ch.t: Resolved Not to Defile Himself with the King’s Food
ch.sub: The Name Changed, the Heart Did Not
sec: The Siege and the Vessels: The First Exiles
Chosen for the Palace, Taught Chaldean Learning, Given New Names
Daniel Resolves: Vegetables and Water for Ten Days
God Gives Wisdom, and “Daniel Continued”

pts: They Changed Your Name, but They Could Not Change Your Heart
Exile took away their surroundings and their names, but it could not take away a person’s resolve.
Resolve, at a Small Table
Victory and defeat often turn on small details: do not let the king’s table become your master.
Wisdom Is God’s Gift; the King Is Only a Witness
God gives understanding; the king examines them and finds them ten times better; dynasties change, and God’s servant is still there.

ch.q: Has there ever been a time when your circumstances did not force you to give up your faith, but slowly handed you a new name, a new position, a new standard, until little by little you became what they wanted you to be? Daniel chapter 1 begins with a besieged city, yet it turns at a small table: God’s people were carried off into someone else’s kingdom, their names were changed, their futures were arranged, and Daniel quietly made up his mind in his heart. This chapter asks us: in someone else’s kingdom, who has set my heart in place?
ch.truth: People can change your name and arrange your future, but they cannot take away a heart that has already been set before God; and what makes a person stand is the favor and wisdom God gives.

mv.t: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

card: In the third year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, the king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem, and the Lord gave the king and some of the vessels of the temple into his hand. The king ordered that young men, handsome and well versed in learning, be chosen from among the Israelites, to be taught the writing and language of the Chaldeans, and to be given a daily portion of the king’s food and wine for three years. Among them were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, and they were given new names. But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king’s food, and he asked the chief of the eunuchs for permission. God gave him favor, and after a ten-day test their faces looked even better. God also gave the four young men knowledge and skill, and Daniel understood all kinds of visions and dreams; when the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his whole realm. Until the first year of King Cyrus, Daniel was still there.
“But Daniel resolved”: a name can be changed and circumstances can be arranged, but the decision set in the heart is where God’s servant finally stands.

Every turn in this chapter has God as its subject: “the Lord gave,” “God made him find favor,” “God gave them knowledge.” Grace does not mean I first stand firm and then God helps; he moves first, and only then is it possible for me to have a settled heart.
Selflessness is not suppressing yourself; it is letting go of the thought, “I will arrange the outcome in God’s place”: let the heart settle, ask, and leave the consequences with him.
“Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.”
This week, find the “small table” in your own life, write down one thing you have decided not to touch, and tell it to someone you trust.

Final integration:
The city was besieged, and the Lord handed it over.
The vessels were carried away, and God was not absent.
The name was changed, yet the heart was set by Daniel himself.
Before the king’s food was even laid on the table, he had already settled his heart.
He did not pound the table. He did not run away.
He said: please.
Resolve is hard; speech is gentle.
God gave him favor, and God made his face look well.
God gave understanding, God gave wisdom—not the king.
Dynasties pass; Babylon passes.
Daniel was still there.
You can be too.
ch.self: The definition of self: inside the names and positions others give me, I gradually let my circumstances set my heart; the way out through selflessness is to settle the heart first before God, and then leave the consequences with him.

t321.k: Jesus also lived in a world that was not his own: he had honor, yet did not grasp it; he had authority, yet submitted; he did not change who he was in order to fit in (Phil 2:5--8; Matt 4:1--10).
t321.g: Letting Jesus be King does not begin with big things, but with a small table: inside other people’s standards, first ask whether “the king’s food” has become the master of my life, and give both resolve and speech to him (Dan 1:8--9).
t321.p: God’s system is not an escape from Babylon, but a group of people inside Babylon who still guard one another: four young men resolved together, and God showed wisdom and witness through them (Dan 1:11, 17).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Has anyone ever changed what they call you, or used a different name for you for convenience? What did that feel like?

【2. The Heart of It】 1:3--7 Babylon does not use the whip, but training and good conditions. In your present surroundings, which “very good condition” is quietly making you stop mentioning your faith?

【3. Scripture】 The “resolve” in 1:8 means “set upon the heart,” and it came before the pressure. Is there something you set upon your heart long ago and no longer renegotiate? If not, what are you willing to settle now?
【4. Gospel】 God first made Daniel find favor, and only then was the road open (1:9). How does this free us from relying on our own willpower to hold on to a decision?
【5. Action】 This week, in what concrete setting will you state your position by asking rather than protesting? What time, who is the person, and what is the one sentence?

prac.main: Resolve first, speak afterward; leave the outcome with God
items: Toward God: every day take one minute to say to God, “Lord, my heart was set by you, not by my circumstances.”
Toward yourself: write down the “small table” in your life, and write down one thing you have decided not to touch.
Toward others: when you meet someone who disagrees with you, first ask yourself: is he an enemy, or only afraid? Answer him with one gentle sentence.
Toward daily life: choose one small detail you have been compromising on, and this week, in the way of asking, put a clear arrangement that can be checked to the people concerned.
Toward mission: find a companion, say to each other, “I will not touch this,” and ask once a week: are you still there?

safe: ① Wrong teaching: turning the ten days of vegetables into “only eating vegetarian is spiritual” or “vegetarian food is healthier”

Right understanding: the text does not teach dietary rules; 1:8 speaks of not defiling, and the result after ten days is God’s witness to a conscience that had resolved, not the power of the food itself.
Test: does the congregation become more willing to obey conscience, or do they use diet to measure other people’s spirituality?
② Wrong teaching: turning “resolve” into willpower, man conquering all
Right understanding: resolve is setting upon the heart, but God first gave Daniel favor (1:9), and later wisdom was also God’s gift (1:17); resolve and dependence are the same thing.
Test: does the congregation depend on God more, or do they bind themselves tighter by effort?
③ Wrong teaching: turning “faces looked fairer” in 1:15 into “hold firm and you will certainly get benefits”
Right understanding: this is a witness for this occasion, not a guarantee; chapter 3 still has “But if not,” and chapter 6 still has a night in the pit.
Test: those who suffer without seeing results—are they comforted, or are they told, “You did not hold firm enough”?
④ Wrong teaching: turning the learning of Chaldean learning into “believers should not receive worldly education”
Right understanding: 1:17 says that God gave these four knowledge and skill in all kinds of learning; the text opposes being assimilated, not learning.
Test: do young people study and work with more devotion while keeping their hearts, or are they frightened away from learning?

ch.arc: The Dream of the Four Kingdoms
sec: The King Forgets the Dream, the Wise Men Are Helpless, the King Orders Destruction
Daniel Asks for Time, the Four Pray Together, and He Blesses the God of Heaven
The Introduction: “Not Because of Any Wisdom of Mine”
The Dream: The Great Image and the Stone
The Interpretation: Gold, Silver, Bronze, Iron, Clay, and God Sets Up a Kingdom
The King Falls Down, and Daniel and His Three Friends Are Promoted

pts: The King Forgot the Dream, and No One Had a Way
When the wisdom of the world comes to an end, it is the turn of the God of heaven to speak.
Pray First, Then Interpret the Dream
The secret was not revealed because someone’s wisdom surpassed that of living people, but God revealed it; the four prayed together, and Daniel blessed first.
The Stone Cut Out Without Hands
Human kingdoms have gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay; God’s Kingdom is set up separately, never destroyed, and fills the whole earth.

ch.q: Has there been a night when you had already used up every way you knew, and still your heart was uneasy? Daniel chapter 2 begins with the most powerful man in the world unable to sleep: the king had a dream and forgot it, all the experts said there was no way, and the king ordered all the wise men killed, with Daniel and his three friends on the list. This chapter asks us: when human wisdom comes to an end, do we first go looking for the next method, or do we first, before the God of heaven, seek together and bless first?
ch.truth: Human wisdom has a day when it comes to an end, but the God of heaven changes times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings, and himself sets up a Kingdom that will never be destroyed, one cut out without human hands.

mv.t: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, nor will its sovereignty be left to another people; but it will break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it will stand forever.

card: Nebuchadnezzar had a dream and was troubled in his heart. He summoned the magicians and the Chaldeans and told them to declare the dream and its interpretation, or be cut in pieces; when they said there was no one on earth who could, the king ordered the wise men destroyed, and the four, Daniel and his friends, were to be killed as well. Daniel asked for time, and with his three companions sought mercy from the God of heaven; the secret was revealed in a night vision, and he blessed first, then went before the king and said, “not because of any wisdom of mine.” The dream was a great image: a head of gold, breast of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay; a stone cut out without hands struck the image and became a great mountain that filled the whole earth. God gave the kingdom to the head of gold, and said he would set up a Kingdom that would never be destroyed. The king fell on his face and said that Daniel’s God is the God of gods; Daniel was promoted, and he raised up his three companions.
“Not because of any wisdom of mine”: human wisdom has an end, the secret was revealed by the God of heaven, and God’s Kingdom is a stone cut out without hands, not built by man.

God reveals first, and then a person can say, “He reveals the deep and secret things. He knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.” Grace in this chapter is God first giving the dream, giving the interpretation, giving protection, and a person has only to ask and to bless.

Selflessness is, at the moment when you stand in the most advantageous position and could say the most pleasing words, still saying first, “not because of any wisdom of mine,” and giving the glory back to God.
“He changes the times and the seasons. He removes kings, and sets up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding.”
This week, find a companion, say to each other one thing where “human ways have run out,” and agree to pray for each other’s matter every day: bless first, then ask.

Final integration:
The king could not sleep, because there was a dream.
The experts all said: no one can.
The decree went out, and the killing was on its way.
Daniel did not run away, and did not cry injustice.
He asked first, prayed first, and found his companions first.
In the night, the secret was revealed.
He blessed first, and then spoke.
He said: not because of any wisdom of mine.
A great image could not stand; a stone cut out without hands broke it.
Human kingdoms have a beginning and an end.
God’s Kingdom is never destroyed.
We do not build it; he brings us in.
ch.self: The definition of pride: taking the wisdom, position and ability God has given as one’s own skill, leaving the entrusted position and grasping God’s glory.

t321.k: Jesus also prayed in the night; in Gethsemane he gave everything to the Father, saying, “not my will, but yours” (Luke 22:41--42); he is the foundation of that Kingdom not made with human hands (Matt 16:18; Mark 14:58; Heb 9:11).
t321.g: Letting Jesus be King means that before human ways run out, we first hand one thing over to him: bless first, then speak; seek together first, then act (Dan 2:18--23).
t321.p: God’s system is not built by man but is a Kingdom God himself sets up; we are not those who build it but the people brought into it, guarding one another in the small group (Dan 2:44; 2:17--18).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Have you ever had a night when your heart was very uneasy and you could not say why? Whom or what did you look for first?

【2. The Heart of It】 In 2:10--11 the Chaldeans say, “There is not a man on the earth.” In your life, is there something you have tried every way for, and still you do not dare say to God, “I have no way”?
【3. Scripture】 In 2:20--23 Daniel blessed God before giving the answer. Do you have a habit of remembering to thank God only after you have received the answer?
【4. Gospel】 In 2:44 God says that he will set up a kingdom, set up by himself. How does this free you from treating any kingdom or situation as your final hope?
【5. Action】 In 2:17--18 Daniel found three companions to pray together. This week, whom will you find, and for what matter will you seek together? Please give the name and the time.

prac.main: Bless first, then speak; seek together, then act
items: Toward God: this week, every day before you ask anything of God, first take one minute to bless him: “You change the times and the seasons; you remove kings and set up kings; wisdom and might are yours.”
Toward yourself: write down one thing that has recently succeeded for you, and write beside it: “This was God’s gift, not my wisdom beating others.”
Toward others: find a companion, say to each other one thing where human ways have run out, and agree to pray for each other every day this week.
Toward daily life: on an uneasy night, do not rush to find a method; first be quiet for five minutes, hand the matter to God, and then sleep.
Toward mission: where you have ability, speak up for someone who is treated unfairly and in a weak position, as Daniel pleaded for all the wise men.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: matching the four metals one by one with specific empires, years and today’s nations, and drawing up a timetable

Right understanding: the text names only the head of gold as Babylon (2:38); the other three kingdoms are not named; the views of the various schools are set side by side, and what these notes hold to is: “human kingdoms have a beginning and an end, and God’s Kingdom is not made by human hands.”
Test: does the congregation look up more to the Kingdom that is never destroyed, or are they busier counting times and identifying nations?
② Wrong teaching: turning the stone of 2:44, or God’s Kingdom, into a spiritual kingdom that people can build by striving or by political means
Right understanding: the stone was “cut out without hands,” and the Kingdom is “set up” by God; people are not the builders but the people brought in.
Test: does the congregation wait and obey more humbly, or do they want more to remake the world by force?
③ Wrong teaching: turning “not because of any wisdom of mine” in 2:30 into “people do not need to learn or work hard”
Right understanding: in chapter 1 Daniel had already received three years of training in learning; what he spoke of is where the glory belongs, not a denial of learning.
Test: do young people study with more effort and give the glory to God more, or do they despise study?
④ Wrong teaching: turning the king’s falling down before Daniel in 2:46 into Daniel accepting human worship, or into believers being honored because of this
Right understanding: the text says only that the king fell down and commanded that an offering be made, and does not say that Daniel accepted it; the king’s words in 2:47 point to Daniel’s God.
Test: does the congregation give the glory to God more, or care more about being honored by others?

sec: The Golden Image and the Sound of Music: All the Earth Bows Down
The Chaldeans Accuse, the King Questions
“But If Not”
The Furnace Heated Seven Times, and the Fourth in the Fire
Out of the Furnace, the King Blesses, and the Three Friends Are Promoted

pts: The Golden Image, the Sound of Music, and Everyone’s Knees
The knees of all the earth bent; the three who did not bend became the accused.
“But If Not”
They did not guarantee that God would surely save; they guaranteed only for themselves that they would never serve another god.
The Fourth in the Fire
God did not keep them from entering the fire, but was with them in the fire; the king himself said: there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.

ch.q: Have you ever had a moment when you knew that if you only bowed your head a little, along with everyone else, all would be well? Daniel chapter 3 begins with a piece of music: when the music sounded, people of every province, nation and language fell down, and only three stood. They were accused, questioned, and thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. This chapter asks us: when God may save, and may also not save in the way we wish, what do we stand on?
ch.truth: Being saved is God’s matter, and being faithful is man’s matter; God did not promise us we would not enter the fire, yet he is with us in the fire, so that every mouth confesses that there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.

mv.t: But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”

card: Nebuchadnezzar made a golden image and gathered the officials of the provinces on the plain of Dura; when the music sounded, all were to fall down and worship, and whoever did not worship would be thrown into the burning fiery furnace. Some Chaldeans accused Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego of ignoring the king, not serving the king’s gods, and not worshiping the golden image. The king was furious, gave them one more chance, and asked: what god will deliver you out of my hands? The three answered: our God whom we serve is able to deliver; but if not, we will not serve your gods. The king ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter, and the three were bound and thrown in, while the strong men who carried them were themselves burned to death. The king was astonished, and saw four men walking in the fire, unbound and unharmed. The three came out of the furnace without even the smell of fire; the king blessed their God, issued a decree of protection, and promoted the three.
“But if not”: being saved is God’s matter, and being faithful is man’s matter; they did not guarantee the outcome for God, but guaranteed only for themselves that they would never serve another god.
God did not first put out the fire and then let them in; he went in while the fire was still burning; grace in this chapter is God’s presence in the fire, not the removal of the fire.
Selflessness is, at the moment of greatest pressure, not making one’s own rescue the condition of faithfulness: he may not act as I wish, but he is still the King.
“But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”
This week, write down one thing that you will hold to even “if not,” and find a companion, tell him why you will hold to it, and ask him to pray for you.

Final integration:
When the music sounded, everyone knelt down.
Three stood, accused and questioned.
The king asked: what god will deliver you?
They said: our God is able.
But if not, we will not serve your gods.
The furnace was heated seven times, and they were bound and thrown in.
In the fire there were four, unbound, walking.
When they came out, there was not even the smell of fire.
The king said: there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.
God did not keep them from entering the fire.
He was in the fire, with them.
ch.self: The definition of pride: making one’s own rescue a condition, requiring God to act as I wish, or else leaving one’s position and grasping God’s authority.

t321.k: Jesus in Gethsemane said, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matt 26:39), and on the cross walked into the deepest fire; he promised, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matt 28:20).
t321.g: Letting Jesus be King means that, while the fire has not gone out and the outcome is not clear, we still say: he may not act as I wish, but he is still the King (Dan 3:17--18).
t321.p: God’s system is a group of people who still stand where everyone else bows their heads, present with one another and guarding one another; the three companions went in together and came out together, and no one faced the fire alone (Dan 3:12--30).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Tell of one time you “went along with everyone” in doing something: was there a bit of unease in your heart then? And afterward?

【2. The Heart of It】 In 3:15 the king asks, “Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?” Today, what words, from others or from your own heart, are used to ask you, “Does what you believe work?”
【3. Scripture】 In 3:17--18 the first sentence is faith and the second is obedience. Have you made “God must save” a condition of your faithfulness? Please say one thing honestly.
【4. Gospel】 In 3:25 the king saw a fourth in the fire. How does this lead you to believe that God did not promise you would not enter the fire, but promised to be with you in the fire?
【5. Action】 In 3:12 the accusation came from people nearby. This week, for whom will you pray, someone misunderstood or shut out because of faith? Please say the name and the time.

prac.main: But if not, still standing; in the fire he is with us
items: Toward God: this week, every day take one minute to say to God: “You are able to save me; but if not, I will still follow you.”
Toward yourself: write down one thing you have been unwilling to put down because you fear the outcome, and write: “Being saved is God’s matter; being faithful is my matter.”
Toward others: notice someone near you who has been shut out or misunderstood because of faith, greet him first, do not comment, only keep him company.
Toward daily life: on an occasion where “everyone does it this way,” pick one small thing you will not follow, and do it quietly, without argument.
Toward mission: tell the story of “But if not,” in three sentences, to a friend who is going through the fire, and pray for him.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: turning “But if not” into “if you have enough faith, God will surely save you”

Right understanding: what the three said is that God is able to save, and may also not save as people wish; being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is man’s matter, and faithfulness is not conditional on being saved.
Test: is the congregation better able to stay faithful when the outcome is unclear, or do they take not being rescued as their own lack of faith?
② Wrong teaching: turning the fourth into doctrinal evidence that must be believed, or declaring “that is” Christ

Right understanding: the king said “like a son of the gods,” and 3:28 calls him “his angel”; the views of the various schools are set side by side, and we say only that this brings to mind Immanuel, God with us.
Test: is the congregation more sure that God is present in the fire, or do they argue more about who this was?
③ Wrong teaching: turning the promotion for faithfulness (3:30) into a reward and guarantee of faithfulness
Right understanding: promotion was a result, not a reason; when the three said “But if not,” they did not know they would be promoted.
Test: is the congregation more able to be faithful without seeking a reward, or do they treat faithfulness as a way to exchange for success?
④ Wrong teaching: turning the three’s refusal to worship into permission to confront those in authority loudly on any occasion

Right understanding: they did not shout slogans or protest; they simply did not bow, and calmly stated their position; for brothers and sisters who are under persecution, we should especially not press for or make public any traceable details.
Test: does the congregation have a calm and firm witness, or are they more combative and more hurtful?

ch.t: The Most High Rules in the Kingdom of Men
sec: The King’s Decree and Doxology
The King’s Dream: A Tree Reaching to Heaven Is Cut Down
Daniel Interprets and Counsels
Fulfillment: “Is Not This Great Babylon, Which I Have Built”
Eyes Lifted to Heaven, the King’s Confession

pts: A Tree Whose Height Reached to Heaven
The weight of the dream is not the cutting down of the tree, but “that the living may know”; Daniel’s counsel is: practice righteousness, show mercy to the poor.
“Is Not This Great Babylon, Which I Have Built”
While the word was still in his mouth, the kingdom had departed from him.
I Lifted Up My Eyes to Heaven
The first act of returning understanding was to look up; those who walk in pride he is able to abase.

ch.q: Have you ever had a moment when everything is going well, yet there is an unease you cannot name? Daniel chapter 4 is a witness written by a king himself: he was at rest in his house, yet had a dream: a tree reaching to heaven was cut down, and the stump left in the earth. Twelve months later, in the royal palace, he said: is not this great Babylon what I built? Before he had finished speaking, the kingdom departed from him. This chapter asks us: when we succeed, to whom does the glory go?
ch.truth: The Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he will; the proud he is able to abase, and the one who lifts his eyes to heaven he restores.

mv.t: “ ‘The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones; to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.’

card: King Nebuchadnezzar proclaimed to all the earth, by decree, the signs and wonders God had worked toward him. He was at rest in his palace, yet troubled by a dream: a tree whose top reached to heaven, giving food to all, was commanded by a watcher to be cut down, with only the stump left, bound with a band of iron and bronze, so that he would live with the animals and eat grass, for seven times, that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. No wise man could interpret it, but Daniel, astonished for a moment, said the tree was the king, and urged the king to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by mercy to the poor. Twelve months later the king said in his palace that great Babylon was what he had built by his own great might; before he had finished speaking, a voice from heaven said the kingdom had departed from him. He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox. When the days were fulfilled he lifted up his eyes to heaven, his understanding returned, and he blessed the Most High, saying that those who walk in pride, God is able to abase.
“The Most High rules in the kingdom of men”: every position and every kingdom is given; God abases the proud, and restores those who lift their eyes to heaven.

God’s judgment carries grace that remains: the stump was left, and after seven times the kingdom was returned; grace in this chapter is twelve months of patience, and the restoration after looking up.
Selflessness is, in the moment of success, not saying “I built this,” but saying “you gave this,” returning the glory to God.
“Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”

This week, write down one thing for which others praised you, and write beside it: this was given by God; then find a companion, and say to each other where it is easiest for you to “take the glory for yourself.”

Final integration:
The king was at rest in his palace, yet he had a dream.
A tree, its height reaching to heaven, giving food to all.
The watcher said: cut it down. The stump is to be left.
Daniel said: O king, the tree is you.
He said also: break off your sins by righteousness, by mercy to the poor.
Twelve months, and nothing happened.
The king said: is not this great Babylon what I built?
Before the words were finished, the kingdom had departed from him.
After seven times, he lifted up his eyes to heaven.
Understanding returned, and he blessed the King of heaven.
Those who walk in pride, God is able to abase.
The Most High rules in the kingdom of men.
ch.self: The definition of pride: calling the position, the achievement and the ability God has given “mine,” leaving the place of one entrusted, and grasping God’s glory.

t321.k: Jesus, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:6--7); he said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).
t321.g: Letting Jesus be King means that in success and when praised we still say: you gave this; and lift our eyes to heaven, and give the glory to him (Dan 4:34, 4:37).
t321.p: In God’s system, everyone’s position is given, and we guard and remind one another; like Daniel, who did not avoid telling the king the truth, and did not give up giving him a way out (Dan 4:24--27).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Tell of one thing for which others have recently praised you. What was the first thought in your heart then: thanking God, thinking you did well, or embarrassment?
【2. The Heart of It】 4:4 says the king was “at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace,” yet had a dream that troubled him. Have you ever felt uneasy at the very time things were smoothest?
【3. Scripture】 In 4:30 the king says, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built.” Is there a place in your life where you often say “I did this,” and forget to say “God gave this”?
【4. Gospel】 In 4:34 the king lifted up his eyes to heaven, and his understanding returned. How does this lead you to believe that you need not wait until you lose everything, but can look up now?
【5. Action】 In 4:27 Daniel urged the king to show “mercy to the poor.” This week, for which person in a weak position will you do one concrete thing? Please say the name and the time.

prac.main: Lift Your Eyes to Heaven, Give the Glory Back to God
items: Toward God: this week, after each thing for which you are praised or succeed, say in one sentence to God: “You gave this; the glory is yours.”
Toward yourself: write down one thing for which you most easily say “it was all me,” and write beside it: “This is a position given, not my capital.”
Toward others: find a companion, and remind each other: when the other says “it was all my credit,” gently say, “look up.”
Toward daily life: every day stop for thirty seconds, leave the screen, lift your eyes to heaven once, ask nothing, and say only “you are King.”
Toward mission: in a place where you have influence, do one concrete thing for someone in a weak position, as Daniel urged the king to show mercy to the poor.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: forcing “seven times” into seven years and matching it with some year, event or person today

Right understanding: the original says only seven “times,” without saying whether days, months or years; the various views are set side by side, and what this chapter holds is “that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.”
Test: is the congregation more ready to bow and acknowledge God’s rule, or more busy counting days and pointing out who is who?
② Wrong teaching: describing the king’s illness as some medical diagnosis, or using it to mock or judge those who struggle in mind

Right understanding: the text describes only “ate grass like an ox, hair grown like eagles’ feathers,” and gives no medical name; this passage is a reminder to all the proud, not a comment on any patient.
Test: does the congregation see more of its own pride, or look down more on those who are suffering?
③ Wrong teaching: turning 4:27, “righteousness, mercy to the poor,” into a way of exchanging good deeds for peace or forgiveness
Right understanding: Daniel describes what repentance looks like, and says “perhaps,” with no guarantee; being forgiven is God’s grace, and doing good is the fruit of repentance.
Test: is the congregation more willing to show mercy to the poor, or does it treat good deeds as a chip to trade with God?
④ Wrong teaching: concluding from 4:34--37 that Nebuchadnezzar was saved and became a believer, or asserting that he was not saved
Right understanding: the text records only that he lifted his eyes, praised and confessed, and does not state his eternal end; we stay with what the text says and do not pass a verdict for God.
Test: is the congregation more looking to God’s mercy and sovereignty, or more eager to judge someone’s final end?

ch.t: Weighed in the Balances and Found Lacking
sec: The Great Feast and the Vessels of the Temple
The Fingers on the Wall, the Queen Mother Recommends Daniel
Daniel Is Called: Let Your Gifts Be to Yourself
The Accusation: “You Have Not Humbled Your Heart”
MENE, TEKEL, PERES
That Night, the Kingdom Changed Hands

pts: Drinking From the Vessels of the Temple
It was not that he did not know; he knew, and did not care.
You have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this
The weight of sin is in “knowing”: the lessons of history were set before him, and he did not learn.
MENE, TEKEL, PERES
Counted, weighed, divided: that very night the kingdom changed hands.

ch.q: Have you ever had a moment when you already knew what to do, yet kept putting it off, finding reasons, saying “in a little while”? Daniel chapter 5 is a lively night: Belshazzar made a great feast, drank wine from the golden vessels of the temple in Jerusalem, and praised the gods made of wood and stone, gold and silver. Suddenly the fingers of a hand appeared on the wall and wrote four words. Daniel said: you have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this. This chapter asks us: what we lack, is it information, or a bowed head?
ch.truth: God’s judgment is never sudden; it comes after long patience. The greatest debt is not that one did not know, but that one knew and still would not humble himself, would not give the glory to God.

mv.t: “You, his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this,

card: King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his lords, and in the midst of the drinking commanded that the gold and silver vessels from the temple in Jerusalem be brought, and praised the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. Suddenly the fingers of a man’s hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall; the king’s face changed and his knees struck together; the wise men could not read it. The queen mother remembered Daniel, saying that in him was the spirit of the holy gods. Daniel refused rewards, first recounted the story of Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling, and pointed out that Belshazzar, though he knew all this, had not humbled his heart, but had lifted himself up against the Lord of heaven, and had not glorified the God in whose hand his breath is. The writing on the wall was MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN: God has counted your kingdom, you are weighed in the balances and found wanting, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. That night Belshazzar was slain, and Darius took the kingdom.
“You are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting”: God’s standard is real; the greatest debt is not that one did not know, but that one knew and did not humble himself.
God’s judgment is not sudden: first there was the story of Nebuchadnezzar, first the long patience; grace in this chapter is that he already knew, and there was still a chance to bow.
Selflessness is, on a relaxed night, not treating holy things as things for amusement, and after knowing, bowing at once, without delay and without finding reasons.
“You are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.”
This week, write down one thing you have long known you should do, yet have kept putting off, and find a companion, agree on a concrete time, and do it.

Final integration:
A lively night, a great feast.
The vessels of the temple were brought out for amusement.
On the wall, a hand appeared.
The wise men could not read it, could not even read.
The queen mother remembered a name.
Daniel did not speak for a reward.
He said: you have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.
MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.
You are weighed in the balances, and found wanting.
That night, the kingdom changed hands.
The Most High rules in the kingdom of men.
When you know, bow down.
ch.self: The definition of pride: knowing God’s word and God’s works, and not humbling oneself; treating holy things as one’s own, leaving one’s place, and grasping God’s authority.

t321.k: Jesus, though he knew who he was, humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross (Phil 2:8); he stands for us at the other end of the balances, so that we do not stand by our own weight (Rom 5:8).
t321.g: Letting Jesus be King means that after knowing God’s word, we bow at once, without delay and without finding reasons; and even when relaxed, we do not treat holy things as our own (Dan 5:22--23).
t321.p: In God’s system there are those who remember you and remind you, and those who speak the truth without a reward; like the queen mother who remembered Daniel, like Daniel who proclaimed faithfully (Dan 5:10--17).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Tell of one small thing you “already knew, yet kept putting off.” Why did you put it off?

【2. The Heart of It】 In 5:2 Belshazzar, in the midst of the drinking, brought the temple vessels out for amusement. In your life, is there something that originally belonged to God (time, a gift, or money) that you have casually used elsewhere?
【3. Scripture】 5:22 says, “You have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.” Recently, which matter is one where you “knew, yet have not bowed”? Please say it honestly.
【4. Gospel】 5:27 says you are weighed in the balances. How does this help you understand that we do not stand by our own weight, but Christ stands on our side?
【5. Action】 In 5:10 the queen mother remembered Daniel. This week, for whom will you “remember,” saying one quiet word when he is in panic? Please say the name and the time.

prac.main: When You Know, Bow Down; No Delay, No Reasons
items: Toward God: this week, every day be quiet for three minutes and say to God: “The one thing I know, today I will bow.”
Toward yourself: write down one thing you have long known you should do, yet have kept putting off, and write a concrete date.
Toward others: find a companion, tell each other the one thing you each put off, and agree on a time to report back.
Toward daily life: review your time and money once; which part was meant for God, yet has been taken for amusement? Return it to God.
Toward mission: say one quiet word to someone in panic, and pray for him, like the queen mother who remembered Daniel.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: turning “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” into a code for working out some nation or event today
Right understanding: Daniel’s interpretation points to the end of Babylon that very night; the text does not ask us to turn it into a tool for counting days or identifying nations.
Test: is the congregation more willing to bow in response to God, or more eager to calculate and guess?
② Wrong teaching: turning the judgment into gloating over others, or using the “balances” to judge others’ shortfall
Right understanding: when Daniel spoke of the shortfall, he did not mock or gloat; this chapter is spoken to everyone who knows and does not humble himself, ourselves included.
Test: does the congregation first look at its own balances, or is it busier weighing others?
③ Wrong teaching: turning the “balances” into “people must reach the standard by their deeds in order to be saved”
Right understanding: the balances show the shortfall so that people see their need; the gospel is that Christ already stands on our side, not that we stand by our own weight.
Test: does the congregation rely more on Christ’s grace, or is it more anxious about whether it is doing enough?
④ Wrong teaching: saying that Daniel’s refusing rewards in 5:17 and accepting the purple in 5:29 shows he was inconsistent or hypocritical
Right understanding: what he refused was speaking on condition of a reward; the reward was ordered by the king himself afterward, and he did not make it a precondition of the interpretation.
Test: is the congregation more faithful without a reward, or does it treat rewards as a chip for faithfulness?

ch.t: Praying as He Had Always Done
sec: Daniel Surpasses All, and No Ground for Accusation Is Found
A Decree Is Designed and Sealed with the Royal Signet
Praying As Usual, Accused, the King Distressed
Thrown into the Lions’ Den, the Mouth of the Den Sealed
Dawn: The Servant of the Living God
The Accusers Repaid, the King’s Decree

pts: A Man with Nothing to Hold Against Him
No fault is found in him, so they can only look in the law of his God; devotion becomes the charge.
As Before
He knows about the decree and still kneels three times a day; he does nothing new, he only refuses to stop what he has always done.
The Servant of the Living God
What is shut is the lions’ mouths; even the king declares: his kingdom will not be destroyed.

ch.q: Is there a habit you would be first to change under pressure? In Daniel chapter 6, someone designs a decree aimed only at Daniel: for thirty days, whoever asks anything of any god or man will be thrown into the lions’ den. Daniel knows the decree has been signed, goes up to his room, with his window open toward Jerusalem, kneels three times a day, prays and gives thanks, as he did before. This chapter asks us: when pressure wants to change the shape of our worship, do we perform, hide, or carry on as usual?
ch.truth: Carrying on as usual is the quietest witness under pressure; and at dawn God sends his angel to shut the lions’ mouths, so that the nations may know he is the living God and his kingdom will not be destroyed.

mv.t: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.

card: Darius appoints one hundred twenty satraps and three presidents, and Daniel surpasses them all; his enemies can find no ground for accusation, and can only look in the law of his God. They design a thirty-day decree: whoever asks anything of any god or man except the king will be thrown into the lions’ den; the king signs it. Daniel knows, and still returns upstairs, with his window open toward Jerusalem, kneels three times a day, prays and gives thanks, as before. He is accused, and the king is distressed; he wants to rescue Daniel but cannot change the decree, until sunset. The king says: your God, whom you serve continually, will deliver you. Daniel is thrown into the den, the mouth of the den is sealed, and the king fasts all night. At dawn the king calls out, and Daniel says that God sent his angel to shut the lions’ mouths, because he was found innocent before God. He is lifted out of the den, with no injury, because he trusted in his God. The accusers are thrown into the den, and the king issues a decree that all the land should tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God.
“As before”: the quietest witness under pressure is to carry on as usual; the one who shut the lions’ mouths is the angel whom God sent.

God’s way of saving is not to spare us the den but to be in the den with us: the angel shuts the lions’ mouths, and at dawn someone hears Daniel’s voice; grace in this chapter is God’s keeping watch in the dark of night.
Selflessness is not performing to prove something to others, and not changing because of danger; it is simply to return to God as usual, and, when hurt, still to bless first.
“Three times a day he knelt on his knees, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.”
This week, write down one spiritual habit that you most easily change under pressure, and find a companion; agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: “as usual.”

Final integration:
Daniel surpasses all, and his enemies find no ground for accusation.
They can only look in the law of his God.
The decree is signed, and the window faces Jerusalem.
He knows, and still kneels, prays and gives thanks, as before.
The king is distressed; he wants to save him but cannot change it.
The lions’ den, a stone, a seal, a night of fasting.
At dawn, the angel shuts the lions’ mouths.
He says: I was found innocent before God.
There is no injury on his body, because he trusted in God.
The king declares to all the earth: he is the living God, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.
As usual.
ch.self: Definition of pride: putting my own safety, face and circumstances above God’s will, and changing my obedience to God out of fear of loss; or, the reverse, turning obedience into a performance and boasting of it before others.

t321.k: Jesus too was one who prayed “as usual”: he came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39), and under the greatest pressure still returned to the Father and said: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).
t321.g: Let Jesus be King means that before any law, unwritten rule or pressure, we still return to him first, praying and giving thanks as usual; and when hurt, still blessing (Dan 6:10, 6:21).
t321.p: God’s system is a company of people whose windows stay open toward God, living as usual in every kingdom, not with confrontation as the aim but with faithfulness as the witness; beyond the three presidents there are companions who remind one another (Dan 6:4, 6:10).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Name one small habit you do every day. If you were forced to stop one day, would you feel something was missing?

【2. The Heart of It】 The decree in 6:7 did not mention Daniel’s name, yet it made his ordinary life illegal. Is there a rule or a pressure in your life that makes “worshiping as usual” cost something?
【3. The Text】 6:10 says “as he did before.” Under pressure, do you usually increase, decrease, or change your spiritual habits? Please honestly tell about the most recent time.

【4. The Gospel】 In 6:22 Daniel says God sent his angel to shut the lions’ mouths. How does this help you believe that God’s keeping is not necessarily sparing us the den, but being in the den with us?
【5. Action】 In 6:21 Daniel blesses the king first. This week, whom will you bless, especially the one who has hurt you? Please say the name and the time.

prac.main: As Usual Under Pressure, Still Blessing When Hurt
items: Toward God: this week, at a fixed time and place each day, pray and give thanks quietly for five minutes, not shortening it because of busyness or circumstances.
Toward yourself: write down the most recent spiritual habit you changed because you feared trouble, and write down one smallest step to restore it.
Toward others: find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: “as usual”; no showing off, no comparing.
Toward daily life: for someone who has hurt you, say one word of blessing each day, without needing him to know.
Toward mission: in the setting where you are, do one unnoticed daily thing that no one can find fault with, so that your witness builds up in ordinary days.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: turning Daniel’s prayer into “believers may break any government law at any time”

Right understanding: Daniel was faithful in everything reasonable and gave way only on the one matter of “asking from God”; Acts 5:29 says, “We must obey God rather than men,” but that is a line between obedience and apostasy, not a pass for defiance.
Test: is the congregation better able to discern the limits of obedience, or more ready to use “being spiritual” as an excuse for defiance?
② Wrong teaching: turning the punishment of the accusers’ wives and children in 6:24 into a retribution God delights in, or using it to curse enemies

Right understanding: the text describes an ancient punishment that fell on whole families and does not say it was good; Deuteronomy 24:16 says each man shall be put to death for his own sin, and we do not defend any violence.
Test: is the congregation more compassionate toward those who are victims, or more willing to use this verse as an excuse for revenge?
③ Wrong teaching: turning Daniel’s rescue into “as long as you pray, you will surely not be hurt”

Right understanding: Daniel’s rescue was God’s work, and chapter 3’s “But if not” is in the same book; some people prayed and still suffered, even died as martyrs, and it was not because they had less faith.
Test: is the congregation trusting more in God’s presence, or treating prayer as a way to buy safety?
④ Wrong teaching: turning “praying as usual” into a public performance, or encouraging public declarations in dangerous places

Right understanding: Daniel went back to his own house with his window open; he did not call a press conference. For brothers and sisters under persecution, we must protect people even more, and not make public any details that could be traced.
Test: is the congregation quieter and steadier, or more eager to display courage?

ch.t: The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
ch.arc: The Four Beasts and the Son of Man
sec: Four Beasts Come Up from the Sea, the Little Horn Grows
The Throne, the Judgment, One Like a Son of Man Coming with the Clouds
Daniel Alarmed, an Attendant Explains: The Saints Receive the Kingdom
The Fourth Beast and the Little Horn Explained
The Judge Sits, the Kingdom Is Given to the Saints

pts: Four Beasts Rising from the Sea
The powers of the ages rise out of a churning sea, and the last grows a little horn that speaks great things.
The Throne and the Clouds of Heaven
The one who sits in judgment is the Ancient of Days; the one who receives the kingdom is the one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven.
The Saints Receive the Kingdom
The saints first suffer “a time, times, and half a time,” yet the kingdom and dominion will at last be given to the saints of the Most High.

ch.q: Have you ever been crushed breathless by a great force? Daniel chapter 7 is Daniel’s own dream: four great beasts come up from the sea, the last with iron teeth and a little horn with a mouth speaking great things. Then the scene turns: thrones are placed, the Ancient of Days sits, the books are opened; one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, is brought near before him, and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom. This chapter asks us: when everything around us looks like beasts, do we look at the teeth of the beasts, or at the throne quietly set up?
ch.truth: Even the greatest power is given, and is beneath the throne; the kingdom is not seized but given to the one like a son of man, and also to the saints of the Most High.

mv.t: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.

card: In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel saw a vision by night: the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea, and four great beasts came up from the sea. The first was like a lion with eagle’s wings; its wings were plucked off, and a man’s heart was given to it. The second was like a bear, and it was told: arise, devour much flesh. The third was like a leopard with four wings and four heads, and dominion was given to it. The fourth was terrible and strong, with great iron teeth and ten horns, and another little horn came up, with eyes and a mouth speaking great things. Then thrones were placed, the Ancient of Days sat, the books were opened, and the beast was slain; the dominion of the other beasts was taken away. One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven, was brought near before him, and was given dominion, glory and a kingdom. An attendant explained: the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom forever; the Judge sits, and the kingdom and dominion are given to the saints. Daniel was alarmed, but kept the matter in his heart.
The beasts come up from the sea; the kingdom comes down from heaven. What is given is not to the strongest, but to the one like a son of man and to the saints of the Most High.
Even the beasts’ wings, a man’s heart and dominion are all “given”; God’s grace in this chapter is that, above the chaos, he has already quietly set up a throne.
Selflessness is not scrambling for the kingdom or holding ourselves up with big words; we receive the kingdom not because we are strong but because the kingdom is given.
“His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.”

This week, write down the one power or the one big word you fear most, say it out loud before God, and agree with a companion to remind each other each day with one phrase: the throne has been set up.

Final integration:
The four winds of heaven break on the great sea.
Four beasts come up, each more terrible than the last.
Their wings, the man’s heart and the dominion were all given.
The little horn has eyes and a mouth, and speaks great things.
Thrones are placed, and the Ancient of Days sits.
The books are opened, and nothing is overlooked.
The voice of great words is stopped by judgment.
One like a son of man is brought before him and given the kingdom.
The kingdom is also given to the saints of the Most High.
Daniel is alarmed, but keeps it in his heart.
The wind is heaven’s wind.
The throne is one that was set up.
ch.self: Definition of pride: holding up one’s position with big words and power, or, before a power greater than oneself, forgetting the throne and, out of fear, fixing one’s focus on the beast’s teeth; leaving one’s place and grasping a dominion that is not one’s own.

t321.k: Jesus himself used the title Son of Man and said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45); he gains the kingdom not by devouring but in the form of a servant.
t321.g: Let Jesus be King means that before all big words and pressure we still keep our focus on the throne, acknowledging that the kingdom, dominion and glory are all given, and all belong to him (Dan 7:13–14).
t321.p: God’s system is a company of people called the saints of the Most High, who do not scramble but receive, and who in the chaos remind one another: the throne has been set up, and the kingdom will surely be given (Dan 7:18, 7:27).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Name the dream or shadow you feared most as a child. Looking back now, is it still so big?
【2. The Heart of It】 In 7:8 the little horn has eyes and a mouth that speaks great things. In your life, is there a “big word” that seems impossible to answer, so that you can only dodge it?
【3. The Text】 In 7:9–10 the thrones were “placed” and the Judge “sat.” How do these two pictures change your heart when you face chaos? Please name one thing you want to hand over.
【4. The Gospel】 In 7:13–14 the one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given the kingdom. How does this help you believe that the kingdom is not seized but entrusted?

【5. Action】 In 7:28 Daniel kept the matter in his heart. This week, what is one thing you do not yet understand that you will first keep in your heart while remaining faithful? Please name the matter and the time.

prac.main: See the Throne, Not the Teeth of the Beast; Receive the Kingdom, Do Not Scramble for It
items: Toward God: this week, spend five minutes each day bringing before God one power that makes you afraid, saying only: “The wind is heaven’s wind, and the throne has been set up.”
Toward yourself: write down the most recent sentence that made you shrink, or made you want to speak big words yourself, and write down one small step back to your own place.
Toward others: find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: “the throne is set up”; no comparing, no showing off.
Toward daily life: take one revenge, accusation or worry you cannot give away, hand it in one prayer to the One who sits in judgment, and do not bring it up again.
Toward mission: in the setting where you are, do one small, faithful thing that does not grab for power or speak big words, so that your witness builds up in ordinary days.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: matching the four beasts to certain nations or organizations of today, and setting out a timetable

Right understanding: the four beasts have long been read in different ways, and these notes set them side by side without charting a schedule; the point of the text is “given and judged,” not to make people count days.
Test: is the congregation more quietly seeing the throne, or more eager to guess at times?
② Wrong teaching: identifying the little horn with a person or regime of today and calling him the antichrist

Right understanding: the text describes features, speaking great things, wearing out the saints, planning to change the times and the law, and names no one of today; identifying someone makes the congregation panic and also hurts the innocent.
Test: is the congregation more watchful and patient, or more fearful and more ready to put labels on people?
③ Wrong teaching: giving “one like a son of man” only a single answer and belittling other readings, or setting the son of man and the saints against each other

Right understanding: the son of man and the saints have long been read as individual, as collective, and as both; in the New Testament Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, and we see the connection while respecting each view, not letting the two be set against each other.
Test: does the congregation see more that Jesus is King, and more that they themselves are people to whom the kingdom is given, or is it more eager to debate?
④ Wrong teaching: teaching “the saints will receive the kingdom” as “believers will surely win and not be hurt”

Right understanding: 7:21 says plainly that this horn made war with the saints and prevailed against them; receiving the kingdom comes after the judgment and is given, not an exemption from suffering now.
Test: is the congregation better able to endure and hope in suffering, or does it treat faith as a guarantee against suffering?

ch.t: The Ram, the Goat, and the Little Horn
sec: The Ram and the Male Goat
The Little Horn, the Sanctuary, and “How Long?”
Gabriel: “Understand, Son of Man”
The Explanation and the Sealing
Daniel Sick for Some Days

pts: The Ram, the Male Goat and the Little Horn
One after another they exalt themselves, and the last styles himself as great as the prince of the host and tramples the sanctuary.
“Understand, Son of Man”
What the vision gives is “understanding,” not a schedule of days; Daniel is called “son of man” and is raised up.
Sick for Some Days, and Still Doing the King’s Business
The vision does not make him leave his post: he fainted, was sick, then rose up and did the king’s business.

ch.q: Have you ever, on some night, asked heaven: how long? Daniel chapter 8 has a ram, a male goat, and a little horn, one after another exalting themselves, the last destroying the sanctuary and taking away the continual burnt offering. Even the holy one in heaven asks: how long will this be? The answer is a number made of evenings and mornings. Then Gabriel comes, calls Daniel “son of man,” touches him as he lies in a deep sleep of fright, and sets him upright. This chapter asks us: when you cannot understand and no one can tell you the days, do you hurry to calculate, or do you let God raise you up?
ch.truth: The nights are numbered; what God gives is understanding, not a schedule of days. When we are frightened and fallen asleep he reaches out and sets us upright, and we can return to our post.

mv.t: Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me, and set me upright.

card: In the third year of King Belshazzar, Daniel in a vision stood by the river Ulai at Susa and saw a ram with two horns pushing west, north and south; no beast could stand before it, and it did as it pleased and magnified itself. A male goat came from the west, not touching the ground, with a notable horn between his eyes, and broke the ram’s two horns; when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and four came up in its place. Out of one of them came a little horn, growing toward the south, the east and the glorious land, reaching to the host of heaven, taking away the continual burnt offering and casting down the sanctuary, and prospering in all it did. A holy one in heaven asked: how long? The answer: two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings, then the sanctuary will be cleansed. Gabriel was commanded to make Daniel understand; he was frightened and fell on his face, was called “son of man,” and was touched and set upright. The explanation: the ram is Media and Persia, the male goat is Greece; later a king of fierce countenance arises, and is broken without hand. The vision is sealed up. Daniel was sick for some days, then rose up and did the king’s business.
The same verb, “magnified himself,” is said of four subjects; what God gives is understanding and being raised up, not a schedule of days.

God’s grace in this chapter is that he sends an angel to touch a man fallen asleep in fright and set him upright, and gives “how long?” an answer with a limit: the nights are numbered, and the morning will come.
Selflessness is not using the counting of days to gain security, and not leaving one’s post because of not understanding; it is, after being raised up, returning to the duties of today.
“I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me, and set me upright.”
This week, write before God the one “how long?” you most want to ask, and agree with a companion to remind each other each day with one phrase: the nights are numbered, and the Lord raises me up.

Final integration:
The ram magnifies himself.
The male goat magnifies himself.
The little horn magnifies himself and casts down the sanctuary.
The holy one asks: how long?
The answer: there are evenings and mornings, and the sanctuary will be cleansed.
Gabriel is commanded to make him understand.
Understand, son of man.
A man fallen asleep in fright is touched and raised up.
The vision is sealed; the time is not yet.
Sick for some days, then he rose up and did the king’s business.
The nights are numbered.
God raises me up.
ch.self: Definition of pride: replacing trust in God with counting days and rushing ahead to know; or, before a great power, using not understanding as a reason to leave one’s place and put down what one should do today.

t321.k: Jesus too is the Lord who reaches out to touch people and raise them up: “He came and took her by the hand, and raised her up” (Mark 1:31), and he stretched out his hand and touched the leper, saying, “I want to. Be made clean” (Matt 8:3).
t321.g: Let Jesus be King means handing the question “how long?” to him and not using a schedule of days in place of trust; and after being raised up, returning to the duties and the post of today (Dan 8:14, 8:27).
t321.p: God’s system is a company of people who have been raised up: in not understanding they keep one another company, do not frighten one another, and do not chart schedules; each returns to his post and faithfully does the business at hand (Dan 8:18, 8:26–27).

grp: 【1. Icebreaker】 Name the “how long?” you most often asked the grown-ups as a child, such as when the holiday comes, or when you will grow up. Do you still have questions like that now?
【2. The Heart of It】 In 8:13 even the holy one in heaven asks “how long?” What is the one “how long?” you most want to ask God now? Please say it honestly, with no polishing.
【3. The Text】 The answer in 8:14 is a number of “evenings and mornings,” and we do not use it to count days. How does this answer make you quieter, or more unsettled? Please say why.
【4. The Gospel】 In 8:18 Gabriel touches Daniel and sets him upright. How does this help you believe that God’s first move toward the weak is to raise them up, not to blame?

【5. Action】 In 8:27 Daniel was sick for some days, then rose up and did the king’s business. This week, what post or duty will you still return to, even when you do not understand? Please name the matter and the time.

prac.main: When We Do Not Understand, Let God Raise Us Up; After Being Raised, Return to Our Post
items: Toward God: this week, be quiet for five minutes each day, tell God one “how long?”, and then say only one sentence: “Please set me upright.”
Toward yourself: write down one thing for which you are anxious to know the day or the outcome, and write down one small thing you can do today, so that you are not trapped by this question.
Toward others: find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: “the nights are numbered”; do not pass around schedules of days, and do not frighten one another.
Toward daily life: on days when you do not understand, are very tired or are sick, still do the one duty in front of you, such as going to work on time or caring for your family.
Toward mission: when someone wants to use this chapter to chart a timetable, gently bring him back to the purpose Gabriel gives: to make people understand, not to make them panic.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: working out the two thousand three hundred as calendar dates, or matching it to some event of today

Right understanding: the original is “two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings”; it has long been read as 2,300 days, as 1,150 days, and as a symbolic number; these notes set them side by side and do not count days.
Test: is the congregation trusting God more and better able to endure, or more eager to guess at dates?
② Wrong teaching: identifying the little horn or little king with a person or regime of today, and calling him the antichrist

Right understanding: what the text gives is features and an end: speaking great things, casting down the sanctuary, attacking the saints, broken without hand; it has long been read as a king of the Greek period, as a figure of the last days, and as a pattern; these notes set them side by side and identify no one of today.
Test: is the congregation more watchful and patient, or more fearful and more ready to put labels on people?
③ Wrong teaching: confusing the “son of man” of 8:17 with the “one like a son of man” of chapter 7

Right understanding: 8:17 is a Hebrew form of address meaning that Daniel is a finite human being; chapter 7 is Aramaic and describes the one who comes with the clouds of heaven. The wording and the position of the two differ, and we do not force them together.
Test: is the congregation discerning the text’s own context, or being carried along by the similarity of the forms of address?
④ Wrong teaching: turning 8:12 “through disobedience” into “people who suffer must have done something wrong”
Right understanding: the text does not say whose sin it was, and does not say every suffering is because of someone’s sin; for the suffering we do not blame, we only accompany.
Test: is the congregation more compassionate toward the suffering, or quicker to find who should be blamed?

sec: Learning from the Book: Fasting and Prayer
Confession: “We” Have Sinned and Done Wrong
Asking the Lord to Forgive: Not Because of Our Righteousness
Gabriel Comes: “You Are Greatly Beloved”
Seventy Sevens

pts: Learning from the Books
He read Jeremiah and learned of the seventy years. He did not take it to calculate; he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes, and prayed.
We Have Sinned and Done Wrong
Confession uses “we,” and the ground of asking for forgiveness is “not for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.”
Seventy Sevens
Before the prayer was finished the answer went out; the center of the answer is that God will put an end to transgression, make an end of sins and make atonement for iniquity.

ch.q: When you read one of God’s promises, what is your first reaction? Do you take out a calculator and start to calculate, or do you kneel down? In Daniel chapter 9, Daniel learned from the books the seventy years of which Jeremiah spoke. He did not calculate days; he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes, turned his face to God, and confessed with “we”: we have sinned and done wrong, have done wickedly and rebelled. He asked for forgiveness on one ground only: “not for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.” Before the prayer was finished, Gabriel flew to him: at the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, for you are greatly beloved. This chapter asks us: when God’s word comes to you, do you use it to calculate, or to pray?
ch.truth: A promise is for praying, not for calculating; the ground of our asking is not our own righteousness but God’s great mercy, and his word has already gone out when we open our mouths.

mv.t: My God, turn your ear, and hear. Open your eyes, and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name; for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.

card: In the first year of Darius, Daniel learned from the books of Jeremiah’s word that the desolations of Jerusalem would last seventy years, and he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes, and prayed and made petitions to the Lord God. He first praised God who keeps covenant and loving kindness, then confessed with “we”: we have sinned, dealt perversely, done wickedly, rebelled, turned aside from your precepts and not listened to the prophets; righteousness belongs to the Lord, confusion of face to us, and mercy and forgiveness also to the Lord. He remembered the exodus from Egypt and asked the Lord to turn his anger away from Jerusalem, and said, “we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake,” asking the Lord to hear, forgive and act, and not to defer for his own sake. Before the prayer was finished, Gabriel flew swiftly to him about the time of the evening offering and said: at the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, for you are greatly beloved. Then come the seventy sevens: to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy; the last three verses speak of the anointed one cut off, of desolations and of the end.
A promise is not for calculating but for praying; the ground is not our own righteousness but God’s great mercy.
God’s grace in this chapter is that the commandment went out when we began to ask, and that he calls us greatly beloved; what the seventy sevens deal with is sin and righteousness.
Having no self is confessing with “we” before God, not putting ourselves outside to point the finger; and not measuring prayer by “am I worthy?” but simply setting the petition down.
“We do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.”
This week, each day pray with “we” for five minutes for a group you belong to (family, church or country), and turn one promise you want to “calculate” into prayer.

Final integration:
He learned from the books of the seventy years.
He did not calculate; he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes.
First praise: keeping covenant, showing loving kindness.
Then confession: we have sinned and done wrong.
Righteousness belongs to him, confusion of face to us.
Mercy and forgiveness also belong to him.
We ask, not for our righteousness, but for his great mercy.
Before the prayer was finished, Gabriel came.
The commandment went out, for you are greatly beloved.
The seventy sevens deal with sin and righteousness.
Desolation was decreed, and the end was decreed too.
Take the promise to prayer.
ch.self: Definition of pride: turning God’s promise into a timetable that can be calculated and controlled, or putting the ground of prayer on our own righteousness and qualification; leaving our place and trying, in our own way, to exchange for God’s response.

t321.k: Jesus taught us to pray, and also opened his mouth with “we”: “Our Father in heaven” (Matt 6:9), “Forgive us our debts” (Matt 6:12); on the cross he spoke for others: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).
t321.g: To let Jesus reign is to bring God’s promise to him in prayer, not letting calculating take the place of trust; and in confession not to defend ourselves but to look only to his mercy (Dan 9:2–3, 9:18).
t321.p: The God-ordered system is a people who pray with “we”: not standing outside to point the finger, but confessing together and interceding for one another, placing the petition on God’s mercy and not on our own righteousness (Dan 9:5, 9:18).

grp: [1. Icebreaker] Share a piece of good news or a promise you received recently. What was your first reaction: joy, calculating, or wanting to tell someone?
[2. Piercing] In 9:2–3 Daniel read the seventy years and did not calculate days; he fasted and prayed. Is there a promise of God that you have always wanted to “calculate”? Please say what it is.
[3. Scripture] In 9:5 Daniel confessed with “we,” putting even himself in. When you pray for a group you belong to, do you say “they” or “we”? Please say honestly about the most recent time.
[4. Gospel] 9:18: “not for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.” How does this help you believe that you need not be worthy in order to set your petition down?
[5. Action] 9:23 says the commandment went out as the petitions began. This week, which prayer without an answer will you keep setting down? Please say the matter, the time and your companion.

prac.main: Take the promise to prayer, confess with “we,” ask on the ground of mercy
items: Toward God: this week, each day spend five minutes reading one verse of God’s promise; do not calculate, only turn your face to him and say one sentence: “Don’t defer, for your own sake.”
Toward yourself: write down one promise you want to “calculate,” and write one sentence of prayer you can say to God in place of that calculation.
Toward others: find a companion and agree once a week to pray together with “we” for a group you belong to, without blaming others.
Toward daily life: at a fixed time each day, like the “evening offering,” be quiet for five minutes and put the day’s burden before God.

Toward mission: when someone wants to use this chapter to calculate days or set up a timetable, gently bring him back to prayer and mercy, so that people love the Lord more rather than become more anxious.

safe: ① Wrong teaching: calculating the seventy sevens into dates, or laying out a timetable of history and the end

Right understanding: the original says only “seventy sevens,” and does not say days, months or years; there have long been different readings, and these notes set them side by side, do not count days and do not lay out a chart; the point of this passage is that sin and righteousness are dealt with.
Test: is the congregation returning more to prayer and mercy, or becoming more eager for calculating and arguing?
② Wrong teaching: turning “the commandment went out” into “if only we pray, God will surely answer in our time and our way”

Right understanding: the text says that God’s word had gone out as the petitions began; it does not say that we can control the outcome; Daniel waited for God’s work, and still asked on the ground of mercy.
Test: is the congregation trusting more in God’s sovereignty, or treating prayer as a method of exchanging for results?
③ Wrong teaching: turning “we have sinned” into condemning the victims, or turning collective confession into blaming those who suffer
Right understanding: Daniel confesses before God on behalf of the people; he does not blame any individual who suffers; for the suffering we do not blame, we only accompany and show mercy.
Test: is the congregation more compassionate toward the suffering, or quicker to find who should be blamed?
④ Wrong teaching: identifying 9:26–27 as some figure or regime of today, or calling brothers and sisters who hold a different reading unbelieving

Right understanding: the anointed one, the most holy, and the people of a prince have long been read in many ways, and these notes set them side by side; we identify no one today, and we respect the faithfulness of each tradition.
Test: is the congregation more united and more patient, or more fearful and more ready to judge one another?

ch.t: From the First Day You Set Your Heart to Understand
sec: Three Weeks of Mourning, the Great Vision by the River
A Hand: “Your Words Were Heard”
The Speechless Is Touched and Strengthened
Return to Fight; What Is Inscribed in the Writing of Truth

pts: Mourning Three Weeks
He mourned for the future of God’s people, saw the glory, and it was he himself who fell down.
Your Words Were Heard
From the first day he set his heart to understand, heaven had responded; delay does not mean not heard.
Peace Be to You, Be Strong
The speechless one is touched and strengthened: not by his own strength, but by being raised up.

ch.q: Have you ever mourned over something not your own, prayed, waited a long time, and had no response? In Daniel chapter 10, Daniel mourned for the people for three whole weeks, ate no pleasant bread and did not anoint himself. Then he saw a glory beyond description; those with him fled, and he fell to the ground, speechless. The messenger from heaven touched him, raised him, and said: do not be afraid; from the first day that you set your heart to understand, your words were heard. This chapter asks us: when delay looks like silence, do you trust time, or the God who heard from the first day?
ch.truth: Your words were heard from the first day; delay does not mean not heard. He first touches us and gives us strength, and only then says: be strong.

mv.t: Then he said to me, “Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard. I have come for your words’ sake.

card: In the third year of Cyrus, Daniel mourned for the people three whole weeks: he ate no pleasant bread, no meat or wine came into his mouth, and he did not anoint himself.
