“Those who are wise among the people will instruct many; yet they will fall by the sword and by flame, by captivity and by plunder, many days.
Now when they fall, they will be helped with a little help; but many will join themselves to them with flatteries.
Some of those who are wise will fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.

“The king will do according to his will. He will exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and will speak marvelous things against the God of gods. He will prosper until the indignation is accomplished; for that which is determined will be done.
He won’t regard the gods of his fathers, or the desire of women, or regard any god; for he will magnify himself above all.
But in his place he will honor the god of fortresses. He will honor a god whom his fathers didn’t know with gold, silver, and with precious stones and pleasant things.

He will deal with the strongest fortresses by the help of a foreign god. He will increase with glory whoever acknowledges him. He will cause them to rule over many, and will divide the land for a price.

“At the time of the end the king of the south will contend with him; and the king of the north will come against him like a whirlwind, with chariots, with horsemen, and with many ships. He will enter into the countries, and will overflow and pass through.
He will enter also into the glorious land, and many countries will be overthrown; but these will be delivered out of his hand: Edom, Moab, and the chief of the children of Ammon.
He will also stretch out his hand on the countries. The land of Egypt won’t escape.
But he will have power over the treasures of gold and of silver, and over all the precious things of Egypt. The Libyans and the Ethiopians will be at his steps.
But news out of the east and out of the north will trouble him; and he will go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.
He will plant the tents of his palace between the sea and the glorious holy mountain; yet he will come to his end, and no one will help him.
12: “At that time Michael will stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there will be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time. At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.
Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse. Those who turn many to righteousness will shine as the stars forever and ever.
But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end. Many will run back and forth, and knowledge will be increased.”
Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on the river bank on this side, and the other on the river bank on that side.
One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, “How long will it be to the end of these wonders?”

I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it will be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have finished breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things will be finished.
I heard, but I didn’t understand. Then I said, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?”
He said, “Go your way, Daniel; for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.
Many will purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked will do wickedly; and none of the wicked will understand; but those who are wise will understand.
“From the time that the continual burnt offering is taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there will be one thousand two hundred ninety days.
Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days.
“But go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.”

1.grk: בִּשְׁנַת שָׁלוֹשׁ לְמַלְכוּת יְהוֹיָקִים מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָה בָּא נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל יְרוּשָׁלִַם וַיָּצַר עָלֶֽיהָ׃ וַיִּתֵּן אֲדֹנָי בְּיָדוֹ אֶת־יְהוֹיָקִים מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָה וּמִקְצָת כְּלֵי בֵית־הָֽאֱלֹהִים וַיְבִיאֵם אֶֽרֶץ־שִׁנְעָר בֵּית אֱלֹהָיו וְאֶת־הַכֵּלִים הֵבִיא בֵּית אוֹצַר אֱלֹהָֽיו׃
1.lit: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God; and he carried them into the land of Shinar to the house of his god. He brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god.”

1.gram:
וַיִּתֵּן אֲדֹנָי (the Lord gave): the active verb that opens the whole book, and its subject is not Nebuchadnezzar but אֲדֹנָי (the Lord). Verse 1 looks like a military move by the king of Babylon, but verse 2 at once corrects it: it was the Lord who handed the king over.

אֶרֶץ־שִׁנְעָר (the land of Shinar) is the plain where the tower of Babel was built in Genesis 11; from its very first line the book leads the reader back to that city that wanted to “make a name” for itself.
1.exp:
Verse 1 says that Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city; verse 2 says that it was the Lord who gave the king into his hand. It is the same event read two ways, and this whole book is teaching us to read it the second way.

First, the history: the third year of Jehoiakim was about the time when Babylon first reached out its hand toward Judah. The city was not destroyed, only besieged; the king was not killed, only handed over; the temple was not burned, only some of its vessels were taken. This was the first group of exiles, not large in scale, but already a signal: God’s people could no longer count on the protection of walls and sanctuary.

Now the wording. The word “gave” recurs through this chapter: the Lord gave the king, God gave Daniel favor before the chief of the eunuchs, and God gave knowledge and skill to the four young men. Who gives and who receives—the text reminds us again and again: the hand of history is not in the hand of the king of Babylon.

The vessels were brought into “the house of his god” and put into “the treasure house of his god.” In Babylonian eyes, this was proof that their god had beaten Yahweh. But the text speaks very quietly: not beaten, but handed over by the Lord himself. The most painful thing about exile is that it looks as if God lost; this book is going to tell us that God did not lose, he has only begun to work in another place.

Today we too often see only the besiegers in our own days of being “besieged.” Verse 1 lets us know: the siege is real, the pain is real, but the subject of verse 2 is the Lord.

1.grk: וַיֹּאמֶר הַמֶּלֶךְ לְאַשְׁפְּנַז רַב סָרִיסָיו לְהָבִיא מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמִזֶּרַע הַמְּלוּכָה וּמִן־הַֽפַּרְתְּמִֽים׃ יְלָדִים אֲשֶׁר אֵֽין־בָּהֶם כָּל־וְטוֹבֵי מַרְאֶה וּמַשְׂכִּילִים בְּכָל־חָכְמָה וְיֹדְעֵי דַעַת וּמְבִינֵי מַדָּע וַאֲשֶׁר כֹּחַ בָּהֶם לַעֲמֹד בְּהֵיכַל הַמֶּלֶךְ וּֽלֲלַמְּדָם סֵפֶר וּלְשׁוֹן כַּשְׂדִּֽים׃ וַיְמַן לָהֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ דְּבַר־יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ מִפַּת־בַּג הַמֶּלֶךְ וּמִיֵּין מִשְׁתָּיו וּֽלְגַדְּלָם שָׁנִים שָׁלוֹשׁ וּמִקְצָתָם יַֽעַמְדוּ לִפְנֵי הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ וַיְהִי בָהֶם מִבְּנֵי יְהוּדָה דָּנִיֵּאל חֲנַנְיָה מִֽישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָֽה׃ וַיָּשֶׂם לָהֶם שַׂר הַסָּרִיסִים שֵׁמוֹת וַיָּשֶׂם לְדָֽנִיֵּאל בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר וְלַֽחֲנַנְיָה שַׁדְרַךְ וּלְמִֽישָׁאֵל מֵישַׁךְ וְלַעֲזַרְיָה עֲבֵד נְגֽוֹ׃
1.lit: “The king spoke to Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of Israel, even of the royal offspring and of the nobles; youths in whom was no defect, but well-favored, and skillful in all wisdom, and endowed with knowledge, and understanding science, and who had the ability to stand in the king’s palace; and that he should teach them the learning and the language of the Chaldeans. The king appointed for them a daily portion of the king’s dainties, and of the wine which he drank, and that they should be nourished three years; that at its end they should stand before the king. Now among these were of the children of Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The prince of the eunuchs gave names to them: to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego.”

ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning

ChaldeanכַּשְׂדִּֽיםKasdimH3778Babylonians; here it refers to their writing and learning
to nourishוּֽלְגַדְּלָםgaddelH1431to make grow, to train; the king meant to raise them into his own men

1.gram:
לְלַמְּדָם סֵפֶר וּלְשׁוֹן כַּשְׂדִּים (to teach them the writing and language of the Chaldeans): סֵפֶר originally meant “something written,” and here it covers a whole body of learning and literature, not only literacy. A three-year course is a complete replacement of the mind.

The וַיָּשֶׂם (he set) of 1:7 and the וַיָּשֶׂם (he resolved) of 1:8 are the same verb in the same form: the chief of the eunuchs “set” new names, and Daniel “set” his heart. The two “settings” meet face to face in the next verse.
1.exp:
Babylon did not want prisoners; it wanted colleagues. This passage is the first trap of the whole book, and it is laid very gently.

Look at the conditions for choosing them: royal family, nobles, young, without blemish, handsome, intelligent, knowledgeable, able to stand. This is not picking forced labor; it is picking successors. Then look at the treatment: the king himself appointed their food and wine, nourished them for three years, and then they would “stand” before the king. They ate the king’s meal, studied the king’s books, and would one day stand in the king’s palace. All the conditions were so good that one could hardly feel anything but gratitude.

Then the names. Daniel means “God is my judge,” Hananiah “Yahweh has been gracious,” Mishael is generally taken as “Who is what God is?”, and Azariah “Yahweh has helped.” Four names, and every one of them carries Yahweh. And the new names? Belteshazzar is generally thought to be connected with the Babylonian god Bel; Abednego means “servant of Nego (Nabu)”; the origins of Shadrach and Meshach are disputed among scholars, and we need not force an answer. The point is: names were “set,” not “asked.” They were not asked whether they were willing; they were simply given new titles.

Please notice one detail: the text uses the same verb for two things. The chief of the eunuchs “set” names, and in the next verse Daniel “set” his heart. People can change your name, but they cannot change what you have set in your heart.

This is the situation of many people today: workplace, school, and surroundings do not need to force you; they only need to give you very good conditions, and you slowly become what they want. Only when we see this “gentle assimilation” do we understand why Daniel was so serious in the next verse.

1.grk: וַיָּשֶׂם דָּנִיֵּאל עַל־לִבּוֹ אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־יִתְגָּאַל בְּפַתְבַּג הַמֶּלֶךְ וּבְיֵין מִשְׁתָּיו וַיְבַקֵּשׁ מִשַּׂר הַסָּרִיסִים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִתְגָּאָֽל׃
1.lit: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.”
1.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
resolveוַיָּשֶׂםsimH7760to place, to set; the same verb as “gave names” in 1:7
heartלִבּוֹlevH3820heart; in Hebrew the “heart” is the place of decision, not only of feeling

king’s foodבְּפַתְבַּגpatbagH6598the king’s dainties; a Persian loanword for fine court food

1.gram:
וַיָּשֶׂם דָּנִיֵּאל עַל־לִבּוֹ (Daniel set it upon his heart): this is the Hebrew idiom for “making up one’s mind.” The text does not say he “felt” or “hoped”; it says “set upon the heart,” that is, before anything happened, there was already an unmoving place in his heart.

The stem of יִתְגָּאַל (to defile himself) is reflexive: he was unwilling to let himself become one who is defiled. The second occurrence, יִתְגָּאָל, carries different vowel points, a difference in the traditional reading; the meaning is unchanged.
1.exp:
The most important act of the whole book takes place at a dinner table, and before anyone forced him.

The word “resolve” in the original is “set upon the heart.” The timing matters: the king’s food had just been assigned, no one had yet said that refusing to eat meant death, and no one had stepped forward to object, yet Daniel already had his answer. Many people’s failure is not at the moment of greatest pressure but in not having resolved beforehand: deciding only when the pressure comes is usually too late.

What he resolved was not “shall I eat or not,” but “I will not defile myself.” The text does not explain why he considered the king’s food defiling: perhaps the meat and wine had been offered to idols, perhaps it was food forbidden by the law, or perhaps accepting the king’s table meant accepting the king’s sovereignty. This is where the text deliberately says nothing, and we need not supply Daniel with a single answer; what is truly worth watching is the way he handled the problem.

He did not protest publicly, refuse to attend, or secretly pour out the food. He “asked” the chief of the eunuchs. The word is gentle: resolve is hard; speech is gentle. His firmness was not wrapped in arrogance, and his respect was not bought with compromise. This is wisdom for life in someone else’s kingdom: the heart must be settled, and the attitude must be humble.

Back to 1:7: their names were set, and Daniel set his own heart. What people can take away is name, surroundings, and future; what they cannot take away is a decision already set upon the heart. Today, at work, at home, at school, you may have a “small table.” You do not have to change the world at once, but you can decide in your heart today: this one thing, I will not touch.

1.grk: וַיִּתֵּן הָֽאֱלֹהִים אֶת־דָּנִיֵּאל לְחֶסֶד וּֽלְרַחֲמִים לִפְנֵי שַׂר הַסָּרִיסִֽים׃ וַיֹּאמֶר שַׂר הַסָּרִיסִים לְדָנִיֵּאל יָרֵא אֲנִי אֶת־אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲשֶׁר מִנָּה אֶת־מַאֲכַלְכֶם וְאֶת־מִשְׁתֵּיכֶם אֲשֶׁר לָמָּה יִרְאֶה אֶת־פְּנֵיכֶם זֹֽעֲפִים מִן־הַיְלָדִים אֲשֶׁר כְּגִֽילְכֶם וְחִיַּבְתֶּם אֶת־רֹאשִׁי לַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
1.lit: “Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. For why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? Then you would endanger my head with the king.””
1.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
kindnessלְחֶסֶדchesedH2617steadfast love, kindness; in the Old Testament often used of God’s faithful love for his covenant people
compassionוּֽלְרַחֲמִיםrachamimH7356compassion; the root is related to “womb,” the closest kind of tenderness
fearיָרֵאyareH3373to be afraid, to revere; here it is a man fearing the king, not fearing God
worse lookingזֹֽעֲפִיםza'afH2196to be angry, to look sullen; it refers to a poor complexion
1.gram:
וַיִּתֵּן הָאֱלֹהִים (God gave): the subject is God and the verb is “give,” echoing the “the Lord gave” of 1:2. לְחֶסֶד וּלְרַחֲמִים (kindness and compassion) are two words used together; in the Old Testament they are often paired like this only when explaining God’s character.

וְחִיַּבְתֶּם אֶת־רֹאשִׁי (you would endanger my head): literally, “you would make my head guilty,” a way of speaking in which the head is the payment.
1.exp:
The chief of the eunuchs was not the villain; he feared the king, but God had already begun working in his heart.

The order in verse 9 is delicate: God first gave Daniel favor, and only then came the chief’s answer. Daniel did not get his answer first and then resolve; he resolved, and then God opened the way. Many people reverse the order: they wait until every condition is clear before deciding. The order the text gives us is: first settle the heart, then the road opens.

Now look at what the chief said. He said, “I fear my lord the king.” It is not that he lacked sympathy; he simply did not dare. His “head” was at stake. If these four young men looked worse, he would pay with his life. This is not obstruction; it is a person living wedged under power telling his real fear.

This gives us a reminder: in an unbelieving environment, those who oppose you are not necessarily bad people; very often they are only afraid. If we treat everyone who disagrees as an enemy, we cannot see the favor God has already prepared in their hearts.

What God gave was “kindness and compassion.” This was not Daniel’s eloquence or his popularity. All he did was settle his heart and open his mouth; the rest was God’s work.

In 321 language, this is the starting point of “selflessness”: not suppressing yourself, but no longer preparing outcomes in God’s place. A person settles the heart and leaves the consequences with him.

1.grk: וַיֹּאמֶר דָּנִיֵּאל אֶל־הַמֶּלְצַר אֲשֶׁר מִנָּה שַׂר הַסָּֽרִיסִים עַל־דָּנִיֵּאל חֲנַנְיָה מִֽישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָֽה׃ נַס־נָא אֶת־עֲבָדֶיךָ יָמִים עֲשָׂרָה וְיִתְּנוּ־לָנוּ מִן־הַזֵּרֹעִים וְנֹאכְלָה וּמַיִם וְנִשְׁתֶּֽה׃ וְיֵרָאוּ לְפָנֶיךָ מַרְאֵינוּ וּמַרְאֵה הַיְלָדִים הָאֹכְלִים אֵת פַּתְבַּג הַמֶּלֶךְ וְכַאֲשֶׁר תִּרְאֵה עֲשֵׂה עִם־עֲבָדֶֽיךָ׃ וַיִּשְׁמַע לָהֶם לַדָּבָר הַזֶּה וַיְנַסֵּם יָמִים עֲשָׂרָֽה׃ וּמִקְצָת יָמִים עֲשָׂרָה נִרְאָה מַרְאֵיהֶם טוֹב וּבְרִיאֵי בָּשָׂר מִן־כָּל־הַיְלָדִים הָאֹכְלִים אֵת פַּתְבַּג הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ וַיְהִי הַמֶּלְצַר נֹשֵׂא אֶת־פַּתְבָּגָם וְיֵין מִשְׁתֵּיהֶם וְנֹתֵן לָהֶם זֵרְעֹנִֽים׃
1.lit: “Then Daniel said to the steward whom the prince of the eunuchs had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat, and water to drink. Then let our faces be examined before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s dainties; and as you see, deal with your servants.” So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days. At the end of ten days, their faces appeared fairer, and they were fatter in flesh, than all the youths who ate of the king’s dainties. So the steward took away their dainties, and the wine that they would drink, and gave them vegetables.”

ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
testנַסnasahH5254to test, to try; he gave the other side a way to check with their own eyes
vegetablesהַזֵּרֹעִיםzero'imH2235things that grow from seed; a general term for vegetables and grains

1.gram:
הַזֵּרֹעִים (vegetables) comes from the root for “seed,” literally “things sown.” It does not refer only to greens; it can include legumes and grains. The English “vegetables” is enough, and there is no need to speculate further.

The ten-day “test” is a proposal that can be checked: Daniel did not say, “Trust me, God will keep us,” but “see for yourself.” Faith does not shy away from testing.
1.exp:
Daniel did not demand a miracle; he offered a method the other side could accept.

The chief of the eunuchs said no, so Daniel changed the person he spoke to: he went to the steward who managed them directly, and set out one condition. Ten days, vegetables and water, and then look with your own eyes, and deal with us according to what you see. This was not a gamble; it was handing the decision to the other side, and handing over the consequences with it: if it does not work, you may go back to the king’s way.

There is a spiritual order worth noticing here: he did not demand that others be like him, and he did not criticize the king’s food. He simply asked, for himself and for his three companions, for a space in which to obey conscience. Firm in position, calm in tone, clear in terms, transparent in result.

The result in the text is simple: after ten days, their faces looked better and their bodies were fatter. The steward took away the king’s food and wine and gave them vegetables. Please notice that this does not say vegetarian food is healthier, and it is not any teaching about diet; the text does not say that the result came from the food itself. What it says is: when a person resolves in conscience not to defile himself, God takes responsibility for the consequence that person was afraid of. They feared looking worse, and God made their faces look better.

We need not turn the ten days of vegetables into a set of rules, nor expect that every act of holding firm will bring a visible good result. Chapter 3 will say: even if not. But here, God first gave these four a small witness: he remembers the decisions set upon the heart.

1.grk: וְהַיְלָדִים הָאֵלֶּה אַרְבַּעְתָּם נָתַן לָהֶם הָֽאֱלֹהִים מַדָּע וְהַשְׂכֵּל בְּכָל־סֵפֶר וְחָכְמָה וְדָנִיֵּאל הֵבִין בְּכָל־חָזוֹן וַחֲלֹמֽוֹת׃
1.lit: “Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”

ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning

1.gram:
נָתַן לָהֶם הָאֱלֹהִים (God gave them): this is the same verb as the וַיִּתֵּן אֲדֹנָי of 1:2 and the וַיִּתֵּן הָאֱלֹהִים of 1:9. Three times in chapter 1 there is a “giving”: the Lord gave the king, God gave favor, God gave wisdom.

הֵבִין (understand) is a causative stem, with the sense of “making others understand.” Daniel’s “understanding” was not something he worked out himself; it was given to him.
1.exp:
This verse turns the first chapter over and reads it from the other side: the one truly “educating” these four young men was not Babylon’s three-year course, but God.

The king’s conditions were: intelligent, knowledgeable, well versed in all learning. But this verse says that these things were given by God. The same intelligence that the Babylonians thought they had trained, the text says God gave. They used the king’s books and learned the king’s learning, but the source of wisdom lay somewhere else.

One person is singled out by name: Daniel “had understanding in all visions and dreams.” That sentence prepares every story that follows: in chapter 2 he interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream; in chapter 4 he interprets the king’s second dream; from chapter 7 on, he himself is given visions. Notice: his ability did not come from an examination; God gave it to him specially, and not for his own sake.

This is a reminder to believers who study and work in the world: you can study well, and you should; but what finally lets you stand is not your degree but the understanding God gave. This is not a call to stop working hard; it is knowing, while working hard, to whom the credit finally belongs.

One more thing: the verb “understand” later becomes a mark of the whole book. In chapters 8, 9 and 10, Daniel asks God again and again to “make me understand,” which shows that he never treated this understanding as his own possession.

1.grk: וּלְמִקְצָת הַיָּמִים אֲשֶׁר־אָמַר הַמֶּלֶךְ לַהֲבִיאָם וַיְבִיאֵם שַׂר הַסָּרִיסִים לִפְנֵי נְבֻכַדְנֶצַּֽר׃ וַיְדַבֵּר אִתָּם הַמֶּלֶךְ וְלֹא נִמְצָא מִכֻּלָּם כְּדָנִיֵּאל חֲנַנְיָה מִֽישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה וַיַּֽעַמְדוּ לִפְנֵי הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ וְכֹל דְּבַר חָכְמַת בִּינָה אֲשֶׁר־בִּקֵּשׁ מֵהֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ וַֽיִּמְצָאֵם עֶשֶׂר יָדוֹת עַל כָּל־הַֽחַרְטֻמִּים הָֽאַשָּׁפִים אֲשֶׁר בְּכָל־מַלְכוּתֽוֹ׃

The king talked with them; and among them all was found no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore stood they before the king. In every matter of wisdom and understanding, concerning which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters who were in all his realm.”

1.gram:
עֶשֶׂר יָדוֹת (ten times) is literally “ten hands,” a way of stressing “far better”; it need not be taken as an exact number.

הַחַרְטֻמִּים הָאַשָּׁפִים (the magicians and the enchanters) are a group that recurs in chapter 2 and again in chapters 4 and 5. They make their first appearance here, and later they will be put to shame again and again by God’s servant.
1.exp:
The three years of study were over, the king examined them himself, and the result was: among all these, none could compare with these four.

The point of this passage is not the grades but “the standard used.” What the king asked about was “matters of wisdom and understanding,” that is, the ability to govern and to judge, not whether they were vegetarian. The four stood firm before the king because God gave them understanding; but they were “seen” before the king because they were first seen by God at the table.

Notice another detail: they “stood before the king.” That word, in verse 4, was what Babylon wanted them to do. Now they really stood before the king, but the ones who stood were those who had not defiled themselves. The position was still the one Babylon gave, but the people inside had not been replaced by Babylon.

“Ten times better” is the small climax of chapter 1, and it also previews the next chapters: the magicians cannot interpret the dream, but Daniel can; in the furnace no one can save, yet a fourth is present with them; in the lions’ den no one can come out, but Daniel comes out. From here the book keeps asking: in this kingdom, who is truly wise?

This does not ask us to become the best in order to prove something; it reminds us that when we do not strive for ourselves, God will, at the right time, put us in the right place, so that his name may be seen.

1.grk: וַֽיְהִי דָּֽנִיֵּאל עַד־שְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃פ
1.lit: “Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus.”

ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning

1.gram:
וַיְהִי דָּנִיֵּאל (Daniel was): the verb הָיָה only means “to be.” The last sentence of the chapter uses no verb of power; it says only: he was there.

“The first year of King Cyrus” (about 539–538 BC) is the end of the exile. But 10:1 says that in “the third year of Cyrus king of Persia” Daniel received another revelation; how the two passages relate is explained in the issues section: 1:21 says that he stayed on until this moment, not that he ended in this year.
1.exp:
The last sentence of chapter 1 has only a few words: Daniel was still there.

The weight of this sentence can only be read against the whole history. Nebuchadnezzar’s dynasty ended, Babylon fell, Media and Persia took over; all the power that once changed names, set banquets, and picked talent passed away, one after another. Only one young man who had been carried off was still there. He did not stand by power, and he did not stand by compromise, but because his heart, at that first table, had already been set.

The text uses the most ordinary verb: “was.” It does not say he “succeeded,” “held power,” or “was honored”; it says only that he “was there.” Sometimes the greatest praise God gives a person is not what he accomplished, but that, through long years and one king after another, he still stood before God.

This sets the tone for the next eleven chapters: this is not a book asking “when is the end,” but a book about how, in someone else’s kingdom, God’s servant stays. Kingdoms will change, but the God who rules in heaven does not change; and those who serve him therefore have a reason to stand. You and I can also, in our own generation and at our own post, simply be someone who is “still there.”

2.grk: וּבִשְׁנַת שְׁתַּיִם לְמַלְכוּת נְבֻֽכַדְנֶצַּר חָלַם נְבֻֽכַדְנֶצַּר חֲלֹמוֹת וַתִּתְפָּעֶם רוּחוֹ וּשְׁנָתוֹ נִהְיְתָה עָלָֽיו׃ וַיֹּאמֶר הַמֶּלֶךְ לִקְרֹא לַֽחַרְטֻמִּים וְלָֽאַשָּׁפִים וְלַֽמְכַשְּׁפִים וְלַכַּשְׂדִּים לְהַגִּיד לַמֶּלֶךְ חֲלֹמֹתָיו וַיָּבֹאוּ וַיַּֽעַמְדוּ לִפְנֵי הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲלוֹם חָלָמְתִּי וַתִּפָּעֶם רוּחִי לָדַעַת אֶֽת־הַחֲלֽוֹם׃
2.lit: “In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him. Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be called to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king. The king said to them, “I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream.””

2.gram:
וַתִּתְפָּעֶם רוּחוֹ (his spirit was troubled): the verb is a reflexive stem, literally “his spirit was struck of itself.” The same verb is used in Gen 41:8 for Pharaoh’s dream, and in Ps 77:4 for “I am so troubled”; it is “the kind of unease that will not let you sleep.”

“The second year” seems to differ from the three years of training in 1:5. A common explanation is that Babylon counted the year of a king’s accession as the “accession year,” not counting it as year one, so that the three years of training span several calendar years without needing to be three full twelve-month periods. The text does not ask us to count days here.
2.exp:
The most powerful man in the world could not sleep. This chapter begins with a bed that could not sleep.

Nebuchadnezzar was the world power of his day: he had besieged Jerusalem, subdued many nations, and even the vessels of the temple were in his treasury. Yet as soon as he had a dream, “his spirit was troubled.” There is an unease that power and wealth cannot soothe. Somewhere inside he knew that this dream was no ordinary dream; it had to do with his kingdom.

His first reaction was to gather all the experts: the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, the Chaldeans. This was a list of Babylon’s think tank, each with a specialty, each with a teacher behind him. At the end of chapter 1 this group had been “ten times” surpassed by the four of Daniel; now they were to stand before the king themselves.

Please notice: “stand before the king” uses the same verb as the four young men “standing” in 1:5. The difference is that this time those standing did not know what to say. Human wisdom has to be measured first before the most powerful man.

Today too, in our most uneasy nights, we often first look for experts, for methods, for ways. The text does not rebuke seeking help; it only lets us see first: there is an unease that human ways cannot reach.

2.lit: “Then the Chaldeans spoke to the king in the Syrian language, “O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation.” The king answered the Chaldeans, “The thing has gone from me. If you don’t make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut in pieces, and your houses will be made a dunghill. But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you will receive of me gifts and rewards and great honor. Therefore show me the dream and its interpretation.” They answered the second time and said, “Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation.” The king answered, “I know of a certainty that you are trying to gain time, because you see the thing has gone from me. But if you don’t make known to me the dream, there is but one law for you; for you have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, until the situation changes. Therefore tell me the dream, and I will know that you can show me its interpretation.” The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, “There is not a man on the earth who can show the king’s matter, because no king, lord, or ruler, has asked such a thing of any magician, or enchanter, or Chaldean. It is a rare thing that the king requires, and there is no other who can show it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.””

2.gram:
אֲרָמִית (Aramaic) is the marker of the language switch in the Old Testament: from 2:4b, through 7:28, the original changes to Aramaic. Why the switch comes here is discussed in the issues section; for now notice the scene where the switch happens: the Chaldeans spoke in Aramaic, that is, the common language of the court, and the text simply continues writing in that language.

אַזְדָּא מִנִּי מִלְּתָא (2:5, 8): “the matter is settled by me” or “the matter has gone from me.” אַזְדָּא is a Persian loanword whose meaning is disputed: one view is “certain, decided,” another “gone, forgotten.” The CUV takes the latter (“I have forgotten”); whichever is taken, what the king wants is: “first tell me the dream.”
2.exp:
The king made a demand no one could meet: not only the interpretation but the dream itself had to be told first.

This is a very interesting conversation. The Chaldeans said in polite court language: “O king, live forever; tell your servants the dream.” This was their usual way: first hear the dream, then interpret it, and the interpretation looks very professional but no one can ever verify it. But the king changed the rules: you tell me the dream first, and then I will believe your interpretation. “The dream is settled by me” (or “forgotten”)—whichever reading is taken, the king’s meaning is clear: I want to know whether you really see, or are making up a story.

The Chaldeans’ answer is the most honest sentence in the passage: “There is not a man on the earth who can show the king’s matter.” Then they said a theological sentence: “except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.” They were half right. The gods they spoke of “do not dwell with flesh,” that is, they are far from people and do not live among them; but in verse 22 that follows, Daniel will say: “the light dwells with him.” The true God is a God who is with people.

Human expertise shows its limit just when it is truly needed. Today too we often use “more methods, more experts” to deal with unease; the text reminds us that there is a kind of problem where only when people say, “We have no way,” does the God of heaven have room to speak.

2.gram: וְחַכִּימַיָּא מִתְקַטְּלִין (the wise men were to be slain) is a participle, describing “in progress”: as soon as the decree went out, the killing was already on its way. Daniel and his three friends had not appeared before the king, yet were counted among the “wise men,” a group caught up in it.
2.exp:
Human cruelty often begins with the sentence “I have no way.”

The king’s anger was not at one person but at the whole system: he “commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed.” He was not punishing those who had failed in duty; he was announcing: this group I once trusted is useless.

The reader should see a detail here: Daniel and his three friends had not been part of that failure, yet were to be killed along with them. They had not failed, but they belonged to that group, and so they faced the same judgment. This is the situation of exiles: you have done nothing wrong, yet because you “belong to the system,” you are counted in with the rest.

In any environment where power is unstable, there are such moments: a sudden order, a sudden purge, a sudden fear. The text does not gloss over it; it says directly: the decree has gone out, and the killing is on its way. God’s servants are not exempted from such situations.

But then, in verse 14, the story turns. He did not run, did not cry injustice, did not fight; he answered with a tactful word. He took in the pressure first, and only then acted. This order is worth learning in every sudden pressure: do not rush to strike back, and do not rush to flee; ask first, and then speak.

2.grk: בֵּאדַיִן דָּנִיֵּאל הֲתִיב עֵטָא וּטְעֵם לְאַרְיוֹךְ רַב־טַבָּחַיָּא דִּי מַלְכָּא דִּי נְפַק לְקַטָּלָה לְחַכִּימֵי בָּבֶֽל׃ עָנֵה וְאָמַר לְאַרְיוֹךְ שַׁלִּיטָא דִֽי־מַלְכָּא עַל־מָה דָתָא מְהַחְצְפָה מִן־קֳדָם מַלְכָּא אֱדַיִן מִלְּתָא הוֹדַע אַרְיוֹךְ לְדָנִיֵּֽאל׃ וְדָנִיֵּאל עַל וּבְעָה מִן־מַלְכָּא דִּי זְמָן יִנְתֵּן־לֵהּ וּפִשְׁרָא לְהַֽחֲוָיָה לְמַלְכָּֽא׃פ אֱדַיִן דָּֽנִיֵּאל לְבַיְתֵהּ אֲזַל וְלַחֲנַנְיָה מִֽישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה חַבְרוֹהִי מִלְּתָא הוֹדַֽע׃ וְרַחֲמִין לְמִבְעֵא מִן־קֳדָם אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא עַל־רָזָה דְּנָה דִּי לָא יְהֹֽבְדוּן דָּנִיֵּאל וְחַבְרוֹהִי עִם־שְׁאָר חַכִּימֵי בָבֶֽל׃
2.lit: “Then Daniel returned answer with counsel and prudence to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon. He answered Arioch the king’s captain, “Why is the decree so urgent from the king?” Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel. Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would appoint him a time, and he would show the king the interpretation. Then Daniel went to his house and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions: that they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his companions would not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.”

2.gram:
עֵטָא וּטְעֵם (counsel and discretion) are two words used together: עֵטָא is “counsel,” טְעֵם is “judgment, taste, tact.” Together they mean “the wisdom of measured, skillful speech.” Daniel did not clash and did not beg; he first asked one question: why is it so urgent?

אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא (the God of heaven) is the central title of this chapter and the ones that follow, and it occurs many times in the Aramaic sections. With the “Lord” of 1:2 and the “God” of 1:9, it forms a line of names: this God is not limited by the gods of any empire; he is in heaven.
2.exp:
A man who still asks quiet questions under a death order is one who truly knows who rules.

Arioch, the captain of the guard, had come to carry out the order. Daniel did not resist him but asked: “Why is the decree so urgent from the king?” It was a very quiet question, and it made a man who was ready to kill stop and talk.

Daniel then did three things: first, he went in to see the king and asked for time, and he did not say “I guarantee I can,” only “grant me a delay”; second, he returned to his house and told his companions; third, he asked them to “desire mercies of the God of heaven.” The order of the three things is very clear: ask first, seek first, pray first, and only then the interpretation.

Please notice especially the word “companions.” He did not carry this alone but called in three friends to seek together. In chapter 1 they resolved together; in chapter 2 they prayed together. In someone else’s kingdom we are not isolated individuals; we are a small group that guards one another.

And that title: “the God of heaven.” It is the most common title in the Aramaic sections. The Babylonians said: the gods do not dwell with flesh. They could not find the answer on earth. Daniel said: we seek the God of heaven. A different direction gives a different answer. When people meet something they cannot solve, they often look first for a way on earth; the text teaches us to look up first.

2.grk: אֱדַיִן לְדָנִיֵּאל בְּחֶזְוָא דִֽי־לֵילְיָא רָזָה גֲלִי אֱדַיִן דָּֽנִיֵּאל בָּרִךְ לֶאֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּֽא׃ עָנֵה דָֽנִיֵּאל וְאָמַר לֶהֱוֵא שְׁמֵהּ דִּֽי־אֱלָהָא מְבָרַךְ מִן־עָלְמָא וְעַד־עָלְמָא דִּי חָכְמְתָא וּגְבוּרְתָא דִּי לֵֽהּ־הִֽיא׃ וְהוּא מְהַשְׁנֵא עִדָּנַיָּא וְזִמְנַיָּא מְהַעְדֵּה מַלְכִין וּמְהָקֵים מַלְכִין יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין וּמַנְדְּעָא לְיָדְעֵי בִינָֽה׃ הוּא גָּלֵא עַמִּיקָתָא וּמְסַתְּרָתָא יָדַע מָה בַחֲשׁוֹכָא עִמֵּהּ שְׁרֵֽא׃ לָךְ׀ אֱלָהּ אֲבָהָתִי מְהוֹדֵא וּמְשַׁבַּח אֲנָה דִּי חָכְמְתָא וּגְבוּרְתָא יְהַבְתְּ לִי וּכְעַן הֽוֹדַעְתַּנִי דִּֽי־בְעֵינָא מִנָּךְ דִּֽי־מִלַּת מַלְכָּא הוֹדַעְתֶּֽנָא׃
2.lit: “Then the secret was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven. Daniel answered, “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his. He changes the times and the seasons. He removes kings, and sets up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding. He reveals the deep and secret things. He knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.””

2.gram:
דִּי־חָכְמְתָא וּגְבוּרְתָא דִּי הִיא (for wisdom and might are his): the two words “wisdom” and “might” are used of the same God; Babylon’s wise men had wisdom but no power, Babylon’s king had power but no wisdom, and only this God has both.

מְהַשְׁנֵא עִדָּנַיָּא וְזִמְנַיָּא מְהַעְדֵּה מַלְכִין וּמְהָקֵים מַלְכִין: three participles, all “present continuous”: he “keeps” changing, removing kings, setting up kings. This is not a single act but a continuing rule.
2.exp:
Before giving the answer, he spoke a hymn of praise. This is the heart of the chapter, and the first prayer of the whole book.

Look at the order: God had revealed the secret, and Daniel did not run straight to the king; he stopped first and blessed the God of heaven. This praise is a miniature map of the world: time is in his hand (“changes the times and the seasons”), kingship is in his hand (“removes kings, and sets up kings”), wisdom is in his hand (“gives wisdom to the wise”), and even darkness is in his hand (“knows what is in the darkness”).

Then comes the sentence that answers the Chaldeans: “the light dwells with him.” Earlier they said: the gods do not dwell with flesh. Now Daniel says: this God not only dwells with people, he himself is the dwelling of light. This is the greatest rebuttal of this chapter, and also its gentlest comfort: the God we serve is not a God far away.

He also said: “wisdom and might are his.” Then in verse 23 he says in the first person: “You have given me wisdom and might.” Please notice that this “give” is on the same line as the “give” of chapter 1: wisdom is given, not one’s own.

In 321 language, this is the starting point of “Let Jesus receive all the glory”: first see to whom the credit belongs. This passage is not the result of one person’s prayer, but of a small group seeking together, and then God himself answering. God’s answer often comes in the night; and people’s praise need not wait for the morning.

2.lit: “Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said this to him: “Don’t destroy the wise men of Babylon. Bring me in before the king, and I will show to the king the interpretation.” Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said this to him: “I have found a man of the children of the captivity of Judah who will make known to the king the interpretation.” The king answered Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Are you able to make known to me the dream which I have seen, and its interpretation?” Daniel answered before the king, and said, “The secret which the king has demanded can’t be shown to the king by wise men, enchanters, magicians, or soothsayers; but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: “As for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what will happen. But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but to the intent that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your heart.”

2.gram:
בְּאַחֲרִית יוֹמַיָּא (in the latter days): literally “at the end of the days,” often used in the prophets for “some moment in the future.” Here it is the “later things” that Nebuchadnezzar’s dream is concerned with, and the interpretation is to explain the order of the kingdoms that follow, not a fixed day.

לָא בְחָכְמָה (not for wisdom) is an emphatic negative. Daniel did not say “I am not very smart,” but: it is not that my wisdom surpasses all the living; this secret was revealed so that the king might know.
2.exp:
Daniel’s first words were not “I can,” but “I am not.”

First look at the first thing he did on going in: he did not rush to claim credit but said to Arioch: “Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon.” He pleaded for those who could not interpret the dream. These were his “colleagues” and also his “rivals,” and he did not let them be killed just because he could interpret the dream. His ability was to save people, not to beat others.

Then he stood before the king. The king asked him: “Are you able?” This is a question that makes it very easy to say “I can,” because saying “I can” brings a future. But Daniel’s answer first says “cannot”: “wise men, enchanters, magicians, or soothsayers” cannot tell the king, and then “there is a God in heaven.” He turned the king’s eyes away from people and pointed to heaven.

Most important is verse 30: “But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living.” This is a humble declaration and also the watershed of the whole book: pride is leaving one’s position and grasping power; humility is returning to one’s position and giving the glory back to God. Before him was a king used to hearing praise; behind him was a post that would keep being raised by the king. Yet what he said at that moment was: this is not me.

We too often stand in such a position: able to do what others cannot. At that moment, what is the first thing we say? “I am good,” or “This was given by God”?

2.lit: ““You, O king, saw, and behold, a great image. This image, which was mighty, and whose brightness was excellent, stood before you; and its appearance was terrifying. As for this image, its head was of fine gold, its breast and its arms of silver, its belly and its thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, its feet part of iron, and part of clay. You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors. The wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them. The stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.”

2.gram:
דִּי לָא בִידַיִן (not by hands): this negation is the pivot of the passage. The image was made by human hands, but the stone was “not by hands.” This expression is later used in the New Testament to describe “what is made by God, not made by hands” (compare Mark 14:58; Heb 9:11), a connection the New Testament itself makes; here we say only: the source of this stone is not in the world of men.

הִתְגְּזֶרֶת (cut out) is a reflexive-passive form that does not say who cut it, but makes clear that it was “not cut by man.” This passive is a theological passive, pointing to God.
2.exp:
The biggest role in the dream is not the image but the stone.

First look at the image: tall, bright, terrifying. “Stood before you”: what the king saw was a projection of his own kingdom: head of gold, breast of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and the lower it went, the harder and the less precious the metal; at the feet, half iron and half clay. This image, from top to bottom, goes from precious to cheap, from pure to mixed, and finally stands on an unstable foundation.

Then a stone appeared. Notice its source: “cut out without hands.” The image was made by hands and set up by a human kingdom, but the stone was not. This “without hands” is the key phrase of the chapter: God’s Kingdom does not grow out of human kingdoms, and is not built by human strength.

Where did the stone strike? Not at the head of gold but at the feet, at the most fragile place. The image fell, and gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay were broken in pieces “together,” becoming chaff of the threshing floor, carried away by the wind, with “no place found for them.” This is a total end: all the kingdoms, high or low, vanish at the same moment.

Then the stone that broke everything became a great mountain, filling the whole earth. Human kingdoms will at last be replaced; God’s Kingdom will fill. This dream is not a historical timetable but a declaration: everything people build, however splendid, is not final.

2.lit: ““This is the dream; and we will tell its interpretation before the king. You, O king, are king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory. Wherever the children of men dwell, he has given the animals of the field and the birds of the sky into your hand, and has made you rule over them all. You are the head of gold.”

2.gram:
מַלְכוּתָא חִסְנָא וְתָקְפָּא וִיקָרָא יְהַב: four things, all “given.” יְהַב (give) is the verb on the same line as the verb of chapter 1. Kingdom, power, strength and glory were not seized by Nebuchadnezzar; the God of heaven gave them to him.

“King of kings” is a royal title of the ancient Near East; here it is rewritten: you, this “king of kings,” were set up by another “God.”
2.exp:
The highest compliment, and the heaviest reminder: “the God of heaven has given the kingdom to you.”

Daniel spoke to a world ruler without avoiding the point. He first respected his rank: “You are king of kings,” and then at once put the title back in its right place: “the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory.” All four were given.

This is a shrewd way of speaking, and also a big message: kingdom, power and glory were not taken by the king through his own ability; they were entrusted. One who is entrusted must give account to the one who entrusted. This sentence will appear again in chapter 4, and that time the king will pay a very great price for forgetting it.

Look at one more detail: “You are the head of gold.” The head of gold is the most precious part of the whole image, and the first to appear. Nebuchadnezzar must have been very pleased to hear this. But the text has already prepared the words that follow: after the head of gold come silver, bronze, iron and clay, and the head of gold itself will end. Being called “most precious” does not mean “forever.”

For us today this is also a reminder: the positions, talents and influence we have were all given. They are not unimportant, but we must not forget who gave them.

2.lit: ““After you, another kingdom will arise that is inferior to you; and another third kingdom of bronze, which will rule over all the earth. The fourth kingdom will be strong as iron, because iron breaks in pieces and subdues all things; and as iron that crushes all these, it will break in pieces and crush. Whereas you saw the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay, and part of iron, it will be a divided kingdom; but there will be in it of the strength of the iron, because you saw the iron mixed with miry clay. As the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom will be partly strong, and partly broken. Whereas you saw the iron mixed with miry clay, they will mingle themselves with the seed of men; but they won’t cling to one another, even as iron does not mix with clay.”

2.gram:
This passage names only the “head of gold” as Nebuchadnezzar (2:38); for the other three kingdoms the text says only “another kingdom,” “a third kingdom,” “a fourth kingdom,” without naming them. This is why later generations read the “four kingdoms” in different ways (Babylon—Medo-Persia—Greece—Rome, or Babylon—Media—Persia—Greece); the views of the various schools are set out in the issues section.

לָא דָּבְקִין (not joining): this word describes a mixed kingdom whose parts do not cling to one another. The weight of the text lies not on “which two peoples,” but on “mixed, yet unable to be one.”
2.exp:
This passage is the one that most tempts people to draw up a chart, and it most needs the reader to put his hands down.

The text says clearly only: the head of gold is Babylon. The silver, bronze and iron that follow are not named. Many people reading this immediately want to match each metal with an empire, a year, a present-day nation. This is the road most easily taken by those who read this book through the ages, and also the road that most easily takes people away from the point of the text.

So what is this passage really saying? Look at the “character” it describes: the second kingdom is “inferior to you,” the third “will bear rule over all the earth,” the fourth “will be strong as iron, because iron breaks in pieces and subdues all things,” and the last is “partly strong and partly broken,” iron mixed with clay, “not holding together.” Every kingdom has a beginning and an end; every one grows worse and more mixed, and in the end stands on an unstable foundation.

This is a very honest view of history: human kingdoms grow harder and also more brittle the later they come. The hardest iron is at last mixed with the softest clay, becoming a kingdom whose parts cannot cling together. Power can break everything, but it cannot make people truly one.

So we need not turn this passage into a map. We need only remember what it says to us: any kingdom that looks solid, strong and splendid is limited; and there is one Kingdom that is different. That is the point of the next verse.

Because you saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God has made known to the king what will happen hereafter. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure.””

2.gram:
יְקִים אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא מַלְכוּ (the God of heaven will set up a kingdom): the verb is יְקִים (to make stand), the subject is “the God of heaven,” the object is “a kingdom.” It comes from the same root as “removes kings, and sets up kings” in 2:21: he sets up kings, and he sets up a kingdom.

וּמַלְכוּתָה לְעַם אָחֳרָן לָא תִשְׁתְּבִק (nor will its sovereignty be left to another people): literally “its kingship will not be left to another people,” meaning this kingdom will not be transferred or replaced. Human kingdoms change hands; God’s Kingdom will not.
2.exp:
The most important verse of the whole chapter: human kingdoms come one after another, and God’s Kingdom does not grow out of them.

“In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom.” Please notice the subject and the verb: the subject is the God of heaven, the verb is “set up.” It was not set up by man, not reformed into being by man, not the natural evolution of human history, but set up by God himself. Read with 2:21: since he can “remove kings, and set up kings,” now he will “set up a kingdom.”

This kingdom has three characteristics: first, it is never destroyed. All the earlier kingdoms “break in pieces and crush”; this one will not. Second, it is not left to another people. It will not be transferred, absorbed or replaced. Third, it will stand forever. Human kingdoms have a time; God’s Kingdom has no end.

Then verse 45 returns to that stone: “cut out without hands.” This stone is the mark of this Kingdom. God’s Kingdom does not rest on human hands, human armies, economies or systems; its source is outside the human world.

This gives us two comforts today. First, we need not treat any kingdom as our final hope, nor despair at the rise and fall of any kingdom. Second, we are invited to become people of this Kingdom. It is not that we build God’s Kingdom, but that God brings us into the Kingdom he has set up. This is what 321 means by “to build God’s system”: not that we invent a system, but that we live in the Kingdom God has already set up.

2.lit: “Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, worshiped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an offering and sweet odors to him. The king answered to Daniel, and said, “Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, since you have been able to reveal this secret.” Then the king made Daniel great, and gave him many great gifts, and made him rule over the whole province of Babylon, and to be chief governor over all the wise men of Babylon. 2.gram:
סְגִד (fall down, worship) is the Aramaic verb specifically for “worship,” and it will become a key word in chapter 3 (3:5–6, 10–15, 18, 28). In chapter 2 the king “worships” Daniel, and in chapter 3 the king commands people to “worship” the golden image; the contrast between these two will be developed later.

וּמִנְחָה וְנִיחֹחִין (an offering and sweet odors) is the vocabulary of worship, but the text does not say whether Daniel accepted or refused. His response is discussed in the issues section.
2.exp:
The king fell down and worshiped, but the text puts its weight on the sentence in his mouth: “Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings.”

This is a big change. At the beginning of chapter 2 this king trusted magicians, gods and his own power; at the end he says: your God is the God of gods, the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets. His mouth spoke the right words. But please notice: what he said was “your God,” not “my God.” This is an acknowledgment, not necessarily a conversion. In chapters 3 and 4 he still has a long road to walk.

Now look at Daniel being promoted: ruler over the whole province and chief of all the wise men. This was his promotion and also his test. With power came more difficulties in not defiling himself. But he did one thing: he asked the king to appoint his three companions over the affairs of the province too. He did not monopolize it; he raised his friends. This is the 920 practice: the few “2s” beside him, he did not forget.

The last sentence is easily overlooked: “but Daniel was in the gate of the king.” He stayed at the king’s gate, that is, in a place where he could speak at any time and also face risk at any time. He did not leave his calling because he had been promoted; he stayed there, awaiting God’s next entrusting. In chapter 3 his three companions are sent to the plain of Dura; Daniel is not present. The text does not explain this difference, and we leave it there until chapter 3.

3.lit: “Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the local governors, the deputies, and the governors, the judges, the treasurers, the counselors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. Then the local governors, the deputies, and the governors, the judges, the treasurers, the counselors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together to the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then the herald cried aloud, “To you it is commanded, peoples, nations, and languages, that whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music, you fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king has set up. Whoever doesn’t fall down and worship shall be cast into the middle of a burning fiery furnace the same hour.” Therefore at that time, when all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music, all the peoples, the nations, and the languages, fell down and worshiped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.”

3.gram:
הֲקֵים (to set up) appears several times in these seven verses, and each time the subject is “King Nebuchadnezzar.” It is the same verb as יְקִים (God sets up kings, God sets up a kingdom) in 2:21, 44: in chapter 2 it is God who sets up, in chapter 3 it is the king who sets up. Two “settings up,” face to face in this chapter.

The list of instruments repeats in 3:5, 7, 10, 15. Many of the names are Greek loanwords (such as פְּסַנְתֵּרִין and סוּמְפֹּנְיָה), and later discussions of the book’s date and language arise from this; see the issues.
3.exp:
This chapter begins with a very clever design: not forcing people to believe, but letting them “kneel the moment they hear the music.”

First look at the image. It was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (about twenty-seven meters high and 2.7 meters wide), a strange proportion, more like a pillar than a person. In chapter 2 the king saw an image whose “head was of gold”; now he built an image that was gold all over. He did not accept the explanation “you are the head of gold, and after you another kingdom will arise”; he made the whole image of gold. This is his answer to chapter 2: my kingdom will not be replaced.

Then look at the list of those summoned: satraps, prefects, governors … the officials of the provinces. This was an assembly of imperial loyalty. When the music sounds, everyone falls down. The text, in a tone close to irony, repeats the list of instruments word by word: each time the same, each time in perfect order. The greatest pressure is often not the sword but “everybody does it.” Across three verses, “all the peoples, nations, and languages” fell down. No one said no, and no one needed to be forced; one piece of music was enough.

This is the situation many face today: not that faith is forbidden, but that they are invited to “be like everyone else.” The text first lets us see how natural and orderly this invitation is, and only then lets us see that three people did not bend their knees.

3.grk: כָּל־קֳבֵל דְּנָה בֵּהּ־זִמְנָא קְרִבוּ גֻּבְרִין כַּשְׂדָּאִין וַאֲכַלוּ קַרְצֵיהוֹן דִּי יְהוּדָיֵֽא׃ עֲנוֹ וְאָמְרִין לִנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִֽי׃ מַלְכָּא שָׂמְתָּ טְּעֵם דִּי כָל־אֱנָשׁ דִּֽי־יִשְׁמַע קָל קַרְנָא מַשְׁרֹקִיתָא שַׂבְּכָא פְסַנְתֵּרִין וְכֹל זְנֵי זְמָרָא יִפֵּל וְיִסְגֻּד לְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָֽא׃ וּמַן־דִּי־לָא יִפֵּל וְיִסְגֻּד יִתְרְמֵא לְגֽוֹא־אַתּוּן נוּרָא יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃ אִיתַי גֻּבְרִין יְהוּדָאיִן דִּֽי־מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן עַל־עֲבִידַת מְדִינַת בָּבֶל שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ לָא־שָׂמֽוּ מַלְכָּא טְעֵם לָא פָלְחִין וּלְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָא דִּי הֲקֵימְתָּ לָא סָגְדִֽין׃ס
3.lit: “Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near, and brought accusation against the Jews. They answered Nebuchadnezzar the king, “O king, live for ever! You, O king, have made a decree, that every man that hears the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image; and whoever doesn’t fall down and worship shall be cast into the middle of a burning fiery furnace. There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, have not respected you. They don’t serve your gods, and don’t worship the golden image which you have set up.””

3.gram:
וַאֲכַלוּ קַרְצֵיהוֹן (accused): literally “ate their pieces,” a vivid idiom, like biting a piece of flesh and tearing off a person’s name. The Chinese translation says only “accused” and loses that flavor of tearing.

פָּלְחִין (serve) is a tracked word starting from 3:12: the accusers say they “do not serve your gods,” the king says “you do not serve my gods,” the three friends say “our God whom we serve,” and the king finally says they would not “serve any god.” The same verb, in one chapter, changes masters four times.
3.exp:
The accusers are often not enemies, but colleagues.

This passage has only five verses, yet it is very precise. “Certain Chaldeans” are the very group that Daniel outshone in chapter 2. They did not speak to the three friends, they did not warn them privately; they went straight to the king. Some accusations are not because you were wrong, but because your “being different” pierces everyone’s uniformity.

Notice the wording of the accusation: first they restate the king’s command, as if only guarding the king’s majesty; only then do they name names: “Jews,” and they add the line, “whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon.” This is a very precise knife: the position of the three came from the king; now they “pay no heed to the king.” In other words: you gave them high office, and they are not grateful.

Then come two charges: not serving the king’s gods, not worshiping the golden image the king set up. “Serve” and “worship,” two words. These two words recur in this chapter, and each time it is the same choice: who is your Lord?

This passage does not record how the three friends responded, because the text wants us to see one thing first: they were seen because they did not bend with the music. They shouted no slogans and staged no protest; they only kept standing in the midst of the uniformity. Sometimes a witness is not in what is said but in what is not done.

3.grk: בֵּאדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר בִּרְגַז וַחֲמָה אֲמַר לְהַיְתָיָה לְשַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ בֵּאדַיִן גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ הֵיתָיוּ קֳדָם מַלְכָּֽא׃ עָנֵה נְבֻֽכַדְנֶצַּר וְאָמַר לְהוֹן הַצְדָּא שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ לֵֽאלָהַי לָא אִֽיתֵיכוֹן פָּֽלְחִין וּלְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָא דִּי הֲקֵימֶת לָא סָֽגְדִֽין׃ כְּעַן הֵן אִֽיתֵיכוֹן עֲתִידִין דִּי בְעִדָּנָא דִּֽי־תִשְׁמְעוּן קָל קַרְנָא מַשְׁרוֹקִיתָא שַׂבְּכָא פְּסַנְתֵּרִין וְסוּמְפֹּנְיָה וְכֹל׀ זְנֵי זְמָרָא תִּפְּלוּן וְתִסְגְּדוּן לְצַלְמָא דִֽי־עַבְדֵת וְהֵן לָא תִסְגְּדוּן בַּהּ־שַׁעֲתָה תִתְרְמוֹן לְגֽוֹא־אַתּוּן נוּרָא יָקִֽדְתָּא וּמַן־הוּא אֱלָהּ דֵּי יְשֵֽׁיזְבִנְכוֹן מִן־יְדָֽי׃
3.lit: “Then Nebuchadnezzar in rage and fury commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. Then these men were brought before the king. Nebuchadnezzar answered them, “Is it on purpose, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you don’t serve my god, nor worship the golden image which I have set up? Now if you are ready whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music to fall down and worship the image which I have made, good; but if you don’t worship, you shall be cast the same hour into the middle of a burning fiery furnace. Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?””

3.gram:
הַצְדָּא (is it on purpose): traditionally this word has two readings, “is it deliberate” and “is it true”; both say the same thing, that the king is giving them a chance to reconsider.

מַן הוּא אֱלָהּ דִּי יְשֵׁיזִבְנְכוֹן מִן־יְדָי (what god is there who can deliver you out of my hands): the king uses a rhetorical question, and he assumes the answer is “none.” In 3:29 the king himself answers it: “there is no other god who is able to deliver in this way.” This is the greatest irony of the chapter.
3.exp:
The king gave them a chance, and also gave them a challenge: “What god is there who can deliver you out of my hands?”

First look at the king’s attitude: furious, and yet still giving a chance. “If you are ready … fall down and worship.” This is a very polite threat: bend now, and everything can be treated as if it never happened. This is the hardest form of pressure: not that no road is given to you, but that the road is near, easy, and reasonable.

Then look at the challenge itself: “What god is there who can deliver you out of my hands?” This is the central question of the whole chapter. The king does not ask, “Why will you not worship?” He asks, “Is your God able?” He turns faith into a contest of power. If your God cannot save you, it makes no difference whether you kneel or not.

Notice a detail: the king says “my hands.” In chapter 2 the stone was cut out “without hands”; now the king uses the strength of “my hands” to define who can be delivered. The hands of man and the hand of God face each other in this chapter.

We also hear this question today in different forms: “Why does your God not save you?” “Is what you believe any use?” This question cannot be answered by argument. The answer of the three friends is not a debate; it is the three verses of the next passage.

3.grk: עֲנוֹ שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ וְאָמְרִין לְמַלְכָּא נְבֽוּכַדְנֶצַּר לָֽא־חַשְׁחִין אֲנַחְנָה עַל־דְּנָה פִּתְגָם לַהֲתָבוּתָֽךְ׃ הֵן אִיתַי אֱלָהַנָא דִּֽי־אֲנַחְנָא פָֽלְחִין יָכִל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתַנָא מִן־אַתּוּן נוּרָא יָקִֽדְתָּא וּמִן־יְדָךְ מַלְכָּא יְשֵׁיזִֽב׃ וְהֵן לָא יְדִיעַ לֶהֱוֵא־לָךְ מַלְכָּא דִּי לָא־פָֽלְחִין וּלְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָא דִּי הֲקֵימְתָּ לָא נִסְגֻּֽד׃ס
3.lit: “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, “Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.””

3.gram:
הֵן אִיתַי אֱלָהַנָא ... יָכִל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתַנָא (3:17): הֵן can be “if,” and it can also be “behold.” So there are two readings:
① “If it be so (that you throw us into the fire), our God whom we serve is able to deliver us”;
② “If our God exists and is able to deliver, he will deliver us” (less common).
The CUV’s “even so” takes the former. Whichever is taken, the point is: they are sure that God has the power, but they do not guarantee the outcome on God’s behalf.

וְהֵן לָא (but if not, 3:18): “and if not,” meaning “even if he does not deliver.” These words became one of the most famous declarations of faith in the Old Testament.
3.exp:
This is the heart of the chapter: they do not guarantee the outcome for God; they guarantee only their own faithfulness.

First look at the first words of the three: “We have no need to answer you in this matter.” They did not defend themselves, did not plead, did not say “please spare us.” They were calm, not because they were not afraid, but because the answer had long been settled. This is the same thing as Daniel’s “resolve” in chapter 1: first have the answer in the heart, and then face the pressure.

Then come two sentences, a very precise structure of faith. The first: “Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us out of your hand.” This is trust, with no doubt about God’s power. The second: “But if not …” This is obedience, with no condition on God’s will. The first is trust in God; the second is a decision about themselves. They were not sure that God had to deliver, but they were sure that they would not worship.

These four words are often misused. Some turn “But if not” into “God will surely deliver you, if only you have enough faith,” which is exactly upside down. What these words say is: being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is man’s matter. They did not make their own rescue a condition of faithfulness.

For us today this is a very great comfort: you may not know whether God will deliver you, you may not know how things will end, and still you can choose not to be defiled. This is not cold calculation, but the freedom of living under God’s sovereignty.

In the words of 321, this is letting Jesus be King: he may not act as I wish, but he is still the King.

3.grk: בֵּאדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר הִתְמְלִי חֱמָא וּצְלֵם אַנְפּוֹהִי עַל־שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ עָנֵה וְאָמַר לְמֵזֵא לְאַתּוּנָא חַד־שִׁבְעָה עַל דִּי חֲזֵה לְמֵזְיֵֽהּ׃ וּלְגֻבְרִין גִּבָּֽרֵי־חַיִל דִּי בְחַיְלֵהּ אֲמַר לְכַפָּתָה לְשַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ לְמִרְמֵא לְאַתּוּן נוּרָא יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃ בֵּאדַיִן גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ כְּפִתוּ בְּסַרְבָּלֵיהוֹן וְכַרְבְּלָתְהוֹן וּלְבֻשֵׁיהוֹן וּרְמִיו לְגֽוֹא־אַתּוּן נוּרָא יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃ כָּל־קֳבֵל דְּנָה מִן־דִּי מִלַּת מַלְכָּא מַחְצְפָה וְאַתּוּנָא אֵזֵה יַתִּירָא גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ דִּי הַסִּקוּ לְשַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ קַטִּל הִמּוֹן שְׁבִיבָא דִּי נוּרָֽא׃ וְגֻבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ תְּלָתֵּהוֹן שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ נְפַלוּ לְגֽוֹא־אַתּוּן־נוּרָא יָֽקִדְתָּא מְכַפְּתִֽין׃פ
3.lit: “Then Nebuchadnezzar was full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated. He commanded certain mighty men who were in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their pants, their tunics, and their mantles, and their other clothes, and were cast into the middle of the burning fiery furnace. Therefore because the king’s commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceedingly hot, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell down bound into the middle of the burning fiery furnace.”

3.gram:
חַד שִׁבְעָה עַל דִּי חֲזֵה: “seven times more than it was usually seen to be heated.” In the Bible “seven” often expresses completeness; here it may be a literal number, or it may mean “to the extreme.” The text does not choose for us, and the issues discuss it further.

מְכַפְּתִין (being bound) is a participle, echoing at the end of 3:23 the picture of “bound” in 3:24, preparing the way for the later contrast of “not bound.”
3.exp:
In the end, the king’s wrath burned up his own strongest men.

The pace of this passage is fast: wrath filling him, his countenance changed, the furnace heated seven times, strong men binding, throwing in. Every action adds more. This is what power looks like when it is angry: the less it can be refused, the more it must prove that it cannot be refused.

But notice two details. First, “in their trousers, their coats, and their hats,” bound, they were thrown in: they were not stripped and not treated specially; in their ordinary appearance they went into the fire. This detail will be taken up again in verse 27: their clothes were not changed. Second, the strong men who carried them were killed by the flame. The king who wanted to prove that “no god can deliver you” lost his strongest men before he had even thrown the three in.

There is no miracle here, only a cold fact: the fire was real, the furnace was real, death was real. The text does not play down what the three friends faced. This is why the four words “But if not” are so heavy. They were not speaking on the premise that God would surely deliver; they stood, knowing that the fire was real.

Today we also need not deny that some fires are very hot: illness, loss, being shut out, being misunderstood. The text will not say to us, “the fire is not that hot”; it will only say: in the hottest place, you are not alone. This is the point of the next passage.

3.grk: אֱדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא תְּוַהּ וְקָם בְּהִתְבְּהָלָה עָנֵה וְאָמַר לְהַדָּֽבְרוֹהִי הֲלָא גֻבְרִין תְּלָתָא רְמֵינָא לְגוֹא־נוּרָא מְכַפְּתִין עָנַיִן וְאָמְרִין לְמַלְכָּא יַצִּיבָא מַלְכָּֽא׃ עָנֵה וְאָמַר הָֽא־אֲנָה חָזֵה גֻּבְרִין אַרְבְּעָה שְׁרַיִן מַהְלְכִין בְּגֽוֹא־נוּרָא וַחֲבָל לָא־אִיתַי בְּהוֹן וְרֵוֵהּ דִּי דָּמֵה לְבַר־אֱלָהִֽין׃ס

He spoke and said to his counselors, “Didn’t we cast three men bound into the middle of the fire?” They answered the king, “True, O king.” He answered, “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed. The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.””

3.gram:
דָּמֵה לְבַר־אֱלָהִין (like a son of the gods): אֱלָהִין is plural, and it can be translated “gods,” or as a plural of majesty for “God”; coming from the mouth of Nebuchadnezzar, it sounds more like “a son of the divine beings, that is, a being of the divine kind.” In 3:28 the king calls this one “his angel” (מַלְאֲכֵהּ), which is his own explanation of who it was.

This verse is the core of the issue “the fourth who looks like a son of the gods.” Later interpreters differ: some hold it was an angel (3:28), some that it was an appearance of Christ in the Old Testament (a Christophany), some that it was a sign of God’s presence. This commentary sets the views side by side in the issues.
3.exp:
God did not keep them from entering the fire; he came into the fire and was with them.

The most breathtaking moment of the whole chapter is not the coming out of the furnace but the word “Look!” The king rose up in haste, not because they had escaped, but because the number in the fire was wrong: “Did we not cast three men bound into the middle of the fire?” “True, O king.” He confirmed it three times, and then said: “I see four men, unbound, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are not hurt.”

When you read this verse, look slowly at each word: four, unbound, walking in the fire, not hurt. Those who went in bound were loosed in the fire. The fire, which had come to devour, became the place where they walked. The most wonderful thing is that the fire was still there, the furnace was still there, and the king’s command had not been revoked. God did not first put out the fire and then let them in; he walked in while the fire was still burning.

Then that line: “the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.” Spoken from the mouth of a foreign king, the phrase does not mean what the church later called “the Son of God.” What the king said was: this one does not belong to humankind. In 3:28 he adds that God “sent his angel.” As for who this one was, the various schools hold different views; this commentary does not make it a required item of doctrinal proof. We say only: this brings to mind Immanuel, God with us (Matt 1:23).

This is the greatest comfort of this chapter: God did not promise us we would not enter the fire, but he promised to be with us in the fire. The fire you are walking through may not yet have gone out, but you are not alone.

3.lit: “Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace. He spoke and said, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!” Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the middle of the fire. The local governors, the deputies, and the governors, and the king’s counselors, being gathered together, saw these men, that the fire had no power on their bodies. The hair of their head wasn’t singed. Their pants weren’t changed, the smell of fire wasn’t even on them. Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said, “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel, and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God. Therefore I make a decree, that every people, nation, and language, which speak anything evil against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, shall be cut in pieces, and their houses shall be made a dunghill; because there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.” Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.”
