3.gram:
אֱלָהָא (God): in 3:26 the king calls the three “servants of the Most High God”; the title “Most High God” will become a key title in chapter 4. That a foreign king opens his mouth with this title begins from his seeing the three friends come out of the furnace with his own eyes.

הִתְרְחִצוּ עֲלוֹהִי (they trusted in him): this verb is rare in the Old Testament, and literally means “to rest oneself upon.” What the king saw was not how strong they were, but the one on whom they relied.
3.exp:
The king’s last words answer the question of the whole chapter: “there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.”

Recall 3:15: “Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?” That was the king’s question. Now he answers it with his own mouth. His answer fits his situation: he no longer asks “who can deliver,” but says “he has delivered.” The same verb, the same king, turned from a question into a confession.

Look again at his first words: “you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!” He calls them “servants.” A few minutes before, they were “the ones who pay no heed to you”; now they are “servants of the Most High God.” This change of address is the quietest witness of the chapter.

Then the officials examine them: no harm to the body, no singed hair, no changed clothes, not even the smell of fire. As they went in, so they came out. This is one of the most careful descriptions in the Bible: the fire left no trace here.

Two last reminders. First, the king’s blessing is for “the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego,” not “my God”; he is still learning. Second, they were promoted. Notice: promotion was a result, not a reason. When they said “But if not,” they did not know they would be promoted. Faithfulness is not for the sake of promotion, but remains faithful even if not promoted. This is the other half of 3:18.

4.gram:
שְׁלָמְכוֹן יִשְׂגֵּא (may your peace be multiplied) is the greeting formula of imperial decrees of that time. Chapter 4 is a rare chapter in the whole book: from beginning to end it is a decree written by a foreign king in his own voice; see the issues.

אָתוֹהִי רַבְרְבִין (how great are his signs): the king attributes “signs and wonders” to the “Most High God,” and this pair of words is often used in the Old Testament to describe what God did in Egypt.
4.exp:
This chapter is a witness written by the king himself, and it is written beginning from the end.

First look at what kind of document this is. An ordinary decree is a king giving orders and setting rules; this one is a king proclaiming to “all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth”: the signs and wonders that God has worked toward me, I am glad to make known. Please notice that he says “toward me.” This is not an onlooker’s comment, but a first-person witness by one who went through it himself.

His doxology is only three verses, yet it has already stated the conclusion of the whole chapter: “His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom; his dominion is from generation to generation.” Compare chapter 3: he once set up a golden image and required the whole earth to bow; now he himself proclaims to the whole earth that only one kingdom is everlasting, and that kingdom is not his. These are the words of a king, spoken from the top of an empire.

The text tells us the ending first so that, as we read the story below, we ask not “how will it end?” but “how did he come to this?” This is also our own story: often it is only when we look back that we can say, God has worked signs and wonders toward me. Your witness can also be like this decree: simple, honest, and in the first person: what God has done toward me.

4.grk: אֲנָה נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר שְׁלֵה הֲוֵית בְּבֵיתִי וְרַעְנַן בְּהֵיכְלִֽי׃ חֵלֶם חֲזֵית וִֽידַחֲלִנַּנִי וְהַרְהֹרִין עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבִי וְחֶזְוֵי רֵאשִׁי יְבַהֲלֻנַּֽנִי׃ וּמִנִּי שִׂים טְעֵם לְהַנְעָלָה קָֽדָמַי לְכֹל חַכִּימֵי בָבֶל דִּֽי־פְשַׁר חֶלְמָא יְהֽוֹדְעֻנַּֽנִי׃ בֵּאדַיִן חַרְטֻמַיָּא אָֽשְׁפַיָּא וְגָזְרַיָּא וְחֶלְמָא אָמַר אֲנָה קֳדָמֵיהוֹן וּפִשְׁרֵהּ לָא־מְהוֹדְעִין לִֽי׃ וְעַד אָחֳרֵין עַל קָֽדָמַי דָּנִיֵּאל דִּֽי־שְׁמֵהּ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר כְּשֻׁם אֱלָהִי וְדִי רֽוּחַ־אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין בֵּהּ וְחֶלְמָא קָֽדָמוֹהִי אַמְרֵֽת׃ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר רַב חַרְטֻמַיָּא דִּי׀ אֲנָה יִדְעֵת דִּי רוּחַ אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין בָּךְ וְכָל־רָז לָא־אָנֵס לָךְ חֶזְוֵי חֶלְמִי דִֽי־חֲזֵית וּפִשְׁרֵהּ אֱמַֽר׃
4.lit: “I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace. I saw a dream which made me afraid; and the thoughts on my bed and the visions of my head troubled me. Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known to me the interpretation of the dream. Then the magicians, the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers came in; and I told the dream before them; but they didn’t make known to me its interpretation. But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods. I told the dream before him, saying, “Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you, and no secret troubles you, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and its interpretation.”

4.gram:
רוּחַ אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין (spirit of the holy gods): אֱלָהִין is plural, and קַדִּישִׁין is also plural, so the literal sense is “spirit of holy gods.” The CUV and most Chinese translations take “holy God” because these are the words of a foreign king in his own vocabulary. Later interpreters understand this in two ways: one, that it is the king’s address within a polytheistic setting; two, that the plural means “the Most Holy God.” See the issues.

שְׁלֵה...וְרַעְנַן (at rest, flourishing): the king used two words, one saying he was secure, one saying he was flourishing like a tree, which lays a clue in advance for the later dream of the “tree.”
4.exp:
The dream began from the place of “I was at ease.”

Verse 4 says: I was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace. The original uses two words, one for “ease” and one for “flourishing.” This was the king at his best: the nation secure, the building works complete, no visible threat. Yet at just that time he had a dream that made him afraid and troubled. This is an important reminder: the greatest unease often does not come from hardship, but from the time when “everything is going well.”

Notice the king’s reaction: he first summoned all the experts. The magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans and diviners: he did what he had done in chapter 2, and the result was the same: “but they couldn’t make known to me its interpretation.” This time the king did not rage or order killing; he only admitted: they could not. Human methods had again reached their end.

Then he remembered Daniel. Listen to how he described him: “Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods.” The king used his own name and the name of his own god, yet he admitted: in this man is a “spirit” that I do not have. This is the king’s language, not our confession of faith. We need not read it as a complete doctrine, but we can see that a foreign king, at his most uneasy, remembered the one for whom “no secret troubles him.”

In your life there are also moments when unease comes in the “smoothest” times. Do not hurry to press it down, and do not hurry to find a method. Like the king, first admit that human methods are limited, and then go find a companion in whom the Spirit of God dwells.

4.grk: וְחֶזְוֵי רֵאשִׁי עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבִי חָזֵה הֲוֵית וַאֲלוּ אִילָן בְּגוֹא אַרְעָא וְרוּמֵהּ שַׂגִּֽיא׃ רְבָה אִֽילָנָא וּתְקִף וְרוּמֵהּ יִמְטֵא לִשְׁמַיָּא וַחֲזוֹתֵהּ לְסוֹף כָּל־אַרְעָֽא׃ עָפְיֵהּ שַׁפִּיר וְאִנְבֵּהּ שַׂגִּיא וּמָזוֹן לְכֹלָּא־בֵהּ תְּחֹתוֹהִי תַּטְלֵל׀ חֵיוַת בָּרָא וּבְעַנְפוֹהִי צִפֲּרֵי שְׁמַיָּא וּמִנֵּהּ יִתְּזִין כָּל־בִּשְׂרָֽא׃
4.lit: “Thus were the visions of my head on my bed: I saw, and behold, a tree in the middle of the earth; and its height was great. The tree grew, and was strong, and its height reached to the sky, and its sight to the end of all the earth. The leaves of it were beautiful, and it had much fruit, and in it was food for all. The animals of the field had shade under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.”

4.gram:
וְרוּמֵהּ יִמְטֵא לִשְׁמַיָּא (its height reached to the sky): the verb יִמְטֵא (to reach) appears again in 4:22, in the interpretation: “your greatness has grown, and reaches to the sky.” The dream and the interpretation use the same word, so that one cannot help seeing that this tree is the king himself.

וּמָזוֹן לְכֹלָּא (food for all): the tree’s merit is not its height but that it fed all life. This is the best part of the dream, and also, in the interpretation that follows, God’s gentlest reminder to this king.
4.exp:
This was a good tree, and that is the most unsettling thing.

In the first scene of the dream there is no bad part. The tree was exceedingly tall and strong, its height reached to the sky, and it could be seen from the ends of the earth; its leaves were beautiful and its fruit plentiful, all were fed from it, the animals had shade under it and the birds lived in its branches. It is an almost perfect picture. This king was not merely a tyrant who oppressed people; his kingdom did feed and shelter many. The text does not deny this.

But notice one detail: this tree’s height “reached to the sky.” How high can human achievement go? In the Bible the picture of “reaching to the sky” brings to mind the tower of Babel, where people wanted to make a name for themselves and reach heaven. This tree is not wrong because it grew badly, but because it grew to a height that did not belong to it. Pride does not grow from bad places; it often grows from good ones. Ability, achievement, being needed are all good, but when we forget that all of it was given, good turns into height.

This gives us a very practical reminder: do not look for the traces of pride only in our failures; look for them even more in our successes. The place where you are most praised, the place where you are most relied upon: is there a little spot there where God’s place has quietly been taken? The tree was not wrong, but it needed someone to remind it: you were planted.

4.grk: חָזֵה הֲוֵית בְּחֶזְוֵי רֵאשִׁי עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבִי וַאֲלוּ עִיר וְקַדִּישׁ מִן־שְׁמַיָּא נָחִֽת׃ קָרֵא בְחַיִל וְכֵן אָמַר גֹּדּוּ אִֽילָנָא וְקַצִּצוּ עַנְפוֹהִי אַתַּרוּ עָפְיֵהּ וּבַדַּרוּ אִנְבֵּהּ תְּנֻד חֵֽיוְתָא מִן־תַּחְתּוֹהִי וְצִפְּרַיָּא מִן־עַנְפֽוֹהִי׃ בְּרַם עִקַּר שָׁרְשׁוֹהִי בְּאַרְעָא שְׁבֻקוּ וּבֶֽאֱסוּר דִּֽי־פַרְזֶל וּנְחָשׁ בְּדִתְאָא דִּי בָרָא וּבְטַל שְׁמַיָּא יִצְטַבַּע וְעִם־חֵיוְתָא חֲלָקֵהּ בַּעֲשַׂב אַרְעָֽא׃ לִבְבֵהּ מִן־יְשַׁנּוֹן וּלְבַב חֵיוָה יִתְיְהִב לֵהּ וְשִׁבְעָה עִדָּנִין יַחְלְפוּן עֲלֽוֹהִי׃ בִּגְזֵרַת עִירִין פִּתְגָמָא וּמֵאמַר קַדִּישִׁין שְׁאֵֽלְתָא עַד־דִּבְרַת דִּי יִנְדְּעוּן חַיַּיָּא דִּֽי־שַׁלִּיט בְּמַלְכוּת וּלְמַן־דִּי יִצְבֵּא יִתְּנִנַּהּ וּשְׁפַל אֲנָשִׁים יְקִים׃ דְּנָה חֶלְמָא חֲזֵית אֲנָה מַלְכָּא נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר פִּשְׁרֵא׀ אֱמַר כָּל־קֳבֵל דִּי׀ כָּל־חַכִּימֵי מַלְכוּתִי לָֽא־יָכְלִין פִּשְׁרָא לְהוֹדָעֻתַנִי כָּהֵל דִּי רֽוּחַ־אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין בָּֽךְ׃
4.lit: ““I saw in the visions of my head on my bed, and behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from the sky. He cried aloud, and said this, ‘Cut down the tree, and cut off its branches! Shake off its leaves, and scatter its fruit! Let the animals get away from under it, and the fowls from its branches. Nevertheless leave the stump of its roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of the sky. Let his portion be with the animals in the grass of the earth. Let his heart be changed from man’s, and let an animal’s heart be given to him. Then let seven times pass over him. “ ‘The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones; to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.’ “This dream I, king Nebuchadnezzar, have seen; and you, Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation; but you are able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in you.””

4.gram:
שִׁבְעָה עִדָּנִין (seven times): עִדָּן is a “period,” without saying whether days, months or years. Some read it as seven years, some as seven seasons or seven months, and some as a symbol of “a full period.” This commentary does not decide the length for the text; see the issues.

דִּי שַׁלִּיט ... בְּמַלְכוּת אֲנָשָׁא (the Most High rules in the kingdom of men): שַׁלִּיט is “having sovereignty,” and is the central sentence of this chapter. It appears three times in 4:17, 25, 32, and is said once more at last as the king’s confession in 4:34–35.

עִיר וְקַדִּישׁ (a watcher, a holy one): “watcher” is rare elsewhere in the Old Testament; here it refers to a heavenly sent one, and echoes 4:24 “the decree of the Most High.”
4.exp:
This passage states the most important sentence of the whole book: “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.”

The second scene of the dream is a watcher coming from heaven. He came down from heaven and cried aloud: cut down this tree. Four commands in a row: cut down, cut off, shake off, scatter. It is a complete demolition. But notice: the stump was left. The root remained in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze. This judgment is not destruction; it is a judgment with something left. The purpose of the judgment was not to wipe out this man, but “let his heart be changed from man’s, and let an animal’s heart be given to him. Then let seven times pass over him.”

Why an animal’s heart? Because this man, in the heights, forgot he was a man. He thought he was a god, so God let him, in the least human way, learn again to be human. It is a very deep picture: pride is leaving the place of man and wanting to take God’s place; and this judgment sent him back to the place of man, even lower.

Then comes the key of this chapter: “to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.” Notice that this sentence is not spoken only to the king; it is “that the living may know,” spoken to everyone. Every kingdom and every position is given. In chapter 2 this sentence was “he changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings,” and in chapter 7 it is “the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High.” The whole book is saying this sentence.

What you are doing, the position where you are, the influence you have: all were given. To admit this is not to make oneself small but to put oneself in the right place: to be a good servant, not a false master.

4.lit: “Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was stricken mute for a while, and his thoughts troubled him. The king answered, “Belteshazzar, don’t let the dream, or the interpretation, trouble you.” Belteshazzar answered, “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation to your adversaries. The tree that you saw, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached to the sky, and its sight to all the earth; whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit plentiful, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation: it is you, O king, that have grown and become strong; for your greatness has grown, and reaches to the sky, and your dominion to the end of the earth. “Whereas the king saw a watcher and a holy one coming down from the sky, and saying, ‘Cut down the tree, and destroy it; nevertheless leave the stump of its roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field, and let it be wet with the dew of the sky. Let his portion be with the animals of the field, until seven times pass over him. “This is the interpretation, O king, and it is the decree of the Most High, which has come on my lord the king: that you shall be driven from men, and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You shall be made to eat grass as oxen, and shall be wet with the dew of the sky, and seven times shall pass over you; until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will. Whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the roots of the tree; your kingdom shall be sure to you, after that you will have known that the heavens do rule. Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.””

4.gram:
שְׁמַיָּא שַׁלִּטִן (heaven rules, 4:26): “heaven” here stands for God, a circumlocution of the late Old Testament, meaning “the God of heaven rules.” This usage later echoes in the New Testament phrase “kingdom of heaven.”

פְרֻק (break off, 4:27): the original sense is “to break apart, to tear off,” and some read it as “to redeem, to set free.” The CUV takes “cut off sin,” but the verb can also be understood as “to pull oneself out of sin by righteousness.” See the issues.

צִדְקָה (righteousness): in late Hebrew and Aramaic this word often carries the sense of “almsgiving, doing good,” and so is set beside the next line, “showing mercy to the poor.”
4.exp:
The difficulty of the interpreter is to say a painful truth and still love the person.

First look at Daniel’s reaction: “stricken mute for a while, and his thoughts troubled him.” He was not a man without feeling. He understood the dream, and knew it was a judgment on the king. The king, seeing his face, comforted him instead: do not be troubled. He said, “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you.” This is a very human sentence: he truly hoped the dream was not about the king. A true interpreter comes with tears to speak of judgment.

Then he said very directly: “it is you, O king.” No detours, no technique. He matched each part of the dream with the king’s life: grown and strong, that is you; greatness reaching to the sky, that is you; dominion to the end of the earth, that is you. Then the verdict: you will be driven from men, dwell with the animals of the field, eat grass as oxen. Notice that Daniel did not treat the verdict as his own matter; he said, “the decree of the Most High.” It was not his idea or his judgment; he only carried the word from heaven into the palace.

Then the most important line: he did not stop at judgment, he gave the king a way: “let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.” There is a word here to look at slowly: “perhaps.” He gave no guarantee and made no promise on God’s behalf. The judgment was set, yet the door of repentance remained open. To a mighty king he said: see the poor. This is the most concrete repentance: not more sacrifices, but more mercy.

If one day you need to say a hard truth to someone, remember Daniel: first grieve for the person, then speak clearly, and finally give a way out.

4.lit: “All this came on the king Nebuchadnezzar. At the end of twelve months he was walking in the royal palace of Babylon. The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, “O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: ‘The kingdom has departed from you. You shall be driven from men; and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You shall be made to eat grass as oxen. Seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.’ ” This was fulfilled the same hour on Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from men, and ate grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky, until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.”

4.gram:
בָּבֶל רַבְּתָא דִי־אֲנָה בֱנַיְתַהּ (this great Babylon, which I have built): in the king’s words, “I” occurs most; he says “I,” by “my power,” for “the glory of my majesty.” In the original the “I” is piled word by word into one sentence.

עִלָּיָא (the Most High, 4:32): the Aramaic Old Testament title for God, its root meaning “high.” This contrasts with the king’s tree that “reached to the sky”: the one truly on high is not the tree but the Most High.
4.exp:
Judgment did not come at once; God first gave twelve months.

Verse 29 says: “At the end of twelve months.” The dream, the interpretation and the counsel were all given, and yet nothing happened. One month, two months, half a year, a year. These twelve months were God’s patience, and also the most dangerous time for man: because nothing happened, people think it does not matter. God’s patience is often taken as God’s silence, and God’s silence is again taken as one’s own safety.

Then the king walked in the royal palace of Babylon, looking over his city. He said one sentence: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” Count them: I, my power, my majesty, my glory. In this one sentence there is only one protagonist. This is not an evil man speaking evil; it is a very successful man speaking the truth: the city really was built by him, the works really were completed by him. But he turned “a position given” into “my achievement.”

This is the most exact definition of pride: leaving the place of man, and taking God’s glory for oneself. “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky.” God did not wait for him to finish, because the sentence had already been finished. The verdict did not change: the kingdom has departed from you, you will be driven out, and seven times will pass over you. Then the text uses only one verse to write the end: eating grass as oxen, hair grown like eagles’ feathers, nails like birds’ claws.

Notice that the text gives this condition no medical name and does not ask us to diagnose it. It lets us see only this: a man who thought he was a god became one who was not like a man. We need not use this picture to mock anyone, and still less to judge people near us who struggle in mind. This passage is a reminder to every one of us: when you begin to say “it was all me,” stop, and look up.

4.lit: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever; for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation. All the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing; and he does according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth; and no one can stop his hand, or ask him, “What are you doing?””

4.gram:
עַיְנַי לִשְׁמַיָּא נִטְלֵת (I lifted up my eyes to heaven): נטל is “to lift.” His eyes had always been fixed on his own city and his own glory; now he raised his gaze from below to heaven.

וּמַנְדְּעִי עֲלַי יְתוּב (my understanding returned to me): יְתוּב is “to turn back.” The order of the text is important: he first lifted his eyes, and then understanding came back. Not first recovery and then looking up, but first looking up, and then being restored.

וְלָא אִית דִּי־יְמַחֵא בִידֵהּ (no one can stop his hand): “stop his hand” is an ancient phrase meaning to hinder God’s work.
4.exp:
His understanding came back at the moment he lifted his eyes to heaven.

After seven times, when the days were over, the text uses the simplest action: “I lifted up my eyes to heaven.” No ceremony, no great religious act, only a man raising his eyes from the ground. Think how hard this action is. He had been looking at his own city, his own achievement, his own glory; for seven times he had only bent his head to eat grass. Now he looked up. And understanding returned at that very moment.

Notice the order: he did not first find his understanding and then bless; he first lifted his eyes, and then was restored. It is not that I get well first and then look to God, but that when I look up, I am healed. Today, is there something you have been bending your head over to handle? Perhaps it is not to solve it first, but to lift your head first.

Then his doxology: “his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.” This echoes the decree of verses 1 to 3, beginning and end. But here is one more sentence, the deepest: “All the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing; and he does according to his will … and no one can stop his hand, or ask him, ‘What are you doing?’” This king once asked the three companions: “Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?” Now he says: no one can stop God’s hand. “My hand” and “his hand,” he has at last told apart.

One important reminder: we stay with what the text says, that he lifted his eyes, blessed, and confessed. As for his later life and eternal end, the text does not say, and we do not pass a verdict for God. We see only this: God was pleased to let a man, in the lowest place, lift up his head.

4.gram:
מְשַׁבַּח וּמְרוֹמֵם וּמְהַדַּר (praise, extol, honor): three participles, present tense, not a one-time act but a continuing state. The king’s first person turns from “I lifted up” in 4:34 to the continuing “I praise” in 4:37.

וְדִי הָלְכִין בְּגֵוָה יָכִל לְהַשְׁפָּלָה (those who walk in pride he is able to abase): the verb יָכִל, “is able,” is the same as in 3:17, “our God is able to deliver us.” From “he is able to deliver” to “he is able to abase,” the same God.
4.exp:
The last sentence of this chapter is the conclusion written by one who had been proud: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”

First see how the text writes the king’s restoration: understanding returned, glory returned, and his counselors and lords came to seek him. His kingdom and his position lost nothing, and “excellent greatness was added to me.” This is a surprising ending: God did not take his kingdom away, but let him, with another kind of eyes, possess it anew. The same position, a different man. Before, his kingdom was what “I built by the might of my power”; now it is what is “given.”

Then his confession: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven.” Notice the title he uses: “the King of heaven.” He himself was a king, yet he said there is a greater King in heaven. What he praises is that “all his works are truth, and his ways justice.” These are words only one who has suffered can say: I did not understand, but now I know that he is true and just.

The last sentence has a very deep honesty: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” This sentence was not said to him by someone else; he said it of himself. This is a witness with no defense. When you hear it, there is nothing in it of looking down from above. Because this sentence is what every one of us needs. In the words of 321: pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place. Let man be man, and let God be God.

This chapter is the center of the whole book, and also an invitation: you need not wait until you have lost everything to look up. Today you can lift your eyes to heaven and say: you are King.

5.grk: בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר מַלְכָּא עֲבַד לְחֶם רַב לְרַבְרְבָנוֹהִי אֲלַף וְלָקֳבֵל אַלְפָּא חַמְרָא שָׁתֵֽה׃ בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר אֲמַר׀ בִּטְעֵם חַמְרָא לְהַיְתָיָה לְמָאנֵי דַּהֲבָא וְכַסְפָּא דִּי הַנְפֵּק נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר אֲבוּהִי מִן־הֵיכְלָא דִּי בִירוּשְׁלֶם וְיִשְׁתּוֹן בְּהוֹן מַלְכָּא וְרַבְרְבָנוֹהִי שֵׁגְלָתֵהּ וּלְחֵנָתֵֽהּ׃ בֵּאדַיִן הַיְתִיו מָאנֵי דַהֲבָא דִּי הַנְפִּקוּ מִן־הֵֽיכְלָא דִּֽי־בֵית אֱלָהָא דִּי בִירֽוּשְׁלֶם וְאִשְׁתִּיו בְּהוֹן מַלְכָּא וְרַבְרְבָנוֹהִי שֵׁגְלָתֵהּ וּלְחֵנָתֵֽהּ׃ אִשְׁתִּיו חַמְרָא וְשַׁבַּחוּ לֵֽאלָהֵי דַּהֲבָא וְכַסְפָּא נְחָשָׁא פַרְזְלָא אָעָא וְאַבְנָֽא׃
5.lit: “Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand. Belshazzar, while he tasted the wine, commanded that the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem be brought to him; that the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, might drink from them. Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of God’s house which was at Jerusalem; and the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, drank from them. They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of bronze, of iron, of wood, and of stone.”

5.gram:
בִּטְעֵם חַמְרָא (while he tasted the wine): literally “in the taste of the wine,” that is, at the moment when the wine was at its height and judgment had loosened. The decision to order the temple vessels brought was made at such a moment.

אֲבוּהִי (his father): the Aramaic “father” may mean a biological father, an ancestor, or a former king; the relation between Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar is in the issues, and this commentary does not decide it for the text.
5.exp:
This was a very lively night, and also a very quiet moment before judgment.

A thousand lords, a great feast, the king and the crowd drinking face to face. Imagine the scene: the lamps blazing, laughter without end, wine cup after cup. The text does not say this night was unusual in any way; it says only that it was the liveliest and most relaxed of nights. Judgment often draws quietly near on just such a night.

Then comes that decision: “while he tasted the wine, commanded that the golden and silver vessels … be brought.” Notice the moment: not when he was sober, but when the wine was at its height. These vessels had been taken from the temple of God in Jerusalem, and were originally for serving God. Now they were used to hold wine and to raise a cup in praise of gods made of wood and stone, gold and silver. The most dangerous thing is often not one great sin but, in a relaxed moment, treating holy things as things for amusement.

The text writes this passage in detail: gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, stone. This list brings to mind the great image of chapter 2 and the golden image of chapter 3. People again and again treat what their own hands made as gods. When reading this passage, we need not look only at the king; we can ask ourselves: what holy things have we grown used to? What time, gifts and resources that were meant for serving the Lord have we, in relaxed moments, casually used elsewhere?

5.lit: “In the same hour, the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall of the king’s palace. The king saw the part of the hand that wrote. Then the king’s face was changed in him, and his thoughts troubled him; and the joints of his thighs were loosened, and his knees struck one against another. The king cried aloud to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. The king spoke and said to the wise men of Babylon, “Whoever reads this writing, and shows me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.” Then all the king’s wise men came in; but they could not read the writing, and couldn’t make known to the king the interpretation. Then king Belshazzar was greatly troubled, and his face was changed in him, and his lords were perplexed.”

5.gram:
אֶצְבְּעָן דִּי יַד־אֱנָשׁ (fingers of a man’s hand): the original does not say whose hand, only “like a man’s hand,” and this restraint makes the scene more unsettling.

קִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן (the joints of his thighs were loosened): משׁתרין is “loosened,” from the same root as the “dissolving of doubts” (untying knots) said by the queen mother in 5:12: the king’s own joints were “untied,” yet he had to ask someone to “untie a difficulty.”
5.exp:
The most powerful man in the room was frightened, his knees knocking, by a hand with no body.

Verse 5 says: “In the same hour, the fingers of a man’s hand came out.” Not an angel, not a voice, only a hand, part of a hand. It wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall, in the place where the light was brightest. The picture is very quiet and very powerful: God does not need to say much; one hand is enough to stop the whole feast.

Then the text gives the king’s reaction in four actions: his face changed, his thoughts troubled him, the joints of his thighs were loosened, his knees struck one against another. It is a very real bodily reaction. The thousand lords, the gold and silver vessels, the feast: none of it mattered any more. When God’s hand appears on the wall, the strongest part of a person is often the first to give way.

Then he did what his predecessor had done: he summoned the wise men, and promised a great reward: purple, a chain of gold, the third place in the kingdom. But the wise men “could not read the writing.” Notice this: not only could they not interpret, they could not even read. Human wisdom, before God’s handwriting, could not take even the first step. This is the same as in chapters 2 and 4: human methods always come to an end.

This passage does not say what the words were, and leaves us a blank, so that we wait with the king in dismay. Sometimes God’s word comes in a way we cannot read, and what we need is not more experts but one “in whom is the spirit of God.”

5.grk: מַלְכְּתָא לָקֳבֵל מִלֵּי מַלְכָּא וְרַבְרְבָנוֹהִי לְבֵית מִשְׁתְּיָא עֲנָת מַלְכְּתָא וַאֲמֶרֶת מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִי אַֽל־יְבַהֲלוּךְ רַעְיוֹנָךְ וְזִיוָיךְ אַל־יִשְׁתַּנּֽוֹ׃ אִיתַי גְּבַר בְּמַלְכוּתָךְ דִּי רוּחַ אֱלָהִין קַדִּישִׁין בֵּהּ וּבְיוֹמֵי אֲבוּךְ נַהִירוּ וְשָׂכְלְתָנוּ וְחָכְמָה כְּחָכְמַת־אֱלָהִין הִשְׁתְּכַחַת בֵּהּ וּמַלְכָּא נְבֻֽכַדְנֶצַּר אֲבוּךְ רַב חַרְטֻמִּין אָֽשְׁפִין כַּשְׂדָּאִין גָּזְרִין הֲקִימֵהּ אֲבוּךְ מַלְכָּֽא׃ כָּל־קֳבֵל דִּי רוּחַ׀ יַתִּירָה וּמַנְדַּע וְשָׂכְלְתָנוּ מְפַשַּׁר חֶלְמִין וַֽאַֽחֲוָיַת אֲחִידָן וּמְשָׁרֵא קִטְרִין הִשְׁתְּכַחַת בֵּהּ בְּדָנִיֵּאל דִּֽי־מַלְכָּא שָׂם־שְׁמֵהּ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר כְּעַן דָּנִיֵּאל יִתְקְרֵי וּפִשְׁרָה יְהַֽחֲוֵֽה׃פ

The queen spoke and said, “O king, live forever; don’t let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your face be changed. The king Nebuchadnezzar your father, yes, the king, your father, made him master of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers; because an excellent spirit, knowledge, understanding, interpreting of dreams, showing of dark sentences, and dissolving of doubts were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation.””

5.gram:
וּמְשָׁרֵא קִטְרִין (dissolving doubts): literally “untying knotted things,” a vivid figure: a difficulty is like a rope tied in a hard knot. In 5:6 the king’s “joints were loosened” uses the same set of words: the king himself was “untied,” yet had to ask someone to “untie knots.”

מַלְכְּתָא (the queen mother): the original is “queen,” different from the “wives and concubines” (שֵׁגְלָתֵהּ) of 5:2, 3, and refers to an older woman of standing who remembered the previous reign. Who she was, see the issues.
5.exp:
When the whole room was in panic, one elder remembered a name.

The queen mother had not been at the feast. It was “by reason of the words of the king and his lords” that she came into the banquet house. Notice her first words: “don’t let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your face be changed.” She was the only one in the whole scene who spoke quietly. She did not scream or blame; she only remembered.

Whom did she remember? One man: Daniel. Listen to how she described him: “light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods.” She said twice that in him was the spirit of the holy gods. An older woman, in the simplest language, pushed that forgotten man to the front. Some people, in the midst of chaos, are not the strongest, but the ones who remember. They remember who once stood firm before God.

Then she listed Daniel’s abilities: interpreting dreams, showing dark sentences, dissolving doubts. “Dissolving doubts” in the original is “untying knots,” a delicate figure. This elder did not say he could foretell the future, or that he had any magic; she said only: he can untie what is knotted.

This passage lets us see a very small role at a very large turning point. Is there someone like the queen mother near you? In the midst of everyone’s panic, remembering a name, saying one quiet word? You too can be that kind of person.

5.lit: “Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Are you that Daniel of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Judah? I have heard of you, that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light, understanding, and excellent wisdom are found in you. Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me, that they should read this writing, and make known to me its interpretation; but they could not show the interpretation of the thing. But I have heard of you, that you can give interpretations, and dissolve doubts. Now if you can read the writing, and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple, and have a chain of gold around your neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.” Then Daniel answered before the king, “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.”

5.gram:
מַתְּנָתָךְ לֶהֱוְיָן לָךְ (let your gifts be to yourself): this is a courteous but clean refusal. Daniel did not say “I do not want it,” only “to yourself”; what he refused was “on condition of payment,” not serving the king.

אֶקְרֵא (I will read): he did not first agree to the reward and then work, but said “I will read to the king”: this is the order of “not for a reward.” See the discussion in the issues of “later accepting the purple.”
5.exp:
He was not one who spoke for a reward, and that is why he could speak the truth.

The king’s first words are interesting: “Are you that Daniel of the children of the captivity of Judah?” He called him “of the captivity.” This king did not know the man well, only a label. He seems to have remembered that his father the king once brought some people out of Judah. But he did not remember that this man had once stood before his father and spoken of the future of the whole empire. People often remember only your label, and not what you have done. Daniel did not argue, and did not state his credentials.

Then the king repeated the great reward of verse 7: purple, a chain of gold, the third place. This reward said: if you speak, you will be the third man in this kingdom. It was an invitation of power. Listen to Daniel’s answer: “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another.” He did not rage and did not bargain; he only said very clearly: this is not why I came.

Behind this sentence is a more important one: “Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.” He spoke not because of a prize but because the words needed to be spoken. Only one who does not speak for a reward can say the truth others do not like to hear. Because what he was about to say was not good news. This brings to mind: if our motive in serving is to be seen and rewarded, it will be hard for us, when needed, to say what must be said.

5.lit: ““You, king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father the kingdom, and greatness, and glory, and majesty. Because of the greatness that he gave him, all the peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. He killed whom he wanted to, and he kept alive whom he wanted to. He raised up whom he wanted to, and he put down whom he wanted to. But when his heart was lifted up, and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him. He was driven from the sons of men, and his heart was made like the animals’, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. He was fed with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky; until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men, and that he sets up over it whomever he will. “You, his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this, but have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines, have drunk wine from them. You have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which don’t see, or hear, or know; and you have not glorified the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways. Then the part of the hand was sent from before him, and this writing was inscribed.”

5.gram:
כָל־דְּנָה יְדַעְתָּ (you knew all this): ידע is the “know” that recurs in chapter 4. Nebuchadnezzar “knew” that the Most High rules at the cost of seven times; Belshazzar “knew all this,” yet paid no price and did not humble himself. This is the central charge of the whole chapter.

הִתְרוֹמַמְתָּ (you have lifted up yourself): the word רום (to lift up) appears in 4:37, “those who walk in pride he is able to abase”; here it is used to accuse Belshazzar: he lifted himself above the Lord of heaven.
5.exp:
This is the heaviest passage of the chapter: not “you did not know,” but “you knew all this, and have not humbled your heart.”

Daniel’s words begin with history. He first spoke of his father Nebuchadnezzar: God gave him the kingdom, greatness, glory and majesty, and all peoples, nations and languages trembled before him; he could kill and keep alive, raise up and put down. But his heart was lifted up and his spirit hardened, and he was driven out, to live with the wild donkeys and eat grass as oxen, until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men. Notice that this is the whole story of chapter 4, condensed into a few sentences, spoken to this night and this man.

Then he turned and pointed directly at Belshazzar: “You have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.” This is the charge of the chapter. He did not say “you did not know”; he said “you knew, and did not bow.” The greatest debt is not ignorance, but knowing and still not humbling oneself. This sentence is especially important for us today: we have heard much truth, read many verses, know many stories; what we lack is often not information but a bowed head.

Then he made the charge concrete: you have lifted yourself up against the Lord of heaven, you brought the vessels of his house and drank from them, you praised gods that cannot see or hear, and have not glorified the God “in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways.” This is not a lecture of doctrine but a very near reminder: every breath you take is in God’s hand.

The last line: “Then the part of the hand was sent from before him, and this writing was inscribed.” The writing on the wall was not without cause; it had a reason, a charge and an interpretation. God’s judgment is never sudden; it comes after long patience.

מְנֵא מְנֵא תְּקֵל וּפַרְסִין: the four words can be read as three units of weight (mina, shekel, half-shekel), or as three verbs (numbered, weighed, divided). Daniel’s interpretation takes the second reading, and brings out a wordplay at the same time: פְּרֵס (divided) and פָּרָס (Persia) share the same root.

חַסִּיר (wanting, deficient): the word means “lacking.” What is on the other side of the balances is “God’s standard”; this man, before the standard, was not enough.
5.exp:
The writing on the wall had only four words, yet it had already written the end of a kingdom.

Did the wise men fail to read it because it was too simple? Or because it was too direct? MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. These words could be a merchant’s ledger: one mina, one mina, one shekel, half-shekels; or they could be God’s judgment: numbered, weighed, divided. Daniel was not deceived by the first reading; what he saw at once was the second: this was not an account but a verdict.

Three sentences, each nearer than the last. “MENE”: God has counted your kingdom and brought it to an end. Notice, it is not “your kingdom is about to end,” but “God has already counted”: a process that began long ago. “TEKEL”: you are weighed in the balances and found wanting. This is the theme of the chapter, and the most honest word in it. Every person will be placed on the balances, and what is on the other side is not another person but God’s standard. “PERES”: your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. This is the result.

Notice one detail: when Daniel spoke of the “shortfall,” there was no mockery, no gloating. He only said it very clearly. This is how one who interprets judgment should be: not pleased, not exaggerating, only faithfully proclaiming.

For us today, “weighed in the balances” is a very solemn word, and one that needs to be heard. But on our side there is another truth: there is one who has already stood for us at the other end of the balances. We do not reach that standard by ourselves; we rely on Christ. This gospel means we need not run from the balances, because we do not stand there by our own weight.

5.gram:
וְדָרְיָוֶשׁ מָדָיָא קַבֵּל מַלְכוּתָא (Darius the Mede received the kingdom): the verb is קַבֵּל, “received,” not “seized.” This detail echoes “God sets up kings” in 2:21 and 4:17: a kingdom is “received.”

בְּלֵילְיָא (in that night): the words “that night” are the shortest and coldest sentence of this chapter, with no adornment.
5.exp:
The reward had only just been put on, and the kingdom had already changed hands.

Verse 29 is a very ironic scene: Belshazzar gave the order, and they clothed Daniel with purple, put a chain of gold about his neck, and proclaimed that he would be the third ruler. This king, after hearing his own verdict, still kept his promise. A detail worth stopping at: he did not kill the one who brought the word, and did not change his promise, yet he also did not repent. His action was a perfectly complete “courtesy,” without one repentance.

Then comes the shortest narrative of the whole book: “In that night Belshazzar the Chaldean King was slain.” No description, no scene, only one sentence. This night began with a great feast and ended in a sudden change of dynasty. God’s judgment is not always loud; it can be quiet, yet on time.

The last verse changes the name: “Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.” Notice the verb: not “seized,” but “received.” The kingdom is received. This brings us once again back to the center: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.

Daniel, that night, put on the purple, and before daybreak the king had changed. He did not rise higher because of it, and lost nothing because of it. He knew that his position had never been given by the king; it was given by God. This is the best rest for us whenever our position rises or falls.

מִתְנַצַּח (distinguished above): this is a reflexive verb, meaning “to show oneself continually surpassing.” Daniel’s excellence was not a single performance but something ongoing and daily.

בְּדָת אֱלָהֵהּ (in the law of his God): דָּת appears five times in this chapter: “the law of his God” (6:5) and “the law of the Medes and Persians” (6:8, 12, 15). The same word, two kinds of law: one God’s, one the king’s. This chapter is the two laws standing face to face.
6.exp:
His enemies could find ground against him in only one thing: his faithfulness to God.

The first picture of this passage is a very large administrative system: one hundred twenty satraps and three presidents, with Daniel one of them. He had lived through Babylon’s prime and then walked into a new regime, and he was not pushed out. “He clearly surpassed the other presidents and satraps”: not by connections, not by tactics, but by “an excellent spirit,” that is, the faithfulness he had held steadily from chapter 1.

Then comes jealousy. It is the oldest story in the human world: someone does well, and someone else begins to look for ground against him. But notice this sentence: “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful.” They searched everywhere: accounts, administration, speech; there was not one thing they could use to accuse him. The strongest witness is not a beautiful speech but a daily life no one can find fault with.

So they came to a conclusion: “unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.” This sentence is the highest praise an enemy ever gave Daniel. They admitted that this man’s only “weakness” was his obedience to God. The reversal is ironic: they wanted to find his fault, and found his greatest glory. If your life were examined closely one day, would the only thing they could find be your faithfulness to God?

6.grk: אֱדַיִן סָרְכַיָּא וַאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּא אִלֵּן הַרְגִּשׁוּ עַל־מַלְכָּא וְכֵן אָמְרִין לֵהּ דָּרְיָוֶשׁ מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִֽי׃ אִתְיָעַטוּ כֹּל׀ סָרְכֵי מַלְכוּתָא סִגְנַיָּא וַֽאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּא הַדָּֽבְרַיָּא וּפַחֲוָתָא לְקַיָּמָה קְיָם מַלְכָּא וּלְתַקָּפָה אֱסָר דִּי כָל־דִּֽי־יִבְעֵה בָעוּ מִן־כָּל־אֱלָהּ וֶֽאֱנָשׁ עַד־יוֹמִין תְּלָתִין לָהֵן מִנָּךְ מַלְכָּא יִתְרְמֵא לְגֹב אַרְיָוָתָֽא׃ כְּעַן מַלְכָּא תְּקִים אֱסָרָא וְתִרְשֻׁם כְּתָבָא דִּי לָא לְהַשְׁנָיָה כְּדָת־מָדַי וּפָרַס דִּי־לָא תֶעְדֵּֽא׃ כָּל־קֳבֵל דְּנָה מַלְכָּא דָּֽרְיָוֶשׁ רְשַׁם כְּתָבָא וֶאֱסָרָֽא׃
6.lit: “Then these presidents and local governors assembled together to the king, and said this to him, “King Darius, live forever! All the presidents of the kingdom, the deputies and the local governors, the counselors and the governors, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a strong decree, that whoever asks a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions. Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it not be changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.” Therefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree.”

6.gram:
כֹּל סָרְכֵי מַלְכוּתָא (all the presidents of the kingdom): the accusers say “all the officials of the kingdom have consulted together,” yet Daniel was one of the three presidents, so this was plainly untrue. It is a lie that says only “everyone,” and it was later used to put pressure on the king.

כְּדָת מָדַי וּפָרַס דִּי־לָא תֶעְדֵּא (according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be altered): “law” (דָּת) is the key word of this chapter. The king’s law is given the same unchangeability as God’s law. It is both the irony of this chapter and its dilemma.
6.exp:
A decree that looks as if it honors the king is in fact a trap made for one man.

These men did not go straight to accuse Daniel. They were clever: they designed a law. The content sounded good: for thirty days, whoever asks a petition of any god or man except the king shall be thrown into the lions’ den. On the surface it honored the king and put him in the place of God, a thirty-day loyalty test. This decree did not mention Daniel in a single word, yet it turned Daniel’s daily life into a crime.

Notice the language they used: “consulted together,” “all agreed.” It is a very common method: to use “everyone is doing it” to apply pressure. In fact Daniel, one of the three presidents, was never asked. The most dangerous law is not the one that plainly targets you, but the one that looks ordinary and happens to make it impossible for you to worship as usual.

Then comes the key moment: “make it unchangeable, according to the law of the Medes and Persians.” Darius signed. With this one act the king too became a prisoner: the law he had established, even he could not take back. It is a deep irony and also a foreshadowing in this chapter: a law made by man can trap the one who made it, while the law of God is what sets people free.

This passage contains no miracle and no voice from heaven, only a decision by a group of clever people in a meeting room. But perhaps that is exactly what many believers face more often today: not an obvious persecution, but a seemingly reasonable rule that makes “worshiping as usual” something that costs us.

Then these men assembled together, and found Daniel making petition and supplication before his God.”

6.gram:
יְדַע דִּי־רְשִׁים כְּתָבָא (knew that the writing was signed): יְדַע is “to know,” a word that recurs throughout the book. He was not ignorant; he “knew, and still…”. This is another picture of 3:18, “let it be known to you.”

וְכַוִּין פְּתִיחָן לֵהּ בְּעִלִּיתֵהּ נֶגֶד יְרוּשְׁלֶם (his windows open in his upper room toward Jerusalem): “open” is a participle, meaning “always open.” It was not opened for the occasion; it was his habit all along.

כְּדִי־הֲוָא עָבֵד מִן־קַדְמַת דְּנָה (as he did before): the word “before” (from earlier times) stresses not this one time but continuity over many years.
6.exp:
He knew, and then, as before.

This is the quietest verse of the chapter, and one of the most important in the whole book. Verse 10 says: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house.” He did not call a press conference, did not rally companions, did not go around asking for help, and did not hide. He simply went home, went upstairs, and went to that window. The greatest witness is often not a big action but carrying on as usual under pressure.

Notice these details. First, the window was open “toward Jerusalem.” This was Solomon’s hope in the temple dedication prayer: when the people are carried away captive and pray toward this house, God will hear (1 Kings 8:48). His window was a memory of home and also a direction of hope. Second, “open”: the original suggests the window was always open. It was not for today; it was his daily habit. He did not open it specially to make a statement, nor close it to avoid trouble.

Third, “he kneeled on his knees before his God, and gave thanks.” Hear that word: thanks. This is a man about to be thrown into the lions’ den, and his prayer has thanksgiving in it. Fourth, “as he did before”: these words are the strength of the whole chapter. He did not increase the number of times because of danger, and he did not reduce it because of danger. He did not perform, and he did not retreat.

Today we may not meet a lions’ den, but there are many “little lions”: the unwritten rules of the workplace, the pressure to work on the Lord’s Day, a setting where you feel awkward saying “let me pray first.” Daniel is not teaching us how to confront others; he is teaching us how to carry on as usual under pressure. This is one picture of selflessness: I do not need to prove anything to anyone; I simply return, as usual, into God’s presence.

6.grk: בֵּאדַיִן קְרִיבוּ וְאָמְרִין קֳדָם־מַלְכָּא עַל־אֱסָר מַלְכָּא הֲלָא אֱסָר רְשַׁמְתָּ דִּי כָל־אֱנָשׁ דִּֽי־יִבְעֵה מִן־כָּל־אֱלָהּ וֶֽאֱנָשׁ עַד־יוֹמִין תְּלָתִין לָהֵן מִנָּךְ מַלְכָּא יִתְרְמֵא לְגוֹב אַרְיָותָא עָנֵה מַלְכָּא וְאָמַר יַצִּיבָא מִלְּתָא כְּדָת־מָדַי וּפָרַס דִּי־לָא תֶעְדֵּֽא׃ בֵּאדַיִן עֲנוֹ וְאָמְרִין קֳדָם מַלְכָּא דִּי דָנִיֵּאל דִּי מִן־בְּנֵי גָלוּתָא דִּי יְהוּד לָא־שָׂם מַלְכָּא טְעֵם וְעַל־אֱסָרָא דִּי רְשַׁמְתָּ וְזִמְנִין תְּלָתָה בְּיוֹמָא בָּעֵא בָּעוּתֵֽהּ׃ אֱדַיִן מַלְכָּא כְּדִי מִלְּתָא שְׁמַע שַׂגִּיא בְּאֵשׁ עֲלוֹהִי וְעַל דָּנִיֵּאל שָׂם בָּל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתֵהּ וְעַד מֶֽעָלֵי שִׁמְשָׁא הֲוָא מִשְׁתַּדַּר לְהַצָּלוּתֵֽהּ׃ בֵּאדַיִן גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ הַרְגִּשׁוּ עַל־מַלְכָּא וְאָמְרִין לְמַלְכָּא דַּע מַלְכָּא דִּֽי־דָת לְמָדַי וּפָרַס דִּֽי־כָל־אֱסָר וּקְיָם דִּֽי־מַלְכָּא יְהָקֵים לָא לְהַשְׁנָיָֽה׃
6.lit: “Then they came near, and spoke before the king concerning the king’s decree: “Haven’t you signed a decree that every man who makes a petition to any god or man within thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?” The king answered, “This thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.” Then they answered and said before the king, “That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day.” Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him. Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, “Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians, that no decree nor statute which the king establishes may be changed.””

6.gram:
לָא־שָׂם עֲלָיִךְ מַלְכָּא טְעֵם (pays no attention to you): שָׂם טְעֵם (to set a command / to take to heart) is the same wording as the accusation against the three friends in 3:12: “these men pay no heed to you.” The same charge, in the same way; this is the enemy’s consistent language.

שָׂם בָּל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתֵהּ (set his heart to deliver him): literally “he put his heart on delivering him,” that is, “he thought with his whole heart how to deliver him.” The king wanted to “deliver” (שֵׁיזִב), the key verb of the book: in 3:15 the king asked, “what god is there that can deliver you?” and now the king himself is the one who wants to deliver and cannot.
6.exp:
The king has supreme power, yet cannot save the man he most wants to save.

The camera turns to the king’s side. The accusers come in and first remind the king: you signed the decree. It is a very shrewd step: first make the king nod, then bring up Daniel’s name. The king answered, “The thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be altered.” When he said this he did not yet know that those words would become a rope binding himself.

Then they said: “Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, pays no attention to you.” Notice how they named Daniel: one of the exiles. They did not say “your president” or “Daniel, who has served the king for years”; they said only “of the captivity.” It was a stripping of identity: turning a man from a contributor into an outsider. And “pays no attention to you” is exactly the wording used against the three friends in chapter 3. The enemy’s language is always alike.

Then the king’s reaction: “Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored till the going down of the sun to rescue him.” This king is not a bad man. He loved this man; he wanted to save him; he spent the whole day looking for a way. But his way was blocked by his own signature. The accusers came again: “Know, O king… no decree or statute which the king establishes may be changed.” Human power can set up laws, but it cannot save a man from a law it has set up itself.

Do you remember Nebuchadnezzar’s sentence in chapter 3? “Who is that god who will deliver you out of my hands?” In this chapter the king himself becomes the one asking that question: who can deliver me from the law I made myself? Only God can answer that question.

6.gram:
אֱלָהָךְ דִּי אַנְתְּ פָּלַח־לֵהּ בִּתְדִירָא הוּא יְשֵׁיזְבִנָּךְ (your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you): תְּדִירָא (continually) appears in the whole book only in 6:16 and 6:20; both times the king says it, and both times it goes with “serve.” What the king says is what he has observed in Daniel: a man who serves continually.

וְחַתְמַהּ מַלְכָּא בְּעִזְקְתֵהּ (the king sealed it with his own signet): the den the king sealed and the decree the king signed in 6:8 form a closed circle: the king’s seal locks Daniel in, and locks the king in too.
6.exp:
The king said something he himself was not sure of: “Your God whom you serve continually will deliver you.”

They brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. Notice that the text does not describe his reaction; no cry, no plea, only the king’s sentence: “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.” This sentence is a little like comfort, a little like a blessing, and more like a man with no assurance, grasping at the one hope left at the last moment. The king’s sentence is the most honest of the whole chapter. All his power could not save him; he could only hand Daniel over to Daniel’s God.

Notice the word “continually”: “your God whom you serve continually.” What the king saw was not one brave moment of Daniel’s, but his long years. This is an important reminder: a person’s trust in a time of crisis is built up, day by day, in ordinary days. Though the king was a foreigner, from Daniel’s long life he reached this conclusion: the God this man serves is real.

Then a stone was laid at the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his nobles. This picture reminds us of another mouth of a tomb, another stone, also sealed (Matt 27:66). We do not treat it as a type; we can only say: it reminds us. People seal death in the firmest way, and at dawn God has his own work to do.

Finally, the king’s night: fasting, no musical instruments, no sleep. That night the king was less at peace than Daniel. In the palace there was no one who could comfort him. Human power can seal a den, but it cannot seal a conscience.

6.lit: “Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste to the den of lions. When he came near to the den to Daniel, he cried with a troubled voice. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?” Then Daniel said to the king, “O king, live forever! My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.” Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.”

6.gram:
עֲבֵד אֱלָהָא חַיָּא (servant of the living God): the phrase אֱלָהָא חַיָּא (the living God) is used in the Old Testament in contrast with dead idols (Jer 10:10). Here a foreign king, in the fear of early morning, says the deepest title.

זָכוּ קֳדָמוֹהִי הִשְׁתְּכַחַת לִי (innocence was found in me before him): “innocence” (זָכוּ) is a courtroom word meaning “clear.” Daniel is not saying he has no sin, but that in this matter, before God and before the king, he has done no wrong. See the issues.

הֵימִן בֵּאלָהֵהּ (trusted in his God): הֵימִן (to trust) is the Aramaic “to believe,” from the same root as the “faithful” (מְהֵימַן) of 6:4. His faithfulness and his trust are one and the same thing.
6.exp:
At dawn it is the king who speaks first, and then Daniel who bears witness.

Verse 19 says: “Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste to the den of lions.” This king probably did not sleep. He went “in haste,” with a word from the same root as his own fright in chapter 5. His hurry was that of a frightened man at daybreak, rushing to confirm something he dared not confirm. Coming near the den, he cried out “with a troubled voice”: “Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?” Notice his title for Daniel: servant of the living God. He had not said that yesterday. One night of silence changed his title.

Then Daniel’s voice: “O king, live forever!” His first words were a blessing for the king. A man who had just come out of the lions’ den did not blame, did not accuse, did not cry injustice; he first blessed the king who had thrown him in. This is one picture of selflessness: when hurt, still blessing. Then he gave his witness: “My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths.” Notice: the one who shut the lions’ mouths was God, not his prayer and not his faith, but the angel God sent.

He went on: “because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.” We will discuss this sentence separately later, but notice one order first: first “before God,” then “before the king.” He answers to God first, and then to the king. He said it very calmly: he had not disobeyed the king in anything reasonable; he had only, on the matter of “asking from God,” chosen God.

Finally the text gives a conclusion: “no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.” This sentence is not saying how great Daniel’s faith was, but that the One he trusted is trustworthy. His faith is not a condition to be filled up; it is a place: he placed himself in God’s hand.

6.lit: “The king commanded, and they brought those men who had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions mauled them, and broke all their bones in pieces, before they came to the bottom of the den. Then king Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: “Peace be multiplied to you. “I make a decree that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; “for he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end. He delivers and rescues. He works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who has delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.” So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.”

6.gram:
אֲכַלוּ קַרְצוֹהִי דִּי דָנִיֵּאל (accused Daniel): literally “ate the pieces of Daniel,” exactly the same phrase as in 3:8, where the three friends were accused. The accusers of the two chapters appear in the same way and end in the same way.

וְאָתִין וְתִמְהִין (signs and wonders): this pair of words appears in Nebuchadnezzar’s decree in 4:2–3, and here Darius’s decree uses it again. Two foreign kings, each with a decree, proclaim the same God to all the earth.
6.exp:
The ending of this chapter has a very heavy picture and a very glorious decree.

Verse 24 is the hardest verse of the chapter to read: the king ordered the accusers, together with their wives and children, to be thrown into the lions’ den. We cannot pretend this verse is not there. The laws of the ancient Near East often practiced collective punishment; the text describes what happened and does not say it was good. Deuteronomy 24:16 says: “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers. Every man shall be put to death for his own sin.” So when we read this verse we are not celebrating, and we are not making excuses for any violence; we see that one who used harming the innocent as his means finally fell into the pit he himself dug. Whether this collective sentence was just, we set out the different views in the issues.

Then comes the decree. Like Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 4, this king also proclaims to all the earth: “men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed.” Notice that these words are almost word for word the same as those of chapters 2 and 4. Two foreign kings in a row use the same language to bear witness to all the earth. This is what the whole long Aramaic section keeps saying: God’s kingdom is indestructible, and human kingdoms, however great, will come to bow before him.

The last verse: “So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” He outlived one empire, and then another. From the youth of chapter 1 he walked to here, a man who carried on “as usual”: resolving as usual, serving as usual, praying as usual. This is the theme of the chapter and the pattern the whole book wants us to learn: in different kingdoms, still the servant of the same God.

7.lit: “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon Daniel had a dream and visions of his head on his bed. Then he wrote the dream and told the sum of the matters. Daniel spoke and said, “I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea. Four great animals came up from the sea, different from one another.”

7.gram:
אַרְבַּע רוּחֵי שְׁמַיָּא מְגִיחָן לְיַמָּא רַבָּא (the four winds of the sky stirring up the great sea): “wind” (רוּחַ) is the same word as “spirit,” and in the Old Testament “the sea” is often a symbol of chaos and the nations. This picture recalls Genesis 1: the Spirit of God moving over the face of the waters; only here it is the winds of heaven stirring up a great water.

שָׁנְיָן (different): the root שׁנה (to change, to differ) appears many times in this book: 2:21 “changes the times and the seasons,” 3:19 “his face was changed,” 5:6 “his face was changed,” 6:8 “which doesn’t alter,” 7:3 and 7:19 “different.” “Change” is a word that keeps recurring in this book.
7.exp:
This chapter is the hinge of the whole book: the six chapters before are stories, and the six after are visions, beginning with this night.

Chapter 7 differs from chapters 1–6 in one important way: the earlier chapters are stories about “others,” telling of Daniel and his three friends living in the court of foreign kings; this chapter is “Daniel’s own” dream. Verse 1 says: “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon,” a date that falls before chapter 5 yet is placed after chapter 6. Why was it arranged this way? We set out the various views in the issues. We can say first: whichever came first, the author lets us start here, looking at the world from a different angle.

Then a very large picture: the four winds of heaven stirring up the great sea. In the Bible the sea is often a symbol of unrest and chaos, the place where the nations surge. “Four great animals came up from the sea, different from one another.” Notice that these beasts “came up from the sea”; they did not come down from heaven. They are powers that grow out of human chaos. The great image of chapter 2 was seen through human eyes: gold, silver, bronze and iron, one statue; chapter 7 is seen through heaven’s eyes: these kingdoms are a pack of beasts.

What people see is splendor; what heaven sees is beasts. This does not say that every kingdom is evil; it reminds us that power not lit by the light of God shows what it really is. This chapter is not meant to frighten, but so that when we see the wind rising on the sea, we remember: the wind is “heaven’s” wind. Even chaos is in heaven’s hand.

7.lit: ““The first was like a lion, and had eagle’s wings. I watched until its wings were plucked, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made to stand on two feet as a man. A man’s heart was given to it. “Behold, there was another animal, a second, like a bear. It was raised up on one side, and three ribs were in its mouth between its teeth. They said this to it: ‘Arise! Devour much flesh!’ “After this I saw, and behold, another, like a leopard, which had on its back four wings of a bird. The animal also had four heads; and dominion was given to it. “After this I saw in the night visions, and, behold, there was a fourth animal, awesome and powerful, and exceedingly strong. פֻם מְמַלִּל רַבְרְבָן (a mouth speaking great things): this expression appears in 7:8, 11, 20 and is the mark of the little horn. “Great words” are the chief feature of this chapter’s little horn.
7.exp:
All four beasts are given: wings plucked off, a man’s heart given, dominion given. Even the beasts are in God’s hand.

The first was like a lion with eagle’s wings. It is a noble combination: the king of beasts joined to the king of birds. But “I watched until its wings were plucked, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made to stand on two feet as a man. A man’s heart was given to it.” This is the shadow of Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 4: brought low, and given “a man’s heart.” What was taken from this beast was the power to fly; what was given was a human form.

The second was like a bear, raised up on one side, with three ribs in its mouth between its teeth, and they said to it: “Arise! Devour much flesh!” Notice that even this command was “spoken”: even the authority to devour has a source of command. The third was like a leopard, with four wings and four heads, and dominion was given to it. Its speed was not its own ability either; it too was “given.” The text repeatedly uses the passive to make us see that behind the four beasts there is an unseen hand.

The fourth is the hardest to describe: “awesome and powerful, and exceedingly strong,” with great iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces, and stamping the residue with its feet. It has no name, because no animal can be compared to it. Then it has ten horns, among which came up a little horn with eyes like the eyes of a man and a mouth speaking great things. This is a horn “with eyes and a mouth, but no heart”: able to see and to speak, but without a man’s heart.

Which kingdom each of the four beasts is has long been read in different ways; we set them side by side in the issues and do not chart a timetable. What helps us most is this: the greatest powers all have a limit; they were all given, and they will all be taken back. The pressure you face, however much it looks like a beast, is beneath that hand.

7.grk: חָזֵה הֲוֵית עַד דִּי כָרְסָוָן רְמִיו וְעַתִּיק יוֹמִין יְתִב לְבוּשֵׁהּ׀ כִּתְלַג חִוָּר וּשְׂעַר רֵאשֵׁהּ כַּעֲמַר נְקֵא כָּרְסְיֵהּ שְׁבִיבִין דִּי־נוּר גַּלְגִּלּוֹהִי נוּר דָּלִֽק׃ נְהַר דִּי־נוּר נָגֵד וְנָפֵק מִן־קֳדָמוֹהִי אֶלֶף יְשַׁמְּשׁוּנֵּהּ וְרִבּוֹ קָֽדָמוֹהִי יְקוּמוּן דִּינָא יְתִב וְסִפְרִין פְּתִֽיחוּ׃

His throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him. Thousands of thousands ministered to him. Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The judgment was set. The books were opened.”

7.gram:
עַתִּיק יוֹמִין (the Ancient of Days): literally “the aged of days” or “advanced in years.” In the Bible “old” is tied to wisdom, dignity and eternity; it does not say God is an old man, but that he is before all days and above all days.

כָּרְסָוָן רְמִיו (thrones were placed): the verb is passive and plural, “were set up”; not “put down somewhere” but “set in order.” The scene of judgment is prepared, not improvised.

דִּינָא יְתִב (the judgment was set, he sat): דִּין (judgment) and יְתִב (sit) appear together and are repeated in 7:10 and 7:26: judgment is carried out “seated,” an unhurried authority that is never in a rush.
7.exp:
This scene forms the greatest contrast with the chaos before it: no clamor, only one throne, quietly set up.

The rhythm of the text changes at this verse. Before, four beasts came up one after another; now there is one sentence: “I watched until thrones were placed.” Notice that it is not “a son of David” and not “an army,” but “thrones.” The beasts are busy scrambling for position; in heaven a place has long since been prepared.

Then the one who sat, “the Ancient of Days.” His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. This is a picture of “old,” and also of “pure”: not the old of decline, but the old of one who was there from the beginning and has always been there. The beasts before were all newcomers; he is the one who has always been. His throne was fiery flames and its wheels burning fire, and a fiery stream issued from before him. This is a holy God, whose holiness no one dares look upon.

Then the numbers: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The purpose of the number is not for us to count but to feel: in heaven there is an order we cannot see, greater than all the armies of earth. The last sentence: “The judgment was set. The books were opened.” Judgment is carried out “seated,” not hurried, not anxious. The books are opened, and nothing is forgotten.

This picture gives us a deep rest: history’s end is not a free-for-all but a throne of judgment. The injustice you have suffered and the evil you have seen, not one thing has been missed by this Judge. This is not meant to make us afraid, but so that we can place things in his hand and not take revenge ourselves.

7.gram:
הֶעְדִּיו שָׁלְטָנְהוֹן (their dominion was taken away): the verb עדא (to take away, to remove) also appears in 7:14, “his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away (לָא יֶעְדֵּה).” The same verb: on one side “taken away” (the beasts), on the other “not taken away” (the dominion of the son of man): a sharp contrast.

זְמַן וְעִדָּן (a season and a time): the same pair of words as in 2:21, “changes the times and the seasons (עִדָּנַיָּא וְזִמְנַיָּא).” God rules over times and seasons; even “how much longer” the beasts will last he sets.
7.exp:
The beast’s end is decided by its “mouth”: because it spoke great things.

Verse 11 says: “I watched at that time because of the voice of the great words which the horn spoke.” This sentence is interesting: the little horn’s end came because of its mouth. It had eyes like the eyes of a man and a mouth speaking great things. Its greatest power was speech, and its end came because of speech. This is a very consistent theme in the Bible: the proud mouth is stopped by God’s judgment. You need not wait until the end to know that the one who speaks big words will not have the last word.

Then the ending: “slain, and its body destroyed, and it was given to be burned with fire.” The text gives no detail and no exaggeration, only a fact: it was dealt with. We do not need to turn this verse into a forecast about anyone today, and we do not need to identify who the little horn is. What the text wants us to see is this: however great a power is, however loud its words, in the end it is the judgment of heaven that settles it.

Verse 12 says that the rest of the beasts had their dominion taken away, yet their lives were prolonged for a season and a time. There is a very gentle detail in this sentence: the other beasts were not destroyed, only had their dominion taken away, and remained for a time. This is the same gentleness as in chapter 4, where the tree was cut down but the stump was left. God’s judgment is not indiscriminate destruction; it has measure, and even the season and the time are in his hand.

Dominion can be given and can be taken away; the One who “takes away” has always been there. When you see a power that seems never to fall, remember: its “season and time” were not set by itself.
