7.gram:
כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ (one like a son of man): בַּר אֱנָשׁ is literally “son of man,” which in Aramaic means “a human being”; the prefix “like” (כְּ) gives “one like a human being.” In contrast with the four beasts before: the beasts were “like a lion,” “like a bear,” “like a leopard,” but this one is “like a man.”

יִפְלְחוּן (should serve him): פלח (to serve) is a tracked word of this book: in chapter 3 the object of service was the golden image or the gods; in this chapter what all the peoples serve is this one like a son of man. See the issues, where these notes set out the various views and also see the New Testament connection.

עַתִּיק יוֹמַיָּא מְטָה (he came even to the Ancient of Days): he did not walk up to the throne himself; he was “brought near” (הַקְרְבוּהִי) before him. The authority was given: this is again the theme of “being given.”
7.exp:
The four beasts before were “like beasts”; this one is “like a man.”

We come to the highest point of the whole book. Before there were four beasts: like a lion, like a bear, like a leopard, and one beyond description. Now it changes: “there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man.” It is a strong contrast: what came up from the sea were beasts; what came with the clouds from heaven was “one like a man.” Human kingdoms in history have often been beastly; the kingdom God establishes has a human face.

Notice that he did not walk up to the throne himself; he was “brought near” before the Ancient of Days. The kingdom was not seized by him; it was given. “Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom.” These three stand in sharp contrast with the fourth beast’s “devoured and broke in pieces”: the beast seizes, the son of man receives; the beast swallows, the son of man is given. The true kingdom is not taken by force; it is entrusted.

Then the range of this kingdom: peoples, nations and languages should serve him. These words are exactly the same as the herald’s “peoples, nations, and languages” in chapter 3. In chapter 3 all were commanded to fall down and worship the golden image; in chapter 7 all will serve this one like a son of man. The same words, two kingdoms. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed; this joins in one line with the words of chapters 2, 4 and 6.

Who is the “son of man”? There have long been different views: some take it as an individual, some as a collective representative of the saints, some as both. In the New Testament Jesus often calls himself the Son of Man, and at his trial he cites this verse, saying: “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming on the clouds of the sky” (Matt 26:64). We see this connection and also respect the various views; see the issues. However it is read, this scene tells us: history’s end is not a still greater beast, but one like a man, given the kingdom.

7.gram:
קַדִּישֵׁי עֶלְיוֹנִין (the saints of the Most High): עֶלְיוֹנִין (Most High) is plural, meaning “the Highest (One),” a plural of majesty. קַדִּישֵׁי “holy ones” is also plural. “The saints of the Most High” are the holy people who belong to the Most High. Later interpreters differ on who the “saints” are: the people of God on earth, the angels of heaven, or both. See the issues.

יְקַבְּלוּן מַלְכוּתָא (will receive the kingdom): קבל (to receive): in 5:31 Darius “received” the kingdom, and here the saints too will “receive” the kingdom. The same verb: the kingdom is something received.
7.exp:
Even Daniel was frightened by this dream; he did not rush to say he understood, he went and asked.

Verse 15 says: “my spirit was grieved within my body, and the visions of my head troubled me.” A man who did not waver in the lions’ den this time was frightened by a dream. This is important: faith is not the absence of feeling. Daniel was frightened, but he did one thing: he came near to one of those who stood by and asked him the truth. He did not interpret it himself, and did not guess; he went and asked.

The attendant’s explanation was short: “These great animals, which are four, are four kings, who will arise out of the earth.” The four beasts arise out of the “earth,” consistent with what was said before, that they came up from the “sea.” Then a very powerful sentence: “But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.” The word “But” is the turn of the whole explanation: before it, four beasts, rising and falling; after it, an everlasting kingdom.

Notice that the saints’ receiving the kingdom is also a “receiving,” the same verb as Darius’s “received the kingdom” in 5:31. The kingdom is not gained by seizing or by human effort; it is given. Who are the “saints”? They may be God’s people on earth, or may include a company in heaven; the various views read it differently. We need not draw a line here to set the son of man against the saints: between them there is a connection, not a conflict, and we set this out in the issues.

For us today this sentence holds a deep comfort: the people you belong to may look very small and overlooked in the world’s eyes, yet the text says they will receive the kingdom. This is not a hope with pride in it but a hope with humility: we receive the kingdom not because we are strong but because the kingdom is given.

7.lit: ““Then I desired to know the truth concerning the fourth animal, which was different from all of them, exceedingly terrible, whose teeth were of iron, and its nails of bronze; which devoured, broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet; and concerning the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn which came up, and before which three fell, even that horn that had eyes, and a mouth that spoke great things, whose look was more stout than its fellows. I saw, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them, until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. “Thus he said, ‘The fourth animal will be a fourth kingdom on earth, which will be different from all the kingdoms, and will devour the whole earth, and will tread it down, and break it in pieces. As for the ten horns, ten kings will arise out of this kingdom. Another will arise after them; and he will be different from the former, and he will put down three kings. He will speak words against the Most High, and will wear out the saints of the Most High. He will plan to change the times and the law; and they will be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.”

7.gram:
וְדִינָא יְהַב לְקַדִּישֵׁי עֶלְיוֹנִין (judgment was given to the saints of the Most High): literally “judgment was given to the saints of the Most High.” This can be read as “the judgment was pronounced in their favor” (vindicating them), or as “the authority to judge was given to them.” The two readings are set side by side, but both point to the saints receiving justice.

יִסְבַּר לְהַשְׁנָיָה זִמְנִין וְדָת (he will plan to change the times and the law): סבר (to plan) is joined with שנה (to change): what this little horn wants to change is not one thing but “time” and “law,” that is, the framework of time in which people live and the norms by which they live.

עִדָּן וְעִדָּנִין וּפְלַג עִדָּן (a time and times and half a time): the original is “a time, two times, and half a time,” using the same word (עִדָּן) as the “seven times” of 4:16, 23. The length is unclear; see the issues.
7.exp:
Even Daniel most wanted to know about the fourth beast, because that one was the hardest to face.

Verse 19 is a very honest sentence: “Then I desired to know the truth concerning the fourth animal.” He did not ask especially about the first three. He asked especially about the fourth, because that one was different from the others, exceedingly terrible. He said his fear plainly. This is a very good example: there is no need to pretend we are not afraid. Bring the thing you fear most before God, and ask: what is this?

The attendant’s explanation has three layers. First: the fourth beast is a fourth kingdom on earth, different from all the kingdoms. Second: the ten horns are ten kings; afterward another arises, different from the former. Third: this king does three things: he speaks words against the Most High; he wears out the saints of the Most High; he plans to change the times and the law. All three put God somewhere else: speaking big words belittles God; wearing out the saints attacks those who belong to God; changing the times and the law means rewriting the times and norms God has set.

Who this little horn is has long been read in many different ways; we set them side by side in the issues, and the position of these notes is clear: we do not identify anyone of today, and we do not count days. “A time and times and half a time” is in the original “a time, two times, and half a time,” and we do not decide its length for it. What we see is its direction: the saints “given into his hand” is limited, bounded, and has an end.

Then comes the turn. Verse 22 says: “until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.” These words are spoken to all who are in suffering. What you have suffered was not suffered in vain; what you are waiting for is not something you will wait for in vain. The text does not say which day this time is; it says only: it will come. For those under persecution this is a great comfort; for those not under persecution it is a reminder: do not make light of, or make use of, someone else’s suffering.

7.grk: וְדִינָא יִתִּב וְשָׁלְטָנֵהּ יְהַעְדּוֹן לְהַשְׁמָדָה וּלְהוֹבָדָה עַד־סוֹפָֽא׃ וּמַלְכוּתָה וְשָׁלְטָנָא וּרְבוּתָא דִּי מַלְכְוָת תְּחוֹת כָּל־שְׁמַיָּא יְהִיבַת לְעַם קַדִּישֵׁי עֶלְיוֹנִין מַלְכוּתֵהּ מַלְכוּת עָלַם וְכֹל שָׁלְטָנַיָּא לֵהּ יִפְלְחוּן וְיִֽשְׁתַּמְּעֽוּן׃ עַד־כָּה סוֹפָא דִֽי־מִלְּתָא אֲנָה דָֽנִיֵּאל שַׂגִּיא׀ רַעְיוֹנַי יְבַהֲלֻנַּנִי וְזִיוַי יִשְׁתַּנּוֹן עֲלַי וּמִלְּתָא בְּלִבִּי נִטְרֵֽת׃פ

7.gram:
וְדִינָא יִתִּב (but the judgment will be set): the same sentence pattern as 7:10, “the judgment was set.” In this chapter the sentence repeats and forms a “frame”: 7:10 and 7:26 both say “judgment sits,” and judgment is placed between two “sittings.”

כָּל־שָׁלְטָנַיָּא לֵהּ יִפְלְחוּן וְיִשְׁתַּמְּעוּן (all dominions will serve and obey him): who “him” is, the original may refer to “the Most High,” or to “the people of the saints” or to the “son of man.” This ambiguity is deliberate: the kingdom is given to the saints, yet it is also God’s kingdom. See the issues.

בְּלִבִּי נִטְרֵת (I kept the matter in my heart): “kept” (נטר) means “to guard,” “to preserve.” This verb recalls Luke 2:19, where Mary “kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.” Daniel did not at that moment tell the vision to everyone; he first kept it in his heart.
7.exp:
This chapter ends not with a shout but with one person keeping it in his heart.

Verse 26 says: “But the judgment will be set.” This echoes 7:10: judgment is “seated.” Before, there was the rushing, warring, devouring of the beasts, a scene of chaos; now there is one who sits. “They will take away his dominion, to consume and to destroy it to the end.” This is the final announcement against the little horn. Notice that it is not a war but a verdict: not “defeated” but “judged.”

Then the most important sentence of the chapter: “The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High.” This sentence echoes 7:14, where the son of man receives the kingdom: on one side “him,” on the other “the saints.” The kingdom is not taken by force but given; not given to the strongest but to the saints of the Most High. All the greatness will be given to them. It is the gentlest and also the most subversive sentence: all the kingdoms of the earth will in the end be handed to those who never scrambled for them.

“All dominions will serve and obey him.” The “serve” and “obey” in this sentence stand opposite chapter 3, where everyone served the golden image. Chapter 3 was forced service; in chapter 7 all powers freely serve the true kingdom. This is the conclusion of the whole long Aramaic section of the book: God’s kingdom is everlasting, and all who hold power will in the end serve him.

Finally, Daniel. “Here is the end of the matter,” he says, and he himself was “much troubled, and his face was changed.” Even a man who had seen so great a vision was frightened. Yet he said: “but I kept the matter in my heart.” He did not hurry to explain, and did not hurry to proclaim. He first kept it. This is something we can learn: some words God gives us not to be spoken at once but to be kept in the heart first, so that they change us. When we cannot yet understand, we can first keep it, and go on being faithful.

Now it was so, that when I saw, I was in the citadel of Susa, which is in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision, and I was by the river Ulai.”

8.gram:
חָזוֹן נִרְאָה אֵלַי אֲנִי דָנִיֵּאל (a vision appeared to me, even to me, Daniel): the verb here is a passive form, “appeared” (נִרְאָה); Daniel did not go looking for the vision, it “appeared” to him. This follows from chapter 7, where Daniel “wrote the dream”: the vision is something given.

עִבְרִית / אֲרָמִית: from 8:1 the original returns from Aramaic to Hebrew. These notes have set out the various views on this shift in the stance of the whole book; we do not use it to date the book, and only see that the earlier section (2:4–7:28) was in the language of “the nations,” and now we return to the language of “the holy people” themselves.
8.exp:
The opening of chapter 8 has only one verb, “appeared”: the vision appeared to Daniel; he did not go looking for it.

This chapter differs from chapter 7 in one obvious way: the language returns from Aramaic to Hebrew. Why? There have long been different views, and we have set them out in the stance of the whole book; we do not draw a conclusion here. We can quietly see this: the long section before spoke of “the nations’ affairs” in the language the nations shared; from this chapter on, speaking of the holy people, the sanctuary and the end, it uses the holy people’s own language. You need not agree with any one view in order to read this chapter.

Then the text gives two places. “Susa, which is in the province of Elam”: a place that later became the royal city of Persia; “by the river Ulai”: a river. Notice: this is the position “in the vision”; he had not really moved there. His body may still have been in Babylon, but his eyes were carried to a center of power that was still to come. This reminds us that visions often let us see that a kingdom that looks very stable today is, in God’s eyes, only a location, a stage.

The third year of King Belshazzar is a few years after chapter 7. Daniel had already seen one dream, and now there is another. God does not tell everything at once. He gives us a little at a time, waits for us to “keep it in the heart,” and then gives the next. This is his patience with people: not pouring it out on us, but leading us to see, step by step.

8.lit: “Then I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns. The two horns were high; but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last. I saw the ram pushing westward, northward, and southward. No animals could stand before him. There wasn’t any who could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and magnified himself. As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west over the surface of the whole earth, and didn’t touch the ground. The goat had a notable horn between his eyes. He came to the ram that had the two horns, which I saw standing before the river, and ran on him in the fury of his power. I saw him come close to the ram, and he was moved with anger against him, and struck the ram, and broke his two horns. There was no power in the ram to stand before him; but he cast him down to the ground, and trampled on him. There was no one who could deliver the ram out of his hand. The male goat magnified himself exceedingly. When he was strong, the great horn was broken; and instead of it there came up four notable horns toward the four winds of the sky.”

וַיַּעֲשֶׂה כִרְצוֹנוֹ וְהִגְדִּיל (he did according to his will, and magnified himself): the verb הִגְדִּיל (to make oneself great) appears again and again in 8:4 (the ram), 8:8 (the male goat), 8:11 (the little horn) and 8:25 (the little king). Four times, the same word, pointing to four different subjects.

וְאֵין מַצִּיל מִיָּדוֹ (there was none who could deliver out of his hand): this pattern also appears twice, in 8:4 and 8:7. It says that before these great powers people have no one to rely on for rescue. This despair prepares a contrast for the later “broken without hand.”
8.exp:
The verb “magnify himself” appears four times in this chapter: the ram, the male goat, the little horn and the little king all use the same word.

The text first gives us two animals: a ram standing by the river with two horns, the later one higher; and a male goat coming from the west, crossing the whole earth, not touching the ground, with a notable horn between his eyes. These two animals are explained by the text itself later (8:20–21), and we will speak of it when we come to that passage. For now notice the text’s manner of writing: it does not describe their majesty in detail, but lets us hear verb after verb: pushing, could not stand, none who could deliver, magnified himself.

The ram “did according to his will, and magnified himself”; the male goat “magnified himself exceedingly.” The same word, said of two different powers. This tells us: whichever power it is, as long as it forgets that it was given, it walks the same road: “making itself great.” We have already seen such a man in chapter 4: Nebuchadnezzar, on the roof of his palace, said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling-place, by the might of my power?” This chapter is only that in the form of a different animal.

The coldest sentence is: “There wasn’t any who could deliver out of his hand.” This sentence is said twice in the ram’s story. Before great powers people are helpless; this is true, and the text does not hide it. But please remember this sentence, because later, when the little king “stands up against the prince of princes,” his end is “broken without hand.” That phrase reminds us of the stone in chapter 2 that was “cut out without hands.” People cannot save people; but there is One who does not need human hands.

Also, when the male goat was strong, the great horn was broken; and in its place four notable horns came up toward the four winds of the sky. Notice the text’s word: “broken” (שָׁבַר). The highest point of strength is the beginning of breaking. The peak of power is often its turning point. This is not a threat but a very quiet reminder: no horn can keep rising forever.

8.grk: וּמִן־הָאַחַת מֵהֶם יָצָא קֶֽרֶן־אַחַת מִצְּעִירָה וַתִּגְדַּל־יֶתֶר אֶל־הַנֶּגֶב וְאֶל־הַמִּזְרָח וְאֶל־הַצֶּֽבִי׃ וַתִּגְדַּל עַד־צְבָא הַשָּׁמָיִם וַתַּפֵּל אַרְצָה מִן־הַצָּבָא וּמִן־הַכּוֹכָבִים וַֽתִּרְמְסֵֽם׃ וְעַד שַֽׂר־הַצָּבָא הִגְדִּיל וּמִמֶּנּוּ הַתָּמִיד וְהֻשְׁלַךְ מְכוֹן מִקְדָּשֽׁוֹ׃ וְצָבָא תִּנָּתֵן עַל־הַתָּמִיד בְּפָשַׁע וְתַשְׁלֵךְ אֱמֶת אַרְצָה וְעָשְׂתָה וְהִצְלִֽיחָה׃
8.lit: “Out of one of them came out a little horn, which grew exceedingly great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the glorious land. It grew great, even to the army of the sky; and it cast down some of the army and of the stars to the ground, and trampled on them. Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down. The army was given over to it together with the continual burnt offering through disobedience. It cast down truth to the ground, and it did its pleasure and prospered.”

8.gram:
וַתִּגְדַּל עַד־צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם (it grew great, even to the army of the sky): וַתִּגְדַּל (it grew great) is from the same root as the earlier הִגְדִּיל (magnified himself). From “becoming great” to “making oneself great” is a downward line.

הַתָּמִיד (the continual burnt offering): this word is the thing taken away in 8:11, 12 and 13. תָּמִיד is literally “continual, uninterrupted.” The worship of the sanctuary being interrupted is the most painful picture in this passage.

וְהִצְלִיחָה (and prospered): the same verb recurs in 8:12, 24 and 25. The “prospering” of evil is, in the text, something specially pointed out, not hidden.
8.exp:
This little horn did three things to the “sanctuary”: reached up to the host of heaven, took away the continual offering, and cast down the sanctuary. And what is most disturbing is that the text says it “prospered.”

From one of the four horns came a “little” horn. Notice: first “little,” and then, toward the south, the east and “the glorious land,” it grew great. “The glorious land” is in the Bible often what the land God promised is called. This horn’s direction pointed to where God’s people were.

Then its three actions. First, it grew great even to the army of the sky, and cast some of the stars to the ground and trampled on them. This is a very large picture: pulling things of heaven down and trampling them under foot. Second, it “magnified itself, even to the prince of the army,” and “took away from him the continual burnt offering.” This lays hands directly on God, and on the worship of God. Third, “the place of his sanctuary was cast down.” For one person to carry off another’s home is one thing; to tear down the place where a people worship God is another. For that is where they are “seen,” where they meet with God.

The text then says something very heavy: “The army was given over to it together with the continual burnt offering through disobedience.” Please read this sentence slowly. The original verb is passive: “was given over.” The text does not say that God’s people had no responsibility. It says that under God’s sovereignty there is a kind of “being given over” that is connected with “disobedience.” But the text does not say which sin, and does not say that every suffering is because of someone’s sin. Please do not turn this verse into blame for the suffering.

Finally, “It cast down truth to the ground, and it did its pleasure and prospered.” This sentence lets us see that evil may have a season of “prospering.” If you have seen someone who speaks big words, tears down God’s house, and seems impossible to stop, you are not the first to be confused. The text wrote this plainly. It does not deceive you. It only, in the next verse, lets us hear someone in heaven asking: “How long?”

Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.””

8.gram:
עֶרֶב בֹּקֶר אַלְפַּיִם וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת (two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings): the original is “evening, morning, two thousand three hundred”; it does not say “days” (יוֹם). “Evening and morning” is similar to the wording of Genesis 1, “there was evening and there was morning”: whether this is “2,300 days” or “1,150 days, with two offerings, morning and evening, each day,” has long been read in different ways; see the issues.

וְנִצְדַּק קֹדֶשׁ (the sanctuary will be cleansed): the Niphal form of the verb צָדַק (to be righteous), literally “to be vindicated” or “to be restored to rightness,” which the CUV renders “cleansed.” That rendering places the emphasis on the sanctuary being washed; the original is more like saying: the “rightness” of the sanctuary is declared anew.
8.exp:
The holy one in heaven asked a question we too often ask: “How long?” And the answer is a number made of “evenings and mornings.”

Verse 13 is very special: Daniel heard two holy ones speaking to each other. One was speaking, and the other asked: “How long will the vision … be?” This question is not Daniel’s; it is asked by those in heaven. It reminds us that the question “how long?” is not only asked by the weak. Heaven asks too. How many times in the Psalms have we heard the holy people cry like this: “How long, Yahweh?” This is not unbelief but an honest faith.

Then the answer: “To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.” Look at the original: “two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings.” This number has been read in many ways: some think it is 2,300 days; some think that “evening and morning” refers to the twice-daily continual offerings, so that it is 1,150 days; and some think it is a symbolic number that need not be exact. We set them side by side in the issues, and the position of these notes is clear: we do not use this number to count days.

Why? Because the point of the answer is not the number but the second half: “the sanctuary will be cleansed,” or “vindicated.” What the text gives is an answer with a “limit”: this destruction has an end. It has an “evening” and also a “morning.” For someone who is in the dark of night this is a very great comfort: the night is numbered.

Think for a moment: have you asked recently, “How long?” Perhaps about an illness, a prayer with no answer, a relationship not yet repaired. Do not feel your faith is weak because of it. The holy one in heaven has asked too. The text does not tell you not to ask. It only gives you a gentle answer: there is an evening, and there is also a morning; this night has a limit.

I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called, and said, “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.” So he came near where I stood; and when he came, I was frightened, and fell on my face; but he said to me, “Understand, son of man; for the vision belongs to the time of the end.” Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me, and set me upright. He said, “Behold, I will make you know what will be in the latter time of the indignation; for it belongs to the appointed time of the end.”

8.gram:
בֶּן־אָדָם (son of man): this word is literally “son of man,” and in Hebrew it means “a human being, a mortal”; it differs in wording and in context from the Aramaic בַּר אֱנָשׁ (one like a son of man) of chapter 7. Here an angel addresses Daniel; in Ezekiel, God repeatedly addresses the prophet this way. It is a form of address for “man” before God, and is not the one in chapter 7 who “came with the clouds of the sky.”

וַיַּעֲמִידֵנִי עַל־עָמְדִי (he set me upright where I stood): the causative form of the verb עָמַד (to stand). Before, the ram “could not stand”; now Daniel is “raised to his feet.” “Standing” is an undercurrent of this chapter.

לְעֶת־קֵץ (it belongs to the time of the end): קֵץ (end) is one of the tracked words of this book, appearing once each in 8:17 and 8:19, and together with 11:27, 35, 40 and 12:4, 9, 13 forming the trail of “the end” through the whole book.
8.exp:
The angel calls him “son of man,” not as praise but as a reminder: you are only a man, so you need to be raised up.

When Daniel saw the vision he “sought to understand it.” This is a very good habit: having seen, he did not hurry to speak, nor hurry to worry, but sought to understand. Then something like the appearance of a man stood before him; at the same time a man’s voice called: “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.” This is the first time in the whole Bible that an angel’s name appears: Gabriel. The name means “mighty one of God” or “God is my mighty one.” Notice this: it was the voice of God that commanded Gabriel to make Daniel understand. Understanding is given; it is not squeezed out by our own hard thinking.

Then Daniel’s reaction: “I was frightened, and fell on my face.” As in chapter 7, even Daniel was frightened. Then the angel said to him: “Understand, son of man.” Notice: this “son of man” is the Hebrew בֶּן־אָדָם, which in Ezekiel God repeatedly uses of the prophet, to remind him: you are a man, a finite man. It is a different word and a different position from the “one like a son of man coming with the clouds” of chapter 7. We do not mix the two together.

Daniel said: “Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground.” Even before the most important revelation, a man falls asleep. So the angel “touched me, and set me upright.” Before, the ram “could not stand”; now Daniel was raised up by a hand. The first thing God’s messenger did for a weak man was not to blame him but to raise him up.

Finally the angel said: “the vision belongs to the time of the end,” “the appointed time of the end.” Notice: what was given to Daniel was “understanding,” not a schedule of days. The purpose of the vision is to let people know that there is an “end” and an “appointed time,” and that all of it is in the hand of one God. We need not count it either; we only need to be raised up and then to stand.

8.gram:
מַלְכֵי מָדַי וּפָרָס (the kings of Media and Persia): “kings” is plural, and “Media and Persia” taken together form the two-horned ram. In this verse the text itself gives the answer, one of the rare places in the whole book where “the symbol is directly opened.”

מֶלֶךְ יָוָן (the king of Greece): יָוָן (Javan, Greece) in Genesis 10 is one of the descendants of Japheth; in the prophets it often refers to a people of the western coastlands.

וְלֹא בְכֹחוֹ (but not with his power): the four kingdoms did not have the power of the original great horn. The text does not say who the four kingdoms are, and gives no names.
8.exp:
In this chapter, rarely, the text itself opens the symbols: the ram is Media and Persia; the male goat is Greece.

In the whole book of Daniel there are a few times when the text tells us directly what the symbol means: in chapter 2, “you are the head of gold”; in chapter 7, “these great animals, which are four, are four kings”; in this chapter, “the ram which you saw, that had the two horns, they are the kings of Media and Persia.” These places are the steadiest footing when we read this book: what the text itself says, we follow in saying, without adding and without changing carelessly.

So in this passage there is nothing we need to “guess”: the two-horned ram is Media and Persia, two horns, one higher and one lower, the later one higher, which does not conflict with Persia’s coming later to surpass; the rough male goat is the king of Greece; the great horn between his eyes is the first king. The text goes this far, and gives him no name and no dates. We do not say more than the text.

Then the horn that was broken: “in the place where four stood up, four kingdoms will stand up out of the nation, but not with his power.” We have already seen this picture: when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and four came up in its place. The text does not say which four nations, and we do not chart a schedule. But notice one detail: “but not with his power.”

Why does the text say this specially? Perhaps as a reminder: power is diluted. A very great horn, once broken, is replaced by four that do not equal it. The powers people build, passed from one generation to the next, often become smaller, more fragmented, more quarrelsome than the original. This is not a prophecy about any country, but a very deep view of history: power that does not rest on authority God gave cannot last.

8.lit: ““In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, will stand up. His power will be mighty, but not by his own power. He will destroy awesomely, and will prosper in what he does. He will destroy the mighty ones and the holy people. Through his policy he will cause deceit to prosper in his hand. He will magnify himself in his heart, and he will destroy many in their security. He will also stand up against the prince of princes; but he will be broken without hand. “The vision of the evenings and mornings which has been told is true; but seal up the vision, for it belongs to many days to come.””

8.gram:
וּבְאֶפֶס יָד יִשָּׁבֵר (he will be broken without hand): literally “in the absence of a hand, he is broken.” “Broken” (שָׁבַר) is the same verb as the ram’s horns broken and the male goat’s horn broken in 8:7, 8: in the end even the one who broke others is broken.

וְלֹא בְכֹחוֹ (but not by his own power): 8:24 says his power will be mighty, “but not by his own power.” The power is not his own; it is given, or permitted; this follows from chapter 7, where the four beasts were “given dominion.”

סְתֹם הֶחָזוֹן (seal up the vision): the verb סָתַם (to seal up) shares a root with the “seal up” of 12:4, 9, and it is the close of the whole book: sealed, until the time comes.
8.exp:
The text says that this king’s power is “not by his own power,” and that his end is “broken without hand.” These are his two marks.

At the end of his explanation to Daniel the angel speaks of a king “of fierce face.” The text gives this king’s features: fierce face, understanding dark sentences; his power will be mighty, but not by his own power; he prospers in what he does; he destroys the mighty ones and the holy people; in his heart he magnifies himself; he stands up against the prince of princes. Notice that when we read this verse we must follow the features the text gives, not the names we have in mind.

Who this king is has long been read in many different ways: many scholars think it refers to a king of the Greek period who persecuted the Jews, including his defiling the sanctuary and abolishing the continual burnt offering, which resemble the description of this chapter; others think the little horn of this chapter is at the same time a foreshadowing of some figure of the last days; still others stress that it describes a “pattern”: in any generation, whoever speaks big words, tears down God’s house and attacks those who belong to God is in this pattern. We set the views side by side in the issues, and the position of these notes is: we do not identify anyone today, and we do not use it to chart a timetable. The fruit of the text is that people endure, not that they panic.

This king has three contrasts. First, his power is “not by his own power”; he is in fact permitted. Second, he destroys people “in their security,” by deceit, not openly. Third, he “stands up against the prince of princes,” which is opposition to God, in the same direction as the little horn of chapter 7 who “speaks words against the Most High.”

Then the ending: “he will be broken without hand.” This reminds us of the stone in chapter 2 that was “cut out without hands.” The text does not connect the two verses; we say only that it reminds us. The point is: his end does not come by human strength but by God’s work. Finally the angel said: “seal up the vision.” This is not because it is unimportant, but because the time has not yet come.

8.gram:
וָאָקוּם וָאֶעֱשֶׂה מְלֶאכֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ (I rose up, and did the king’s business): two verbs, “rose up” and “did,” the first קוּם (to stand up), the second עָשָׂה (to do). The text adds no adjective; it does not say how brave or faithful he was; it says only that he rose up and did the work.

וָאֶשְׁתּוֹמֵם עַל־הַמַּרְאֶה (I wondered at the vision): שׁמם (to be appalled) is from the same root as the “desolate” (שֹׁמֵם) of 8:13. The sanctuary was desolate, and Daniel too was stunned: the desolation was not only a matter outside him; it was also inside him.
8.exp:
After seeing the greatest vision, Daniel was sick for some days; then he rose up and did the king’s business.

The last verse is the most “ordinary” verse of this chapter, yet it is the one I most want you to stop and look at. Before it were the ram, the male goat, the little horn, the sanctuary destroyed, the two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings, Gabriel, the appointed time of the end. But at the end the text says: “I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick for some days. Then I rose up, and did the king’s business.”

Notice three things. First, he “was sick.” This vision was more than his body could bear. The text does not say that spiritual people do not get sick. It is very honest: having seen such things, he could not hold up. Second, he “rose up.” Sick for some days, he still rose. Not because he was strong, but because the angel had “set me upright”; this rising is something only someone who has been raised up can do. Third, he “did the king’s business.” He did not resign his post because he had seen a vision, and did not hide because he thought the world would have suffering. He returned to his work.

Then the text says another very honest sentence: “I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it.” Even the one who saw did not fully understand. His “wondering” is from the same root as the “desolate” of the sanctuary in 8:13. The desolation of the sanctuary was desolation in his heart too: he was a man who hurt together with his people.

This verse gives us a very practical practice: when we do not understand, return to our post. You may be sick, you may be stunned, you may not understand; but you need not put down today’s duties because of it. This chapter does not teach us to count days; it teaches us: go to work, care for your family, do what you should do today, and at the same time keep that vision you do not understand in your heart. Because the One who raised you up will also be waiting for you in the next morning.

9.gram:
בִּינֹתִי בַּסְּפָרִים (I understood by the books): בִּין (to understand) is the “understand” that Gabriel said to Daniel in chapter 8 (8:16, 17); now Daniel himself goes to “understand.” סְפָרִים is plural, “the books,” showing that at that time God’s word had already been collected and read.

וָאֶתְּנָה פָנַי אֶל־אֲדֹנָי הָאֱלֹהִים (I set my face to the Lord God): the action “set the face” also appears in Isaiah and Jeremiah; it is turning the face toward someone. He was not facing a schedule of days; he turned toward a Person.
9.exp:
When Daniel read the seventy years in the books, he did not pick up a pen to calculate; he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes, and turned his face to God.

Chapter 9 is, in the whole book, the chapter most like a “prayer book.” But please notice that it does not begin with prayer; it begins with reading: “In the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet, for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years.” He was reading Jeremiah. In Jeremiah there are two places that speak of seventy years (Jer 25:11–12; 29:10). He had read them.

Then what did he do? An ordinary person who read “seventy years” might calculate the days, might get excited, might say: it is nearly time. Daniel did not. The text says: “I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.” He turned his face to God. This is the first lesson of this chapter: God’s promise is not for calculating; it is for praying.

Why? Because a promise is a word of relationship, not a timetable. When God said seventy years, he was not sending Daniel a countdown timer; he was saying: I remember you, and I will bring you back. When Daniel read this sentence, his reaction was: “I must go and meet the God who is speaking.”

Is there a promise of God in your life that you have always wanted to “calculate”? Perhaps about a child, a job, the reconciliation of a family. Try, like Daniel, first putting down the abacus and turning your face to him. Fasting and sackcloth and ashes, these outward postures, are not the goal; they are ways of putting the whole person down. We will talk about their meaning in the issues.

We haven’t listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.”

9.gram:
וָאֶתְוַדֶּה (I made confession): the root of the Hithpael of יָדָה in Hebrew means both “to give thanks” and “to confess.” Confession and praise are in the same root: admitting what we are, and admitting what God is.

חָטָאנוּ וְעָוִינוּ וְהִרְשַׁעְנוּ וּמָרָדְנוּ (we have sinned, dealt perversely, done wickedly, and rebelled): four verbs, all in the first person “plural”: “we.” Not one is “they.”
9.exp:
As soon as he opened his mouth he first said who God is: great and dreadful, keeping covenant and showing loving kindness. Only then did he say that “we” have sinned.

The structure of this prayer is very clear: first praise, then confession. Verse 4: “Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments.” God is the one who “keeps covenant” and shows “loving kindness” (chesed). This is the foundation of the whole prayer. He was not confessing to a cold judge; he was confessing to a covenant-keeping God. You see, before the confession there is loving kindness.

Then come four verbs, one after another: we have sinned, dealt perversely, done wickedly and rebelled, even turning aside from the commandments and ordinances. These four words are different faces of sin in the Bible: missing the mark, twisting, wickedness, rebellion. Please notice: every verb is “we.” Not one “they.”

This point is very important and very counterintuitive. Daniel is the most praised person in the whole book. He had committed no great sin, and the text in this book records no fault of his. Yet when he prayed he said, “we have sinned.” This is the attitude of an intercessor: he puts himself inside the people and does not stand outside pointing the finger. It also reminds us of Ezra chapter 9 and Nehemiah chapter 9, the same “we.”

Have you ever prayed for a group you love, or a country, church or family you belong to? When you prayed, did you say “they,” or “we”? Daniel teaches us a very gentle posture: first praise, then say “we.”

9.lit: ““Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face, as it is today; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, who are near, and who are far off, through all the countries where you have driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against you. Lord, to us belongs confusion of face, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you. To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him. We haven’t obeyed Yahweh our God’s voice, to walk in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets. Yes, all Israel have transgressed your law, turning aside, that they should not obey your voice. “Therefore the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us; for we have sinned against him. He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us, and against our judges who judged us, by bringing on us a great evil; for under the whole sky, such has not been done as has been done to Jerusalem. As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil has come on us. Yet we have not entreated the favor of Yahweh our God, that we should turn from our iniquities and have discernment in your truth. Therefore Yahweh has watched over the evil, and brought it on us; for Yahweh our God is righteous in all his works which he does, and we have not obeyed his voice.”

לְךָ אֲדֹנָי הַצְּדָקָה וְלָנוּ בֹּשֶׁת הַפָּנִים (righteousness belongs to you, Lord, but to us confusion of face): two “belongs”: לְ you, לָ us. 9:7 sets God’s righteousness beside human shame; 9:9 says that mercies and forgiveness also belong to the Lord our God. The same sentence pattern: first righteousness and shame, then mercies and forgiveness.

לַאדֹנָי אֱלֹהֵינוּ הָרַחֲמִים וְהַסְּלִחוֹת (to the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness): both nouns are plural (רַחֲמִים、סְלִחוֹת), stressing abundance and repetition. He first admitted righteousness before speaking of mercy; and mercy was already present in the midst of judgment.
9.exp:
Righteousness belongs to him, shame belongs to us; and mercies and forgiveness also belong to him.

This is the middle of the whole prayer, and the longest stretch of confession. Notice its sentence pattern: “Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face.” Two “belongs” separate the two sides very clearly: God is righteous; we are ashamed. This is not self-belittling but honesty, which gives the prayer a place to stand.

But look at verse 9, the same pattern, but the content turned over: “To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him.” Mercies and forgiveness also belong to him. This sentence, placed in the middle of the confession, is the hinge of the whole prayer. As he confesses he remembers: he is a forgiving God. Without this, confession would become only heavy self-blame.

Then he mentions the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses, poured out on them (9:11). For many modern readers this is hard. We talk about its meaning in the issues. The point is: Daniel did not defend God or make excuses for him; he only said that God is righteous, and that all this is not that he broke the covenant but that we did. In verse 13 he adds a very deep word: “Yet we have not entreated the favor of Yahweh our God, that we should turn from our iniquities and have discernment in your truth.” The calamity came, and they had not yet turned.

Please do not turn this passage into blame on anyone who suffers. This is Daniel, on behalf of the whole people, speaking a review of history before God. He himself was one of the exiles. If you are suffering, the text does not ask you to say “I deserved it”; it wants you to know that there is a God who is righteous and also merciful, and you may bring your pain, and your weakness, into his presence.

9.grk: וְעַתָּה׀ אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהֵינוּ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתָ אֶֽת־עַמְּךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בְּיָד חֲזָקָה וַתַּֽעַשׂ־לְךָ שֵׁם כַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה חָטָאנוּ רָשָֽׁעְנוּ׃ אֲדֹנָי כְּכָל־צִדְקֹתֶךָ יָֽשָׁב־נָא אַפְּךָ וַחֲמָתְךָ מֵעִֽירְךָ יְרוּשָׁלִַם הַר־קָדְשֶׁךָ כִּי בַחֲטָאֵינוּ וּבַעֲוֺנוֹת אֲבֹתֵינוּ יְרוּשָׁלִַם וְעַמְּךָ לְחֶרְפָּה לְכָל־סְבִיבֹתֵֽינוּ׃ וְעַתָּה׀ שְׁמַע אֱלֹהֵינוּ אֶל־תְּפִלַּת עַבְדְּךָ וְאֶל־תַּחֲנוּנָיו וְהָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ עַל־מִקְדָּשְׁךָ הַשָּׁמֵם לְמַעַן אֲדֹנָֽי׃ הַטֵּה אֱלֹהַי׀ אָזְנְךָ וּֽשֲׁמָע עֵינֶיךָ וּרְאֵה שֹֽׁמְמֹתֵינוּ וְהָעִיר אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָא שִׁמְךָ עָלֶיהָ כִּי׀ לֹא עַל־צִדְקֹתֵינוּ אֲנַחְנוּ מַפִּילִים תַּחֲנוּנֵינוּ לְפָנֶיךָ כִּי עַל־רַחֲמֶיךָ הָרַבִּֽים׃ אֲדֹנָי׀ שְׁמָעָה אֲדֹנָי׀ סְלָחָה אֲדֹנָי הַֽקֲשִׁיבָה וַעֲשֵׂה אַל־תְּאַחַר לְמַֽעֲנְךָ אֱלֹהַי כִּֽי־שִׁמְךָ נִקְרָא עַל־עִירְךָ וְעַל־עַמֶּֽךָ׃
9.lit: ““Now, Lord our God, who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have gotten yourself renown, as it is today; we have sinned. We have done wickedly. Lord, according to all your righteousness, let your anger and please let your wrath be turned away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain; because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a reproach to all who are around us. “Now therefore, our God, listen to the prayer of your servant, and to his petitions, and cause your face to shine on your sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord’s sake. My God, turn your ear, and hear. Open your eyes, and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name; for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake. Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do. Don’t defer, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people are called by your name.””

9.gram:
אֲנַחְנוּ מַפִּילִים תַּחֲנוּנֵינוּ לְפָנֶיךָ (we present our petitions before you): the verb הִפִּיל is “to cause to fall”; literally “we cause our petitions to fall before you.” Like putting down a heavy load: the petition is not held up in the hand but set down.

אֲדֹנָי שְׁמָעָה אֲדֹנָי סְלָחָה אֲדֹנָי הַקְשִׁיבָה וַעֲשֵׂה (Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do): three “Lord”s, three verbs: hear, forgive, listen and act. This is the shortest and most urgent sentence of the whole prayer.

לְמַעַנְךָ אֱלֹהַי (for your own sake, my God): the final ground of prayer is not I, nor the people, but “you yourself,” “your name.”
9.exp:
The final ground of his petition is only three words: “for your own sake.”

This is the most moving stretch of prayer in the whole chapter. He first remembers the exodus from Egypt: “who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have gotten yourself renown, as it is today.” In the darkest hour he first remembers what God has done. That memory gives him courage to open his mouth. Then he asks God to turn his anger away from Jerusalem, “your holy mountain.” Then he says: “cause your face to shine on your sanctuary that is desolate.” This “face to shine” recalls the blessing in Numbers: “Yahweh make his face to shine on you.”

Then the heart of the chapter: “we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.” Please read this sentence slowly: we ask, not because we have any merit. Even prayer is not our merit. The verb in the original is more vivid: “we cast our petitions down before you.” Like putting down a heavy load. That load is shame, desolation, helplessness. He did not say, “Lord, look how repentant we are”; he said, “look at your mercy.”

The last verse is three short cries: “Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do. Don’t defer, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people are called by your name.” The ground of the whole prayer moves from the people to God’s name. This is the steadiest place in prayer: what we ask is not our face but his name.

If you have ever measured your prayer by “am I worthy?” this passage will set you free. You need not be worthy; you only need to bring your petition and set it down. Exchange “my righteousness” for “your mercy.” This is the deepest grace of this chapter.

9.grk: וְעוֹד אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר וּמִתְפַּלֵּל וּמִתְוַדֶּה חַטָּאתִי וְחַטַּאת עַמִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמַפִּיל תְּחִנָּתִי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהַי עַל הַר־קֹדֶשׁ אֱלֹהָֽי׃ וְעוֹד אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר בַּתְּפִלָּה וְהָאִישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵל אֲשֶׁר רָאִיתִי בֶחָזוֹן בַּתְּחִלָּה מֻעָף בִּיעָף נֹגֵעַ אֵלַי כְּעֵת מִנְחַת־עָֽרֶב׃ וַיָּבֶן וַיְדַבֵּר עִמִּי וַיֹּאמַר דָּנִיֵּאל עַתָּה יָצָאתִי לְהַשְׂכִּילְךָ בִינָֽה׃ בִּתְחִלַּת תַּחֲנוּנֶיךָ יָצָא דָבָר וַאֲנִי בָּאתִי לְהַגִּיד כִּי חֲמוּדוֹת אָתָּה וּבִין בַּדָּבָר וְהָבֵן בַּמַּרְאֶֽה׃
9.lit: “While I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God; yes, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering. He instructed me and talked with me, and said, Daniel, “I have now come to give you wisdom and understanding. At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, and I have come to tell you; for you are greatly beloved. Therefore consider the matter, and understand the vision.”

9.gram:
עוֹד אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר בַּתְּפִלָּה (while I was still speaking in prayer): his prayer was not yet finished. The participle מְדַבֵּר (speaking) appears in 9:20 and 21, stressing that the answer arrived in the midst of the prayer, not after the prayer was over.

בִּתְחִלַּת תַּחֲנוּנֶיךָ יָצָא דָבָר (at the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out): דָּבָר can be “word,” “command” or “matter.” This “word” had already “gone out” (יָצָא). At the moment you began to ask, God’s word was already on the way.

חֲמוּדוֹת (greatly beloved): literally “desired, very precious”; in the book of Daniel it appears three times, in 9:23 and 10:11, 19, as Gabriel’s name for him.
9.exp:
Before the prayer was finished the answer was already flying to him; and the name he was given was “greatly beloved.”

Verses 20 and 21 each have “while I was speaking,” a very deliberate repetition: Gabriel arrived in the midst of his prayer. His prayer was not yet finished, and the answer came. This reminds us that God’s response does not wait until we have finished speaking before it begins to move. His word had gone out long before.

Look at the second thing Gabriel said: “At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, and I have come to tell you.” From the moment you began to ask, God’s “word” went out, and I (Gabriel) have come to tell it to you. This sentence deserves a pause and slow thought: one of your prayers may look as if it has no answer yet; but the text says the word has already gone out. He moves earlier than we do.

Then this name: “for you are greatly beloved.” The original is חֲמוּדוֹת, literally “very precious, very much desired.” He was not called beloved because he prayed well; he was beloved before the prayer. Prayer is not an exchange to earn love; it is speaking within love. For a man who had just confessed sin for a whole chapter, how his heart must have been comforted to hear this sentence.

One more thing: “the time of the evening offering.” At that time the temple was gone and the evening offering had stopped, but Daniel still remembered that hour. Prayer became his evening offering: Psalm 141 says, “the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.” With no temple, there was still an evening offering: he had carried the altar into his own prayer.

שָׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעִים (seventy sevens): שָׁבֻעִים is the plural of “seven,” meaning “a set of seven”; the original does not say days, months or years. In the Bible there is a sabbath year every seven years (Lev 25), and a jubilee after seven times seven years, so the reading “years” has a basis, but the original does not say it directly.

לְכַלֵּא הַפֶּשַׁע וּלְחַתֵּם חַטָּאוֹת (to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins): in the standard manuscripts there is a difference of writing and reading here, which has long been handled in different ways; but the direction of the text is clear: sin is stopped, ended and atoned for.

לִמְשֹׁחַ קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (to anoint the most holy): קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (most holy) in the Old Testament can mean “the most holy place,” and can also mean a “most holy” person or thing. This phrase has long been read in different ways; see the issues.
9.exp:
What the seventy sevens are to accomplish is six things: to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy.

This verse is the most studied in the whole book, and also the one that most easily leads people to calculate days. First, our position: in the stance of the whole book we have already said that these notes do not count days and do not set up a timetable. There have long been many different readings, and we set them side by side in the issues, including: that the seventy sevens point to a stretch of history beginning in ancient times; that they point to the coming of Christ; that they point to a time still further on; or that they are a symbolic, structured period. We do not decide for you which one.

Here I want you to look at the direction of this verse. Gabriel came to answer Daniel’s prayer. Daniel had prayed: the seventy years are up; forgive, and let Jerusalem be desolate no more. God’s answer was a larger vision: “Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city” (the word is literally “sevens”). The seventy years stretched into “seventy sevens.” God did not answer only the matter of seventy years; he lifted the eyes to something farther.

This verse lists six things in two groups. The first group, three things, is about “sin”: to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make atonement for iniquity. The second group, three things, is about “fulfillment”: to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy. Please notice that not one of these six is military, political or geographical; all of them deal with sin and righteousness.

This is the center of this chapter: God’s answer to Daniel was not a schedule of days but a promise that sin would be dealt with. If today you are confused by a complicated history or a great suffering, please remember: what God cares about most is dealing with sin and bringing in everlasting righteousness.

9.grk: וְתֵדַע וְתַשְׂכֵּל מִן־מֹצָא דָבָר לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת יְרֽוּשָׁלִַם עַד־מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד שָׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעָה וְשָׁבֻעִים שִׁשִּׁים וּשְׁנַיִם תָּשׁוּב וְנִבְנְתָה רְחוֹב וְחָרוּץ וּבְצוֹק הָעִתִּֽים׃ וְאַחֲרֵי הַשָּׁבֻעִים שִׁשִּׁים וּשְׁנַיִם יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ וְאֵין לוֹ וְהָעִיר וְהַקֹּדֶשׁ יַשְׁחִית עַם נָגִיד הַבָּא וְקִצּוֹ בַשֶּׁטֶף וְעַד קֵץ מִלְחָמָה נֶחֱרֶצֶת שֹׁמֵמֽוֹת׃ וְהִגְבִּיר בְּרִית לָרַבִּים שָׁבוּעַ אֶחָד וַחֲצִי הַשָּׁבוּעַ יַשְׁבִּית׀ זֶבַח וּמִנְחָה וְעַל כְּנַף שִׁקּוּצִים מְשֹׁמֵם וְעַד־כָּלָה וְנֶחֱרָצָה תִּתַּךְ עַל־שֹׁמֵֽם׃פ
9.lit: ““Know therefore and discern that from the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be built again, with street and moat, even in troubled times. After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One will be cut off, and will have nothing. The people of the prince who come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end will be with a flood, and war will be even to the end. Desolations are determined. He will make a firm covenant with many for one week. In the middle of the week he will cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease. On the wing of abominations will come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, wrath will be poured out on the desolate.””

מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד (the Anointed One, the prince): מָשִׁיחַ (anointed one) in the Old Testament can refer to a king or a priest, and also to Cyrus (Isa 45:1). The “Anointed One, the prince” of 9:25 and the “Anointed One” of 9:26 are the same word, but whether they refer to the same person has long been read in different ways.

יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ וְאֵין לוֹ (the Anointed One will be cut off, and will have nothing): כָּרַת (to cut off) is passive, and in the Old Testament is often used of being “cut off from the people.” וְאֵין לוֹ is literally “and there is not to him”; its translation and reading have long differed.

וְהִגְבִּיר בְּרִית לָרַבִּים (he will make a firm covenant with many): who the subject is, and what kind of time “one week” is, have long been read in different ways; see the issues.
9.exp:
These three verses are the hardest passage in the whole book. We do not calculate; we look only at their direction: the Anointed One is cut off, desolation is decreed, and God’s end is decreed too.

First let us say plainly: these three verses are among the most disputed texts in the whole Bible. There have long been many different readings. Some point the “Anointed One, the prince” to Cyrus or to a certain high priest; some to Christ; some point “the people of the prince” to an ancient empire, some to later Rome, some to a figure of the last days. We set the views side by side in the issues; we do not decide for you, and we certainly do not set up a timetable here.

So what can we say? First, we see the order the text gives: first the rebuilding of Jerusalem, in troubled times; then the Anointed One is cut off; then destruction and war, to the end. Second, we see a word that recurs in this passage: desolation. “Desolations are determined” (9:26); “one who makes desolate” (9:27). This reminds us of chapter 8, the desolation of the sanctuary. Third, we see the last sentence: “wrath will be poured out on the desolate,” to the full end that was determined. The one who destroys is, in the end, also met by God’s wrath poured out.

Please notice: this passage stands between two “seventies,” inside the answer to a prayer. Its purpose is not to make people anxious but to say: desolation is decreed, but desolation also has an end. This is the same answer we saw in chapter 8: the night is numbered.

If you want to know more, the issues have each view, and you can read slowly. If you want to carry away only one sentence, it is this: these three verses are not a schedule of days; in a very large history, God is still dealing with sin and still decreeing the end. When you reach this point, do not be anxious; go back to 9:18: we ask, not because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.

10.grk: בִּשְׁנַת שָׁלוֹשׁ לְכוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס דָּבָר נִגְלָה לְדָֽנִיֵּאל אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר וֶאֱמֶת הַדָּבָר וְצָבָא גָדוֹל וּבִין אֶת־הַדָּבָר וּבִינָה לוֹ בַּמַּרְאֶֽה׃ בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֲנִי דָֽנִיֵּאל הָיִיתִי מִתְאַבֵּל שְׁלֹשָׁה שָׁבֻעִים יָמִֽים׃ לֶחֶם חֲמֻדוֹת לֹא אָכַלְתִּי וּבָשָׂר וָיַיִן לֹא־בָא אֶל־פִּי וְסוֹךְ לֹא־סָכְתִּי עַד־מְלֹאת שְׁלֹשֶׁת שָׁבֻעִים יָמִֽים׃פ וּבְיוֹם עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה לַחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי הָיִיתִי עַל יַד הַנָּהָר הַגָּדוֹל הוּא חִדָּֽקֶל׃
10.lit: “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the thing was true, even a great warfare. He understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision. In those days I, Daniel, was mourning three whole weeks. I ate no pleasant bread. No meat or wine came into my mouth. I didn’t anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled. In the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel,”

10.gram:
וְצָבָא גָדוֹל (even a great warfare): צָבָא can be “army,” and can also be “hard service, warfare”; גָדוֹל is “great.” This phrase has long been translated variously as “great warfare,” “great hardship” and “great army”; see the issues.

שְׁלֹשָׁה שָׁבֻעִים יָמִים (three whole weeks): the word “days” (יָמִים) is added specially to distinguish this from the “seventy sevens” (שָׁבֻעִים) of chapter 9: here it is three sevens of “days,” not a set of seven “years.” This detail shows that the same word “seven” is decided by its context.
10.exp:
He mourned three whole weeks, ate no pleasant bread and did not anoint himself; this is a man mourning for the future of the people.

This is the last vision of the whole book, running from chapter 10 to chapter 12. The text first gives the time: the third year of Cyrus king of Persia. Notice that this is already the Persian era. Babylon is past. Chapter 1 said, “even to the first year of king Cyrus,” and Daniel was still there; now it is the third year of Cyrus, and the old man is still there. His name is still called Belteshazzar, the name Babylon gave, which has followed him all along. But in this chapter his name makes us see that in a foreign land he is still Daniel, “God is my judge.”

The text says, “the thing was true, even a great warfare.” The original צָבָא גָדוֹל has long been read in many ways, and we set them side by side in the issues. We can quietly say first: whichever it is, this is a word about something hard and very great.

Then Daniel himself: “I, Daniel, was mourning three whole weeks.” Why was he mourning? The text does not say. We only know that he ate no pleasant bread and did not anoint himself with oil. This is the look of mourning. Over the years some have guessed that it was for the situation of the returned people, or for the state of Jerusalem; the text gives none of these, and we do not supply it for him. But we can see this: he was not a man for himself alone. His mourning was for the future of God’s people.

Please think: have you ever mourned over something not your own? For a church, a country, a child’s future. Such mourning is not weakness; it is love. This chapter begins with the mourning of an old man, and then God’s answer comes.

10.grk: וָאֶשָּׂא אֶת־עֵינַי וָאֵרֶא וְהִנֵּה אִישׁ־אֶחָד לָבוּשׁ בַּדִּים וּמָתְנָיו חֲגֻרִים בְּכֶתֶם אוּפָֽז׃ וּגְוִיָּתוֹ כְתַרְשִׁישׁ וּפָנָיו כְּמַרְאֵה בָרָק וְעֵינָיו כְּלַפִּידֵי אֵשׁ וּזְרֹֽעֹתָיו וּמַרְגְּלֹתָיו כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל וְקוֹל דְּבָרָיו כְּקוֹל הָמֽוֹן׃ וְרָאִיתִי אֲנִי דָנִיֵּאל לְבַדִּי אֶת־הַמַּרְאָה וְהָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ עִמִּי לֹא רָאוּ אֶת־הַמַּרְאָה אֲבָל חֲרָדָה גְדֹלָה נָפְלָה עֲלֵיהֶם וַֽיִּבְרְחוּ בְּהֵחָבֵֽא׃ וַאֲנִי נִשְׁאַרְתִּי לְבַדִּי וָֽאֶרְאֶה אֶת־הַמַּרְאָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר־בִּי כֹּח וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית וְלֹא עָצַרְתִּי כֹּֽחַ׃ וָאֶשְׁמַע אֶת־קוֹל דְּבָרָיו וּכְשָׁמְעִי אֶת־קוֹל דְּבָרָיו וַאֲנִי הָיִיתִי נִרְדָּם עַל־פָּנַי וּפָנַי אָֽרְצָה׃
10.lit: “I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, there was a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz. His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches. His arms and his feet were like burnished bronze. The voice of his words was like the voice of a multitude. I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone, and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; for my face grew deathly pale, and I retained no strength. Yet I heard the voice of his words. When I heard the voice of his words, then I fell into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.”

10.gram:
אִישׁ אֶחָד לָבוּשׁ בַּדִּים (a man clothed in linen): אִישׁ (man), בַּדִּים (linen). In Ezekiel 9–10 the man in linen is also a messenger from heaven. The appearance here has some similarity to the descriptions in Ezekiel 1:26–28 and Revelation 1:13–15, but we do not equate them; see the issues.

וְלֹא רָאוּ אֶת־הַמַּרְאָה (they did not see the vision): those with him did not see it, yet fled in quaking. This has a similar structure to Acts 9:7, where Saul’s companions “heard the voice, but saw no one,” though each stands on its own.
10.exp:
Only Daniel saw this vision; those with him did not see it, yet fled in quaking; only he was left.

The text gives the appearance of this one who comes: clothed in linen, with a belt of pure gold; his body like beryl, his face like lightning, his eyes like torches, his arms and feet like burnished bronze, the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude. This is a glory beyond description. Who this is has long been read variously: some think he is a glorious angel, like Gabriel; some think he is a higher being, even Christ, because the description of Christ in Revelation 1 has some similarity; and some think the text does not say, and we need not guess. We set the views side by side in the issues; we do not decide for you.

I want you to notice another detail: “I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision.” Those with him did not see it, yet fled in quaking. There is an experience others cannot see. You may have had it: a burden others do not understand; a moment only you and God know. Please do not doubt its reality because no one saw, and please do not feel alone because others did not see. God is the one who sees.

Then Daniel’s reaction: no strength remained in him, his face grew deathly pale, and he retained no strength; when he heard the voice of his words, he fell into a deep sleep on his face. A man who had mourned for the people for three weeks, at the sight of the glory, fell down. This reminds us of chapter 8, where he also fell asleep; and it reminds us of Isaiah, who said, “Woe is me! For I am undone.” Before glory man has no strength; this is honest.

But this chapter does not stop here. Read on: a hand came.

וְעֲמֹד עַל־עָמְדֶךָ (stand upright where you stand): the root עמד (to stand) twice: first “stand up,” then “stand in your place.” He was not raised to another place; he was raised and returned to the place where he had been.

אִישׁ־חֲמֻדוֹת (greatly beloved man): the same word (חֲמוּדוֹת) as Gabriel’s “you are greatly beloved” in 9:23. In this book it appears three times: 9:23, 10:11, 10:19.
10.exp:
A hand touched him and he rose a little on his knees and the palms of his hands; then a voice called him: greatly beloved man.

The man on the ground did not get up by himself. The text says: “a hand touched me, which set me on my knees and on the palms of my hands.” Notice this picture: he had not yet stood; he only rose a little on his knees and palms. This is a very gentle, step-by-step raising. God does not force a man who has fallen to stand straight at once; he first touches him and lets him prop himself up a little with knee and hand.

Then the first words this visitor spoke were not blame, not a command, but a name: “Daniel, you greatly beloved man.” Do you remember? In chapter 9 Gabriel called him this too. The same name appears three times in this book. To a man on the ground without strength, before saying anything else, he was first called “greatly beloved.” This is what God says first to the weak: not “be strong” but “you are beloved.”

Then came the command: “understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright; for I have been sent to you, now.” Please notice that the original has two “stands”: “stand up, in the place where you stand.” The first stand is being raised; the second is returning to your place. This is the same undercurrent as chapter 8: standing. The ram could not stand; Daniel was raised up.

Finally the text honestly says: “I stood trembling.” When he stood, he was still trembling. This detail is warm: God does not require that we stop trembling before we stand. We can tremble and stand at the same time. If you are trembling today, you need not wait to stop trembling before you come.

But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me because I remained there with the kings of Persia. Now I have come to make you understand what will happen to your people in the latter days; for the vision is yet for many days.””

נִשְׁמְעוּ דְבָרֶיךָ (your words were heard): the passive נִשְׁמְעוּ, literally “were heard.” The verb is passive, the subject “your words”; God is the one who hears, and this passive is a respectful way of speaking.

שַׂר מַלְכוּת פָּרַס עֹמֵד לְנֶגְדִּי (the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me): שַׂר (prince, chief) is also the word used in 8:11, “the prince of the army,” and in 10:21, “Michael your prince”; “withstood me” (עֹמֵד לְנֶגְדִּי) is a posture of “opposing.” In this book the word שַׂר can refer to a heavenly or an earthly one, as context decides; see the issues.
10.exp:
The messenger said: from the first day you set your heart to understand, your words were heard; delay does not mean not heard.

This is the most important verse of this chapter: “Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard. I have come for your words’ sake.” Notice three things. First, do not be afraid. This is the first thing God’s messenger said to a trembling man. Second, from the first day. Not the twenty-first day, not when he had fasted and prayed the full three weeks, but “from the first day” his words were heard. Third, I have come for your words’ sake. His prayer was the reason the messenger came.

Have you felt that you prayed a long time and there was no response? Sometimes we think God has not heard. This verse says to you: “from the first day.” Your words were heard from the first day. Delay does not mean not heard.

Then the text says one thing: “But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days.” This sentence has long been read in many different ways, and we set them side by side in the issues. Some think it refers to a spiritual power; some think it refers to the rulers of Persia, or the king’s representatives; and some think the text uses a language in which heaven and earth correspond. We do not turn this verse into a teaching of “territorial spirit warfare”: we do not teach you to identify and attack the spirit of a place. What this verse gives us is a deep comfort: in heaven, over your prayer, much is going on that we cannot see. You need not know the details; you only need to know: the words have been heard.

Michael came to help. Please notice: help is given. Verse 12 is the whole point: from the first day. Not from the twenty-first day. This is the sentence this chapter wants you to remember.

10.lit: “When he had spoken these words to me, I set my face toward the ground, and was mute. Behold, one in the likeness of the sons of men touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth, and spoke and said to him who stood before me, “My lord, by reason of the vision my sorrows have overtaken me, and I retain no strength. For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? For as for me, immediately there remained no strength in me. There was no breath left in me.” Then one like the appearance of a man touched me again, and he strengthened me. He said, “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid. Peace be to you. Be strong. Yes, be strong.” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened, and said, “Let my lord speak; for you have strengthened me.””

10.gram:
וַיְחַזְּקֵנִי (he strengthened me): the Piel of חָזַק (to be strong): “made me strong.” It occurs in 10:18 and 19; then the command of 10:19, “be strong” (חֲזַק), is the same root. Notice: first he was “made strong,” and only then “commanded to be strong.”

שָׁלוֹם לָךְ אִישׁ־חֲמֻדוֹת (peace be to you, greatly beloved man): in Israel שָׁלוֹם is a blessing, not only “no conflict” but “wholeness.” This is the blessing the messenger gave Daniel in this chapter.
10.exp:
The speechless man had his lips touched; the man with no strength was touched twice before he was told: be strong.

This is the gentlest passage of this chapter. “I set my face toward the ground, and was mute.” A man who had mourned for the people for three weeks, at the sight of the vision, could not even speak. Then one in the likeness of the sons of men “touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth.” Notice: he opened his mouth because his lips were touched. God not only raises people to stand; he also lets the mute open their mouths.

Then the first thing he said was honest: “For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? For as for me, immediately there remained no strength in me. There was no breath left in me.” See, he did not pretend to be strong and did not say “I am fine.” He said his helplessness just as it was. God does not despise such words.

Then: “one like the appearance of a man touched me again, and he strengthened me.” This is the second touch. The first raised him to stand; the second gave him strength. Then came the command: “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid. Peace be to you. Be strong. Yes, be strong.” See this order: first he touched and gave strength, and only then said: be strong. This is not asking a man without strength to make himself strong; it is first making him strong, and then telling him to be strong.

You may have had such moments: told to “be strong,” and with no strength. This passage tells you: true strength is not gritted teeth. It is touched into you, spoken into you, given. In the end he said: “Let my lord speak; for you have strengthened me.” He had strength not because of himself but “because of you.” This is the strength of having no self.

10.gram:
בִּכְתָב אֱמֶת (in the writing of truth): כְּתָב (writing) and אֱמֶת (truth): this is a way of saying “truth already written down.” In this book it forms a line with 7:10, “the books were opened,” and 12:1, “everyone who is found written in the book”: in heaven there is a book.

שַׂרְכֶם (your prince): שַׂר (prince) with “your” (־כֶם): Michael is “your prince,” one who belongs to God’s people. 12:1 also has “Michael, the great prince who stands for the children of your people,” which echoes this.
10.exp:
He did not tell everything; he told Daniel only: there is a book of truth, and there is a prince who is yours.

The messenger said: “Do you know why I have come to you?” This is a question, and also an invitation. He went on to say that he would return to fight with the prince of Persia, and afterward the prince of Greece would come. This sentence has long been read in various ways, and we set them side by side in the issues. We do not turn this verse into a tool for predicting geopolitics, nor into a call to “go and attack the spirit of a place.” This is a description in which heaven and earth correspond, and its aim is to let Daniel understand: in the history he saw it is not only people who are moving; a greater God is in charge.

Then he said: “I will tell you that which is inscribed in the writing of truth.” “The writing of truth” is a book written down. In chapter 7 we saw “the books were opened”; in chapter 12 we will see “everyone who is found written in the book.” In heaven there is a book. What God will accomplish is “already written,” not on a sudden whim. This gives us a very deep security: history is not a tangle of threads; one has already written its direction.

Finally he said: “There is no one who holds with me against these, but Michael your prince.” Michael is “your prince”: he belongs to God’s people. This sentence is not meant to make us learn the details of angelology but to say: you are not alone. In heaven, one stands on your side.

This chapter ends very quietly. He did not finish, and gave no dates. He left only one answer: your words were heard; you were touched twice; be strong; there is a book of truth. This is the reply to a man who mourned for his people.

11.lit: ““As for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him. “Now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings will stand up in Persia; and the fourth will be far richer than all of them. When he has grown strong through his riches, he will stir up all against the realm of Greece. A mighty king will stand up, who will rule with great dominion, and do according to his will. When he stands up, his kingdom will be broken, and will be divided toward the four winds of the sky, but not to his posterity, nor according to his dominion with which he ruled; for his kingdom will be plucked up, even for others besides these.”
