11.gram:
אֱמֶת אַגִּיד (I will declare the truth): אֱמֶת means words that are reliable and can stand; the many details that follow in this chapter are all said under this word “truth.”

עָמְדִי לְמַחֲזִיק וּלְמָעוֹז: “I stood by him to support and to protect him”; עמד (to stand) is an undercurrent of the whole book, and here even a messenger from heaven “stands” beside a king.
11.exp:
The messenger from heaven said: truth I will show you; and even in the first year of Darius, I stood beside him.

Chapter 11 does not start anew; it continues chapter 10, and the same messenger is still speaking. His very first sentence lifts the camera higher: “In the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.” How the subject and object of this sentence are to be understood has long been read in different ways, and we set them side by side among the issues; what we can see first is this: between the changes of empires on earth, in heaven someone stands and supports.

Then he uses a very weighty word: “truth.” The long run of kings and kings that follows is not a novel and not arbitrary prediction but something called true. In a few sentences the text passes through Persia and comes to a “mighty king,” whose realm is at its height and yet breaks at the very top, divided toward the four winds of heaven and given to others than his posterity. Most readers through the ages have read this king as the beginning of the Hellenistic age; we do not match them one by one here, but first hold on to one point: the moment a man is strongest is the moment his kingdom breaks most easily.

This gives a very practical comfort: whatever power stands before our eyes, in the eyes of “truth” it has its limit; and the one who “stands beside” is always there.

11.gram:
וּלְקֵץ שָׁנִים (after some years; literally, at the end of years): this is the first time קֵץ appears in this chapter; it is not “the end of the world” but “the end of a stretch of time.” In this chapter the word appears several times, and its meaning has to be judged from the context.

הַנֶּגֶב／הַצָּפוֹן: “the south / the north” are directions seen from Israel’s position, not from the king’s; the text always looks from the side of the “glorious land.”
11.exp:
The kings of the south and of the north rise and fall, all seen from the position of the “glorious land.”

From verse 5 the text begins to speak of the comings and goings of the two kings, south and north. Notice the text’s viewpoint: “south” and “north” are directions seen from Israel. Most readers through the ages have understood them as the Hellenistic age, the marriages, alliances, broken covenants and wars between two dynasties around Egypt and Syria; the details have long been matched in different ways, and we set them side by side among the issues, and say plainly that these notes do not match them one by one for you and set no dates for these details.

Look at the tone of this passage: marriage and covenant look like peace, “but she will not retain the strength.” Human alliances often cover the deepest calculation with the most beautiful form; and the text finishes such a covenant in two words: “cannot stand.” This echoes the undercurrent of the whole book: what truly “stands” is not the kings joined by scheming but the God of heaven.

Reading such history today we may feel it is remote, but the human nature it speaks of is not remote at all: we too often wrap the deepest self-protection in the most beautiful relationship. This passage reminds us: do not put your security on such powers that cannot stand.

11.lit: “His sons will wage war, and will assemble a multitude of great forces, which will come on, and overflow, and pass through. They will return and wage war, even to his fortress. “The king of the south will be moved with anger, and will come out and fight with him, even with the king of the north. He will send out a great multitude, and the multitude will be given into his hand. The multitude will be lifted up, and his heart will be exalted. He will cast down tens of thousands, but he won’t prevail. The king of the north will return, and will send out a multitude greater than the former. He will come on at the end of the times, even of years, with a great army and with much substance. “In those times many will stand up against the king of the south. Also the children of the violent among your people will lift themselves up to establish the vision; but they will fall. So the king of the north will come and cast up a mound, and take a well-fortified city. The forces of the south won’t stand, neither will his chosen people, neither will there be any strength to stand. But he who comes against him will do according to his own will, and no one will stand before him. He will stand in the glorious land, and destruction will be in his hand. He will set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and with him equitable conditions. He will perform them. He will give him the daughter of women, to corrupt her; but she will not stand, and won’t be for him. After this he will turn his face to the islands, and will take many; but a prince will cause the reproach offered by him to cease. Yes, moreover, he will cause his reproach to turn on him. Then he will turn his face toward the fortresses of his own land; but he will stumble and fall, and won’t be found. “Then one who will cause a tax collector to pass through the kingdom to maintain its glory will stand up in his place; but within few days he shall be destroyed, not in anger, and not in battle.”

11.gram:
בְּאֶרֶץ הַצְּבִי (in the glorious land): this title appears three times in this chapter (verses 16, 41, 45) and is the coordinate of the whole chapter: all the comings and goings of the nations happen at the edge of the “glorious land.”

וַיִּנָּשְׂאוּ חָזוֹן לְהַעֲמִיד (11:14): “to fulfill the vision”; the original literally says “to make the vision stand.” Some have read it this way: these violent men wanted to “accomplish” the vision themselves, and this do-it-yourself way made them fall instead.
11.exp:
Wars come and go, yet the text keeps saying: cannot stand, fall, not prevail; the only one who stays unmoved in the middle is the “glorious land.”

These eleven verses are the longest stretch of the chapter and the one where readers most easily get lost: wave after wave of armies, marriages and broken covenants, victories and retreats. We do not match them one by one here, because scholars through the ages have matched the details in many and differing ways; we only hold on to three words that keep recurring.

The first is “stand” (עמד): the text says again and again that no one can stand before him, that the arms of the south cannot stand, that this thing will not stand. Human strength falls one after another. The second is “fall” (כשל), used of the ambitious, of those who try to fulfill the vision with their own hands, and also of the proud commander: he turns toward the strongholds of his own land, but “he will stumble and fall, and won’t be found.” The third is the “glorious land”: the two kings go back and forth, and both must pass through it, tread on it and use it. For God’s people this is a heavy situation: their own land has become someone else’s battlefield.

But notice: not one line here says which king God’s people should follow in this war. The purpose of the text is not to teach us to take sides but to let us see: when great nations fight each other, God’s people are to fix their eyes on the God who “stands unmoved,” not on who wins and who loses.

11.grk: וְעָמַד עַל־כַּנּוֹ נִבְזֶה וְלֹא־נָתְנוּ עָלָיו הוֹד מַלְכוּת וּבָא בְשַׁלְוָה וְהֶחֱזִיק מַלְכוּת בַּחֲלַקְלַקּֽוֹת׃ וּזְרֹעוֹת הַשֶּׁטֶף יִשָּׁטְפוּ מִלְּפָנָיו וְיִשָּׁבֵרוּ וְגַם נְגִיד בְּרִֽית׃ וּמִן־הִֽתְחַבְּרוּת אֵלָיו יַעֲשֶׂה מִרְמָה וְעָלָה וְעָצַם בִּמְעַט־גּֽוֹי׃ בְּשַׁלְוָה וּבְמִשְׁמַנֵּי מְדִינָה יָבוֹא וְעָשָׂה אֲשֶׁר לֹא־עָשׂוּ אֲבֹתָיו וַאֲבוֹת אֲבֹתָיו בִּזָּה וְשָׁלָל וּרְכוּשׁ לָהֶם יִבְזוֹר וְעַל מִבְצָרִים יְחַשֵּׁב מַחְשְׁבֹתָיו וְעַד־עֵֽת׃
11.lit: ““In his place a contemptible person will stand up, to whom they had not given the honor of the kingdom; but he will come in time of security, and will obtain the kingdom by flatteries. The overwhelming forces will be overwhelmed from before him, and will be broken. Yes, also the prince of the covenant. After the treaty made with him he will work deceitfully; for he will come up, and will become strong, with a small people. In time of security he will come even on the fattest places of the province. He will do that which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers’ fathers. He will scatter among them prey, plunder, and substance. Yes, he will devise his plans against the strongholds, even for a time.”

11.gram:
נִבְזֶה (contemptible): literally “one who is despised,” a passive form: this man, in men’s eyes, was originally looked down on and had no right; he gains the kingdom not by lawful succession but by “smooth words.”

עַד־עֵת (only for a time): this “time” is a boundary; however fine his scheming, it lies only within this line.
11.exp:
He was not invited up; he slipped up with smooth words; and the text sums up all his scheming in five words: only until a time.

In verse 21 the text changes the camera: no longer the comings and goings of two kings but one man, “a contemptible person.” The original means “one who is despised”: men had not given him the honor of the kingdom, yet when people were unguarded he took power with flattering words. Most readers through the ages have understood this man as a ruler of the Hellenistic age who persecuted the Jews; others read from other angles; we set them side by side among the issues, and say plainly that these notes do not connect this man to any person or regime today, and do not use him to identify anyone in the future as in prophecy.

This man’s way is written out clearly by a few verbs: flatter, deceive, plan, scatter wealth. It is a very familiar pattern of power: not by lawful trust but by smooth words, by pleasing people, by handing out benefits to buy hearts. We have seen it today too, in small versions in companies, churches and clans.

But the text leaves a very quiet sentence: “yet only for a time.” However refined his plans and however skillful his means, all are placed inside a boundary. This is the greatest comfort of this chapter: human scheming has a timetable, and that timetable is not in his hands.

11.grk: וְיָעֵר כֹּחוֹ וּלְבָבוֹ עַל־מֶלֶךְ הַנֶּגֶב בְּחַיִל גָּדוֹל וּמֶלֶךְ הַנֶּגֶב יִתְגָּרֶה לַמִּלְחָמָה בְּחַֽיִל־גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם עַד־מְאֹד וְלֹא יַעֲמֹד כִּֽי־יַחְשְׁבוּ עָלָיו מַחֲשָׁבֽוֹת׃ וְאֹכְלֵי פַת־בָּגוֹ יִשְׁבְּרוּהוּ וְחֵילוֹ יִשְׁטוֹף וְנָפְלוּ חֲלָלִים רַבִּֽים׃ וּשְׁנֵיהֶם הַמְּלָכִים לְבָבָם לְמֵרָע וְעַל־שֻׁלְחָן אֶחָד כָּזָב יְדַבֵּרוּ וְלֹא תִצְלָח כִּי־עוֹד קֵץ לַמּוֹעֵֽד׃ וְיָשֹׁב אַרְצוֹ בִּרְכוּשׁ גָּדוֹל וּלְבָבוֹ עַל־בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ וְעָשָׂה וְשָׁב לְאַרְצֽוֹ׃ לַמּוֹעֵד יָשׁוּב וּבָא בַנֶּגֶב וְלֹֽא־תִהְיֶה כָרִאשֹׁנָה וְכָאַחֲרֹנָֽה׃ וּבָאוּ בוֹ צִיִּים כִּתִּים וְנִכְאָה וְשָׁב וְזָעַם עַל־בְּרִֽית־קוֹדֶשׁ וְעָשָׂה וְשָׁב וְיָבֵן עַל־עֹזְבֵי בְּרִית קֹֽדֶשׁ׃
11.lit: ““He will stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south will wage war in battle with an exceedingly great and mighty army; but he won’t stand; for they will devise plans against him. Yes, those who eat of his dainties will destroy him, and his army will be swept away. Many will fall down slain. As for both these kings, their hearts will be to do mischief, and they will speak lies at one table; but it won’t prosper, for the end will still be at the appointed time. Then he will return into his land with great wealth. His heart will be against the holy covenant. He will take action, and return to his own land. “He will return at the appointed time, and come into the south; but it won’t be in the latter time as it was in the former. For ships of Kittim will come against him. Therefore he will be grieved, and will return, and have indignation against the holy covenant, and will take action. He will even return, and have regard to those who forsake the holy covenant.”

11.gram:
כִּי־עוֹד קֵץ לַמּוֹעֵד (11:27): “for the end is still at the appointed time.” קֵץ (end) together with מוֹעֵד (appointed time) is the twin word of this chapter: the end is not in men’s hands but in “the appointed time.” The same pairing returns in 11:35.

בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ (holy covenant): this is the key word of the whole turn: his anger no longer falls only on the king of the south but reaches toward God’s covenant, and toward those who forsake the covenant.
11.exp:
At one table two kings tell lies; and the text says: the end is still at the appointed time.

Verse 27 is the sharpest picture of the chapter: two kings sit at one table, drinking, each plotting in his heart how to harm the other, lying to each other and calculating against each other. The verdict the text gives this scene is short: the plan will not prosper, because “the end will still be at the appointed time.” The meaning of the original is: the end is still at the appointed time. It is not their strategies that decide the ending but a timetable they cannot touch.

This sentence will appear again in this chapter (11:35, 11:40, 11:45). We must be careful not to turn this “end” into a day that can be calculated; the point of the text is that the end belongs to God and not to human calculation.

Then the text turns the camera another way: “his heart will be against the holy covenant.” From here all the fighting is no longer only a matter between kings but is turned toward the “holy covenant” and toward “those who forsake the covenant.” In other words, this game of power at last touches the core of the faith of God’s people. The ships of Kittim come against him, he loses heart and turns back, and he vents his anger on the holy covenant. This is an old pattern: a man frustrated outside often vents his anger on someone weaker than himself.

11.lit: ““Forces will stand on his part, and they will profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and will take away the continual burnt offering. Then they will set up the abomination that makes desolate. He will corrupt those who do wickedly against the covenant by flatteries; but the people who know their God will be strong, and take action. “Those who are wise among the people will instruct many; yet they will fall by the sword and by flame, by captivity and by plunder, many days. Now when they fall, they will be helped with a little help; but many will join themselves to them with flatteries. Some of those who are wise will fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.”

11.gram:
וְעַם יֹדְעֵי אֱלֹהָיו יַחֲזִקוּ וְעָשׂוּ (11:32): יֹדְעֵי (know) is a participle, meaning “those who are knowing”; יַחֲזִקוּ (will be firm) comes from the same root as “support, make strong” in 11:1; this continues chapter 10’s “first given strength, then strong.”

מַשְׂכִּילֵי עָם (the wise among the people): this word is the same as “the wise” in Dan 12:3; 11:33–35 prepares for 12:3.
11.exp:
In the darkest time the text leaves only a small group: the people who know their God will be firm and take action; and the wise, by falling, refine others.

These five verses are the heart of the chapter and the verses that most need care. 11:31 says that armies rise, profane the sanctuary, take away the continual offering and set up the abomination that makes desolate; this echoes the descriptions in 8:11–13 and 9:27, which have long been matched to history in different ways, and we set them side by side among the issues. Here we must say plainly: these notes set no date for this verse and do not match it to any person of today; we look only at the conclusion the text gives this darkness.

The conclusion is one sentence: “the people who know their God will be strong and take action.” In this time when everything is defiled, the text does not say “those with force,” does not say “those with cunning,” but says: those who know God. This “knowing” is not knowing some doctrines but living in relationship with God. More surprising is the “wise” the text speaks of next: they make many understand, yet fall by the sword, by flame, into captivity and plunder. This is not a story that “if you believe in God you will surely be safe.” But the text gives their falling a meaning: “to refine, to purify, and to make them white.”

We need to be especially careful here: this does not say God delights in suffering, nor that the suffering are more spiritual. It says: in God’s hand even falling is not falling for nothing. This is a great comfort to believers today in pressure, in persecution, and in not being understood; it also reminds us: do not use this passage to tell a person who is suffering, “this is God refining you,” for that is using Scripture to dam up a person’s tears.

11.lit: ““The king will do according to his will. He will exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and will speak marvelous things against the God of gods. He will prosper until the indignation is accomplished; for that which is determined will be done. He won’t regard the gods of his fathers, or the desire of women, or regard any god; for he will magnify himself above all. But in his place he will honor the god of fortresses. He will honor a god whom his fathers didn’t know with gold, silver, and with precious stones and pleasant things. He will deal with the strongest fortresses by the help of a foreign god. He will increase with glory whoever acknowledges him. He will cause them to rule over many, and will divide the land for a price.”

עַד־כָּלָה זַעַם (until the indignation is accomplished): the indignation has a time when it is “accomplished”; this indignation is not the king’s but God’s, and his prospering lies within the limit God allows.

כִּי נֶחֱרָצָה נֶעֱשָׂתָה: “for that which is determined shall be done”; נֶחֱרָצָה also appears in 9:26–27, meaning “that which has been decided,” and is the common word of the whole book for judgment.
11.exp:
He may exalt himself and prosper; but the text draws a line around his prospering: until the indignation is accomplished.

From verse 36 the tone of the text changes: no longer one passage after another of historical detail but one man’s heart: self-exaltation. This “king” has long been read in two main ways: one holds that it is still the earlier “contemptible person” and the text only pulls the camera into his heart; the other holds that here the text turns to another, more end-time figure of self-exaltation; some hold that the two are, in the text, one description that advances layer by layer. These notes set the views side by side, do not decide for you, and do not turn any reading into an identification of a person today.

But three things are clear whichever way one reads it. First, his self-exaltation begins in the heart: “he will do as he pleases,” and “exalt himself above every god.” This is the same illness as the pride of the two kings in 4:30 and 5:20. Second, he has his god: the “god of fortresses,” to whom he gives gold, silver and precious stones; that is, a man without God in fact has a god, and his god is his power and his security. Third, his prospering has a boundary: until the indignation is accomplished.

The text describes it so not for us to guess who he is but for us to see that the end of pride, whatever name it bears, is the same end. This gives us a deep rest: we need not, and should not, identify that man for history; we only need not let our own heart walk the same road.

11.lit: ““At the time of the end the king of the south will contend with him; and the king of the north will come against him like a whirlwind, with chariots, with horsemen, and with many ships. He will enter into the countries, and will overflow and pass through. He will enter also into the glorious land, and many countries will be overthrown; but these will be delivered out of his hand: Edom, Moab, and the chief of the children of Ammon. He will also stretch out his hand on the countries. The land of Egypt won’t escape. But he will have power over the treasures of gold and of silver, and over all the precious things of Egypt. The Libyans and the Ethiopians will be at his steps. But news out of the east and out of the north will trouble him; and he will go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many. He will plant the tents of his palace between the sea and the glorious holy mountain; yet he will come to his end, and no one will help him.”

11.gram:
וּבָא קִצּוֹ וְאֵין עוֹזֵר לוֹ (11:45): “he will come to his end, and no one will help him.” עוֹזֵר (helper): this word shares a root with the “help” Michael gave in 10:13, 21; on one side “there was help,” on the other “no one will help.”

בְּעֵת קֵץ (11:40, at the time of the end): this phrase also appears in 8:17, 12:4 and 12:9; its referent has long been read in two kinds of ways: “the second century BC” and “a still later time.”
11.exp:
The last verse of chapter 11 has no song of victory, only one quiet sentence: his end will come, and no one will help him.

The last six verses are the hardest stretch of the chapter. The series of wars described in 11:40–45 has some details that do not fully fit the reconstruction of Hellenistic history through the ages, and so interpreters have divided here into several readings: some hold that it is still the same king and that the text uses “prophetic writing” whose details are not meant to correspond to the history books item by item; some hold that from here the text turns to a still later time; and some hold that the text uses a structure that advances layer by layer so that details of history and of a later matter reflect each other. We set them side by side among the issues, and say plainly: these notes do not use this passage to draw up any timetable and do not identify any person of today.

But look at what the text finally gives in this passage: a king who has won victory after victory enters the nations, takes the treasures and pitches the tents of his palace; and then one sentence: “he will come to his end, and no one will help him.” This “help” shares a root with the “help” Michael gave Daniel in chapter 10. Seen side by side, this chapter and the one before form a very moving contrast: God’s people have a great prince standing on their side, while the self-exalting man, in the end, has no one standing beside him.

So this chapter is not for teaching us to read the news but for teaching us to rest: however the nations move, whoever rises and whoever sinks, what the text gives us is an ending, and that ending is “appointed.” Our task is not to calculate but, today, to know God and be strong and take action.

וּבָעֵת הַהִיא יַעֲמֹד: this “stand up” is the same word as the undercurrent of the whole book (עמד); in 11:1 the messenger “stood up to support,” in 10:21 Michael “helps,” and here Michael “stands up”: standing is the last hope of God’s people.

כָּל־הַנִּמְצָא כָּתוּב בַּסֵּפֶר: “everyone who is found written in the book.” “Written in the book” belongs to the same line as the “writing of truth” in 10:21 and the “books” in 7:10.
12.exp:
The last chapter begins with a “stand up”: in the greatest trouble, a great prince stands for the children of your people.

Chapter 12 follows the last sentence of chapter 11 and opens: “At that time Michael will stand up.” “At that time” has long been read in different ways: some hold that it follows the darkness described in 11:36–45; some hold that it points to a still later time; and some hold that the descriptions of history and of the end reflect each other. We set them side by side, and say plainly: these notes set no date for this “at that time” and do not connect it to any event of today.

The text gives two things, set against each other. The first is trouble: “such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time.” This is a heavy phrase; Jesus too, in Matthew 24, used similar words of great tribulation, and we set the views side by side among the issues. The second is deliverance: “everyone who is found written in the book” will be delivered. The one who stands up is Michael, the great prince of “the children of your people”; he stands up not to make the trouble vanish but so that the people may be delivered in the trouble.

Notice that what appears first in this chapter is not an answer but a standing figure. This is the summary of the whole book: when empires rise and fall and kings come and go, beside God’s people stands a great prince of heaven who always stands, and the God who rules.

לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם: “to everlasting life”; this is one of the few Old Testament verses that speak plainly of “eternal life.”
12.exp:
In the darkest place of the whole book, the text lights up one word: awake.

Verse 2 of chapter 12 is one of the clearest Old Testament verses on resurrection. “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake.” Death is called “sleep,” and sleep is something one wakes from. This verse gives all who have fallen for the faith a hope: falling is not the end. Do you remember chapter 11? The wise fell by the sword, in flame, into captivity and plunder; here the text answers them: they will awake.

The verse goes on to say that some will have everlasting life, and some shame and everlasting contempt. The scope of “many” has long been read in different ways: some read it as “all,” some as “many, that is, those concerned”; “everlasting contempt” too has been understood in different theological ways. We set them side by side among the issues. But first see the most direct point of the text: death is not the end; God has a final justice and also a final hope.

In the New Testament, Jesus and the apostles also speak again and again of resurrection and judgment (John 5:28–29, Acts 24:15). This quiets us: we need not build a complete end-time chart on this verse; we need only remember that those you love, and those who suffered for the Lord, are not forgotten. In God’s eyes they are asleep, and will awake.

12.exp:
The wise who fall will shine; those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever.

This verse is to be read together with chapter 11. 11:33 says the wise instruct many yet fall; 11:35 says they fall to refine them; 12:3 says they will shine as the brightness of the expanse. The same word, two scenes: on earth, they fall; in heaven, they shine. This is one of the greatest reversals of the whole book: failure in men’s eyes, glory in God’s.

Notice how the text describes these people: not “those of highest standing” and not “those of greatest achievement” but “those who turn many to righteousness.” The meaning of the original is turning people toward righteousness, toward God. This description does not belong to one office alone; anyone who, with life or with words, accompanies others to come nearer to God is within this description.

This verse is also an answer to those who fell by the sword and in flame in chapter 11: they did not fall for nothing. In men’s eyes they failed; in God’s eyes they are the brightness of the sky. If you have grieved for such a person, this verse is worth reading slowly and receiving slowly.

Stars do not shine by themselves; they are set by God in the sky to guide people in the night. In the same way, the wise do not have their own light; they are set by God in the night. This keeps us from pride and from discouragement: our task is not to shine the brightest but, in the night, not to go out.

סְתֹם הַדְּבָרִים וַחֲתֹם הַסֵּפֶר: “shut up the words, and seal the book”: two commands, both terms of ancient document storage; to seal is not to discard but to preserve, waiting for the time of opening.

12.exp:
The book is to be sealed; and sealing is not throwing away but preserving, waiting for the time God sets.

Verse 4 of chapter 12 is a turning point of the whole book: the messenger commands Daniel to shut up the words and seal the book. In the ancient world, to seal was to keep a document safe so that no one could alter it at will, waiting for the time it should be opened. This verse lets us see that God’s arrangement for his own words has its own time.

Then the text says: many will run back and forth, and knowledge will be increased. This verse is often used to speak of “technological progress in the last days”; but the original “run back and forth” can also be read “examine closely, search,” so there are different readings through the ages: some think it means people everywhere seeking out and studying the contents of this book so that understanding grows; some think it means the growth of knowledge in general; some think both. We set them side by side among the issues. We do not turn this verse into a prediction about technology or the times, and do not use it to draw up days.

For us today this verse holds a practical invitation: this book has not been sealed forever; today it has been placed in our hands. We can look it over back and forth, and in looking come to know God. When you read this book, please read not to gain more information but to know more deeply the God who rules history.

12.grk: וְרָאִיתִי אֲנִי דָנִיֵּאל וְהִנֵּה שְׁנַיִם אֲחֵרִים עֹמְדִים אֶחָד הֵנָּה לִשְׂפַת הַיְאֹר וְאֶחָד הֵנָּה לִשְׂפַת הַיְאֹֽר׃ וַיֹּאמֶר לָאִישׁ לְבוּשׁ הַבַּדִּים אֲשֶׁר מִמַּעַל לְמֵימֵי הַיְאֹר עַד־מָתַי קֵץ הַפְּלָאֽוֹת׃ וָאֶשְׁמַע אֶת־הָאִישׁ׀ לְבוּשׁ הַבַּדִּים אֲשֶׁר מִמַּעַל לְמֵימֵי הַיְאֹר וַיָּרֶם יְמִינוֹ וּשְׂמֹאלוֹ אֶל־הַשָּׁמַיִם וַיִּשָּׁבַע בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָם כִּי לְמוֹעֵד מֽוֹעֲדִים וָחֵצִי וּכְכַלּוֹת נַפֵּץ יַד־עַם־קֹדֶשׁ תִּכְלֶינָה כָל־אֵֽלֶּה׃
12.lit: “Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on the river bank on this side, and the other on the river bank on that side. One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, “How long will it be to the end of these wonders?” I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it will be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have finished breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things will be finished.”
12.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
stoodעֹמְדִיםomdimH5975those standing
riverהַיְאֹרye'orH2975the river (the Nile or a great river)
linenהַבַּדִּיםbaddimH906fine linen

12.gram:
קֵץ הַפְּלָאוֹת (the end of these wonders): קֵץ appears four times in this chapter (12:4, 6, 9, 13); פֶּלֶא (wonder) is often used to describe God’s works, linked with “the wonders of God.”

מוֹעֵד מוֹעֲדִים וָחֵצִי (a time, times, and a half): the same expression as in 7:25. These notes do not convert it into years or days and do not use it to draw up tables; see the issues.
12.exp:
Two stand by the river and ask the question we also want to ask: how long?

In verse 5 of chapter 12 the camera goes back to the river. The man clothed in linen stands above the waters; two others stand, one on this bank and one on that. One of them asks the last question of the whole book: “How long will it be to the end of these wonders?” You may find this sentence familiar: “how long” is a cry often found in the Psalms, the cry of everyone waiting in the dark.

The man clothed in linen lifts both hands to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever. It is a very solemn picture: the answer does not come from human calculation but is placed in God’s hand in an oath. The answer: a time, times, and a half, until the breaking in pieces of the power of the holy people is finished. This expression is the same as in 7:25; the readings are many, and we set them side by side among the issues. These notes do not convert it into years and do not tie it to any event of today.

Please notice one thing: this answer has no date, but it has a guarantee: one who lives forever has sworn. Is what you want a timetable, or a God you can trust? This chapter leads us from the former to the latter.

12.grk: וַאֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי וְלֹא אָבִין וָאֹמְרָה אֲדֹנִי מָה אַחֲרִית אֵֽלֶּה׃פ וַיֹּאמֶר לֵךְ דָּנִיֵּאל כִּֽי־סְתֻמִים וַחֲתֻמִים הַדְּבָרִים עַד־עֵת קֵֽץ׃
12.lit: “I heard, but I didn’t understand. Then I said, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” He said, “Go your way, Daniel; for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.”
12.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning

understandאָבִיןavinH995to understand; to grasp
outcomeאַחֲרִיתacharitH319the latter end; the outcome
goלֵךְlekhH3212to go; to walk

sealedוַחֲתֻמִיםchatumimH2856that which is sealed
12.gram:
וַאֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי וְלֹא אָבִין: “I heard, but I didn’t understand”; בִּין (understand) is an important word of the whole book; in 9:2 and 10:1 Daniel understood, and here he says frankly: I do not understand.

לֵךְ דָּנִיֵּאל (go your way, Daniel): לֵךְ is an imperative, the same word as “go your way” in 12:13; in the last chapter there are two “go your way.”
12.exp:
This old man who had understood many things says frankly: I heard, but I didn’t understand; and God’s answer is: go your way.

Verse 8 of chapter 12 holds a very honest sentence: “I heard, but I didn’t understand.” It is Daniel. The man who understood in chapter 9 as he read Scripture, who set his heart on understanding in chapter 10, here says frankly: I do not understand. The text does not hide this and does not say Daniel was therefore not spiritual enough. Even he had times of not understanding.

Then God’s answer gives him no explanation but: “Go your way, Daniel.” This “go” is not being sent away but being entrusted: these words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end; now is not the time when you need to understand everything but the time when you need to keep walking. This is a deep comfort: not understanding does not stop us from walking the way God gives.

We too often have such moments: we read the Bible, we pray, and still do not understand why this, why that. This verse gives us an honest space: we can say, I do not understand; and we can hear God say: go your way. Between these two sentences there is a faith that need not understand everything yet can go forward in peace.

12.grk: יִתְבָּֽרֲרוּ וְיִֽתְלַבְּנוּ וְיִצָּֽרְפוּ רַבִּים וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ רְשָׁעִים וְלֹא יָבִינוּ כָּל־רְשָׁעִים וְהַמַּשְׂכִּלִים יָבִֽינוּ׃
12.lit: “Many will purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked will do wickedly; and none of the wicked will understand; but those who are wise will understand.”
12.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
purifyיִתְבָּֽרֲרוּyitbarruH1305to be purified; to be chosen
make whiteוְיִֽתְלַבְּנוּyitlabbenuH3835to become white; to be made white
refineוְיִצָּֽרְפוּyitstsarefuH6884to be refined (as gold is refined)
the wickedרְשָׁעִיםresha'imH7563the wicked
understandיָבִינוּyavinuH995to understand
the wiseוְהַמַּשְׂכִּלִיםhammaskilimH7919wise ones
12.gram:
יִתְבָּרְרוּ וְיִתְלַבְּנוּ וְיִצָּרְפוּ: three verbs, all reflexive or passive: “be purified, be made white, be refined”; the same set of words as the three verbs of 11:35 (refine, purify, make white).

וְלֹא יָבִינוּ כָל־רְשָׁעִים וְהַמַּשְׂכִּלִים יָבִינוּ: those who do not understand are the wicked; those who understand are the wise; this “understanding” is not the amount of knowledge but the direction of the road.
12.exp:
The answer at the end is not a timetable but a process: being purified, made white, refined.

Verse 10 of chapter 12 answers 11:35. There it said that some of the wise fall, to refine the rest and make them pure and white; here it says that many will purify themselves and be refined. The same set of words, the same line: what God does in history is not only to deal with kings and kingdoms but to carry out a work of purifying among his people.

Notice that these three verbs are reflexive or passive: be purified, be made white, be refined. This lets us see that purity does not come from ourselves, still less from comparison; it is brought out in God’s hand. This is very close to the “no-self” of 321: we do not make ourselves clean; we are willing to be refined by God.

Then the text divides people into two kinds: the wicked still do wickedly and do not understand; the wise understand. This “understanding” is not the amount of knowledge but direction: those willing to be refined gradually understand; those unwilling understand less and less as they go. So what the text gives us is not a calculated timetable but a road we can walk today: being willing to be purified and refined.

12.grk: וּמֵעֵת הוּסַר הַתָּמִיד וְלָתֵת שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם יָמִים אֶלֶף מָאתַיִם וְתִשְׁעִֽים׃ אַשְׁרֵי הַֽמְחַכֶּה וְיַגִּיעַ לְיָמִים אֶלֶף שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שְׁלֹשִׁים וַחֲמִשָּֽׁה׃
12.lit: ““From the time that the continual burnt offering is taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there will be one thousand two hundred ninety days. Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days.”
12.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
taken awayהוּסַרhusarH5493to be removed
the continual offeringהַתָּמִידhatamidH8548the continual (burnt offering)
abominationשִׁקּוּץshiqqutsH8251a detestable idol
daysיָמִיםyamimH3117days
blessedאַשְׁרֵיashreiH835blessed
waitsהַֽמְחַכֶּהhamechakkehH2442the one who waits
12.gram:
אַשְׁרֵי הַמְחַכֶּה (blessed is he who waits): אַשְׁרֵי is the “blessed” that opens the Psalms; חָכָה (to wait) is a waiting with hope.

יָמִים אֶלֶף מָאתַיִם וְתִשְׁעִים: “one thousand two hundred ninety days” and “one thousand three hundred thirty-five days”: these two numbers have been read in many ways through the ages, and are related to 7:25, 8:14 and 9:27; these notes do not calculate, convert or draw up tables; see the issues.
12.exp:
Of the two numbers of days given at the end, neither can be used for calculating; but the word given last is one we can live out: blessed is the one who waits.

Verses 11 and 12 of chapter 12 are the two verses most easily misused in the whole book. The text says that from the time the continual burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there will be one thousand two hundred ninety days; blessed is he who waits and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. Through the ages the explanations of these two numbers have been very many: some explain from the historical profaning of the sanctuary, some from end-time events, and some see them as symbolic numbers. We set them side by side, and say plainly: these notes do not calculate or convert, do not turn them into any timetable, and do not use them to identify people and events of today.

Look at where these two verses really land: not on the number of days but on one word: “blessed.” Blessed is the one who waits. The “waiting” of the original is a watching with hope. This word has similar uses in the Psalms and in Isaiah. What the whole book finally gives God’s people is not a date but a posture: waiting with hope.

We need to be careful: the two numbers are not to make us more tense but more quiet. Any use that turns these numbers into panic, prediction or judgment of others departs from the purpose of the text. The fruit of the text is patience; and Jesus also said that no one knows that day and hour. So we do not count days; we wait.

12.grk: וְאַתָּה לֵךְ לַקֵּץ וְתָנוּחַ וְתַעֲמֹד לְגֹרָלְךָ לְקֵץ הַיָּמִֽין׃
12.lit: ““But go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.””
12.key:
ChineseOriginalTransliterationStrong'sMeaning
go your wayלֵךְlekhH3212to go; to walk
to the endלַקֵּץlaqetzH7093until the end
restוְתָנוּחַvetanuachH5117to rest; to repose

12.gram:
וְאַתָּה לֵךְ לַקֵּץ וְתָנוּחַ: “go your way until the end; for you will rest”; לֵךְ (go), קֵץ (end), נוּחַ (rest): three words that gather the undercurrent of the whole book into one sentence.

וְתַעֲמֹד לְגֹרָלְךָ: “you will stand in your inheritance”; עמד (to stand): the undercurrent of the whole book, appearing for the last time; גּוֹרָל (lot, portion) is a word used in Joshua for the dividing of the land: the inheritance God assigns to you.
12.exp:
The last sentence of the whole book is said to one old man: go your way, you will rest; and at the end of the days you will stand in your inheritance.

The last sentence of the whole book of Daniel is not a proclamation to the whole world but is said to one person: “But go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.” In this sentence there are three movements: go, rest, stand.

The first is “go your way.” This is the same word as “go your way” in 12:9. God wants him to keep walking, carrying his not-understanding. The second is “rest”: this word is not only a gentle way of saying death but also means “to find rest.” This old man went through many years of Babylon and Persia; his life was not a story of victory but a story of faithfulness; God says to him: you will rest. The third is “stand.” It is the same word as Michael’s “stand up” in 12:1: to stand; he was a man who stood before kings, and at last he too will stand and receive his portion.

Notice: this sentence does not say “then you will know everything,” and gives him no date; it gives him only three things: a road, a rest, a hope of standing. This is the conclusion of the whole book: not a heap of answers but the promise of a God who can be trusted. To you who are waiting, this sentence is also said: go, rest, stand.

blocks: “Resolved Not to Defile Himself with the King’s Food”
Brothers and sisters, peace to you.
On your first day at work, did you ever receive a name tag?
What was printed on it was not your name.
It was an English name the company had picked out for you.
Maybe you smiled, and took it.
It was convenient: easy for colleagues to call, easy for clients to remember.
But one day, you stood in front of the mirror.
And suddenly you wanted to ask yourself one question.
This book was written for people who live in someone else’s kingdom.
For those who live as foreigners.
And for those who, at the company, at school, in the city, have had their names changed.
Step one: they changed your name, but they could not change your heart.
Step two: resolve, at a small table.
Step three: wisdom is God’s gift, and the king is only a witness.
In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. (Dan 1:1)
You see, this is a siege.
There are armies, there are walls, there is a king.
The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God. (Dan 1:2)
It was not that Nebuchadnezzar defeated Jehoiakim.
It was the Lord who gave him into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand.
The same event, two ways of reading it.
This book is going to teach us to learn the second way of reading.
The vessels were carried into another god’s temple.
It looked as if the other god had won.
But the text says it was the Lord who handed them over.
It was not that God lost.
It was that God had begun to work in another place.
Then the king gave an order.
The king spoke to Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of Israel, even of the royal offspring and of the nobles; (Dan 1:3)
You see, whom did the king want?
This was not looking for forced labor.
The king appointed for them a daily portion of the king’s dainties, and of the wine which he drank, and that they should be nourished three years. (Dan 1:5)
After three years, stand in the king’s palace.
With conditions this good, who would want to refuse?
This is where Babylon was most skillful.
They did not use the whip.
Don’t you think that being crushed is actually easier to recognize?
Because you will say, this is an opportunity.
The prince of the eunuchs gave names to them: to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego. (Dan 1:7)
What were the four men’s names, originally?
Mishael: who is what God is?
Belteshazzar was connected with a Babylonian god.
Abednego means servant of a certain god.
The names were changed for them.
No one asked them whether they were willing.
Sometimes what we lose is not our faith.
It is the very name by which we speak our faith.
Maybe it is a way of being addressed.
Maybe it is a position that, to fit in, we slowly stop mentioning.
And you become what they want you to be.
But God’s word did not stop here.

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. (Dan 1:8)
Did you see that one word?
Everything before this was done by others.
The chief of the eunuchs changed names.
This “but” is the turning point of the whole book.
The meaning of the original is “set upon the heart.”
The names were set by the chief of the eunuchs.
The heart was set by Daniel.
In this verse, face to face.
People can change where you live.
But there is no way for people to change the decision you have set in your heart.
Before the food was set on the table.
That is, before the pressure came, his heart already had a place.
Many people’s weakness is not at the moment of greatest pressure.
It is at the moment before they have resolved.
Deciding only when the pressure comes is usually too late.
So today I want to ask you.
Is there one thing you have already set upon your heart, and no longer renegotiate?
Not thinking about it only when the boss opens his mouth.
Not thinking about it only when a friend invites you.
This one thing, I will not touch.
He did not pound the table.
He did not go on strike.
He did not declare before the king who was right and who was wrong.
The text says that he asked.
He asked the chief of the eunuchs for permission not to defile himself.
This is the wisdom for living in someone else’s kingdom.
Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. (Dan 1:9)
Many people want to see the road before they decide.
The order the text gives us is the other way around.
But the road was not yet fully open.

The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. For why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? Then you would endanger my head with the king.” (Dan 1:10)
The chief of the eunuchs was not a bad man.
His head was at stake in this matter.
Sometimes we treat everyone who disagrees as an enemy.
But many people are only afraid.
They are caught in the middle.
They also want to save their lives.
Daniel did not push back hard.
He changed the person he spoke to and changed the method.
“Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat, and water to drink. (Dan 1:12)
Then let our faces be examined before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s dainties; and as you see, deal with your servants.” (Dan 1:13)
Then look with your own eyes.
He did not ask others to believe him.
He asked only for one thing: a chance to be tested.
Faith does not shy away from testing.
At the end of ten days, their faces appeared fairer, and they were fatter in flesh, than all the youths who ate of the king’s dainties. (Dan 1:15)
This is not saying that being vegetarian is healthier.
Nor is it teaching dietary rules.
What the text is saying is:
A person, for the sake of conscience, does not defile himself.
And God takes responsibility for the consequence he was afraid of.
They were afraid of looking worse.
God made their faces look better.
Not every act of holding firm brings this kind of result right away.
But in chapter 1, God first gave these four a small witness.
He remembers the decisions you have set upon your heart.
All right, let’s move to the third point.
Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams. (Dan 1:17)
In this chapter it has already appeared three times.
Verse 9: God made him find favor.
Babylon thought it was the teacher.
It had taught them for three years with the king’s books.
But the text says that the true teacher was God.
They thought it was something they had trained.
The text says it was something God gave.
That day, the king examined them himself.
The king talked with them; and among them all was found no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore stood they before the king. (Dan 1:19)
They finally stood before the king.
The position they stood in was one Babylon had given.
But the ones standing were people who had not been defiled.
In every matter of wisdom and understanding, concerning which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters who were in all his realm. (Dan 1:20)
Notice, what did the king ask about?
But in the end, what lets you stand is not your degree.
It is the understanding God gave.
The last verse has only one sentence.
Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus. (Dan 1:21)
Nebuchadnezzar’s dynasty came to an end.
Those in power changed again and again.
He did not say he succeeded.
He did not say he held power.
He did not say he was honored.
It says only, he was there.
Sometimes the greatest praise God gives a person is not what he accomplished.
It is that through long years, he still stood before God.
But the God who rules in heaven does not change.
So those who serve him also have a reason to stand.
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the beginning.
At work you can use a name that others find easy to call.
But in your heart, you must know who you are.
You are someone known by God.
You are someone who belongs to God.
He also lived in a world that was not his own.
He had honor, yet did not grasp it.
He did not change who he was in order to fit in.
Letting Jesus be King does not begin with big things.
It begins at a small table.
It begins with one decision today.
You do not need to hold on to this decision by your own strength.
It is no longer preparing the outcome in God’s place.
You leave the consequences with him.
In your life, is there a small table?
Is there something you need to set upon your heart right now?
Please say to God in your heart.
Lord, this one thing, I will not touch.
Please give me favor, give me wisdom.
Let me, in this generation, be one who is still there.
You are the God who rules.
When the city was besieged, you were there.
When names were changed, you were there.
At the table, you were there too.
Please help us set our hearts before you.
Please give us favor, and give us understanding.
Let us stand before you always.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
Brothers and sisters, peace to you.
Have you ever had a night like this?
You toss and turn in bed.
Your mind is like a machine that cannot stop.
You have thought of many ways.
You have talked with many people.
You have looked up much information.
But your heart is still uneasy.
Today, we read about a man who could not sleep.
He was the most powerful man in the world at the time.
Step one: the king forgot the dream, and no one had a way.
Step two: pray first, then interpret the dream.
Step three: the stone cut out without hands.
In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him. (Dan 2:1)
There is an unease that power cannot soothe.
So he did what he thought would be most effective.
Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be called to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king. (Dan 2:2)
He called in all the experts.

It is said to one person.
In this sentence there are three movements.
This word is not only a gentle way of saying death.
It also means to find rest.
This old man’s life was not a story of victory.
It was a story of faithfulness.
The same word as Michael’s “stand up.”
He was a man who stood before kings.
At last he too will stand up
This portion is the word used in Joshua for dividing the land.
It is the inheritance God assigns to you.
Please notice what this sentence does not say.
It does not say, at that time you will know everything.
It gives him only three things.
This is the conclusion of the whole book.
But the promise of a God who can be trusted.
Let us look back over this book.
Chapter 1: a young man who purposed not to defile himself with the king’s food.
Chapter 2: the stone cut out without hands.
Chapter 4: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.
Chapter 5: you are weighed in the balances.
Chapter 6: praying as he had done before.
Chapter 7: the Ancient of Days and the son of man.
Chapters 8 to 11: kings and kings, coming and going.
Chapter 10: God first touches, and then says, be strong.
Chapter 11: the people who know their God will be strong and take action.
He fell into the dust, and after three days rose.
He is the firstfruits of those who sleep.
Let us hold only to the clearest point of the text.
The Holy Spirit is my Guide.
Let us, when we do not understand, still be willing to go.
The end is in his hand.
Let Jesus receive all the glory.
Even our shining is his light.
One purpose: to build God’s system.
This is a people who wait,
who accompany one another and purify one another,
who in the night do not go out,
and who, when someone falls, do not hurry to explain.
Finally, please be quiet for a moment.
Is there something you do not understand now?
Perhaps a prayer you have waited long for.
Perhaps a person who has gone away.
Perhaps a situation with no end in sight.
No need to understand it all.
What you do is not in vain.
At the end of the days, you will stand up
You are the God who stands up.
You are the hope of those who sleep.
Let us not count days, but wait for you.
When we do not understand, let us still be willing to go.
who in the night do not go out,
Comfort all who have fallen for the Lord.
And comfort those who are still waiting,
until your kingdom fills the whole earth.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray.

issues.t: Date and Two Languages: The Late Sixth Century, or the Second Century BC?
issues.why: What the text asks: When was this book written, and by whom? Is chapter 11 prophecy, or history written after the fact? What does the bilingual structure of Aramaic (2:4b–7:28) and Hebrew show?
pos: Late sixth century (traditional view)

The traditional reading holds that the book was written by Daniel himself, taken captive to Babylon, in the Babylonian and Persian periods; the details of chapter 11 are prophecy given by God through Daniel. Aramaic was the common language of the empire at that time and reflects the world in which he lived.
Second century BC (critical scholarship)

Many scholars hold that the book reached its final form in the Maccabean period; the details of chapter 11 are so precise because the author is describing history that had already happened, with the aim of comforting a people under persecution. The bilingual structure is seen as a mark of editing.
Depends on one’s view of prophecy

Others stress that the difference in positions depends largely on whether one accepts that “God can show the future in advance”; the distribution of Aramaic and Hebrew has several literary and theological explanations.
issues.say: These notes read the book in the setting the text itself gives (the Babylonian and Persian periods) and set the other positions side by side; we do not make the date of composition a condition of faith. Whichever reading one takes, the effect of 4:17 and 7:13–14 on readers today does not change: the Most High rules, and the kingdom will in the end be given to the holy ones.
issues.care: Do not judge the faith of brothers and sisters who hold a different position; and do not, because of scholarly disputes, feel that this book is unreliable. The foundation of faith is this God who rules, not the theory of any one date.

issues.t: Which Four Kingdoms?
issues.why: What the text asks: Which four kingdoms are meant in chapters 2, 7 and 8?
pos: Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, Rome (traditional)

The traditional reading matches the image of chapter 2 and the four beasts of chapter 7 with the four empires of Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece and Rome, and holds that God’s kingdom arises in the time of Rome.
Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (critical scholarship)
Many scholars hold that the author’s horizon runs from Babylon to the Hellenistic kingdoms; “Media” is seen as a separate kingdom, and the fourth kingdom is Greece (and its successors).
The text stresses “beginning and end”

Others stress that the list of four kingdoms is not the text’s most important point; the point is that human kingdoms rise and pass, one after another, while God’s kingdom is a kingdom of another kind.
issues.say: These notes set the various views side by side, reach no absolute conclusion, and draw up no table. What we hold on to is this: human kingdoms have a beginning and an end, and God’s kingdom does not grow out of them (2:44–45).
issues.care: Do not use any one matching to identify some country or regime of today; and do not, because the list is disputed, feel that these visions have nothing to do with you.

issues.t: Who Is “One Like a Son of Man”?
issues.why: What the text asks: Who is the “one like a son of man” of 7:13–14?
pos: Jesus
The traditional Christian reading holds that this “one like a son of man” is the Messiah, Jesus; when on trial Jesus quoted this verse and spoke of himself (Matt 26:64, Mark 14:62).
The holy ones
Others hold that in the context of chapter 7 the “son of man” symbolizes God’s holy people (7:18, 27), who go through suffering and afterward receive the kingdom.
Both
Still others hold that the two are not opposed: the son of man represents the holy ones, and the holy ones receive the kingdom in the son of man; the New Testament made such a link.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and follow the link the New Testament itself made: Jesus quoted this verse at his trial; at the same time we see that 7:18, 27 say the holy ones receive the kingdom, and we do not set the two against each other.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to draw lines among brothers and sisters about who is orthodox; and do not, because “son of man” is complex, overlook the comfort it gives those who suffer: the kingdom will be given to the holy ones of the Most High.

issues.t: How Should We Read the Seventy Sevens?
issues.why: What the text asks: How are the “seventy sevens” of 9:24–27 to be read?
pos: The historical reading
Some read the “seventy sevens” as a historical period from the exile to Christ’s death, and calculate it from various starting points of dates.
The end-time reading
Others hold that a part of it points to the end times and will be completed only in the future.
The symbolic reading
Still others hold that the “seventy sevens” is a symbolic number, indicating a complete period set by God, and need not be converted.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, count no days and draw up no timetable. We speak only of the man in 9:1–19 who read Scripture and prayed, and of the core to which the six things in 9:24 point: God will deal with sin.
issues.care: Do not use any one calculation to set dates for events of today, or to judge those who hold a different calculation; the fruit should be to know better how to confess and pray, not to be keener on calculating.

issues.t: The Fourth Man in the Fire, “Like a Son of the Gods,” and the New Testament
issues.why: What the text asks: The “fourth” in the fire in 3:25, whose “appearance is like a son of the gods”: how does he relate to the New Testament?
pos: A manifestation of Christ
Some hold that this one is an appearance of Christ in the Old Testament, echoing the New Testament Immanuel (Matt 1:23).
An angel
Others hold that this one is an angel sent by God, because in 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar himself says God “sent his angel” and delivered his servants.
In the language of a foreign king
Still others stress that “son of the gods” is the speech of a foreign king, meaning “a son of the divine,” and need not at once be equated with New Testament doctrine.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. We say: the one with them in the fire makes us think of “Immanuel” (Matt 1:23); we do not treat it as required evidence for a creed. We say only: God did not keep them from the fire; he came into the fire and was with them.
issues.care: Do not force this verse to say more in order to prove some doctrine; and do not use this verse to guarantee that believers will not suffer. What the text gives is presence.

issues.t: Nebuchadnezzar’s Madness and His Confession
issues.why: What the text asks: How are Nebuchadnezzar’s madness and confession in chapter 4 to be read? Was he saved?
pos: A historical and medical explanation
Some, from a historical and medical angle, understand his illness as a mental illness of some kind and compare it with ancient documents.
A spiritual judgment
Others stress that this was God’s judgment on pride, with the aim of making him acknowledge that the Most High rules (4:17, 25, 32).
Whether his confession amounts to salvation
Whether his lifting his eyes to heaven and praising the Most High in 4:34–37 means he was saved has long been viewed in different ways.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and stop where the text stops: in 4:34–37 he lifts his eyes to heaven and praises the Most High. We pass no verdict on his eternal life.
issues.care: Do not draw a conclusion on God’s behalf about anyone, living or dead; and do not, because of the uncertainty, reject this witness: even the proudest king can be brought to acknowledge the Most High.

issues.t: Spiritual Warfare: Is “the Prince of the Kingdom of Persia” a Territorial Spirit?
issues.why: What the text asks: Does the battle between “the prince of the kingdom of Persia” and the archangel Michael in chapter 10 support a theology of “territorial spirit warfare”?
pos: For territorial spirit warfare
Some read “the prince of the kingdom of Persia” as a spiritual power over a region, and hold that believers can identify, name and bind territorial spirits.
Heaven corresponding to earth
Others hold that this is a conflict among angels corresponding to empires on earth, a description in the manner of apocalyptic writing.
The text does not instruct believers to act
Still others stress that the text only shows that there is conflict among angels and does not command believers to identify or attack these powers.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and state our position plainly: the text says only that there is conflict among angels and does not teach believers to identify, name or bind territorial spirits. The point of prayer is 10:12: setting the heart to understand, humbling oneself before God, and being heard. We do not write chapter 10 as a manual of warfare.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to label any region, people or group as “controlled by a spirit”; toward those who are suffering, take still more care and add no blame.

issues.t: The Last Days, the Counted Days, and Naming “the Antichrist”
issues.why: What the text asks: How are we to face the times and days of 7:25, 8:14 and 11:36–12:13, and the identifying of “the antichrist”?
pos: The historical reading
Some match these times and days to the history of the profaning of the temple in the second century BC, and hold that the “little horn” was a ruler of that time.
The end-time reading
Others hold that these descriptions point to a still later time and are linked to the lawless one of the New Testament.
History and the end reflect each other layer by layer
Still others hold that the text has two layers of meaning at once, historical events foreshadowing a later matter.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and state our position plainly: we count no days, draw up no table, and do not identify any modern person, regime or organization as the “little horn” or the “antichrist.” We say only: the suffering holy ones are told “go your way until the end” (12:13), and the fruit is patience, not panic.
issues.care: Do not use these passages to create panic or to label particular groups or organizations; for those who are under persecution, or who lose sleep over such teaching, accompany first, and then slowly read the text together.

issues.t: How does “the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim” fit with the dating of 2 Kings 24 and Jeremiah?
issues.why: Daniel says the exile happened in the third year of Jehoiakim’s reign (1:1), but the dating of 2 Kings 24:1 and Jeremiah 25:1 and 46:2 looks different: Jehoiakim’s fourth year corresponds to Nebuchadnezzar’s first year. How are these to be read together?
pos: Two ways of reckoning

Babylon was accustomed to count the year a new king came to the throne as his accession year and the next year as year one; Judah used another reckoning. With the two counts differing, the same year can differ by one, so the third year and the fourth year can refer to the same stretch of time.
Two campaigns
Nebuchadnezzar first pressed Judah in the third year of Jehoiakim and took away a group of people; later Jehoiakim rebelled, and then came a larger military campaign. Daniel records the first.
A historical discrepancy
Some hold this is a gap in the author’s memory or sources and regard it as evidence of a later work.
issues.say: These notes take the first two readings as primary: the two ways of reckoning in use together, and the two campaigns, both let the text agree with itself. Whatever the position, the point lies in 1:2: the Lord gave the king into his hand.
issues.care: Do not let details of dates like these turn into a dispute over “the Bible has errors” or “my view is right.” First hold on to the subject of verse 2, and deal with the dates slowly afterward.

issues.t: The temple vessels taken away: why did God allow it?
issues.why: The vessels of the temple were brought into the temple of Babylon’s god (1:2). The name and house of the LORD were trodden underfoot by other gods; is this God’s defeat? Why did God allow it?
pos: Discipline and judgment

The kings and prophets had long warned: if Judah forsook the covenant, God would let them be taken into exile (2 Kings 20:17; Jeremiah 25). The vessels being taken away was the fulfillment of this warning.
God’s sovereignty
The subject of the text is “the Lord” (אֲדֹנָי); it is he who gave the king over, and it was not that Babylon prevailed over him.
A temporary humiliation
The vessels were later brought out and used in chapter 5, and in the end were returned in Ezra (Ezra 1:7). The humiliation was temporary, and God did not give up.
issues.say: These notes read it this way: this was the Lord’s sovereignty and discipline, and at the same time a preparation for God’s people to still know him in another people’s kingdom. The vessels of chapter 5, and the return in Ezra, will come back to answer this question.
issues.care: To someone going through “why did God allow it,” do not give an answer too quickly. Accompany first, admit that the pain is real; only then let the text say: the Lord was not absent.

issues.t: Is renaming respect or brainwashing? What do the four new names mean?
issues.why: Babylon gave the four young men new names (1:7): Daniel was changed to Belteshazzar, and so on. Was this the ruler’s respect or cultural assimilation? What do the new names mean?
pos: A means of assimilation
The new names mostly carried the name of a Babylonian god, with the aim of cutting their link with the LORD and making them part of the kingdom.
An administrative custom
In the ancient Near East those brought into the court were often renamed, a kind of registration of identity, not always with a religious intent.
Both together
The renaming was both administrative and a cultural remaking; at root it concerns who has the right to name a person.
issues.say: These notes take the third reading: we do not over-guess the meaning of each name (scholars differ on the origins of Shadrach and Meshach), but we see the point of “who has the right to name.” Daniel is still called Daniel later (for example in 2:20 and 10:1), showing that the name did not change him.
issues.care: Do not judge anyone’s faith because of cultural differences in names and ways of address; and do not dismiss the loneliness in the heart of someone who has put down his own name to fit in.

issues.t: Why would Daniel not eat the king’s food? Food, things offered to idols, or a symbol of allegiance?
issues.why: Daniel purposed not to defile himself with the king’s food (1:8). What was his concern? Was something wrong with the food, was the wine offered to idols, or did accepting the king’s table mean pledging loyalty?
pos: Things offered to idols
The king’s food and wine were first offered to Babylonian gods before being brought to the table, and eating meant sharing in idol worship (compare Exodus 34:15; 1 Corinthians 10:20–21).
Unclean food
The king’s food may have included meats forbidden by the Law, or food not prepared according to the rules (Leviticus 11).
A symbol of allegiance
To eat at the king’s table and be supported by the king meant, in the ancient Near East, allegiance and dependence; Daniel wanted to remain undivided toward God.
The text does not explain
The text says only “defile” and gives no reason, perhaps deliberately.
issues.say: These notes admit that the text does not state the reason, and so we do not supply a single answer for him. What can be said for certain is that he took this matter to heart so as not to leave his place, and that he did it by “asking,” not by confronting.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to judge anyone’s eating habits, and do not demand that others hold the same conscience on the same matter. Each person must ask before God: what is my “king’s food”?

issues.t: Vegetables and water for ten days: is this a witness to healthy eating?
issues.why: After ten days of vegetables and water their appearance was better and their bodies stronger (1:12, 15). Is this teaching a kind of healthy eating?
pos: A witness, not dietary teaching

What the text says is God’s care for a person with a settled conscience, not the healing power of vegetarian food. Later, in chapter 10, Daniel also has a time of fasting, and that too is not a dietary rule.
The reasonableness of vegetarian food
Some hold that vegetables and water are in themselves healthier than the king’s food, and that the ten-day difference can be explained by diet.
A miracle
The text links the result with God’s care (1:9, 17), not with a natural outcome.
issues.say: These notes take the first reading: we do not turn this passage into dietary teaching. The ten days are only a small witness that can be tested, and the main character is not the vegetables but God.
issues.care: Do not, because of this passage, judge those who eat meat, and do not treat “persevere and things will get better” as a guarantee; the “But if not” of chapter 3 is waiting just ahead.

issues.t: How should “Daniel continued even to the first year of King Cyrus” be read with the dating of 10:1?
issues.why: 1:21 says Daniel “continued even to the first year of King Cyrus,” yet 10:1 says that in the third year of Cyrus he received another revelation. How are the two to be read together?
pos: The end of a time is not the end of a life
1:21 says that he was there throughout the Babylonian exile, up to the marker of its end; it does not say that he died in that year.
Different angles
1:21 is the closing of the whole chapter, seen from the whole history of the exile; 10:1 is another specific revelation; the two do not conflict.
A mark of editing
Some scholars hold that 1:21 is a later summary, serving as the end of the story.
issues.say: These notes take the first two readings: 1:21 speaks of his remaining there until the turning point of the exile, and 10:1 is another point in time afterward. The two complement each other and do not contradict.
issues.care: Do not, in solving a detail of dating, move the emphasis away from “he was still there”; this sentence itself is a comfort for all who live long in someone else’s kingdom.

issues.t: Why does the text switch to Aramaic here?
issues.why: The book of Daniel begins in Hebrew (1:1–2:4a), changes to Aramaic from 2:4b, and returns to Hebrew only at 7:28. Why the switch here? What does it have to do with composition and editing?
pos: Dictated by the scene
The Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic (2:4), and the narrative goes on being written in that language; Aramaic was the common language of the courts and trade of the Near East at that time.
Dictated by the structure

The Aramaic section (chapters 2–7) centers on the rise and fall of foreign kingdoms and is arranged in a chiastic pattern: the four kingdoms and the kingdom in chapters 2 and 7, the fiery furnace and the lions’ den in chapters 3 and 6, the two humbled kings in chapters 4 and 5. Language and structure correspond.
Editing and composition

Some scholars hold that this is a trace of two sources joined into one book, and it connects with the dispute about the date of composition (see the book-wide positions: composition and bilingual structure).
issues.say: These notes read from the text itself: this Aramaic section speaks of “how God’s people live in foreign kingdoms and how God rules,” which fits the court language it uses. As for the process of composition, we do not treat it as a condition of faith.
issues.care: Do not let the switch of language become a dispute over whether this book can be trusted. First listen to the text: in whichever language, “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (4:17) is the same sentence.

issues.t: Did the king really forget the dream, or was he testing the magicians?
issues.why: The king says, “The thing is gone from me” (2:5, 8), but the meaning of the original is disputed. Did the king truly forget the dream, or had he already made up his mind and was testing the magicians?
pos: He truly forgot
The reading “the dream has gone from me” takes this view; the dream troubled him but he could not grasp its content, which is a real human experience.
He had already decided
The original אַזְדָּא may be a Persian loanword meaning “firm, decided”; the king’s command was “first tell me the dream,” in order to test the magicians.
Both together
Whether or not the king forgot, the result is the same: the king wanted an answer that could not be faked; and the dream’s meaning has a weight even the king himself could not put into words.
issues.say: These notes set both readings side by side and reach no conclusion. The point is not the king’s memory but this: the demand pressed human wisdom to its limit and made the revelation of the God of heaven the only answer.
issues.care: To someone troubled by “an unease that cannot be put into words,” do not hurry to give an explanation. Sometimes the very weight we cannot put into words is what we need to hand over to God.

issues.t: “Whose dwelling is not with flesh”: the Chaldeans’ words set beside Daniel’s
issues.why: The Chaldeans said: “except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh” (2:11). What does this sentence mean? What contrast does it make with the God Daniel serves?
pos: The view of God in polytheism
They held that the gods are far from humankind and do not live with flesh and blood; people cannot directly know the gods’ mind and can only guess through divination and arts.
Contrast with 2:22
Daniel says that God “knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him” (2:22); this God is not far from people but reveals mysteries.
Link to what follows
The fourth who is with them in the fire in chapter 3 (3:25), and Daniel raised up in chapter 10 (10:10), all say the same thing: he is not a God whose dwelling is not with people.
issues.say: These notes take the second and third readings together: God is not a God far from people. “The Word became flesh, and lived among us” in the New Testament (John 1:14) makes us think of this theme, but we say only “makes us think of” and do not call it a direct prophecy of this verse.
issues.care: To someone who feels “God is far from me,” do not answer with “not enough faith”; sit with him for a while first, and then let him hear: the light dwells with him, and he is willing to be with people.

issues.t: Four praying with one heart: what role does prayer play here?
issues.why: Daniel asked his three companions to “desire mercies from the God of heaven” (2:18). What is the relation between the prayer here and the later “revealing of the mystery”? Does prayer change God’s mind, or take part in God’s work?
pos: Prayer as a means
God’s work is set going through human asking; the order of this passage (ask → revealed) shows that prayer is a condition of the revealing.
Prayer as response and participation
God had already prepared; prayer does not change God but lets people stand in faith on what God is doing, and afterward know whom to bless.
A witness of one heart
The text specifically shows this was the prayer of four people with one heart; the emphasis is on “together,” not on “how.”
issues.say: These notes take the latter two readings together: prayer places people beside God’s work, so that when God acts they are not onlookers. The text puts “asking” before “revealing” but gives us no formula to apply.
issues.care: For those whose prayers were not answered as they wished, do not let this passage be said to them as “you did not ask enough.” The “But if not” of chapter 3 and the “blocked prayer” of chapter 10 supply the other half this passage does not say.

issues.t: “Not for any wisdom that I have”: why does Daniel say this first?
issues.why: Daniel said to the king: “this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living man” (2:30). Why does he say this first? Is it a rhetoric of humility, or a theological declaration?
pos: A rhetoric of humility
Messengers in the ancient Near East often stressed “I do not speak from myself” to show that their words carried the authority of the one who sent them.
A theological declaration
Wisdom is given (2:21, 23), so the interpretation is not his own achievement; this is his confession to God and also his witness to the king.
A pointed witness
He states the aim of this: “to the intent that the interpretation may be made known to the king” (2:30), taking the king’s eyes off himself and pointing to the God of heaven.
issues.say: These notes take the latter two readings together: this sentence is a confession and also a witness. It lies on the same line as 1:17, “God gave them knowledge and skill,” and prepares for the story of chapter 4, in which the king is humbled for forgetting.
issues.care: This verse is not asking people to say “I am nothing” in self-belittling. True humility is knowing that all one has is given, and therefore not grasping at glory.

issues.t: Gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay: which four kingdoms?
issues.why: Which kingdoms do the gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay of the great image in the dream point to? The text says plainly only that the head of gold is Babylon (2:38) and names none of the others.
pos: The traditional position
Head of gold = Babylon; silver = Media-Persia; bronze = Greece; iron = Rome; feet of iron mixed with clay = the continuation of Rome or the nations after it.
Another reading
