Gold = Babylon; silver = Media; bronze = Persia; iron = Greece (Alexander and his successors); adopted mostly by critical scholarship and some conservative scholars.
A symbolic reading
The four metals stand for “one worldly kingdom after another”; the point is that the material grows harder and also more brittle, without matching particular empires one by one.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and draw up no table for any. What we hold on to is this: human kingdoms have a beginning and an end, and the later they come the harder and more brittle they are; God’s kingdom is set up separately. This holds whichever reading one takes.
issues.care: Do not turn this passage into an identification of any modern regime or organization, and do not let the discussion of “who is which kingdom” replace the hope of 2:44. Persecuted saints need “God’s kingdom will never be destroyed,” not a timetable.

issues.t: What does “the stone cut out without hands” refer to?
issues.why: What does “the stone cut out without hands” (2:34, 45) refer to? Christ, God’s kingdom, or God’s people?
pos: Christ
Many traditional interpreters hold that the stone points to the Messiah; the New Testament also has similar stone language (Matt 21:44; Luke 20:18; 1 Peter 2:6–8), often seen as echoing Daniel.
God’s kingdom
The text itself explains: what the stone represents is the kingdom the God of heaven “will set up” in 2:44; the stone itself is a symbol of this kingdom.
God’s people
7:27 says the kingdom is given to the holy ones of the Most High; the stone can include those who receive the kingdom.
issues.say: These notes follow the link the New Testament itself made (the language of the stone), and at the same time return to the text’s own explanation (2:44: God’s kingdom), and do not set it against the holy ones of 7:27. The point “not by hands” is the center common to all three readings.
issues.care: Do not debate the details of “who it refers to” more than we look up together. The safest way to say it is: this stone comes from outside the human world, and at last fills the whole earth.

issues.t: When and how does God’s kingdom get “set up”?
issues.why: “The God of heaven will set up a kingdom” (2:44): when and how is this kingdom set up? Did it already begin at Christ’s first coming, or must it wait until it is fully revealed in the future?
pos: Already begun
Jesus preached “the kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15); the kingdom came with Christ’s first coming and spreads gradually through the church and history.
To be established in the future
The stone smashing the image is a picture of a total replacement in the future; God’s kingdom will be fully revealed at the end and replace all human kingdoms.
Already but not yet
The kingdom has begun but is not yet complete; believers live between “already” and “not yet.”
issues.say: These notes take the third reading and set the views side by side: we count no days and draw up no timetable. The text wants us to know that the source of this kingdom is God and that it will never be destroyed; and our present task is to be his people in human kingdoms.
issues.care: For those who suffer and are persecuted, this “already but not yet” is a comfort: before it is fully revealed we will see fragments of the kingdom and also experience pain not yet finished. Do not comfort them with “if your faith is enough you will see it.”

issues.t: The king bows down to Daniel: did Daniel accept it?
issues.why: The king fell on his face and bowed down to Daniel, and commanded that an offering and incense be offered (2:46). Did Daniel accept? Does this conflict with Daniel’s friends later refusing to bow to the golden image?
pos: The text does not say he accepted
The text says only that the king bowed down and commanded an offering; it does not say Daniel accepted; his next words point the emphasis to God.
Etiquette in the ancient Near East
A deep bow to a messenger or high official was a common honor and did not necessarily amount to worship; the king’s confession that follows (2:47) points to God.
Contrast with what follows
In chapter 3 the three friends refuse to bow to the image (3:12, 18); in both places the point is not human glory but who is worthy of worship.
issues.say: These notes do not add to the text what it does not say. What is certain is that the king’s words in 2:47 point to God, not to Daniel. The New Testament story of Paul and Barnabas refusing to be worshiped as gods (Acts 14:11–15) makes us think of the same direction.
issues.care: When a person is lifted up, this passage reminds us that the best response is to give the glory back. To those who are over-worshiped, or who over-worship others, it is the same reminder.

issues.t: Why does Daniel not appear in this chapter?
issues.why: Three times the chapter names Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and not once Daniel. Why does he not appear in this chapter?
pos: The text does not say
The author gives no account of where he was and no explanation; the focus of this chapter rests only on the three companions.
He was not present
Some guess that he was away on official business, or that because of his different rank he was not at this assembly; this is guesswork, and the text does not support it.
The arrangement of the narrative
Chapter 2 is Daniel, chapter 3 the three companions, and chapter 6 returns to Daniel. The author lets different people each face the same question: who is your Lord?
issues.say: These notes do not guess where Daniel was. What the text does not say, we do not supply; what we see is that each person must have his own “purpose,” and God does the same thing in different people.
issues.care: Do not say, because he does not appear, that he compromised, was weak or hid. A silent text is not material for accusation.

issues.t: The golden image sixty cubits high and six cubits wide: whose image is it?
issues.why: The golden image was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (about 27 meters high and 2.7 meters wide), of slender proportion. Whose image is it?
pos: The king himself or a symbol of kingly power
Compare the “head of gold” in chapter 2: the king made the whole image of gold, declaring that his kingdom would not be replaced.
A god of Babylon
The golden image may represent a god the king worshiped, and to worship it was to pledge loyalty to both god and king; the text says only “the image that the king has set up.”
A sign of national loyalty
The point is not whose image it is but the ritual of loyalty: “when you hear the sound, fall down.”
issues.say: The text does not say whose image it is, and we do not pick one answer as the conclusion. What is certain is that people were required to choose, between the king’s image and God, which one to worship.
issues.care: Do not match this image directly with some person or system today. Reading this chapter, first ask yourself: where is the place where I “hear the music and kneel” today?

issues.t: Why is the list of instruments repeated again and again?
issues.why: Horn, flute, lyre, trigon, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music appear several times in this chapter. Why is it repeated so often?
pos: Rhetorical irony
Each time it is repeated word for word, like a tidy mechanical motion, so that one feels worship turned into a standard reflex.
A feature of oral telling and recitation
Repetition was a common device of narrative at that time and also helped oral recitation and memory.
The discussion of language and date
Some names in the list look like Greek loanwords, which is where later scholars’ discussion of the date of composition comes from (see the book-wide positions: composition and date).
issues.say: We read from the effect of the text: the repetition is so that we feel the uniformity and pressure of “as soon as the music sounds, everyone bows.” The discussion of date we do not treat as a condition of faith.
issues.care: Do not let the dispute over the list of instruments replace the question this chapter asks: for whom do your knees bow?

issues.t: “But if not”: will God surely save the faithful?
issues.why: The three companions said, “But if not.” Does this mean that God will surely save the faithful?
pos: The reading of guaranteed success
This holds that if faith is enough, God will surely deliver. This reading is the opposite of the plain sense of “But if not,” and these notes do not adopt it.
God is able, but the outcome is God’s
They said that God is able to save, and also said that even if he does not, they will still not serve other gods. Deliverance is God’s matter; faithfulness is the human matter.
The witness of the martyrs
Hebrews 11:35–38 mentions that some were released and some were tortured and killed, equally witnesses of “faith.”
issues.say: These notes take the second reading: the point of “But if not” is that faithfulness is not conditional on being saved. The chapter ends with their deliverance, but the text first lets us hear them say this sentence when they did not know the ending.
issues.care: This is the point to be most careful about, especially with those going through loss, illness and being shut out. Do not say to anyone, “you were not saved because your faith was not enough.”

issues.t: Who is the fourth whose “appearance is like a son of the gods”?
issues.why: The king said the fourth in the fire had an appearance “like a son of the gods.” Who is he? (Continuing the book-wide position: the fourth figure)
pos: An angel
In 3:28 the king himself calls him one who “sent his angel”; this is the explanation the text itself gives.
An appearance of Christ in the Old Testament
Some interpreters hold that this one is Christ before the incarnation, linked with the promise of Immanuel.
A symbol of God’s presence
Whoever it is, the point is that God himself is with his servants in the fire.
issues.say: These notes follow the book-wide position: three views are set side by side, and we do not treat this figure as required doctrinal evidence. We say only: it makes us think of Immanuel, God with us (Matt 1:23).
issues.care: Do not let the dispute over “who is he” cover the comfort in the fire. Those who are suffering need first to hear: you are not alone.

issues.t: The furnace heated seven times hotter: is this number symbolic?
issues.why: The furnace was heated “seven times more than it was usually heated.” Is this number symbolic?
pos: A literal sevenfold
The king’s anger had reached its height, and he truly made the fire burn fiercer than usual.
A symbol of the extreme
In the Bible “seven” often means completeness or the extreme; here it describes “heated to the utmost.”
Both together
It can be a real act and at the same time show that the king’s anger could go no further.
issues.say: We need not reach a conclusion between the literal and the symbolic. What the text wants us to see is that the fire was really hot; and that when they came out there was not even the smell of fire on them.
issues.care: Do not treat this number as material for calculating or deducing. The point is that in the hottest place God is still there.

issues.t: Why is this chapter a decree written by a king?
issues.why: The first three verses and the closing verses of this chapter are a decree written by King Nebuchadnezzar in the first person; in the middle (from 4:19) the narration switches to the third person. Why is a foreign king’s decree kept in the Bible?
pos: The king’s witness is included
The author included the king’s decree in the book so that a foreign king’s mouth would say “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men,” giving this witness more weight.
A change of narrative form
The alternation of first person (4:1–18, 34–37) and third person (4:19–33) is an arrangement of editing and narration; some hold they are different sources, some hold the author did it deliberately.
Composition and the discussion of sources
This is linked to the discussion of the date of composition and of sources (see the book-wide positions: composition and bilingual structure).
issues.say: These notes read from the text itself: this is a witness a king wrote himself, written starting from the ending. As for the process of composition, we do not treat it as a condition of faith.
issues.care: Do not make this witness small because “a foreign king wrote it”; and do not, because of the dispute over composition, let readers lose confidence in the whole chapter.

issues.t: “The spirit of the holy gods”: what do the words of a foreign king mean?
issues.why: The king says Daniel has “the spirit of the holy gods” in him (4:8, 9, 18). Is he speaking of the Holy Spirit?
pos: The language of a foreign king
The original is the plural “spirit of the holy gods,” a term the king used within his own framework of belief, not a full doctrinal confession.
Pointing to the one God
Some hold that the text uses the plural for honor, pointing to the most holy God, and the king, without knowing it, spoke the truth.
Light from the New Testament
The New Testament says the Holy Spirit lives in believers; but the text of this chapter speaks only of what the king knew.
issues.say: These notes do not treat this sentence as doctrinal evidence for the person of the Holy Spirit. We say only: even a foreign king acknowledged that in Daniel was a spirit beyond the human.
issues.care: Do not force a foreign king’s wording into a proof of doctrine; nor, because it is not a full doctrine, overlook its witness.

issues.t: Are the “seven times” seven years?
issues.why: Are the “seven times” seven years?
pos: Seven years
Taking “times” as years is the most common reading.
Seven seasons, seven months or another period
The original עִדָּנִין means only “periods” and does not specify; some also read it as seven seasons.
A complete period
“Seven” means completeness, pointing to a complete period set by God.
issues.say: These notes do not decide the length for the text. The point is in “until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men”: the length of the time is set by God; the condition for its ending is that the man knows.
issues.care: Do not take the “seven times” and match or calculate it against any year or event.

issues.t: “Break off your sins by righteousness”: is this advice to be saved by works?
issues.why: Daniel advised the king: “break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor” (4:27). Does this mean that doing good can atone for sin?
pos: The concrete fruit of repentance
Daniel is speaking of what repentance looks like: seeing the poor and changing one’s conduct; and he says “if,” with no guarantee.
Doing good in exchange for forgiveness
Some read it literally as “atoning for sin with good deeds”; this does not fit the theme of grace in the whole Bible, and these notes do not adopt it.
Almsgiving and righteousness
The word “righteousness” in later Aramaic and Hebrew can also mean “almsgiving,” set alongside “showing mercy to the poor.”
issues.say: These notes take the first: 4:27 is an invitation to the king to repent, seeing the poor in concrete terms; forgiveness is God’s grace, and doing good is the fruit of repentance.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to make the poor, or those without the ability to do good, feel they do not qualify. Grace always comes first.

issues.t: Nebuchadnezzar’s illness: historical, medical and spiritual explanations
issues.why: What was Nebuchadnezzar’s “illness”? (Continuing the book-wide position: we pass no verdict on Nebuchadnezzar’s eternal life)
pos: A mental illness
From the description of “eating grass like an ox,” some guess some mental illness; but this is a guess, and the text gives no name.
A judgment God carried out
The text attributes this to a decree from heaven and does not classify an illness.
A symbolic and literary description
Others hold that “a beast’s heart” describes a person who has lost his humanity.
issues.say: These notes do not diagnose for the text. What the text wants us to see is that “God can humble those who walk in pride,” and, after he lifts his eyes, the grace of restoration.
issues.care: Do not use this passage to mock or judge those with mental distress, and do not regard anyone’s illness as God’s judgment.

issues.t: He lifted his eyes to heaven and praised the Most High: did he believe in the Lord?
issues.why: The king lifted his eyes to heaven and praised the Most High (4:34–37). Did he come to faith?
pos: True repentance and confession
This is a very clear change: from “my glory” to “the King of heaven.”
A foreign king’s confession, but no conclusion
The text writes only his words; it says nothing of his later life and does not say whether he left his original beliefs.
The purpose of the narrative
The purpose of this passage is to let readers see God’s sovereignty, not to record a king’s conversion.
issues.say: These notes stop where 4:34–37 stops: he lifted his eyes, he praised, he confessed. As for his eternal end, we pass no verdict on God’s behalf.
issues.care: Do not use this question to decide whether anyone is saved or not. We trust only God’s mercy and justice.

issues.t: Who is Belshazzar? How is “his father Nebuchadnezzar” to be read?
issues.why: The text calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar’s “father.” Who is Belshazzar? Was he really Nebuchadnezzar’s son?
pos: A son by birth
Read literally, “father” is father and “son” is son; but historically Belshazzar was a son of Nabonidus, and his relation to Nebuchadnezzar is not clear.
A descendant or successor
In Aramaic “father” and “son” can mean ancestor and descendant, or predecessor and successor, or “one who takes the throne.”
Discussion of the historical sources
In cuneiform sources Belshazzar is a co-regent prince, not formally the king; scholars differ in how they explain the text calling him “king.”
issues.say: These notes do not decide the kinship for the text. What the text wants us to see is that “he knew how those before him had been humbled,” yet did not bow his head.
issues.care: Do not let the dispute over historical detail replace the question this chapter asks: though you know all this, is your heart still hard?

issues.t: Why are the temple vessels especially important?
issues.why: Why are the vessels of the temple so important in this chapter?
pos: Profaning what is holy
These vessels belonged to God’s house, and using them to toast idols was a direct offense against what is holy.
Echoing chapter 1
In 1:2 God gave the vessels of the temple to Nebuchadnezzar; in this chapter these vessels become the spark of judgment.
Symbolic meaning
The vessels symbolize how a person may take what belongs to God and use it to satisfy himself.
issues.say: The emphasis of these notes is on “what is holy being used for entertainment,” and also reminds us: some things are not ours; we are only entrusted with them.
issues.care: Do not turn this passage into teaching about objects alone; the point is the heart’s attitude toward what is holy.

issues.t: Why could the magicians not read “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN”?
issues.why: Why could the magicians not read the words “MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN”?
pos: Too simple in sense, and so hard
These words are everyday units of weight; the wise men did not fail to recognize them but did not know what they pointed to here.
Different readings are possible
The same set of words can be read as units of weight, or as the verbs “numbered, weighed, divided”; the Spirit of God is needed to point it out.
God’s work
In this chapter God not only wrote the words but also chose the one to interpret.
issues.say: These notes take it this way: human expertise cannot replace God’s guidance; the words can be seen, but the meaning God himself must reveal.
issues.care: Do not treat these words as a code for other calculations.

issues.t: Why did Daniel refuse the rewards and later accept the purple robe?
issues.why: Daniel refused the rewards (5:17); why did he later accept the purple robe (5:29)?
pos: What he refused was a condition
What he refused was “speaking in order to get a reward”; the reward was ordered by the king himself afterward.
Obeying the king’s command
As the king’s servant, he accepted the position the king gave and did not treat it as payment for the interpretation.
The circumstances of a life
That night the king was killed, and his purple robe and position did not last.
issues.say: These notes take the first reading: the point is the order, not speaking for reward; and when the reward comes, he is still a servant.
issues.care: Do not use this question to pick at Daniel’s motives, and do not use it to find an excuse for “accepting benefits.”

issues.t: “Though you knew all this, you have not humbled your heart”: are those who do not know God responsible?
issues.why: “Though you knew all this, you have not humbled your heart”: are those who have never heard of God also responsible?
pos: The responsibility of knowledge
Belshazzar knew the story of Nebuchadnezzar and did not humble himself, so he was accused.
General revelation
Romans 1:20 says that creation shows God’s eternal power and divine nature, so that people are without excuse.
An invitation of grace
Before judgment God first gave the chance to “know”; this is grace.
issues.say: These notes stop where the text stops: Belshazzar knew and did not bow his head. As for those who have never heard the gospel, we entrust them to God’s justice and mercy and pass no verdict on God’s behalf.
issues.care: Do not use this question to frighten people, and do not use it to judge any class of people.

issues.t: Who is “Darius the Mede”?
issues.why: Who is “Darius the Mede”?
pos: Another name for Cyrus
Some hold that Darius is another name or a deputy of Cyrus.
Another ruler
Some hold that he was an official appointed to govern Babylon, such as Gubaru and others.
No conclusion yet
The present historical sources do not clearly point to this name, and scholars hold different views.
issues.say: These notes set the various views side by side and do not decide for the text. For this chapter, the point is: the kingdom is given by God and also taken back by God.
issues.care: Do not take this historical puzzle as a test of whether the whole book can be trusted.

issues.t: Godliness made a charge: “unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God”
issues.why: His enemies could find no ground against Daniel, and could only look in “the law of his God” (6:4–5). Why was godliness made into a charge?
pos: Godliness makes people uncomfortable
A person who lives blamelessly makes the faults of others stand out, and so stirs envy.
A conflict of loyalty
Those in power demand complete allegiance, and whoever will not give the “last loyalty” to the king is seen as a threat.
The irony of the narrative
His enemies’ words became the highest witness to Daniel: his only “weakness” was his obedience to God.
issues.say: These notes set the three together and hold on to the last: in the text, this is a witness in which nothing could be faulted in daily life.
issues.care: Do not use this passage to encourage people to look for chances to be persecuted; and do not call every criticism persecution.

issues.t: The “unalterable” decree: why did the king trap himself?
issues.why: The “unalterable” decree (6:8, 12, 15): even the king himself could not withdraw it. Is this a historical fact?
pos: A feature of ancient Persian law
In the text the law of the Medes and Persians is described as unalterable; Esther 1:19 and 8:8 have a similar idea.
The function in the narrative
This “unalterable” puts the king in a bind and also makes the story more tense: human power caught in its own law.
Discussion of the sources
Surviving sources do not clearly prove this legal system, and scholars explain it differently.
issues.say: These notes reach no conclusion on the dispute over sources. The point we see is this: a law made by people can trap the one who made it; and God’s work is not bound by such limits.
issues.care: Do not let this historical question become a test of faith for this chapter.

issues.t: The window toward Jerusalem, three times a day: its relation to 1 Kings 8:48
issues.why: Praying at “the window toward Jerusalem” and “three times a day”: is this a rule?
pos: The tradition of 1 Kings 8:48
Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple: if the people are taken captive and pray toward this house, God will hear.
A pious habit
Three times a day, as in Psalm 55:17, “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will complain and moan,” was a long-standing habit of devotion, not a number the law required.
A symbolic direction
Facing Jerusalem is a hope and an identification, not the worship of a place.
issues.say: These notes do not turn it into a new rule: the point is “as he had done before,” a continuing habit, not a particular direction or number.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to demand that others do it exactly this way; and do not, because you have not done it, feel that your prayer does not count.

issues.t: Was Daniel disobeying? Compare Acts 5:29
issues.why: Was Daniel disobeying? Compare Acts 5:29, “We must obey God rather than men.”
pos: Conditional obedience
In other matters Daniel always served the king faithfully; only in this one matter, “asking from God,” would he not yield.
Peaceful non-compliance
He did not gather a crowd and did not criticize the king, but simply went on as before; this is close to the spirit of Acts 5:29.
Not ordinary defiance
The text does not ask us to use this to despise or resist ordinary authority; Romans 13 stands there too.
issues.say: These notes: this chapter is not “believers may break the law at any time” but “on the root of worship, one cannot yield,” and in a quiet way that does not boast or confront.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to find excuses for all your own disobedience. Also take care: in dangerous situations, do not make public any traceable details.

issues.t: “Innocence was found in me before God”: does Daniel dare to say this?
issues.why: “Innocence was found in me” (6:22): is Daniel saying that he has no sin?
pos: Blameless in this matter
“Innocence” is a court term, meaning that on this one charge he was blameless.
Relative innocence, not sinlessness
He did not say he had never sinned, only that before God and before the king he had done no wrong.
The manner of witness
His words are a witness to the king and a trust in God, not boasting.
issues.say: These notes take the first and second readings: he is stating a fact on this one charge. His words are not a declaration “I am righteous” but “I did nothing wrong in this matter.”
issues.care: Do not use this verse to say that you are a perfect person; and do not, because of your weaknesses, feel you have no right to say “I am innocent.”

issues.t: The accusers’ wives and children punished with them: is this just?
issues.why: The accusers’ wives and children were punished with them (6:24): is this just?
pos: Collective punishment in the ancient world
In the ancient Near East it was common for the families of traitors and false accusers to share the punishment.
The text describes and does not praise
The Bible does not say this punishment was good; Deuteronomy 24:16 says plainly that each person is to die for his own sin.
A warning in the narrative
This verse lets readers see that those who set traps finally fall into their own trap; and at the same time innocent people are drawn in, which is the bitter fruit of sin.
issues.say: These notes do not defend this punishment and do not treat it as a model God approves. What we see is the consequence of evil, and God’s justice shown in human affairs.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to find excuses for any revenge or collective punishment; toward the families who are harmed, have all the more compassion.

issues.t: Why is chapter 7 placed after chapters 5 and 6 when its date is earlier?
issues.why: The date of chapter 7 (the first year of Belshazzar) is before chapter 5, yet it is arranged after chapter 6. What does this arrangement mean?
pos: Arrangement by theme and structure

Chapters 2 to 7 form one large Aramaic section. The image of four kingdoms in chapter 2 and the four beasts of chapter 7 echo each other at beginning and end; this arrangement makes the section a circle: from the statue people see, to the beasts heaven sees.
The dividing line between story and vision
The first six chapters are “stories about others,” and from chapter 7 on come “Daniel’s own visions”; the arrangement makes chapter 7 the pivot of the whole book.
Discussion of date and composition
Scholars hold different views on the date of composition and the arrangement, and this is a question under constant discussion. These notes have set the views side by side in the book-wide positions.
issues.say: These notes take the first two together: whichever came first, the author lets us, from here, look at the world from another angle. The date of composition is not a condition of faith.
issues.care: Do not let the discussion of dates become a reason to attack or look down on others’ faith; and do not, because it cannot be fully resolved, feel that this chapter is unreliable.

issues.t: Which four kingdoms are the four beasts?
issues.why: Which four kingdoms are the four beasts?
pos: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece
Many scholars see the four in order as these four kingdoms, with the fourth being the Greek kingdoms that split after Alexander; this connects with the picture in the second half of chapter 8.
Babylon, Media and Persia, Greece, Rome
Another traditional reading joins Media and Persia as one kingdom and makes the fourth kingdom Rome. This reading has a long line of transmission in the church through the ages.
A reading mainly symbolic
Some hold that the four represent “a series of human powers” and need not match each historical kingdom exactly; the point is their form: beastly, given power, and judged.
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side, draw up no timetable, and do not decide which must be right. What we see is that they were all given power and all judged.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to decide which country of today is which beast; and do not, because experts differ, stop reading this chapter.

issues.t: Who is the little horn?
issues.why: Who is the little horn, with eyes and a mouth speaking great things?
pos: A king of the Greek period
Many scholars hold that this refers to a king after Alexander who persecuted the Jews; the little horn of chapter 8 has similar descriptions.
A figure after Rome or an end-time power
Another traditional reading holds that this is one who arises after the fourth kingdom, connected with the final persecution.
A reading by characteristics
Some stress that the marks of this horn are characteristics: speaking great words, wearing out the holy ones, trying to change times and law; such a power can arise in any generation.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, identify no one today, and do not encourage anyone to identify someone as the antichrist. What the text gives is characteristics and an ending, and the aim is patience, not panic.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to label any political position or person; for those who are being persecuted, protect them all the more, and do not mention traceable details.

issues.t: Who is the “Ancient of Days”?
issues.why: Who is the “Ancient of Days”?
pos: God the Father
The reading of most through the ages: he is God himself seated on the throne; “ancient” means before all days, not aged.
God-centered, not a description of appearance
The title “ancient of days” speaks of his eternity and dignity, not of his age; the New Testament later has a similar picture in describing Christ (Rev 1:14), which makes us think of this link.
A few other readings
A very few hold different views, but within the context of the text the clearest point is: he is the God who judges and gives the kingdom.
issues.say: These notes take the first, and see the link in the New Testament between Christ and God the Father, without further speculation.
issues.care: Do not picture this title as the portrait of an old man; the point is that he is eternal, holy, and sits in judgment.

issues.t: Who is the “one like a son of man”?
issues.why: Who is the “one like a son of man”?
pos: The Messiah, an individual
Many traditional readings: he is a king to whom the kingdom is given, and a portrait of the Messiah.
A representative of the holy ones
Some hold that this is a portrait of the group, the holy ones: the beasts are seen as powers, and the son of man as the image of the holy ones, to whom the kingdom is given (7:18, 27).
A heavenly messenger, or both
Some hold that he is a heavenly representative such as Michael; others hold that individual and group can stand together, linked to each other.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, and see: the son of man and the holy ones are not opposed but linked. However one reads it, this scene tells us that the end of history is one like a man, given the kingdom.
issues.care: Do not turn this issue into a debate of mutual attack; and do not, because it cannot be fully resolved, make light of this hope.

issues.t: “Son of man”: its relation to Jesus’ self-designation and Matthew 26:64
issues.why: What is the relation between “son of man,” Jesus’ self-designation, and Matthew 26:64?
pos: Jesus quoted Daniel 7:13
At his trial Jesus said: “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming on the clouds of the sky” (Matt 26:64); many see a link with Daniel 7:13.
The ordinary meaning of “son of man” in Aramaic and Hebrew
“Son of man” in the Old Testament also often means “a human being” (as in Ezekiel); Jesus’ title may include both levels.
A link is not the whole explanation
The New Testament makes the link, and we follow the New Testament in saying it; how each detail corresponds is read differently by different views.
issues.say: These notes cite only the link the New Testament itself made and add no further inference. We also do not set the son of man against the holy ones.
issues.care: Do not turn this issue into saying there is only one acceptable solution; and do not use it to accuse another church tradition.

issues.t: Who are “the holy ones of the Most High”?
issues.why: Who are “the holy ones of the Most High”?
pos: God’s people on earth
Many readings: they are those who belong to the Most High, who suffer in the world and in the end receive the kingdom (7:21–22, 27).
Heavenly messengers
Some hold that this means a company in heaven; “holy ones” in the Old Testament sometimes means heavenly messengers.
Both
Some also hold that the two are linked: both heaven and earth belong to the holy ones of the Most High.
issues.say: These notes set them side by side. The point we see is that they receive the kingdom as something given, not seized.
issues.care: Do not use this title to build a wall between “us” and “them”; and do not take receiving the kingdom as a guarantee of being free from suffering now.

issues.t: What period is “a time and times and half a time”?
issues.why: What period is “a time and times and half a time”?
pos: A literal three and a half years
Some read this phrase as three and a half years; historically some hold that it relates to a certain period of persecution.
A symbolic, limited time
Some hold that this is a picture of “a limited period”: half of seven means limited, not complete.
Echoes of other texts
Daniel 12:7 and Revelation 12:14 have similar expressions; the views differ in how they match them.
issues.say: These notes count no days and do not decide its length. What we see is its direction: the holy ones are given into his hand for a limited time, within a limit, with an end.
issues.care: Do not use this phrase to calculate dates for any event; to those who are suffering, what to say is: be patient, God knows.

issues.t: Why is there judgment before the kingdom is given?
issues.why: Why is there judgment before the kingdom is given?
pos: Judgment as the handling of justice
Evil is dealt with and those who were wronged are vindicated (7:22); without this step, the giving of the kingdom would be incomplete.
The judgment is a “seated” one
The judgment in 7:10 and 7:26 is quiet and orderly, not emotional revenge.
The kingdom is given
After the judgment the kingdom is given to the son of man and the holy ones; this is God’s sovereignty, not human merit.
issues.say: These notes set the three together: God’s judgment is in justice and also in order; the kingdom is given, not seized.
issues.care: Do not use the theme of judgment to frighten people or to find excuses for your own revenge; you need only hand matters to the one who sits in judgment.

issues.t: Why does the text return to Hebrew from chapter 8?
issues.why: Why does the original return to Hebrew from chapter 8?
pos: A shift of structure and theme
2:4–7:28 is in Aramaic and speaks of the nations and the history of the world; from chapter 8 the return to Hebrew speaks of the sanctuary, the holy people and the end; language and theme correspond.
Discussion of composition and editing

Scholars hold different views on the origin of this bilingual structure, including different stages of composition, editing and intended readers; these discussions have been set side by side in the book-wide positions.
A position that does not affect reading
However this change of language is explained, the message of the text does not change: God rules, and the holy ones receive the kingdom.
issues.say: These notes do not use the change of language to decide the date of composition or the reliability of the book. What we see is that the earlier section speaks to the nations, and this section returns to the language of the holy people themselves.
issues.care: Do not turn this scholarly discussion into a standard for judging others’ faith; and do not, because there are different views, stop reading this chapter.

issues.t: Whom do the ram and the male goat refer to?
issues.why: Whom do the ram and the male goat refer to?
pos: The text’s own explanation
8:20–21 says directly: the ram with two horns is the kings of Media and Persia, the male goat is the king of Greece; and the great horn between his eyes is the first king.
The discussion of the “first king” and the “four kingdoms”
The text does not name the first king or the four kingdoms; the views differ, some matching them to the later split of Greece, some reading otherwise.
The symbolic level
Some stress that the two horns stand for two joined peoples, the later-growing one higher, Persia coming up after; these details are pictures the text gives in symbols.
issues.say: These notes follow the text’s own explanation: the ram is Media and Persia, the male goat is Greece; as for the first king and the four kingdoms, we say no more than the text.
issues.care: Do not take this clear explanation as a reason to match anything to today at will; the text speaks only this far, and we stop here.

issues.t: Who is the little horn? Is it Antiochus IV?
issues.why: Who is the little horn? Is it Antiochus IV?
pos: A king of the Greek period

Many scholars hold that this refers to a king after the split of Greece who defiled the sanctuary and ended the continual burnt offering, matching the description of 8:11–12; Antiochus IV is the one often named.
An end-time figure, or a double correspondence
Another traditional reading holds that this description also foreshadows a later, more end-time figure, and the two can stand together.
A reading by characteristics and pattern

Some stress that the text gives characteristics: speaking great words, destroying God’s house, attacking the holy people, and being broken without human hands; such a pattern may appear in any generation.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, identify no one today, and encourage no one to put a label on anyone. Referring back to the book-wide position: we count no days and identify no antichrist; the fruit is patience, not panic.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to label any political position or person; for those who are being persecuted, do not demand that they go public, and do not press for traceable details.

issues.t: How is “2,300 evenings and mornings” to be counted?
issues.why: How is “2,300 evenings and mornings” counted?
pos: 2,300 days
Reading “2,300 evenings and mornings” as 2,300 days and matching it to a certain period of persecution.
1,150 days
Taking “evenings and mornings” as the two daily continual burnt offerings, each counted once, making 1,150 days in all.
A symbolic number
Some hold that this symbolizes a limited, restricted period and need not match a number of days exactly.
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side, count no days and do not decide its length. The point the text gives is: the destruction of the sanctuary has a limit; there is an evening, and also a morning; and the sanctuary will be shown righteous.
issues.care: Do not use this number to calculate dates for any event; to those who are suffering, what to say is: the nights are numbered, God knows.

issues.t: Why does Gabriel appear here for the first time?
issues.why: Why does Gabriel appear here for the first time?
pos: The first appearance of an angel’s name
Gabriel is the first angel in the Bible whose name appears; before this the text says only “messenger” or “holy one.”
The role of the interpreter
In this chapter Gabriel is commanded to make Daniel understand; in chapter 9 he appears again and explains the seventy sevens.
No discussion of angel details
The text’s emphasis is not on the angel’s appearance and rank but on his task: to make people understand.
issues.say: These notes add no angelology the text does not have. What we see is that understanding is given; the messenger’s first act is to raise him up.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to promote excessive imagining of or worship of angels; and do not, because you cannot see angels, doubt God’s presence.

issues.t: “Seal up the vision”: why seal it up?
issues.why: “Seal up the vision”: why seal it?
pos: The time has not yet come
The vision concerns “many days to come,” so it is sealed first, to wait for its time.
Protection and patience
Some hold that sealing was also to protect those in suffering, so that people would not apply it too early or too lightly.
Echoing 12:4, 9
“Seal” shares a root with 12:4 and 12:9 at the end of the book, a bookend of the whole book: sealed until the time of the end.
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side. Sealing does not mean it is unimportant; it means we need not understand everything now; when we do not understand, we can go back to our post and do our work faithfully.
issues.care: Do not use “sealed” as a reason for refusing to learn; and do not use it to give authority to your own speculation.

issues.t: “I understood by the books”: Jeremiah’s seventy years and Daniel’s prayer
issues.why: Daniel understood the seventy years “by the books”: what was he reading? What is the relation between Jeremiah’s seventy years and his prayer?
pos: Reading Jeremiah

Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10 both speak of seventy years; many readings hold that these are the two places he read. “Books” is plural, showing that God’s word had by then been collected and was being read.
From promise to prayer
He read the promise and did not go off to count days but fasted and prayed; God’s word brought him nearer to God, not more eager to calculate.
The discussion of the starting point of the seventy years
From which year the seventy years are counted and to which year they run has long been read in different ways; the text gives us no conclusion.
issues.say: These notes take the first two readings and reach no conclusion on the starting point of the seventy years. The point is: a promise is not for calculating but for praying.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to argue over who counted right; and do not, because you cannot work it out, stop trusting God’s word.

issues.t: Fasting, sackcloth and ashes: does the posture of prayer matter?
issues.why: Fasting, sackcloth and ashes: does the posture of prayer matter?
pos: Outward posture as an expression of the heart
Fasting, sackcloth and ashes are often in the Bible an expression of repentance and grief; they help a person lay his whole self down.
The posture is not the goal
The prophets also remind us that true fasting is justice and mercy (Isaiah 58), not outward form; a posture without the heart means nothing.
Different circumstances, different ways
People’s bodily conditions and circumstances differ, and they need not do it just the same way; God looks at the heart that turns its face toward him.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side: posture can help us but is not a condition. Daniel’s point is “turning the face to God,” not a particular action.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to demand that others fast; and do not, because of physical illness or being unable to fast, feel your prayer is not enough. Those with health conditions should first consult medical care.

issues.t: Why does Daniel confess using “we”?
issues.why: Why does Daniel confess using “we”?
pos: Intercession on behalf of the people
He puts himself among the people and confesses before God on behalf of the whole nation; this is the posture of an intercessor.
Corporate responsibility
The Bible often treats a group as a whole (as in Ezra 9 and Nehemiah 9); we share one body, one history, one kingdom.
A posture without accusation
Using “we” is not standing outside and accusing; this is a different posture from a prayer that says “they.”
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side. The point is: prayer that begins with “we” is both intercession and humility.
issues.care: Do not use “we” to confess for others or to force others to confess; and do not use this chapter to accuse those who are suffering.

issues.t: The curse written in the law of Moses: why has it come upon all Israel?
issues.why: The curse written in the law of Moses: why has it come upon all Israel?
pos: The structure of the covenant
Deuteronomy 27–30 and Leviticus 26 speak of the blessing of obedience and the curse of breaking the covenant; in 9:11 Daniel understands the exile within the framework of the covenant.
God’s justice and faithfulness
Daniel says this calamity came as written in the law of Moses; God did not break the covenant but acted according to it, and is “righteous” (9:14).
Not an explanation of every suffering

This passage looks back on the historical event of the exile and is not an explanation of every person’s suffering; Job and Jesus (John 9:3) both remind us that not every suffering is because of someone’s sin.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. We do not turn this passage into an accusation against those who suffer. Daniel’s point is to admit that God is righteous and still ask him for mercy.
issues.care: Do not say to someone who is suffering, “you must have done something wrong”; and do not use this passage to defend any harm.

issues.t: “Not for our righteousness, but for your great mercies”: the ground of prayer
issues.why: “Not for our righteousness, but for your great mercies”: what is the ground of prayer?
pos: The ground of prayer is in God, not in people
The plea is not based on human merit but on God’s mercy; this is the hinge of the whole chapter (9:18).
For his name’s sake
9:19 says “for your own sake” and “your name”; the final ground of prayer is God’s name and his reputation.
Link to the New Testament
The New Testament says we are saved not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9); this makes us think that the ground of grace has always been with God.
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side. The point is: you need not be worthy to lay your plea down.
issues.care: Do not preach this verse as “so I need not repent”; the whole of Daniel 9 is confession. Mercy and repentance are not opposed.

issues.t: “The time of the evening offering”: is there an evening offering without a temple?
issues.why: “The time of the evening offering”: is there an evening offering without a temple?
pos: A time kept in memory
The temple had been destroyed, yet Daniel still remembered the time of the evening offering (Exodus 29:38–41); prayer carried on the rhythm of worship.
Prayer as an evening offering
Psalm 141:2 says, “the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice”; prayer can become a kind of offering.
A marker of time
This time is also only a marker showing when Gabriel came, and need not be turned into a rule.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. The point is: where there is no temple, prayer can still be worship.
issues.care: Do not turn this verse into a demand that people pray at one particular moment; God sees your prayer at any time.

issues.t: The six things: who is “the most holy”?
issues.why: The six things: who is “the most holy” who is anointed? (Referring back to the book-wide position: the seventy sevens are not used to count days)
pos: Pointing to Christ
Many church traditions read “the most holy” as Christ; the six things find fulfillment in his death and resurrection.
Pointing to the sanctuary or its cleansing
“Most holy” (קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים) in the Old Testament often means the Most Holy Place; some read it as the sanctuary being set apart as holy again.
Pointing to a historical process
Others see the six things as a gradual historical process, not limited to one event.
issues.say: These notes set the three side by side, do not decide for you, and draw up no timetable. What we see is the direction: sin dealt with, everlasting righteousness brought in.
issues.care: Do not turn this issue into a reason for judging one another; and do not, because of different readings, look down on other brothers and sisters.

issues.t: How are the seventy sevens counted?
issues.why: How are the seventy sevens counted? (Referring back to the book-wide position: the seventy sevens are not used to count days)
pos: The reading in years
Taking each “seven” as seven years, 490 years in all; this is linked to the system of the seventh-year Sabbath.
A symbolic reading
Some hold that the seventy sevens are a symbolic, ordered period and need not correspond exactly to days or years.
Different readings of the starting point and the endpoint
How the starting point of the decree, the seven sevens, the sixty-two sevens and the one seven correspond to history has been read in many different ways down the centuries.
issues.say: These notes count no days and do not decide its length. What we see is that God’s answer to Daniel is a promise about sin and righteousness, not a timetable.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to calculate dates for any event, and do not use it to frighten people; to those who are suffering, what to say is: the nights are numbered, God knows.

issues.t: Who are “the anointed one will be cut off” and “the one who makes desolate”?
issues.why: Who are “the anointed one will be cut off” and “the one who makes desolate”? (Referring back to the book-wide position: the seventy sevens are not used to count days)
pos: Christ and the later destruction
Many traditions read “the anointed one will be cut off” as the death of Christ, and “the one who makes desolate” as the power that later destroyed the holy city and the sanctuary.
Readings by ancient figures
Others point “the anointed one” to Cyrus or to a certain high priest, and “the one who makes desolate” to a king of the Greek period.
A double reading toward the end
Others hold that this passage points at the same time to a figure and events nearer the end, and can have a double fulfillment.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, identify no one today and count no days. The point is: the desolation is decreed, and so is its end; and the one who makes desolate will in the end have God’s wrath poured out on him.
issues.care: Do not use this issue to label any political position, and do not attack one another because of different readings. For those who are persecuted, do not press for traceable details.

issues.t: What does “a great conflict” mean?
issues.why: What does “a great conflict” mean? (10:1)
pos: The great conflict spoken of in this vision
The original reads, “The word is true, and it is a great army (great conflict)”; many readings take this to mean the wars between the nations described in the following chapter.
Hard service
“צָבָא” can also mean hard service or toil; some read it as: the matter is true, and it is also hard.
Warfare in heaven and on earth
Others hold that the conflict in heaven spoken of in 10:13, 20 corresponds to the conflict on earth.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and do not decide for you. What we see is that this vision is true, and also hard; and what Daniel is given is understanding.
issues.care: Do not use this phrase to label any contemporary war or conflict; and do not, because the rendering is uncertain, think this chapter is unreliable.

issues.t: Three weeks of mourning and fasting: what kind of prayer is this?
issues.why: Three weeks of mourning and fasting: what kind of prayer is this? (10:2)
pos: Mourning for the future of the people
He mourned, ate no pleasant food and did not anoint himself; this is mourning for the future of God’s people. The text does not give the reason, and we do not add one.
Fasting and setting the heart to understand
10:12 says he “set your heart to understand” and “humbled yourself”; his fasting is joined to understanding and to humility.
Not a condition for exchanging for an answer
Fasting is an expression, not a formula; those with health conditions need not do the same.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. The point is: he mourned for others, mourned for the people; and God’s messenger heard from the very first day.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to demand that others fast for a number of days; and do not, because of physical illness or being unable to fast, feel your prayer is not enough. Those with health conditions should first consult medical care.

issues.t: Who is the man dressed in linen? Is he Christ?
issues.why: Who is the man dressed in linen? Is he Christ? (10:5)
pos: A glorious angel
Some hold that this is Gabriel or another glorious angel; linen is also the clothing of heavenly messengers in Ezekiel 9–10.
Christ
Others hold that the glory of this visitor resembles the description in Revelation 1:13–15, so it is Christ appearing.
The text does not say
Still others stress that the text does not say who he is and does not have him call himself God; we need not guess.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, do not decide for you, and do not equate the two passages. What we see is that this visitor makes people fall down, and also makes them stand up.
issues.care: Do not turn this issue into a reason for judging one another; and do not, because of different readings, look down on other brothers and sisters.

issues.t: “Your words were heard”: was the delay of the prayer because it was blocked?
issues.why: “Your words were heard”: was the delay of the prayer because it was blocked? (10:12)
pos: Delay does not mean not being heard
From the first day his words were heard; the delay was because things we cannot see were going on in heaven (10:13).
Not every delay has a reason of being blocked
The text speaks of Daniel’s experience this once; it is not an explanation of every delay in prayer. God’s timing and wisdom often exceed our understanding.
Still for the sake of many days to come
10:14 says this vision is for many days to come; in the delay God is also preparing something greater.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. The point is: from the first day, your words were heard; we do not look for an explanation for every delay.
issues.care: Do not say to someone who is waiting, “you must have done something wrong”; and do not turn this verse into an accusation against God.

issues.t: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia”: is this a territorial spirit?
issues.why: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia”: is this a territorial spirit? (Referring back to the book-wide position: chapter 10 does not encourage territorial spirit warfare; the focus is 10:12)
pos: Spiritual powers
Some hold that this refers to a spiritual power behind Persia; the conflict in heaven corresponds to the nations on earth.
Human rulers
Others hold that “prince” (שַׂר) refers to the ruler of Persia or his representative, and that the text uses language in which heaven and earth echo each other.
A description, not an operations manual
Some stress that this verse describes a background Daniel did not know, and does not tell us to identify or attack the spirit of any region.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and state clearly: we do not encourage territorial spirit warfare, and we do not teach identifying or attacking the spirit of any place. The point of this chapter is 10:12: from the first day, your words were heard.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to label any region, people or group as “controlled by a spirit”; with those who are suffering, be especially careful not to blame.

issues.t: Who is Michael?
issues.why: Who is Michael? (Referring back to the book-wide position: chapter 10 does not encourage territorial spirit warfare; the focus is 10:12)
pos: The archangel
Many traditions hold Michael to be the archangel; verse 9 of Jude also calls him the archangel Michael.
A guardian of God’s people
10:21 calls him “your prince,” and 12:1 calls him “the great prince who stands for the children of your people”; he is specially related to God’s people.
No discussion of angelology details
The text’s emphasis is not on Michael’s rank or power but on his role: standing on the side of God’s people.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. What we see is: you are not alone; in heaven, one stands on your side.
issues.care: Do not imagine too much about angels or worship them; and do not, because you cannot see angels, doubt God’s presence.

issues.t: “I stood up to confirm and strengthen him”: who is speaking?
issues.why: “I stood up to confirm and strengthen him”: who is speaking? (11:1)
pos: The speaker is the messenger of chapter 10
The speaker of 11:1 is the messenger who has appeared since 10:5; in the first year of Darius he “stood up” to support Michael and make him strong.
The speaker is Michael’s companion
Others hold that this sentence is only a description of heavenly messengers supporting one another, and need not point to a particular one.
The text is not clear
The person and the object in the original have long been understood differently; some even hold that “I” points to another figure.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and do not decide for you. What we see is: between the successions of earthly empires, someone in heaven is “standing and supporting,” and God’s people are not alone.
issues.care: Do not turn this verse into inferences about the ranks and division of labor of angels; and do not, because the speaker is uncertain, think the whole chapter unreliable.

issues.t: Who are the “three kings” and the “fourth” of Persia?
issues.why: Who are the “three kings” and the “fourth” of Persia? (11:2; referring back to the book-wide position: views on the date of composition set side by side)
pos: The historical kings of Persia
Some match the “three kings” and the “fourth” to historical Persian kings, and read the fourth as the last one who attacked Greece.
The numbers as a rough description
Others hold that the numbers in the text sketch the picture of Persia’s turn from strength to decline, and need not be matched king by king.
Related to readings of the date of composition
Different readings of the date of composition understand the historical details of this verse differently; we set them side by side in the book-wide position.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and settle nothing for you. What we hold on to is: even the strongest empire is within the “truth” that was shown from heaven.
issues.care: Do not turn this verse into a clue for matching any present-day regime; and do not, in order to match history, overlook the rest the text means to give.

issues.t: How do the king of the south and the king of the north correspond to history?
issues.why: How do the king of the south and the king of the north correspond to history? (11:5; referring back to the book-wide position: views on the date of composition set side by side)
pos: Two dynasties of the Hellenistic period

Many scholars read the king of the south and the king of the north as two dynasties in the Hellenistic period, in the region of Egypt and Syria, with marriage alliances and wars matching the history of the time.
A prophetic, general description
Others hold that the text uses typical description to sketch how the nations deal with one another, and not every sentence needs a counterpart in the history books.
The details are still disputed
Scholars do not agree on how each verse corresponds, and the text itself names no one.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and say plainly: we do not match these details one by one and do not fix dates. What we see is that neither king can stand.
issues.care: Do not turn the kings of the south and the north into two countries today; and do not, because the details are hard to match, say this chapter is unimportant.

issues.t: Who is the “contemptible person”?
issues.why: Who is the “contemptible person”? (11:21; referring back to the book-wide position: no antichrist is identified)
pos: A ruler of the Hellenistic period who persecuted the Jews
Many scholars read this “despised person” as a king of the second century BC who persecuted the Jews.
An adversary of the end time
Others hold that he also foreshadows or points to a later adversary nearer the end; the two echo each other.
The text describes only his methods and does not name him
Still others stress that the text is about his way of working: flattery, deceit, scattering wealth; and not about who he is.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and say plainly: we identify no one today as this person and make no timetable from it; we only recognize such a way, and do not walk in it.
issues.care: Do not, in a church or group, put this label on people you dislike; and with those who have been hurt by the powerful, be especially careful not to use this verse to identify for them who hurt them.

issues.t: “The abomination that makes desolate” and its relation to 9:27 and 12:11
issues.why: “The abomination that makes desolate” and its relation to 9:27 and 12:11 (11:31; referring back to the book-wide position: no days counted, no antichrist identified)
pos: All three point to the same historical event
Some hold that what 8:11–13, 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11 speak of is the same event of defiling the sanctuary seen from different angles.
Layers of history and the end echoing each other
Others hold that this description points both to a historical defilement and to a similar later event; the New Testament also cites it in Matthew 24:15.
Each place has its own emphasis
Still others hold that the contexts of the four places differ and need not be forced into one event; look at each in its own place.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, settle nothing for you, and do not use this verse to count days. What we see is that in the darkness of the defiled sanctuary, God’s people still have some who know him.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to label any contemporary event as “the abomination” and cause panic; the fruit should be patience, not fear.

issues.t: “The people who know their God will be strong and do exploits”: what does it mean to know God?
issues.why: “The people who know their God will be strong and do exploits”: what does it mean to know God? (11:32)
pos: Knowing within a relationship
“Know” is a word the Bible often uses; it means living within a relationship with God, and not only knowing doctrine.
Joined to the covenant
The contrast in this verse is “those who do wickedly against the covenant”; knowing God is joined to keeping the covenant and holding fast to the faith.
Strong because held up by God
“Be strong” shares a root with “support” in 11:1; strength is the result of being held up, not of gritting one’s teeth on one’s own.
issues.say: These notes take all three together: knowing God is in a relationship; being strong is being held up by God; and this relationship keeps holding to his covenant even in the dark.
issues.care: Do not turn “knowing God” into how much knowledge one has or how much one serves, and use it to judge who counts as strong; and do not use it to press on those who are weak.

issues.t: Why do the wise ones fall?
issues.why: Why do the wise ones fall? (11:35)
pos: To refine the rest
The text itself says: the falling is to refine, to purify and to make white, until the time of the end.
The wise make people know God by their own witness
Some hold that the fall of the wise becomes part of the refining of the faith of the whole community, so that people see God more.
The text does not explain the cause of all suffering
The text gives only this situation a meaning; it does not say that all suffering has this cause.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side. What we see: in God’s hands even falling has meaning; but this is hope for the sufferer, not an explanation others may lay on pain.
issues.care: Do not say to someone who is suffering or has lost a loved one, “this is God refining you”; using Scripture this way blocks tears and wounds more deeply.

issues.t: From verse 36, is it the same king, or does it turn to another person at the end?
issues.why: From verse 36, is it the same king, or does it turn to another person at the end? (11:36; referring back to the book-wide position: no antichrist is identified)
pos: Still the same king
Many scholars hold that from verse 36 the text still describes the king before, only turning from his outward actions to his heart.
Turning to another at the end
Others hold that from verse 36 the text turns to a self-exalting figure nearer the end, echoing the lawless one the New Testament speaks of.
A description that advances in layers
Still others hold that the text deliberately lets the descriptions of history and of the end overlap, without a hard division.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and say plainly: we identify no contemporary person as the antichrist and make no timetable from it; we look only at the road of pride, and its limit.
issues.care: Do not turn this passage into a guessing game about who “that person” is; and do not use it to stir up fear of any particular people.

issues.t: How should details that do not match history be handled?
issues.why: How should details that do not match history be handled? (11:40; referring back to the book-wide position: views on the date of composition set side by side)
pos: The text is a prophetic generalization
Some hold that verses 40–45 are a prophetic description whose details need not match the history books item by item; the point is the end of the self-exalting one.
Turning to a time nearer the end
Others hold that what this section describes has not yet been fully fulfilled, and points to events nearer the end.
Different readings of the date of composition

Some scholars, following a reading of the date of composition, hold that the difference between this passage and history reflects the writer’s own horizon; we set them side by side in the book-wide position.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and settle nothing for you. We honestly admit the difficulty and hold on to the clearest point of the text: his end comes, and no one helps him.
issues.care: Do not, in defending one reading, attack brothers and sisters who hold another; and do not, because of the difficulty, think the whole book cannot be trusted.

issues.t: Michael standing up, “a time of trouble,” and its relation to Matthew 24:21
issues.why: Michael standing up, “a time of trouble,” and its relation to Matthew 24:21 (12:1; referring back to the book-wide position: no days counted, no antichrist identified)
pos: Tribulation in history
Some hold that this refers to the persecution God’s people went through in the second century BC, the text using heightened language to describe that dark time.
The great tribulation at the end
Others hold that this verse points to a greater tribulation nearer the end, echoing Jesus’ words in Matthew 24:21.
History and the end reflect each other layer by layer
Still others hold that the text deliberately lets the description of history and the description nearer the end overlap, without a hard division.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, do not decide for you, and do not use this verse to draw up a timetable or identify any contemporary event. What we see is that in the greatest tribulation, a great prince stands up.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to label any event today as “the great tribulation” and cause panic; the fruit should be patience, not alarm.

issues.t: Does “everyone who is found written in the book” mean predestination?
issues.why: Does “everyone who is found written in the book” mean predestination? (12:1)
pos: The people God has chosen
Some read it from the angle of predestination, holding that “written in the book” means those God chose and recorded in the book of life.
God’s people who hold on faithfully
Others hold that this refers to those among God’s people who hold on to the faith and are remembered by God; the emphasis is the assurance of being rescued.
The text does not unfold the details of predestination
Still others stress that the point of this verse is comfort, not a debate on predestination.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and do not turn this verse into a dispute over predestination. What we see is: God remembers his people, and their names are written in his book.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to decide whether anyone’s name is in the book; and do not, because of different theological positions, judge other brothers and sisters.

issues.t: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake”: who is included in the resurrection?
issues.why: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake”: who is included in the resurrection? (12:2)
pos: The resurrection of all people
Some read “many” as “all,” holding that here everyone will be raised, some to everlasting life and some to shame.
Many, that is, those concerned
Others hold that “many” refers specifically to those concerned, such as God’s people and their persecutors.
The text does not specify the extent
Still others stress that the point of the text is that death is not the end, and it does not detail the extent of the resurrection.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and settle nothing for you. The New Testament gives clearer revelation about the resurrection (John 5:28–29, Acts 24:15); what we see is that falling is not the end.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to pass judgment on anyone who has died; with those who are grieving, accompany them first, and do not hurry to explain the details of the resurrection.

issues.t: “Everlasting contempt”: how should eternal judgment be read?
issues.why: “Everlasting contempt”: how should eternal judgment be read? (12:2)
pos: Everlasting judgment
Some, from the traditional angle, hold that this refers to everlasting judgment and separation.
Shame in history
Others hold that this verse describes the lasting shame that falls on the persecutors, and need not be refined into a theological eternity.
The text speaks only of the final outcome of justice
Still others stress that the point of the text is God’s final justice, not a detailed picture of judgment.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side, settle nothing for you, and do not turn this verse into a tool for threatening. What we see is that God has a final justice, and also a final hope.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to threaten people or to judge that a certain person has already been condemned; and do not, because it is hard to accept, pretend this verse is not there.

issues.t: “Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse”: who are the wise?
issues.why: “Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse”: who are the wise? (12:3)
pos: The teachers who made many understand
Some hold that the wise are those in 11:33 who instructed the many and suffered for it.
All of God’s faithful people
Others hold that this description covers all the faithful believers who turn people to God.
Especially those who fell for the faith
Still others hold that this verse is especially a comfort to those who fell for the faith.
issues.say: These notes take all three together: the wise are those who, by life and word, accompany others to draw nearer to God; their light is a light God has set in the night.
issues.care: Do not turn this verse into a glory belonging only to a few, or use it to compare who is more spiritual than whom; and do not, because you feel ordinary, deny your own light.

issues.t: Does “knowledge will be increased” mean technology?
issues.why: Does “knowledge will be increased” mean technology? (12:4)
pos: Increase of technology and knowledge in general
Some link this verse to the development of modern technology and hold it is a prophecy of an explosion of knowledge at the end.
People examining and studying this book
Others hold that “run to and fro” can also be read as “search carefully,” meaning people study this book and understanding increases.
Both
Still others hold that the description in this verse includes both the growth of knowledge in general and understanding of this book.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and do not turn this verse into a prediction about technology or the age, nor use it to draw up a timetable.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to put an end-time label on any technology or age; and do not, because information increases, become panicked.

issues.t: “A time, times, and a half, and when they have finished breaking the power of the holy people”
issues.why: “A time, times, and a half, and when they have finished breaking the power of the holy people” (12:7; referring back to the book-wide position: no days counted, no antichrist identified)
pos: A historical period of three and a half years
Some link it with 7:25 and read it as a period of persecution of about three and a half years.
A symbolic limit
Others hold that this is a symbolic expression, meaning a time that is limited and has an end.
A period at the end
Still others hold that this points to a period nearer the end.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and say plainly: we do not convert it into days, use it to draw up a timetable, or identify any contemporary person. What we see is that the One who lives forever has sworn an oath.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to calculate dates or to label any particular people or events; the fruit should be patience, not panic.

issues.t: The 1,290 days and the 1,335 days
issues.why: The 1,290 days and the 1,335 days (12:11; referring back to the book-wide position: no days counted, no antichrist identified)
pos: Days of a historical event
Some explain these two numbers from the history of the defilement of the temple in the second century BC.
Days of an event at the end
Others hold that these two numbers point to an event nearer the end.
Symbolic numbers
Still others hold that these two numbers are symbolic and need not be converted into specific days.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side; they calculate nothing, convert nothing and draw up no table. The text settles on one word at the end: blessed is the one who waits.
issues.care: Do not use these two numbers to fix dates for any contemporary event, or to judge others; any use that causes panic departs from the purpose of the text.

issues.t: “You will rest”: is it death, or rest?
issues.why: “You will rest”: is it death, or rest? (12:13)
pos: It means death
Some hold that “rest” is a gentle word for death, and this verse says to Daniel: you will end this life and wait for the resurrection.
It means finding rest
Others hold that “rest” also carries the sense of finding rest, a comfort to this faithful old man.
Both
Still others hold that this verse holds both meanings together: resting in death, and standing up at the end.
issues.say: These notes set the views side by side and receive both: you will rest, and at the end of the days you will stand in your inheritance. This is a promise to one faithful old man, and a promise to all who wait.
issues.care: Do not use this verse to comfort someone who is grieving too quickly; accompany them first, and read this verse together when they have the strength.

1.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 1 · Daniel Chapter 1
1.title: Resolved Not to Defile Himself with the King’s Food—The Name Changed, the Heart Did Not
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Today I want to begin the lesson with a name tag. You have just started at a company, and the personnel office hands you a name tag. What is printed on it is not your name, but an English name the company picked out for you: Peter, Amy, Jason. You smile and take it, because this way colleagues can call you easily, clients can remember you, and it is all very convenient. But one day you stand in front of the mirror and suddenly ask yourself: am I still me?

Daniel chapter 1 begins in exactly this kind of situation. This book is written for people who live in someone else’s kingdom: the exiled, the foreigners, and also those who, in someone else’s city and someone else’s system, have slowly had their names changed. Verse 1 says that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. It looks like a war. But in verse 2 the subject changes: “The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God.” It was not that Babylon won; the Lord handed them over.

The same event, two ways of reading it. Verse 1 is read with the eyes; verse 2 is read with faith. The whole book of Daniel is going to teach us to learn the second way of reading. Exile really hurts; the vessels were carried into another god’s temple, and it looked as if the other god had triumphed. But the text says that God did not lose; he had only begun to work in another place.

Think about it: what were the three years of study actually teaching? Verse 4 says they were to be taught the writing and language of the Chaldeans. That was not only literacy but a whole way of seeing the world: how to write, how to calculate, how to judge, how to worship. It was a gentle project of replacing the mind. People are not replaced in a single day; they are replaced slowly, in a portion at the table each day, a page in the classroom, a sentence among colleagues. So when we read this chapter today, we are not looking for a villain, but learning to see: when is someone setting my heart for me?

Then the king ordered the selection: members of the royal family and nobles, young, without blemish, handsome, well versed in learning, to be taught the writing and language of the Chaldeans. Each day they would be given the king’s food and wine, and be nourished three years. You see, this is not looking for forced labor; it is picking successors. Babylon’s greatest skill was not the whip but training. Being crushed is easier to recognize; being groomed is the hardest, because you say: this is an opportunity, this is a blessing, I should be grateful.

Next, they were given new names.
