Daniel means “God is my judge”; Hananiah is “Yahweh has been gracious”; Mishael is generally taken as “Who is what God is?”; Azariah is “Yahweh has helped.” Four names, and every one of them carries God. And the new names? Belteshazzar is connected with a Babylonian god, and Abednego is the servant of a certain god. More importantly, the names were “set”; no one asked them whether they were willing. Sometimes what we lose is not our faith, but the very name by which we speak our faith.
Was it malicious of the chief of the eunuchs to change their names?

The text does not state his motive. In ancient courts it was common to register new names for those brought into the palace, so it may have been only an administrative habit, or it may have been a deliberate attempt to reshape their identity. We need not condemn him, but we must see the result: the names carried God, the new names carried other gods, and whoever has the right to name a person has the right to decide who he is. This reminds us that in any environment, what matters most is not what others call me, but whether, before God, I still remember who I am and to whom I belong. A name can be changed, but the identity of being known by God, no one can change.
II. “But”: The Turning Point of the Whole Book (1:8–10)

In verse 8 there is a very small word that I ask you to notice: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.” That word is “But.” Everything before it was done by others: the king gave orders, the chief of the eunuchs changed names, the government assigned the food. Until verse 8: but Daniel. This “but” is the turning point of the whole book.

He resolved. The meaning of the original is “set upon the heart.” The “gave names” of 1:7 and the “resolved” of 1:8 use the same verb, meaning “to set.” The chief of the eunuchs set the names, and Daniel set his own heart. Two “settings,” face to face in this verse. People can change your name, change where you live, change your future, but there is no way for people to change the decision you have set in your heart.

We should also look at verse 10, the chief of the eunuchs’ answer: “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. For why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? Then you would endanger my head with the king.” He was not a bad man; he was afraid. His head was at stake. Sometimes we treat everyone who disagrees as an enemy, but many people are only caught in the middle of power, and also want to save their own lives. When we see this, it is easier to be gentle when we speak: I am not fighting you; I am asking you to give me a chance.

Please notice the timing: when did he resolve? Before anyone threatened him, before the food was set on the table. The pressure had not yet come, and his heart already had a place. Many people’s weakness is not failing at the moment of greatest pressure, but at the moment before they had resolved. Deciding only when the pressure comes is usually too late.

Now look at how he spoke. He did not pound the table, did not go on strike, and did not declare before the king who was right and who was wrong. The text says: he “requested.” Resolve is hard; speech is gentle. The heart must be settled and the attitude humble; this is wisdom for living in someone else’s kingdom. Verse 9 goes on: “Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.” The order is: he resolved first, and then God opened the way. Many people want to see the road before they decide; the order the text gives us is: first settle the heart, then the road opens.
The text does not say what was wrong with the king’s food. May we supply an answer ourselves?

We may guess, but we must not speak too confidently. Perhaps the food came from sacrifices offered to idols, perhaps it involved meat the law did not permit, or perhaps accepting the king’s provision symbolized allegiance. The text deliberately says only “defile,” putting the emphasis on how he handled it, not on which explanation is right. If we insist on supplying a single answer, it is very easy to turn this chapter into a diet list, and miss the real point: his single-mindedness and his gentle attitude. What we are to learn is his heart, not to draw a line in other people’s diets.
III. The Light of the Original: Resolve, Defile, Give (1:8, 9, 17)

There are three words in this chapter worth taking apart. The first is resolve. The verb in the original is שׂוּם, literally “to place, to set,” and together with “upon his heart” it becomes the Hebrew idiom for “making a decision.” Notice that the Hebrew “heart” is not only for feelings; it is the place where decisions are made. So “resolve” is not a sudden burst of emotion, but placing a matter in the position of decision and no longer moving it.

The second is defile, in the original גָּאַל. This word is connected with priestly duty and worship, and means to pollute, to make unclean. The text uses a reflexive form: Daniel was unwilling to “let himself” become one who is defiled. Please notice that his point is not “which food is dirty,” but “what kind of person I will not let myself become.” What he guarded was his own position.

The third is give, in the original נָתַן, the word that occurs most in chapter 1. Verse 2: the Lord gave. Verse 9: God made him find favor. Verse 17: God gave them knowledge. Three times the verb, and the subject is God. Babylon thought it was the one giving: giving names, giving food, giving a curriculum. But the text says, again and again, that the giver is God.

Now put these three words into your week. Resolve is the one thing you are willing to settle first before God; not defiling is the kind of person you are unwilling to let yourself become; give is the favor and wisdom that you know you cannot manage yourself, yet believe God will give. If you have only resolve and no giving, you will grow more and more tired; if you have only giving and no resolve, you will wait until the thing happens and only then start to scramble. You cannot do without either one.

Here is an example from daily life. Someone at work has already decided in his heart beforehand: I will not falsify accounts, I will not lie, I will not tamper with contracts. This decision was set upon his heart before anyone asked him to do anything. One day the supervisor really does open his mouth, and he does not need to think it over again or struggle in panic; he only needs to say in a calm voice: I cannot do this; could there be another way? This is the power of “setting upon the heart”: it lets a person still have his own position at the most tense moment.

Put together, these three words are the roadmap of chapter 1: a person settles the heart, and this is resolve; a person does not let himself leave his position, and this is not defiling; and all the strength that makes him stand and lets things work is not his own but given by God. This is in line with the 321 ideology: letting Jesus be King is not me bracing myself with effort, but my settling the heart, and his doing the work.

No. Willpower is holding up by yourself, and when you cannot hold up, you fail; resolve is placing the heart before God, and then God himself opens the way. After Daniel resolved, the text immediately says, “God made Daniel find favor,” which shows that the road was not one he paved himself. So a person who resolves is not stronger, but clearer about whom he depends on. When we fail, a person of willpower blames himself, while a person of resolve returns to God’s presence and settles the heart again. The biggest difference between the two is which direction one walks after failing. A very practical test: when you have resolved and then failed, what is your first reaction? Is it blaming yourself and gritting your teeth to try again, or returning before God, saying it honestly, and setting it again? The former is often willpower; the latter is resolve.
Is the Hebrew “heart” the same as what we call “mood”?

No. The Hebrew “heart” (לֵב) is the center of thought, will and decision, not only of feeling. So “setting a matter upon the heart” means putting it into the position of decision, so that it does not waver whether the mood is good or bad. This is also why Proverbs says that the springs of life flow from the heart (Prov 4:23). We often say, “With the heart, you are glad; with the head, you worry,” meaning that when we place decisions in the heart and rely on the Spirit, rather than only calculating with the head, we are quieter in the face of pressure and also stronger. So when we say “set the heart before God,” we are not speaking of a feeling but of a decision: whatever my mood today, I choose to let him be Lord.
IV. A Request That Can Be Tested, and One Who Was Still There (1:11–21)

The chief of the eunuchs said no, so Daniel changed the method. He went to the steward who managed them directly and made a request that could be tested: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat, and water to drink. Then let our faces be examined before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s dainties; and as you see, deal with your servants.” He did not ask others to believe him; he asked only for a chance that could be seen with the eyes. Faith does not shy away from testing.

There is another detail: notice that he said “your servants,” not “me.” He spoke for himself and also for Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The four of them resolved together and accepted the ten-day test together. In someone else’s kingdom, one person can easily fail to hold on, but four people who remind one another are very different. This is why we need small groups: not to monitor one another, but so that when we are most likely to relax, someone asks: are you still there?

The result: after ten days, their faces appeared fairer and they were fatter in flesh than the youths who ate the king’s food. Please be careful: this is not teaching vegetarianism, and it is not saying vegetables are healthier. What the text means is that when a person, for conscience’ sake, does not defile himself, God takes responsibility for the consequence he feared. They feared looking worse, and God made their faces look better. But chapter 3 will tell us that not every act of holding firm brings this kind of result right away; so we take this verse as a small witness, not a guarantee.

This is also why the chapter does not stop at “they were better than the others.” Verse 17 says that Daniel also understood all kinds of visions and dreams, a sentence that prepares the road for chapters 2, 4 and 7 that follow. His understanding was not for his own reputation, but so that in the king’s dream and in the king’s fear there would be someone who could speak for God. When God gives a person a gift, it is often not to make him stand high but so that others, in the dark, may see a little light.

Then verse 17: “Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.” They studied the king’s books, but the real teacher was God. Verse 20: when the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters. The last verse has only one sentence: “Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus.” Babylon passed away, dynasties changed again and again, and Daniel was still there.
The greatest praise God gives a person is not necessarily what he accomplished, but that through long years he still stood before God. This is the hope chapter 1 gives us.
May I apply the witness of the ten days of vegetables to my own food decisions?

I do not advise it. The text does not say that vegetables themselves have power, and the subject of the result is God. If you have health concerns, you can consult a doctor and nutrition professionals separately; that is another matter. What to take away from this passage is: when I have settled my heart, God takes responsibility for the consequences; not that if I eat the right things, I will get good results. Turning this verse into a diet formula would not only drift from the text, but would also make those who are sick or cannot follow this way of eating feel they are not spiritual enough. These are people we must be careful to protect. The favor God gives often takes different forms; sometimes it is a visible benefit, sometimes it is peace in the midst of difficulty, and we need not prescribe its shape for God.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is turning this chapter into “only vegetarian is spiritual” or “vegetarian food is healthier.” The text does not teach dietary rules, and the subject of the result is God; using food to measure other people’s spirituality leaves the point of this chapter.

The second deviation is turning “resolve” into willpower, man conquering all. Resolve is setting upon the heart, but God first gave Daniel favor, and the wisdom afterward was also God’s gift; resolve and dependence are the same thing.

The third deviation is turning “faces looked fairer” into “hold firm and you will surely benefit.” This is a witness for this occasion, not a guarantee; chapter 3 has “But if not,” and chapter 6 has a night in the pit. Turning a witness into a transaction hurts those who held firm and did not see the result.

The fourth deviation is turning the learning of Chaldean learning into “believers should not receive worldly education.” The text says that God gave these four knowledge and skill in all learning. What it opposes is being assimilated, not learning; young people can study well and work well, and at the same time keep their hearts.

The fifth deviation is taking this chapter as the basis for “do not associate with unbelievers.” Daniel lived in Babylon and served in the king’s palace, and the text does not rebuke him. What is to be kept is single-heartedness, not isolation; not defiling, not not touching.
If my boss asks me to do something against conscience, should I “request” as Daniel did?

First discern whether it is “a small matter of conscience” or “an obvious sin.” If it is a small matter, ask peacefully as Daniel did, and offer something that can be tested; if it is clearly illegal or harmful to people, you cannot go along, and you must say no clearly and look for someone you trust and for whatever help is needed. “Asking” is an attitude; it is not a cure-all, and it does not mean you must endure forever. In no situation do you need to carry it alone. If you are under this kind of pressure, this week please find someone you trust and tell them what is happening. Finally, remember too that Daniel was not alone before the king: he had three companions, and he had God’s own preparation of favor for him. You do not need to be alone either.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we often say, “when in Rome, do as the Romans do,” and at work and in society, to avoid being excluded we must be like everyone else. This saying has its wisdom, but it also has a trap: little by little, we lose even the judgment of “whether we should go in at all.” Daniel did not refuse Babylon’s learning and work; he went in. What he refused was “defiling.” We must also learn to discern which are cultural differences that I can blend into, and which is the position of the heart that I may not give up. This discernment must be made before God, before the pressure comes. A common way is, in a cultural conflict, to ask first “what will others think of me,” and not “how do I see myself before God.” The result is that we give way a little in every small place, and in the end we can no longer even count how much we have given.

The second question: we are used to “one less trouble,” not wanting to bother people and not wanting to be called unsociable. So many people’s “resolve” often stays only in the heart; they dare not speak, and they dare not ask. Daniel’s way is worth learning: he neither declared it loudly nor swallowed it in silence, but spoke in a clear, courteous way that could be tested. You do not need to confront, and you do not need to hide; in the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, you can say one sentence: “This may not be convenient for me; how could we arrange it?” What we need is first to have a clear position before God, and then to say it in the gentlest tone. This way we do not lose the relationship; very often it makes the relationship more real.
In front of family and elders, how can I “ask” without being disrespectful?

“Asking” is itself a respectful way of speaking. First affirm the other person’s kindness, then state your need, and offer a workable alternative, for example, “Thank you for preparing this; I can’t have this dish. May I have more of the other dishes?” If the other person does not accept it, there is no need to argue or leave; expressing it gently and clearly again and again matters more than winning once. What elders see is not only your words but your attitude. Often a person who is neither servile nor haughty, and who speaks with thanks, helps the family lower their guard more than one who argues his case. If your family is especially sensitive about faith, you can also start with thanks, care and company, letting them see that faith makes you softer, not more distant.

This chapter lets us see the three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model, the Bible is my Standard, the Holy Spirit is my Guide. Jesus also lived in a world that was not his own; he had honor, yet did not grasp it, and he did not change who he was in order to fit in. The Bible is my Standard, because resolve is to be set upon God’s word, not upon circumstances. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because at the table no one sets resolve for you; only he can give us a place in the heart. When we read the Bible, it is not to find a rule to force others to keep, but so that God’s word becomes the place in our heart where, even in the smallest detail, we know to whom we belong.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King does not begin with big things but with a small table: inside other people’s standards, first ask who the master of this table is. Let Jesus receive all the glory, because in every turn of this chapter the verb is God’s: the Lord gave, God made him find favor, God gave them understanding. The credit is not Daniel’s but God’s. If today you can take away only one sentence, please take this one: God moves first, and only then is it possible for me to have a settled heart; it is not that I first stand firm and then God is willing to help.

The one purpose: to build God’s system. Four young men supported one another and resolved together; in a kingdom that did not belong to God, there was still a small group living under God’s sovereignty. This is not escape; it is staying in place and becoming God’s witness. Selflessness is not suppressing yourself, but letting go of the thought “I will arrange the outcome in God’s place”: I settle my heart, and leave the consequences with him.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, and One Who Was Still There

The proud type says: “I don’t need to resolve; I’m very capable, and I’ll deal with it when the time comes.” In fact he wants to be his own master. The text says that Daniel resolved, and also asked others; a truly strong person is one who knows he needs God and needs other people. Think about it: what you really need is not a stronger self, but a willingness to let God stand in front of you.

The fearful type says: “I dare not speak; I’m afraid of being shut out, afraid of losing my job.” The chief of the eunuchs was afraid too; what he feared for was his own head. Fear is real, but God had first prepared favor in his heart; your speaking can be very gentle, and you can begin with just one person.

The ashamed type says: “I have compromised too many times; I have no right to resolve again.” But Daniel’s story does not begin from perfection; it begins from a “but.” Today can be your “but.” Shame makes people hide; grace makes people stand up. You do not need to become a perfect person first to have the right to resolve.

The wounded type says: “I once held firm, and was hurt; I don’t dare trust again.” God did not say that every act of holding firm brings an immediate result; chapter 3 still has “But if not.” You can, even in the wound, still place your heart before God; he remembers.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day take one minute to say to God: Lord, my heart was set by you, not by my circumstances.
Second, write down the “small table” in your life, and write down one thing you have decided not to touch.
Third, when you meet someone who disagrees with you, first ask yourself: is he an enemy, or only afraid? Then answer him with one gentle sentence.
Fourth, find one small detail you have been compromising on, and this week, in the way of “asking,” put a clear, testable arrangement to the people concerned.
Fifth, find a companion, say to each other, “I will not touch this,” and agree to ask each other once a week: are you still there?
I declare: my name was given by God, and my heart was set by God.
I declare: I do not rely on my own willpower; I resolve first, and God will open the way.
I declare: the consequence I fear, God takes responsibility for; I will not turn his grace into a transaction.
I declare: dynasties will change, my God does not change; before him I will stand to the end.
If I have compromised for a long time and only now resolve, is it still in time?

It is in time. Daniel’s “but” appeared only after his name had been changed, which shows that resolve need not come on the first day; it can be any day. What matters is that from today you say one thing before God; you do not need to change your whole life at once, only hold on to one thing first. A small decision is also the beginning of God’s Kingdom. If you feel you have gone too far away, please remember that God was preparing favor before you resolved; at the moment you turn, he is already there, not to rebuke you but to wait for you. You do not need to make one big declaration; you need only, today, to put one thing clearly before God and tell a companion.

Daniel chapter 1 begins with a besieged city and turns at a small table. Four young men had no power to change the king’s kingdom; they had only one very small decision: this one thing, I will not touch. But God, in this very small decision, gave them favor, gave them wisdom, and let the whole land see whose servants are truly wise.

Perhaps you are in a difficult environment, not one of persecution but of slow change. You have not been forbidden to pray; you simply have less and less time. You have not been told to deny your faith; you just feel more and more embarrassed to mention it. Please do not lose heart. Daniel’s story does not say, “You must be strong enough”; it says, “God has already prepared favor in your situation.” Your resolve can be very small; your speaking can be very light; but in God’s hands it can become a very great witness.

Brothers and sisters, today we return to that name tag. You can take it, and at work you can use a name that others find easy to call; but in your heart you must know who you are and to whom you belong. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he is the one who will receive all the glory. The focus is not on how firm I am, but on the God who makes us stand.
May God make us, in every situation, people who are “still there.” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 1:8 says that Daniel “resolved.” In your life, has there been a moment when you clearly knew you had “set one thing upon your heart”? Please say the year or the occasion.
2. ★★ 1:7 says that their names were changed. Have you ever been called by a different name, or stopped stating your position in order to fit in? Please give one example.
3. ★★ In your present surroundings, which “very good condition” is quietly keeping you a little further from God? Please say it in only one sentence.
4. ★★★ Please think quietly about one thing: you know you should not touch it, yet you have never said it aloud. Now write down that thing, and the one person or the one consequence you fear most.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 1:8 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches workplace, family and cultural pressure; if someone mentions long-term oppression, harm or loneliness, do not press for details, do not ask for an immediate decision, and look after the person privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 Please say which place in your life is “a small table.” Please give the time and the setting.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 1:9, “God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.” What sentence is God saying to you? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 Daniel resolved first, and then God opened the way. In the past, did you look at the road first, or settle the heart first? What difference does this make for your present decision?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Please say to the person next to you: “This one thing, I have decided not to touch.” Say only one sentence; no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Step】 This week, you will use “asking” to say one sentence to someone. What is it? Please say the person, the time, the place.

Leader’s reminder: Follow the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, only a sentence, a name, a time is needed; no need to tell a story. If someone’s tears fall, do not rush to comfort and do not press; let him be quiet for a moment, look after him privately after the meeting, and where necessary help him seek professional help.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ At home or at work, is there someone being slowly changed by his surroundings? Please say his name, and decide to pray for him once this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there something “everyone knows should be said, but no one says”? Please say what it is, and say where you could start from yourself.
12. ★★ Is there someone you have seen as an opponent, who is really only afraid? Please say his name, and decide that this week you will say one gentle sentence to him.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “God is not with you only in big things.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not judge anyone’s compromise or silence in the group. If someone shares his wounds, his inability to trust, or long-term hopelessness, do not press for details, do not ask for forgiveness, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” and look after him privately after the meeting.

Please gently close your eyes and place before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read 1:8 together: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

Let the leader pray for each person: ask God to turn the decisions we have set upon our hearts into his own work, so that in the ordinary days of the week we may take that step. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

2.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 2 · Daniel Chapter 2
2.title: The Stone Cut Without Hands—Dream, Stone, Mountain
blocks: I. The Most Powerful Man in the World Could Not Sleep (2:1–13)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Have you ever had a night like this: tomorrow there is something big, you toss and turn in bed, and your mind is like a machine that cannot stop. You have thought of many ways, talked with many people, looked up much information, and still your heart is uneasy. In this lesson we read about a man who could not sleep; he was no ordinary man, he was the most powerful man in the world at that time.

The word “troubled” in the original means to be struck, to be stirred: the king’s spirit, as if struck again and again by a hand, could find no rest. Each of us has such times: the body is very tired and the mind cannot stop; things have been handed off and the heart cannot let go. This kind of unease is not necessarily bad; it is often God reminding us: there is a problem you cannot hold alone.

Daniel 2:1 says: “In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.” Please think about this picture: a king with armies, wealth, the best doctors and the best advisers, and yet he could not sleep. There is an unease that power cannot soothe. So he did what he thought would be most effective: he summoned all of Babylon’s experts, the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, the Chaldeans, and told them to tell him the dream.

Think of the situation of those experts. Each of them, on ordinary days, was a respected person: with a teacher behind him, with experience, with a method that made sense. But when the king wanted a real answer, all their expertise lost its weight in an instant. We have such moments today: the doctor says, we have done all we can; the financial expert says, there is no other way; the counselor says, this is a long-term lesson. People need experts, and also need to admit that experts have limits. Admitting limits is not failure; it is the beginning of learning humility.

But the king made a demand: you tell me my dream first, and then I will believe your interpretation. This demand was both fair and cruel. In the past, no one could ever verify an interpretation of a dream; now the king wanted verification. The Chaldeans said one very honest sentence: “There is not a man on the earth who can show the king’s matter.” Then they added: “except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.”

They were only half right. They said the gods do not dwell with flesh, that is, God is far from people; but Daniel is about to say: “the light dwells with him.” The first point is very simple: human wisdom will always come to a day when it reaches its end. That day is not failure; it is the time when the God of heaven begins to speak. But this end is very dangerous: the king ordered all the wise men destroyed, and Daniel and his three friends were counted in. They had not failed, yet because they belonged to that group, they faced death together. This is the situation of exiles.
Did the king really forget the dream, or was he testing the magicians?

The original can be read two ways: the CUV takes “I have forgotten,” and some read it “the matter is settled by me.” Whichever, the king’s demand is the same: first tell the dream, and only then does it count. The point is not the king’s memory but that this demand pushes human wisdom to its limit, so that the God of heaven becomes the only answer. If we get tangled here too long, we will miss the most important thing in this chapter: God is the God who reveals secrets. And the point of this chapter is not “who is more accurate,” but “who is the one who reveals secrets.” To move the eyes from the details of the dream to the God who lets people know is the best way to read this passage.
II. Ask First, Seek First, Bless First (2:14–30)

When Daniel heard the decree, he did not run away, cry injustice or pick up a sword. To Arioch, the captain of the guard who was going to kill, he asked a very quiet question: “Why is the decree so urgent from the king?” A man ready to kill was stopped by a quiet question. Then he went in to see the king, and did not say “I guarantee I can,” but only “grant me a delay.” Then he returned to his house and told Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, asking them to seek mercy from the God of heaven.

Please do not forget that this Daniel, who could still speak quietly under a death threat, is the Daniel of chapter 1 who resolved at the table. A person’s steadiness in big things is often trained in small things. If he had not learned “seek first, speak afterward” in the small matter of food, he could not have been so quiet when the decree went out and the killing was on its way. So the seemingly small decisions you face today are all preparation for big things to come.

Please notice the order: ask first, seek first, companions first, and only then the interpretation. In chapter 1 they resolved together; in chapter 2 they prayed together. In someone else’s kingdom we are not isolated individuals; we are a small group that guards one another. Do you have someone you can seek together with today? If not, this week is the time to begin looking.

There is another detail worth slowing down to see: when Daniel did all this, there was no guarantee of the outcome. He did not say to the king, “I can surely do it”; he only asked for a chance, and then brought the matter before God. This is a very quiet kind of faith: not guaranteeing one’s own answer, but guaranteeing that one will not leave God. Many people think faith means being very sure of the result, but the faith in this chapter is being sure of the God who can reveal secrets, while the outcome remains open.

Then the answer came in the night. Daniel did not rush off to the king; he stopped first and blessed the God of heaven: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his. He changes the times and the seasons. He removes kings, and sets up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding.” This short prayer is a map of the world: time is in his hand, kingship is in his hand, wisdom is in his hand, and even darkness is in his hand.

At last he stood before the king. The king asked: “Are you able?” This is a question that makes it very easy to say “I can,” because saying “I can” brings a future. But he said “cannot” first: “wise men, enchanters, magicians, or soothsayers” cannot tell the king, and then, “there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets.” Then he said the watershed of the whole book: “not for any wisdom that I have more than any living.” Pride is leaving one’s position, wanting to take away God’s glory; humility is returning to one’s position, giving the glory back to God.
If my prayer does not receive an answer as quickly as Daniel’s, is it that I did not ask enough?

No. The text here records one prayer that was heard, but it is not a formula. In chapter 3 the three friends say “But if not”; in Daniel’s prayer in chapter 10, the angel also says he was held back for twenty-one days. The point of prayer is not intensity but placing ourselves before God. If you are waiting, please do not treat the waiting as your own failure; you can bless first, and then set the matter down. If you are waiting, let yourself and others know: waiting is not the same as having no faith; very often waiting itself is the posture in which faith stands. You can bless first, then be quiet, and you do not need to wait alone.
III. The Light of the Original: Secret, Reveal, Give (2:18–23, 28, 30)

There are three words in this chapter worth taking apart. The first is secret, in Aramaic רָז (raz), a word borrowed from Persian, meaning something hidden that a person cannot know by himself. This word recurs in this chapter. Much of human unease comes from “secrets”: I do not know tomorrow, I do not know the meaning of this event, I do not know what God is doing.

The second is reveal, in Aramaic גְּלָא (gela), meaning to uncover, to disclose. A secret is not untied by people; it is uncovered by God. You can work hard at the puzzle, but the final lid must be opened by God himself. The third is give, in Aramaic יְהַב (yehav), to give. Verse 21: he gives wisdom to the wise; verse 23: you have given me wisdom and might; verse 37: the God of heaven has given you the kingdom.

Look at one more detail: in all three words, the subject is not man. The secret is what God has; the revealing is what God does; the giving is what God gives. Man has only one verb: to ask, and one more: to bless. So this chapter puts people in a very relaxed position: you do not have to be responsible for solving every riddle; you only have to bring the matter before God and give the glory back to him. This is true release: I am not the final answer, and I do not need to be.

Put together, these three words are the roadmap of this chapter: there is a secret, there is God’s revealing, there is God’s giving. The place of man is to ask, to receive, and to bless. This is in line with the 321 ideology: Let Jesus receive all the glory is not a slogan but seeing that everything I have is given.
What is the difference between Aramaic and Hebrew? Why does this chapter suddenly change language?

Aramaic was the common language of the courts and trade of the ancient Near East, and a close relative of Hebrew. From 2:4b the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic, and the text simply continues in Aramaic, until chapter 7. The theme of this section is the foreign kingdoms and God’s sovereignty. As for the details of composition and editing, scholars hold different views, but whichever one we take, what we read is the same sentence from the same God, spoken in different languages. The Aramaic chapters in chapter 7 have the same theme: the rise and fall of foreign kingdoms, and the permanence of God’s Kingdom. This whole Aramaic section is like a large frame that holds God’s sovereignty in the middle.
IV. The Stone Cut Out Without Hands (2:31–45)

Daniel began to tell the dream. A great image: its head was of fine gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, its feet part iron and part clay. The lower it went, the harder and the more mixed, and at last it stood on an unstable foundation. Then a stone: “You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.” Notice that the stone did not strike the head of gold but the most fragile feet. Gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay were broken together, becoming chaff on the threshing floor, carried away by the wind, with no place found for them. This picture is much like many things we see today: splendid outside, inconsistent within; looking solid, yet standing in a place that could split at any time.

Then comes the most important sentence of the chapter: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, nor will its sovereignty be left to another people; but it will break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it will stand forever.” This Kingdom has three marks: never destroyed, not left to another people, standing forever. Human kingdoms change hands; God’s Kingdom does not.

Then Daniel said a very heavy sentence: the God of heaven has given you the kingdom, the power, the strength and the glory, and you are the head of gold. This was said to a world ruler, both an affirmation and a reminder. What was affirmed is that his position was real; what was reminded is that the position was entrusted. One who is entrusted must give account to the one who entrusted. This foreshadowing, in chapter 4, will cost this king a great price, and also teach him a lesson he will never forget.

But this passage is the one that most tempts people to take out a map: the head of gold is Babylon, who is the silver, who is the bronze, who is the iron, and which year is which. But please notice: the text names only the head of gold as Babylon, and none of the others is named. So we do not need to turn this passage into a map. We need only listen to what it says: every kingdom has a beginning and an end; the later it comes, the harder and the more brittle; power can break everything, but it cannot make people truly one.

Please pay special attention to the structure of the image: the more precious the metal, the higher it is; the harder and more mixed the material, the lower it is. This is a picture opposite to our intuition. We often think that history progresses the further it goes; but this dream says that the later a human kingdom comes, the harder, the more divided, the less stable. This is not pessimism but honesty: human history has no power in itself to move toward salvation. Salvation must come from outside, like a stone cut out without hands.

And there are three more words: “without hands.” Human kingdoms are made by human hands; God’s Kingdom is not. God’s Kingdom does not grow out of human kingdoms and does not depend on human armies, systems or effort; its source is outside the human world. So we do not need to treat any kingdom as our final hope, nor despair at the rise and fall of any kingdom.
Which four kingdoms are the gold, silver, bronze and iron? May I ask my pastor?

You may ask, and you may also set the views side by side. The traditional reading is Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome; another is Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece; and some think they are symbolic, representing worldly kingdoms one after another. This book does not ask us to argue about this, much less to draw up a chart or identify some nation today. You can first listen to each view, but please do not divide from brothers and sisters because answers differ. You can also, while reading, write the views side by side and then ask: what does this passage say to those who suffer, wait and hope? The answer is usually more powerful than a timetable.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is matching the gold, silver, bronze and iron one by one with specific empires, years and today’s nations, and drawing up a timetable. The text names only the head of gold as Babylon; what these notes hold to is that human kingdoms have a beginning and an end, and God’s Kingdom is not made by human hands. Turning this passage into a map makes people busy counting and forgetting to look up. This is the most common and most tempting deviation, because it looks very professional and very diligent.

The second deviation is turning God’s Kingdom, or that stone, into a spiritual kingdom that people can build by striving or by political means. The stone was “cut out without hands,” and the Kingdom is “set up” by God. People are not the builders but the people brought in. Turning God’s Kingdom into a human movement often brings weariness, and also pride.

The third deviation is turning “not because of any wisdom of mine” into “people do not need to learn or work hard.” Daniel received three years of training in learning in chapter 1; what he spoke of is where the glory belongs, not a denial of learning. True humility is not belittling oneself but knowing that everything one has was given. True humility is not denying one’s talents but remembering, behind each talent, where it came from.

The fourth deviation is turning the king’s falling down into Daniel accepting human worship, or into believers being honored because of this. The text says only that the king fell down and commanded that an offering be made, and does not say that Daniel accepted it; the king’s words point to Daniel’s God.

The fifth deviation is turning the prayer in this chapter into a formula: “you ask, and God will certainly give you an answer quickly.” This chapter records one prayer that was heard, but chapter 3 has “But if not,” and chapter 10 has a prayer that was held back. Those who did not get what they wished for did not ask too little. What they need more is company, not another rebuke.
When different pastors explain this chapter differently, whom should I listen to?

First distinguish what the text clearly says from what are the views of the various schools. What is clear: God’s Kingdom is set up by him, never destroyed, and outlasts any human kingdom. As for the parts that are guesses, such as the names of the four kingdoms, they can stay in the discussion and need not be made a condition of faith. You can write down the views and read the Scripture with a companion, and you can also ask a pastor for the basis of his view. A mature believer does not need to be afraid because of differing opinions. What matters is not to draw a boundary in the church because of differing opinions. On what is clear in the truth we are one; on what is unclear, we bear with one another, and this too is how people of God’s Kingdom look.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are used to “finding a way in, finding connections, finding a method.” When we meet difficulty, the first thought is often: who knows whom? Is there an acquaintance? These are not necessarily wrong; in reality they are also a kind of wisdom. But this chapter reminds us: there is a kind of problem that human connections cannot reach. At that time, do not hurry to say “I have no way,” but, like Daniel, first ask, first seek, first find companions, bless before God, and then speak. The church is the same. We easily put “methods” before “prayer”: first hold a meeting, first discuss the budget, first find resources, and only at the end say, “let’s pray a bit too.” This chapter does not say meetings are bad; it invites us to adjust the order: first stand firm before God, and then do what needs to be done.

The second question: we are often asked “which side are you on,” and the word “kingdom” is especially sensitive in different settings. Many people therefore have two reactions to the “God’s Kingdom” of this chapter: one is not daring to read it, the other is hurrying to match it with real politics. The direction this chapter gives us is very clear: God’s Kingdom is set up by him, not made by human hands; it is not a regime we are to establish, but a life we are brought into. So we can live quietly in any kingdom, while knowing where our true belonging lies. So we can quietly do the work before us, while knowing where our hope is placed.
If I live in a place where faith cannot be discussed openly, how can I read this chapter?

You can read it as a very quiet hope. In Babylon, Daniel never treated God’s Kingdom as a political platform to oppose the existing regime; he first kept himself from defilement in small things, and before the king he first said “not because of any wisdom of mine.” Within a safe range, in the smallest ways, you can guard your heart, pray, and support one another with companions. There is no need to write or say publicly details that could harm yourself and others. You can also ask a trusted brother or sister to be your prayer partner, and agree on a safe way of contact, so that when you need it, you know someone remembers you.
VII. Living Out 321—Bless First, Then Speak

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. He also prayed at night in Gethsemane, not relying on his own methods but saying: “not what I desire, but what you desire.” The Bible is my Standard, because the blessing in this chapter starts from God’s word and God’s works, not from my own feelings. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because the secret was not untied by reasoning but revealed by God himself in a night vision.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that before human ways run out, we first hand this matter over to him. Let Jesus receive all the glory means doing as Daniel did, and in a position where one could be exalted, saying first: not because of any wisdom of mine. The one purpose: to build God’s system—not that we build God’s Kingdom, but that God brings us into the Kingdom he has set up, and in the small group we guard one another and seek together.

In the small places of every day, this Kingdom is also real: when you choose not to strive for glory by your own methods, when you bring a difficulty to the small group to seek together, when you stop in the midst of busyness to bless, you are living out what “the Kingdom of God has come near” looks like. This is not a distant future but a life that can begin today.
How, concretely, do I “bless first, then speak” in daily life?

You can begin with a very small habit: before you make an important decision or say an important sentence, stop for thirty seconds and say in your heart, “God, wisdom and might are yours.” This is not a ritual but putting the position right. You will find that the tone of your speaking and the speed of your decisions slowly change. You can also agree with companions: before meetings, small groups, or family discussions, bless together for one minute. Over time this habit will change how you see “achievement”: achievement is no longer proving oneself but witnessing to him; failure is no longer being shamed but an invitation to return to him.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, and One Kingdom

The proud type says: “I can handle this; I don’t need others, and I don’t need to keep praying.” Daniel had ability, yet first found companions and first blessed. Your ability is real, but only one who gives the glory to God can go far. You can begin today, hand one small matter to God, and let one companion know.

The fearful type says: “The decree has gone out; we can only wait to die.” Daniel did not wait; he asked first, sought first. Fear is real, but fear is not the last voice; you can, in fear, still open your mouth and ask.

The ashamed type says: “I have no right to be heard by God; I have just made a mistake.” This chapter does not say how perfect Daniel was; it says only that he knew who the God is who reveals secrets. You do not need to be perfect first in order to ask.

The wounded type says: “I once asked, and got no answer.” This wound is real. The hope of this chapter is not a guarantee of an immediate answer every time, but that it tells you: the God of heaven still changes the times and the seasons, he still rules, and you can bring your wound and keep standing before him.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week

First, every day before asking anything of God, take one minute to bless him: you change the times and the seasons, you remove kings and set up kings, wisdom and might are yours. This sentence can be very simple, only one sentence, but please say it every day.

Second, write down one thing that has recently succeeded for you, and write beside it: this was God’s gift, not my wisdom beating others. Writing it down is more powerful than just thinking it in your heart, and better reminds you.
Third, find a companion, say to each other one thing where human ways have run out, and agree to pray for each other every day this week.

Fourth, on an uneasy night, do not rush to find a method; first be quiet for five minutes, hand the matter to God, and then sleep. If you cannot sleep, do not blame yourself; take this unease as an invitation to prayer.
Fifth, where you have ability, speak up for someone in a weak position, as Daniel pleaded for all the wise men.
I declare: the God of heaven changes the times and the seasons, removes kings and sets up kings, and everything is in his hand.
I declare: secrets are revealed by God, not because of any wisdom of mine; I am only one who receives.
I declare: I will bless first, and then speak; seek together first, and then act.
I declare: the kingdom God sets up will never be destroyed; I will not put my hope in any kingdom that will pass away.
If I have not truly blessed God for a long time, how do I begin?

There is no need to begin with beautiful words. You can begin with the simplest sentence: “God, you are the God who rules.” Then add one small thing you saw him doing today. You can also read 2:20–23 straight through and make it your own prayer. The point is not the words but putting the position right: I am the creature, he is the Creator; I am the one who receives, he is the Lord who gives. If you can, ask a companion to read it with you, and after reading, each say one sentence that touched you most today. When the voice says it, prayer becomes more real.

Daniel chapter 2 begins with a king who could not sleep and ends at a stone cut out without hands. What this chapter gives us is not a historical timetable but a declaration: human wisdom has an end, human kingdoms have a beginning and an end, and only the God of heaven changes the times and the seasons, removes kings and sets up kings, and himself sets up a Kingdom that will never be destroyed.

I also want to invite you, this week, to find a quiet moment and slowly read 2:19–23, and make it your own prayer. You do not need many words; just let your heart follow this blessing, again and again putting the position right: he is God, I am man; he rules, I receive. This kind of practice will slowly change how you face unease and difficulty.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that sleepless night. When human ways run out, you can be like Daniel: ask first, seek first, find companions first, bless first. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he is the one who will receive all the glory. The focus is not on whether I have a way, but on the God who holds the times and the seasons.
May God make us live in the Kingdom he has set up, until his Kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 2:1 says that the king’s “spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.” Recently, was there a night when you could not sleep over something? Please say what kind of matter it was.
2. ★★ In 2:10 the Chaldeans say, “There is not a man on the earth.” In your life, is there something for which you have used up every way? Please say it in only one sentence.
3. ★★ When you meet difficulty, whom or what do you look for first: connections, information, experts, or prayer? Please give the most recent example.
4. ★★★ Please think quietly about one thing: you have never dared say to God, “I have no way.” Now write down that thing, and the one point you are most afraid to hand over.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 2:20–23 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches insomnia, anxiety and a sense of powerlessness; if someone mentions long-term fear, oppression or the loss of a loved one, do not press for details, do not ask them to let go at once, and look after the person privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 2:12–13 says that Daniel had not failed, yet was counted on the list. Have you ever been caught up in something because you belonged to a certain group? Please give an example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 2:20–22. What sentence is God saying to you? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 Daniel asked first, sought first, and then spoke. In the past, did you speak first, or seek first? What difference does this make for your present decision?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Please say to the person next to you one sentence blessing God, for example “God, wisdom and might are yours”; only one sentence, no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Step】 This week, whom will you find, and for what matter will you pray together? Please say the person, the time, the place.

Leader’s reminder: Follow the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, only a sentence, a name, a time is needed; no need to tell a story. If someone’s tears fall, do not rush to comfort and do not press; let him be quiet for a moment, look after him privately after the meeting, and where necessary help him seek professional help.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who is “unable to sleep”? Please say his name, and decide to pray for him once this month.

11. ★★ In your church or group, is there something that needs everyone to first bless together and seek together, rather than first discuss methods? Please say what it is, and say where you could begin.

12. ★★ Is there a place where, because of success, you easily forget to say “this was given by God”? Please say the name or the occasion, and decide that this week you will give the glory back to God in one sentence.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “God is the God who reveals secrets.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not judge anyone’s methods or silence in the group, and do not draw conclusions about any regime or person. If someone shares his wounds, long-term hopelessness or the experience of asking without receiving, do not press for details, do not ask for forgiveness, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” and look after him privately after the meeting.
Please gently close your eyes and place before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read 2:20 together: Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his.

Let the leader pray for each person: ask God to teach us to bless first, then speak; to seek together first, then act; and to let us take that step in the ordinary days of the week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

3.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 3 · Daniel Chapter 3
3.title: But If Not—Furnace, Presence, No Bowing
blocks: I. A Piece of Music and an Accusation (3:1–15)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Please imagine a scene: a very large square, packed with people, officials, soldiers and merchants, everyone neatly dressed. In front stands a gleaming colossal image, and beside it a row of musicians. The herald cries aloud: when the music sounds, everyone must kneel. Then the music rises, and a whole field of people, like waves of wheat, bows down layer by layer. In this lesson we read of that scene, and of the few who did not bend in the waves of wheat.

Daniel 3:1 says: “Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.” Think back to chapter 2: the king dreamed of an image whose head was gold, and Daniel said to him, you are that head of gold, and after you there will be other kingdoms. The king heard this explanation and said nothing, but he went back and did one thing: he made an image, and this time not only the head but the whole image was gold. This was his answer: my kingdom will not be replaced. We are sometimes like this too. God says one sentence we do not like to hear; we do not quarrel, nor do we argue back; we only quietly make our own plan again, and make it bigger, brighter, more solid.

Next comes the gathering: the local governors, the deputies, the governors, the judges, the treasurers, the counselors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, all present, an assembly of imperial loyalty. The herald proclaimed: “whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music, you fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king has set up.” Anyone who did not would be cast into the burning fiery furnace. Please notice that this command did not ask everyone to debate, or to take a position; there was only one thing: when the music sounds, kneel. This design is very clever, because you do not need to think, you do not need to decide, you only need to follow everyone.

Then the text records the result in a tone close to irony: “all the peoples, the nations, and the languages, fell down and worshiped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.” No one shouted slogans, no one was dragged away. When the music sounded, everyone bowed their heads. Today the greatest pressure is often not the sword but one sentence: everyone does it this way. This sentence is harder to stand against than a sword, because it is not fierce; it is very polite, very reasonable, and carries a little goodwill. The first point of this lesson is that we must first see clearly how orderly and how natural this invitation is. Only then can we see that three people did not bend.

That three people stood was not a secret. Verse 8 says: “certain Chaldeans came near, and brought accusation against the Jews.” Who accused them? Chaldeans, the very group that Daniel outshone in chapter 2. Some accusations are not because you were wrong, but because your being different pierces everyone’s uniformity. They did not warn them privately, and did not ask first; they went straight to the king, restating the king’s command as if only guarding the king’s majesty, and only then named names: “There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, have not respected you. They don’t serve your gods, and don’t worship the golden image which you have set up.”

Please listen to this knife: you gave them high office, and they pay no heed to you. They did not oppose loudly; they only stood. But standing is itself a word. Sometimes a witness is not what you said but what you did not do. To keep standing in the midst of uniformity was their only action. They did not curse anyone, did not organize, and did not issue any statement.

Then the king was angry. But he did not give the order at once; he gave a chance: “Is it on purpose, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you don’t serve my god, nor worship the golden image which I have set up? Now if you are ready whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music to fall down and worship the image which I have made, good; but if you don’t worship, you shall be cast the same hour into the middle of a burning fiery furnace. Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?” This is the hardest form of pressure: not that no road is given to you, but that the road is near, easy and reasonable. Bend now, and everything can be treated as if it never happened.

That last question is the core of the whole chapter: “Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?” What he asked was not why you will not worship, but whether your God has power. He turned faith into a contest of power. We hear this question today too, in different forms: Is what you believe any use? Why does your God not save you? This question cannot be answered by debate. The three did not debate either; their answer takes only three verses.
Must I refuse every ceremony and occasion? My work requires me to attend some occasions I do not quite agree with. What should I do?

This chapter does not ask us to refuse every occasion. It asks us to discern whether this action gives to something else the worship that should belong only to God. Attending, greeting and courtesy are not the same as worship, pledging loyalty and declaring allegiance. If you are not sure, first talk with a mature brother or sister, and say plainly the occasion, the action and what you feel in your heart; if it would make you declare allegiance to another lord, then, like these three, calmly and firmly do not do it. For the other small things, there is no need to make yourself a difficult person. If you meet an occasion you truly cannot discern, you may first ask a trusted companion, or explain beforehand to the host, and politely decline one particular part.

Now we come to the heart of this chapter. Verse 16: “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, ‘Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter.’” Please notice the first words: they were calm. Not that they were not afraid, but that the answer had long been there. Do you remember chapter 1? Daniel had long ago resolved not to defile himself with the king’s food. First the answer in the heart, then facing the pressure. They did not have to decide on the spot, because the decision had long been made.

Then come two sentences, a very precise structure of faith. The first, verse 17: “If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.” This is trust, with no doubt about God’s power. The second, verse 18: “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.” This is obedience, with no condition on God’s will. They were not sure that God would deliver, but they were sure that they would not worship.

Please think about what fire you are facing right now. Perhaps a prayer with no answer yet, perhaps an illness that has not improved, perhaps a perseverance that no one understands. You do not know whether God will save you in the way you wish, but you can choose: not to be defiled. This is not cold calculation, but a very deep freedom of living under God’s sovereignty. Because you no longer need God to guarantee the outcome before you can feel at peace doing what is right.

I also want to remind you that this sentence does not ask us to grit our teeth. Their calm was not because of how brave they were, but because the God they served is worthy. In the words of 321, this is letting Jesus be King: he may not act as I wish, but he is still the King. You can also make this sentence your own prayer today: Lord, you are able to save; but if not, I will still follow you.
If I say “But if not” and really am not saved, am I abandoned by God?

No. The ending of this chapter is deliverance, but the text first lets us hear that when they said these words they did not know the ending. Hebrews 11:35 and the verses after it also record others: some were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, and others were tried by mocking, scourging, bonds and imprisonment. The text says the world was not worthy of them. Not being saved does not mean being abandoned, and it is not a sign of too little faith. God’s presence is not the same as God’s exemption. You can honestly tell God your pain, and ask someone near you to walk with you for a while. You can also read verses 17 and 18 again and see that when they said these words, they did not know the ending; they knew only who was King.
III. The Light of the Original: Serve, Deliver, But If Not (3:12, 17–18)

There are three groups of words in this chapter worth taking apart. The first is serve and worship. Serve is the Aramaic פְּלַח (pelach), and worship is the Aramaic סְגִד (segid); these two words keep appearing as a pair. The accusers say they do not serve your gods and do not worship your image; the king says, you do not serve my god; the three say, our God whom we serve; the king says at last that they would not serve any other god. The same verb, in one chapter, changes masters four times. What this chapter speaks of is not religious form but this: to whom does your life give its loyalty?

The second group is deliver, the Aramaic שֵׁיזִב (shezav), to rescue, to deliver. The king asks: who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands? The three say: God is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand. The king says at last: there is no other god who is able to deliver like this. The same word, turned from a question into a confession, from the mouth of a king. This is the greatest irony of the chapter: the very thing he most wanted to prove no god could do, he himself in the end acknowledged.

The third group is “but if not,” the Aramaic וְהֵן לָא (vehen la), literally “and if not,” meaning: even if he does not deliver. These four words are often misused. Some teach them as “if only you have enough faith, God will surely save you,” which is exactly upside down. What these words say is: being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is man’s matter. They did not guarantee the outcome for God; they guaranteed only that they would never serve another god. The first is trust in God, and the second is a decision about themselves.

Put together, these three groups are the route of this chapter: Whom do you serve? Who can deliver? What if he does not? You can take these three questions into your own life and ask them one by one. Whom do you serve today? Whom do you believe can deliver? If he does not deliver in the way you wish, what is your decision? These three questions are much easier to ask in quiet than when the fire is already lit.
The originals of “even so” and “but if not” are very similar. How can we tell them apart?

The Aramaic הֵן (hen) at the opening of 3:17 can be “if it be so,” and it can also be “behold,” so some read it as “if God exists, he is able to deliver,” and others as “if you throw us into the fire, our God is able to deliver.” The CUV takes the former, translating it “even so.” The “but if not” of verse 18 clearly points to: even if he does not deliver. The two “ifs” run one positive and one negative, but whichever is read, the point of the two verses is the same: they believed God had power, yet did not make the outcome a condition of their own faithfulness. So we can pause here, first read the meaning of the original, and then put it back into our lives, without arguing about the word for too long.
Is the “deliver” here the same as “being saved” in the New Testament?

Not exactly. The “deliver” of Daniel here is being rescued from the furnace and from the king’s hand, a deliverance of body and circumstance. The “being saved” of the New Testament is mainly being saved from sin and death, and has to do with eternal life. The two do not conflict: God is a God who delivers, who delivers in history and also on the cross. When we read this chapter, we can first hear its own meaning, and then let the New Testament fill in the whole picture, rather than mixing the two together, and still less making “being delivered from the furnace” the necessary treatment of believers. In this way, our reading neither shrinks God’s deliverance nor turns deliverance into a guarantee.
IV. The Fourth in the Fire, and a Witness Without a Singe (3:19–30)

The king’s wrath came. Verse 19 says: “Then Nebuchadnezzar was full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated.” The less it can be refused, the more it must prove that it cannot be refused; this is how power often looks when it is angry. Then the king commanded the strong men of his army to bind the three and cast them into the furnace. Please notice one detail: the three, in their pants, tunics and mantles, were bound and cast in, not treated specially, but went in just as they were. This detail will be taken up again later.

Verse 22 says: “Therefore because the king’s commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceedingly hot, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.” Please listen to this sentence. The king who wanted to prove that no god could save them, before throwing them in, first lost his own strongest men. There is no miracle here; the fire was real, the furnace was real, death was real. The text does not play down what they faced, so “But if not” is so heavy: they did not speak only after being sure that God would deliver, but stood, knowing that the fire was real.

Then the king could not sit still. Verse 24: “Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonished, and rose up in haste. He spoke and said to his counselors, ‘Didn’t we cast three men bound into the middle of the fire?’ They answered the king, ‘True, O king.’” He confirmed it once, and then said: “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed. The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.” Please read slowly: four, unbound, walking in the fire, and unharmed. Those who went in bound were loosed in the fire. The fire, which had come to devour, now became the place where they walked.

The most wonderful thing is that the fire was still there, the furnace was still there, and the king’s command had not been revoked. God did not first put out the fire and then let them in; he walked in while the fire was still burning. As for who the fourth was, the various schools hold different views: some say an angel, some say an appearance of Christ in the Old Testament, and some say a sign of God’s presence. We do not treat it as a required item of doctrinal proof; we say only: this brings to mind Immanuel, God with us. God did not promise us we would not enter the fire, but he promised to be with us in the fire. The fire you are walking through may not yet have gone out, but you are not alone.

The king drew near the mouth of the furnace and said: “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!” Did you hear what he called them? A few minutes before, they were the ones who paid no heed to you; now, they are servants of the Most High God. This is the quietest witness of this chapter. Then the officials together looked them over: the body not harmed by the fire, the hair not singed, the clothes not changed, not even the smell of fire. As they were when they went in, so they were when they came out.

Last, the king’s own words: “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel, and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God.” Do you remember 3:15? Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands? Now the king himself answers: “because there is no other god who is able to deliver like this.” The same word, the same king, turned from a question into a confession. But please notice: he said “their God,” not “my God”; he is still learning. In chapter 4 we will see how he goes on.

The last verse is very short: “Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.” Promotion was a result, not a reason. When they said “But if not,” they did not know they would be promoted. Faithfulness is not for the sake of promotion, but remains faithful even if not promoted. This is the other half of verse 18. If we treat faithfulness as a way to exchange for success, we turn God into someone we can trade with.
Is the fourth in the fire Jesus? May I teach it this way?

The text says only “like a son of the gods,” and in verse 28 the king calls this one “his angel.” The approach of this commentary is to set the views side by side: there is a reading as an angel, and also a reading as an appearance of Christ in the Old Testament, and neither is a clear link made by the New Testament. So we say “this brings to mind Immanuel,” and do not say “this is a type.” In teaching, you can state the various views clearly, and then place the weight on the one thing the text is most sure of: God is with his servants in the fire. Whichever reading you choose, please remember that the real comfort of the text is that God is with his servants in the fire.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is turning “But if not” into “if only you have enough faith, God will surely save you.” This sounds like faith, but it is exactly upside down: the three said that God is able to deliver, and also said that even if he does not, they would still not serve another god. Being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is man’s matter, and faithfulness is not conditional on being saved. Be especially careful here with those who are losing, sick or shut out; do not say to anyone, “you were not saved because your faith was not enough.”

The second deviation is turning the fourth into doctrinal proof that must be believed, or declaring “that is” Christ. The king said “like a son of the gods,” and verse 28 calls him “his angel.” The schools differ: an angel, an appearance of Christ in the Old Testament, a sign of God’s presence. We say only: this brings to mind Immanuel, God with us, and we do not treat it as a creed to be fought for to the end.

The third deviation is turning the promotion for faithfulness into a reward and guarantee of faithfulness. The promotion in verse 30 was a result, not a reason; when the three said “But if not,” they did not know they would be promoted. To treat faithfulness as a method for success is to turn God into someone we can trade with.

The fourth deviation is turning the three’s refusal to worship into permission to confront those in authority loudly on any occasion. They shouted no slogans and staged no protest; they simply did not bow, and calmly stated their position. For brothers and sisters who are under persecution, we should especially not press for details, nor make public any traceable details; protecting people matters more than showing courage.

The fifth deviation is turning the iron rule of this chapter into a contest of who is more brave. “But if not” is obedience to God, not a standard for measuring others. You may not be brave enough, and you may once have knelt; God is still the one who is with you in the fire, and who also calls you to stand again.
If I once knelt, do I still have the right to say “But if not”?

Yes. The text does not say that these three companions never felt fear in their whole lives; it records only that this time they stood. Peter denied the Lord three times, and later was also called to shepherd the flock. What God values is not that you have never fallen, but that today you return to him and decide again who is King.
