You can honestly tell God about the time you knelt, and then say to him today’s “But if not.” He will not reject you, and does not need you to pretend you were never weak. So do not take your past weakness as a reason you cannot stand again today.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are used to the pressure of “everyone does it this way.” Festivals, business dinners, colleagues’ gatherings, family rites: on some occasions, not going is not giving face, and going leaves us unsure whether we are making a statement to another lord. In the Chinese situation, relationships weigh more than principles; this is our strength and often our pressure. This chapter does not ask us to become difficult people, but invites us to discern which things are courtesy and relationship, and which are giving to something else the worship that belongs only to God. In the latter, like the three companions, we can neither argue nor accuse, only quietly not follow, and respect others.

The second question: we often treat “whether God saves” as an exam of faith. Someone at home is sick, we keep praying, and there is no improvement, and those nearby say: your faith is not enough. That sentence wounds, and it does not fit this chapter. When the three said “But if not,” they did not treat the outcome as a report card of faith. So when facing those who are losing, we can accompany and pray, and not draw conclusions for God; when facing ourselves, we can honestly tell God our pain and questions, and still decide: you are King.
If I live in a place where it is not convenient to make faith public, how can I read this chapter?

You can read it as a very quiet hope. The three companions shouted no slogans and staged no protest; they only did not bow, and calmly stated their position. Within a safe range, in the smallest ways, you can guard your heart, pray, and support one another with trusted companions. There is no need to write or say publicly details that could harm yourself and others. Protecting people matters more than showing courage; God also sees the faithfulness that no one else sees. You can also ask a trusted brother or sister to agree with you on a safe way to pray for each other. If you cannot yet find anyone you can trust, you can first speak the words in your heart quietly to God, and he hears them all.
VII. Living Out 321—“But If Not,” Still Standing

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. In Gethsemane he said, “not what I desire, but what you desire,” and he too walked into the deepest fire, and on the cross was not exempted. The Bible is my Standard, because the stand of the three companions did not come from emotion, but from what they had known from childhood, the one only God. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because to stand while everyone bows their heads takes not one’s own courage, but a Spirit who is present within.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that he may not act as I wish, but he is still the King. Let Jesus receive all the glory means that after coming out of the furnace, it is not that people are praised, but that “blessed be their God”; the glory returns to God. The one purpose: to build God’s system. This system is not one person fighting alone, but three people, going in together and coming out together. God’s system is, in a place where everyone bows their heads, still having people who guard one another and stand together.

Changing concepts changes life: when we think “the result of faithfulness must be good,” our life is afraid of failure; when we know “being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is my matter,” our life becomes free. From selfhood to selflessness: the person with self says “God must act as I wish,” the selfless person says “you are King.” In this chapter, selflessness is not nothingness, but no longer making one’s own rescue the condition.
How can “But if not” be lived out in daily life, and not only in big things?

It can begin with the smallest things. For example, you know that a small dishonesty would let you hand in one report fewer and have a little less trouble, yet you decide to be honest; you know that a small retelling could let others see how clever you are, yet you decide to keep your mouth guarded. In these moments you do not know whether God will let you “gain”; you only decide: he is King. Small “But if nots,” one by one, mean that before the great fire you do not have to learn to stand for the first time. As days pass you will find that small faithfulness becomes your best preparation for the great fire. This kind of habit will, little by little, bring you from relying on willpower alone to truly trusting the Lord.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, One Furnace

The proud type says: “My faith is big enough; God will surely save me as I wish.” This sounds like faith, but it puts God under one’s own conditions. The three companions did not speak this way; they said: he is able, but if not, we still will not worship. Please loosen your hand, and let God be God.

The fearful type says: “If I do not follow everyone, I will lose everything.” This fear is real, and the fire is real. But this chapter tells you: in the hottest place, you are not alone. Do not look only at the heat of the fire; look also at the fourth who walks in the fire.

The ashamed type says: “I too once knelt down; I have no right to stand.” The text does not say how perfect these three companions were; it says only that this time they stood. If you once knelt, God still calls you to stand up again today. Return to God, beginning today.

The wounded type says: “I stood, but no one saved me, and I am hurt.” This wound is real. Please do not answer it with “your faith was not enough.” The hope of the text is not a guarantee that you will not enter the fire, but that he came in. You can bring your wound and still honestly say before him: I am in great pain.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day take one minute to say to God: “You are able to save me; but if not, I will still follow you.” You need not say it beautifully, only honestly.
Second, write down one thing you have been unwilling to put down because you fear the outcome, and write beside it: being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is my matter.
Third, notice someone near you who has been shut out or misunderstood because of faith, greet him first, do not comment, only keep him company, and pray for him.
Fourth, on an occasion where “everyone does it this way,” pick one small thing you will not follow, and do it quietly, without argument.
Fifth, tell the story of “But if not,” in three sentences, to a friend who is going through the fire, and pray for him.
I declare: God is able to save me, and he will be with me in the fire.
I declare: but if not, I will still serve the one only God.
I declare: being saved is God’s matter, being faithful is my matter; I will not make being saved a condition of faithfulness.
I declare: there is no other god who is able to deliver like this, and I will give all the glory to him.

Daniel chapter 3 begins with a piece of music and ends with a confession. The knees of a whole empire bent, and only three stood; a furnace heated seven times hotter did not singe a single hair; and a king who wanted to prove that no god could save said at last: there is no other god who is able to deliver like this. What this chapter gives us is not a formula of “faith and be saved,” but a deeper invitation: when the outcome is not yet known, still to decide who is King.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that square. When the music sounds, what will your knees do? The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he also walked into the deepest fire and is with us. The focus is not on whether my faith is big enough, nor on how hot the fire is, but on the Lord who walks in the fire.

May God make us, in the place where everyone bows their heads, still stand, and in the hottest fire still see him, until every mouth confesses that there is no other god who is able to deliver like this. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 3:7 says that everyone fell down as soon as they heard the music. Have you ever had an experience of “everyone does it this way, so I followed”? Please give one example.
2. ★★ 3:12 shows an accusation coming from people nearby. Have you ever been misunderstood or distanced because you were “different”? Please say it in just one sentence.
3. ★★ When you face a question like “Is what you believe any use?”, what is your first reaction in your heart: anger, sadness, or wanting to defend? Please give the most recent example.

4. ★★★ Please think quietly about one thing: something you have been waiting for God to resolve “as you wish.” Now write down that thing, and the one point where you most fear “he will not act as I wish.”

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 3:17–18 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches being shut out, being accused, and pressure at home or work; if someone mentions ongoing persecution, the loss of a loved one, or long-term hopelessness, do not press for details, do not ask them to let go at once, look after them privately after the meeting, and do not make public any traceable information.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.

5. ★★ 【See】 3:17–18, the first sentence is faith and the second is obedience. Which do you see yourself as more like: only the first sentence, or already prepared for the second? Please give an example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 3:25. Which phrase is God saying to you: “loose,” “walking in the middle of the fire,” or “unharmed”? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 Have you made “God must save” a condition of your own faithfulness? If so, what difference would this make to one of your decisions now?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Please say to the person next to you one sentence: “You are able to save; but if not, I will still follow you.” Only one sentence, no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Step】 This week, in which small matter will you quietly “not follow everyone”? Please say the person, the time, the place.

Leader’s reminder: Go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, ask only for one sentence, one name, one time, with no need to tell stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort, do not press for details, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” look after them privately after the meeting, and help them find professional support if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who is in the “furnace”? Please say his name, and decide to reach out to him once this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there something everyone “just follows” and no one has asked why? Please say what it is, and say where you could begin.
12. ★★ Is there a place where, for fear of losing something, you have not dared to say “no”? Please say the name or the occasion, and decide this week to state your position quietly in one sentence.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “God is with us in the fire.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: “But if not” does not ask anyone to compete in bravery, and does not say that those who were not saved had too little faith. Do not judge anyone’s choices, and do not draw conclusions about any regime or person. If someone shares his wounds, losses, or the experience of asking without receiving, do not press for details, do not ask for forgiveness, and look after him privately after the meeting.

Please gently close your eyes and place before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read 3:17–18 together: Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.

Let the leader pray for each person: ask God to teach us, when the outcome is not yet known, still to let Jesus be King; and to let us take that step in the ordinary days of the week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

4.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 4 · Daniel Chapter 4
4.title: The Most High Rules in the Kingdom of Men—Tree, Seven Times, Lifted Eyes
blocks: I. A Witness Written from the End (4:1–18)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Let me first ask you to think of one thing: when was the last time someone praised you to your face? Perhaps your manager said, this project owes much to you; perhaps a friend said, without you I could not have held on. You were glad to hear it, and grateful. But in that instant, was there a voice in your heart that softly said: yes, I did this? In this lesson we read of a man who said that sentence at the top of his voice.

Daniel chapter 4 begins in a very special way. Daniel 4:1 says: “Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you.” An ordinary decree is a king giving orders and setting rules; this one is a king giving witness, and from the end at that: “How great are his signs! How mighty are his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. His dominion is from generation to generation.” Do you remember chapter 3? He once set up a golden image and required the whole earth to bow; now he himself proclaims to the whole earth that only one kingdom is everlasting, and that kingdom is not his. How this king came to this place, he will tell us.

Verse 4 says: “I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace.” Notice the moment: not a time of failure but the best of times. The nation secure, the works complete, no visible threat. Just then he had a dream that made him afraid and troubled. The greatest unease often does not come from hardship but from times that are too smooth. He then did what he knew best: he summoned all the experts. The result was the same as in chapter 2: they could not. This time the king did not rage; he only admitted: human methods had again reached their end. Then he remembered Daniel.

The first scene of the dream is a tree: “I saw, and behold, a tree in the middle of the earth; and its height was great. The tree grew, and was strong, and its height reached to the sky, and its sight to the end of all the earth.” Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit plentiful, the animals had shade under it, the birds lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it. Look: the first scene of this dream has no bad part. This king was not only a tyrant who oppressed people; his kingdom fed many and sheltered many. The text does not deny this. But this tree “reached to the sky,” a picture that brings to mind the tower of Babel. It did not grow badly; it grew to a height that did not belong to it. Pride often does not grow from bad places but from good ones: ability, achievement, being needed are all good, only when we forget that all of it was given, good turns into height.

Then the second scene: a watcher came from heaven and cried aloud: “Cut down the tree, and cut off its branches! Shake off its leaves, and scatter its fruit!” But notice that the stump was left, the root still in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze. This judgment is not destruction; it is a judgment with something left. His heart was to be changed from man’s, and an animal’s heart given to him, so that seven times would pass over him. Why an animal’s heart? Because this man, in the heights, forgot he was a man; so God let him, in the least human way, learn again to be human. The last sentence of this passage is the key of the whole chapter: “that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.”

The two questions share one way out: back before God. Your achievements, set them before him; others’ failures, set them before him too. Before him, no one is high or low, only those who were given, and the God who gives.
Who is the “watcher” in the dream? Is it an angel?

The original says “a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven,” a word rarely used elsewhere in the Old Testament. Most interpreters understand him as a messenger from heaven, sent by God to carry the command of judgment; in 4:24 Daniel says it is “the decree of the Most High,” which also shows that the source of the command is God. The text gives no further description of this watcher’s identity, and we need not guess more details; we need only see that the judgment did not happen by chance, but that the God of heaven rules in the kingdom of men. You can also bring this question to your small group and read the text together, rather than guessing alone. In this chapter we can also learn: first hear what the text says, then ask what it asks of us.
II. Speaking the Truth, and Giving a Way Out (4:19–27)

It was Daniel’s turn to speak. Verse 19 says: “Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was stricken mute for a while, and his thoughts troubled him.” He was not a man without feeling. When he heard this dream, he knew at once that it was a judgment on the king. The king, seeing his face, comforted him instead: “Belteshazzar, don’t let the dream, or the interpretation, trouble you.” Daniel answered: “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation to your adversaries.” This is a very human sentence: he truly hoped the dream was not about the king. A true interpreter comes with tears to speak of judgment.

Then he said very directly: “it is you, O king, that have grown and become strong.” No detours, no technique. He matched each part of the dream with the king’s life: grown and strong, that is you; greatness reaching to the sky, that is you; dominion to the end of the earth, that is you. Then the verdict: you will be driven from men, dwell with the animals of the field, eat grass as oxen, be wet with the dew of the sky, and seven times will pass over you. Notice that Daniel did not treat the verdict as his own matter; he said: “the decree of the Most High, which has come on my lord the king.” It was not his idea or his judgment; he only carried the word from heaven into the palace.

The most important is the last verse. He did not stop at judgment; he gave the king a way: “O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.” Please hear this word: “perhaps.” He gave no guarantee and made no promise on God’s behalf; the judgment was set, yet the door of repentance remained open. To a mighty king he said: see the poor. This is the most concrete repentance: not more sacrifices, but more mercy.

If one day you need to say a hard truth to someone, please remember Daniel: first grieve for the person, then speak clearly, and finally give him a way out. One who speaks the truth does not do it to win, nor to prove himself right, but so that the person still has a road to walk.

This passage also reminds us that interpreting and counseling are two different things. To interpret is to state God’s word clearly; to counsel is to take on a share of responsibility for the other’s road. Daniel did both, and he did not blur his words because the other was a king. May we too have this courage and gentleness: when it needs saying, to say it; when it needs accompanying, to accompany.
If I speak the truth and the other does not accept it, have I wasted my effort?

No. After Daniel spoke, the king did not repent at once; twelve months later the judgment came. Daniel’s responsibility was to say it clearly and faithfully, and the result was in God’s hand. After you have spoken, you can keep praying for this person, and you need not feel you did wrong because he did not change. If you spoke with love, with a way out, and not to shame the other, you have already done what you should. Finally, remember that one who speaks the truth also needs to be accompanied, and should not carry it alone. Remind yourself too: not every time you speak the truth will you see an immediate result.
III. The Light of the Original: Know, Rule, Most High (4:17, 25, 32)

Three words in this chapter recur and are worth taking apart. The first is know, the Aramaic יְדַע (yeda). Verse 17: “that the living may know”; verse 25: “until you know”; verse 32 says it once more. This word does not mean knowing a piece of information, but knowing through experience. The king was driven out and ate grass for seven times, for one purpose only: to make him “know.” God’s judgment is not for revenge, but so that a person truly comes to know him.

The second is rule, the Aramaic שַׁלִּיט (shallit), meaning having sovereignty, having authority to govern. “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men”: this sentence appears three times in this chapter, and is said at last in the king’s confession in 4:34–35: “his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.” This is the central sentence of the whole book, and the same thing that the long Aramaic section, from chapter 2 to chapter 7, keeps saying.

The third is Most High, the Aramaic עִלָּיָא (illaya), its root meaning “high.” Think about it: that tree “reached to the sky,” but the one truly on high is not the tree but the Most High. A man who wants to stand tall can only do so on the earth, and even reaching to the sky is only a tree; he is the one above. These three words together are the route of this chapter: to know, because he rules; he rules, because he is the Most High. Our position is given; our lesson is to know.

These three words also answer a common question: why does God let a person go through such hard days? Because what he wants is not that we bow our heads, but that we “know.” Some lessons we cannot learn at a desk; we can learn them only in the lowest place. This does not say that all suffering is for teaching, but that God can, at any low place, bring us back to his side.
Are the “seven times” seven years? Why is the commentary unsure?

The original says only “seven times”; the Aramaic עִדָּנִין means “periods,” without saying whether days, months or years. Some read it as seven years, some as seven seasons or seven months, and some as a symbol of a full period. The text gives no answer, and we need not decide for it. What this chapter asks us to notice is not the length of time, but the condition for its end: until he knows that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. So where things are uncertain, we would rather honestly say “the text does not say” than hurry to supply an answer. A mature believer is willing to say: this point, the text does not tell us, and we put it in God’s hands.
Is the “spirit of the holy gods” speaking of the Holy Spirit?

In verse 8 the king says that in Daniel is “the spirit of the holy gods”; the original is plural, literally “spirit of holy gods.” This is a foreign king using words familiar to him to state his observation, not a complete doctrinal confession. Some think the plural is a form of dignity pointing to the one God. This commentary does not treat this sentence as doctrinal proof of the person of the Holy Spirit; we see only that even a foreign king admitted that this man had a spirit beyond the human. We need not teach this one phrase as a complete doctrine, nor, because it is incomplete, ignore its witness. This attitude respects both the text and the person before us.
IV. After Twelve Months, He Looked Up (4:28–37)

The dream was given, the interpretation was given, and the counsel was given. But nothing happened. Verse 29 says: “At the end of twelve months.” One month, two months, half a year, a year. These twelve months were God’s patience, and also the most dangerous time for man: because nothing happened, people think it does not matter. God’s patience is often taken as God’s silence, and God’s silence is again taken as one’s own safety. Then he walked in the royal palace of Babylon, looked over his city, and said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”

Please count: I, my power, my majesty, my glory. In this one sentence there is only one protagonist. This is not an evil man speaking evil, but a very successful man speaking the truth: the city really was built by him; the works really were completed by him. But he turned a position given into my achievement. This is the most exact definition of pride: leaving the place of man, and taking God’s glory for oneself. Verse 31 says: “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky.” God did not wait for him to finish, because the sentence had already been finished. Then the text uses one verse to write the end: he was driven out, ate grass as oxen, his hair grew like eagles’ feathers, his nails like birds’ claws.

Notice that the text gives this condition no medical name and does not ask us to diagnose it. It lets us see only this: a man who thought he was a god became one who was not like a man. We need not use this picture to mock anyone, and still less to judge people near us who struggle in mind. This passage is a reminder to every one of us: when you begin to say “it was all me,” stop, and look up.

Then comes the quietest verse of the whole chapter: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High.” No ceremony, no great religious act, only a man raising his eyes from the ground. He had been looking at his own city and his own achievement; for seven times he had only bent his head to eat grass. Now he looked up, and understanding returned at that very moment. Notice the order: he did not first find his understanding and then bless; he first lifted his eyes, and then was restored. It is not that I get well first and then look to God, but that when I look up, I am healed.

The last verse is the conclusion written by one who had been proud: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” This sentence was not said to him by someone else; he said it of himself. This is a witness with no defense. As for his later life and eternal end, the text does not say, and we do not pass a verdict for God. We see only this: God was pleased to let a man, in the lowest place, lift up his head.

Please bring this picture back into your own life: have you had a moment when “the days were over,” and only then found you had been bending your head all along? What many people need is not more information or methods but a moment of looking up. Some find it in a hospital corridor, some on an afternoon of unemployment, some on a very quiet night. Whichever it is, the text says: God waits for that one action. He does not wait for us to be perfect; he waits for us to look up.
What if I am right now in the days of “bending my head to eat grass”?

You need not wait until the days are over to ask. The point of the text is the lifting of the eyes: a very small action, yet the turning point. In the lowest place you can look up and say one sentence: “God, you are King.” You need not say it beautifully, nor first put yourself in order. You can also ask a trusted companion to walk this road with you, and do not take this season as evidence that God has abandoned you; in the text, the stump was kept. Remember, his stump was always kept; so is yours, and God has never given up on you. So you need not hurry to climb out of the low place; you can first come to know God here.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is forcing “seven times” into seven years and matching it with some year, event or person today. The original says only seven “times,” without saying whether days, months or years. What this chapter asks us to hear is “that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men,” not a timetable. If we turn this chapter into material for counting days, we go from bowing the head to turning pages.

The second deviation is describing the king’s illness as some medical diagnosis, or using it to mock or judge those who struggle in mind. The text describes only “ate grass as oxen, hair like eagles’ feathers,” and gives no medical name. This passage is a reminder to all the proud, not a comment on any patient. We need to have compassion on those who suffer, not use them as examples for this chapter.

The third deviation is turning 4:27, “righteousness, mercy to the poor,” into a way of exchanging good deeds for peace or forgiveness. Daniel describes what repentance looks like, and says “perhaps,” with no guarantee; being forgiven is God’s grace, and doing good is the fruit of repentance. Nor are the poor excluded by God because they have not done enough.

The fourth deviation is concluding from 4:34–37 that Nebuchadnezzar was saved and became a believer, or asserting that he was not saved. The text records only that he lifted his eyes, praised and confessed, and does not state his eternal end. We stay with what the text says and do not pass a verdict for God.

The fifth deviation is turning this chapter into “successful people will surely be humbled by God.” The text is not against success, nor does it say that achievement is sin; the tree itself was not wrong. The problem is turning what was given into “mine.” Humility is not refusing success, but knowing, when successful, where it came from.
Does achievement make one prone to pride? Must humility mean deliberately making oneself small?

No. Daniel also had a very high position and ability, yet he said, “not because of any wisdom of mine”; he did not make himself small, he only returned the glory. Humility is not underestimating oneself, but putting things in the right place: ability is given, position is given, and the glory of the result still belongs to God. You can honestly say: I did this well, and also say: this was God’s grace to me. Mature humility sees clearly what one has, and also sees clearly where it came from. Today you might also find one small thing no one saw, do it quietly well, and quietly hand it to God.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are used to “achievement” being a person’s calling card. In Chinese society, who you are, what you have done, which school your child entered often decides how others see you and how you see yourself. Many live inside an invisible comparison: not daring to admit that they are not good enough, and not daring to admit that they did well, for fear of being laughed at or called proud. This chapter gives a way out: you need not deny your achievements, nor lean on them to hold yourself up. You can say: this was given by God; and then quietly, with dignity, return the glory.

The second question: it is easy, when others fall, to feel “this is the end of his pride.” Someone falls ill, someone loses a job, someone’s marriage breaks, and those nearby say: he was just too proud. Such words do not fit this chapter, and they wound. The text asks us to look at ourselves first, not at others. The story of Nebuchadnezzar was written by himself; no one drew the conclusion for him. So when facing others’ failure, we can accompany and pray; when facing our own success, we can look up and say: you gave this.
I am in an environment where an elder or a manager is very forceful. How can I speak the truth as Daniel did?

Daniel’s way of speaking the truth was to respect first, then be direct, and then give a way out: he called the king “my lord,” he said “may the dream be for those who hate you,” he said it clearly, and he left the door of repentance open. In a forceful environment you can first choose the right time and place, and speak privately and quietly; first acknowledge what the other has given, then say what you have seen; and finally offer one concrete way forward. In a situation that could bring danger, please first seek safe support, and do not carry it alone. If you are not sure how to say it, you can first write down what you want to say, and ask a companion to look it over. On the premise of safety and respect, your courage is wisdom, not rashness.
VII. Living Out 321—Lift Your Eyes to Heaven, Give the Glory to God

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. He was in the form of God, yet did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The Bible is my Standard, because what this chapter asks us to know is not a story but a truth: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because looking up is not by willpower but by one within who reminds me: you are King.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that at the moment I say “it was all me,” I lift up my eyes and say: you are King. Let Jesus receive all the glory means that in success and when praised, we neither take it for ourselves nor feign modesty, but honestly say: you gave this. The one purpose: to build God’s system. In God’s system everyone’s position is given, so the great do not look down on the small, and the small do not envy the great; when someone is lifted up, someone reminds him; when someone bows his head, someone accompanies him.

Changing concepts changes life: when we think a position is “what I won,” our life is tense; when we know a position is “given,” our life can relax. From selfhood to selflessness: the person with self says “is not this great Babylon what I built,” the selfless person says “this was given by the King of heaven.” Selflessness is not nothingness, but no longer giving the glory to oneself.

In the family, this means that parents do not take their children’s grades as their own glory, nor their children’s failures as their own shame. In the workplace, this means that supervisors do not take the team’s results for themselves, and colleagues do not scramble for credit in order to be seen. In the church, this means that we do not make the results of our service our calling card, but after each service say together: this is what the Lord did.
How do I practice “no longer giving the glory to myself” in daily life?

You can begin with a very small habit: each time you are praised, first say “thank you,” and then quietly say in your heart “this was given by God.” You can also, each night before sleep, write down three things for which you were praised or thanked that day, and hand them back to God one by one. After a while you will find that you no longer need to be praised so much, nor fear criticism so much, because your worth is no longer placed in others’ mouths. A month later you can look back and see at which times your heart was quieter. This small practice will slowly loosen the hand your heart has kept clenched.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, One Tree Cut Down

The proud type says: “I earned this by my effort, and I have the right to say so.” This may be true: you really did work hard. But please add another sentence beside it: “This was an opportunity God gave me.” Put the two sentences side by side, and you will be freer.

The fearful type says: “If I do not hold on, everything will collapse.” What you fear may be the tree being cut down. But please notice that the text says the stump was left. God’s judgment is not to wipe you out, but to bring you back to the right place. You can let go, because it is not you alone who holds up this world.

The ashamed type says: “I too once said such things; I have no right to look up.” Nebuchadnezzar spoke the proudest words and became the lowest of men, yet he still lifted his eyes, and was still restored. You need not be perfect first to look up; looking up is the first step home.

The wounded type says: “I was not proud, yet I too was brought low.” This is a very honest and very painful feeling. Please do not use this chapter to explain your own pain, and do not let others use this chapter to blame you. Some suffering is not because of pride; some low places are not because of judgment. You can bring your wound, and in the low place still look up and say one sentence: God, I am here.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day after something for which you are praised or succeed, say in one sentence to God: this was what you gave; the glory is yours.
Second, write down one thing for which you most easily say “it was all me,” and write beside it: this is a position given, not my capital.
Third, find a companion, and remind each other: when the other says “it was all my credit,” gently say, “look up.”
Fourth, every day stop for thirty seconds, leave the screen, lift your eyes to heaven once, ask nothing, and say only: you are King.
Fifth, in a place where you have influence, do one concrete thing for someone in a weak position, as Daniel urged the king to show mercy to the poor.
I declare: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men; my position and my ability were all given.
I declare: I will not take the glory for myself; I will give all the glory to the King of heaven.
I declare: I can say “you gave this” in success, and in the low place I can say, “God, you are King.”
I declare: those who walk in pride God is able to abase; those who lift their eyes to heaven God will restore.

Daniel chapter 4 begins with a decree and ends in a confession. A tree that reached to the sky was cut down, and the stump was kept; a king who thought he was a god became one who was not like a man, yet when the days were over he lifted his eyes to heaven. What this chapter gives us is not a frightening story of judgment, but a gentle and clear invitation: you need not wait until you have lost everything to look up.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that word of praise. When someone says, “it is thanks to you,” what does your heart say? The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he is the Lord who was in the form of God yet emptied himself. The focus is not on my achievements, nor on my failures, but on the Most High who rules.
May God make us, in success, say “you gave this,” and in the low place still lift our eyes, until all peoples bless the King of heaven. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 4:4 says the king was “at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace.” Have you ever felt uneasy in your heart at the very time things were smoothest? Please give one example.
2. ★★ In 4:30 the king says, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?” Is there a place where you very easily say “I did this”? Please say it in just one sentence.
3. ★★ When others praise you, what is your first reaction in your heart: thanking God, thinking you did well, or embarrassment? Please give the most recent example.
4. ★★★ Please think quietly about one thing: something you have been bending your head over to handle. Now write down that thing, and the one point you most need to look up and see.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 4:34 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches achievement, comparison and shame; if someone mentions that they or a family member is unemployed, ill or struggling in mind, do not press for details, do not ask them to let go at once, do not treat this chapter as a comment on anyone, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 The tree of 4:10–12 was a good tree. Is there a place where your good is turning into height? Please give an example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 4:34. Which phrase is God saying to you: “lifted up my eyes to heaven,” “my understanding returned,” or “I blessed the Most High”? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 In 4:27 Daniel says, “break off your … iniquities by showing mercy to the poor.” What difference does this make for someone in a weak position whom you now meet?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Please say to the person next to you one sentence, “this was given by God,” and name one thing you want to return to God. Only one sentence, no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Step】 This week, for which person in a weak position will you do one concrete thing? Please say the person, the time, the place.

Leader’s reminder: Go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, ask only for one sentence, one name, one time, with no need to tell stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort, do not press for details, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” look after them privately after the meeting, and help them find professional support if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who is “bending his head to eat grass”? Please say his name, and decide to reach out to him once this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there something everyone often calls “what we did,” and seldom calls “what God gave”? Please say what it is, and say where you could begin.
12. ★★ Is there a place where, because of success, you have not dared say “God gave this”? Please say the name or the occasion, and decide this week to return the glory in one sentence.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not use this chapter in the group to judge anyone’s failure or illness, and do not discuss anyone’s eternal end. If someone shares his wounds, long-term hopelessness or the experience of asking without receiving, do not press for details, do not ask for forgiveness, and look after him privately after the meeting.

Please gently close your eyes and place before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read 4:34 together: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever.

Let the leader pray for each person: ask God to teach us, in success, to say “you gave this”; in the low place, still to lift our eyes; and to let us take that step in the ordinary days of the week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

5.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 5 · Daniel Chapter 5
5.title: Weighed in the Balances and Found Lacking—Finger, Scales, That Night
blocks: I. A Lively Night, a Hand With No Body (5:1–12)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Have you ever had an experience like this: something you already knew in your heart how to do, yet you kept saying “wait a little”? Perhaps a call you should have made, an apology you should have spoken, a habit you should have laid down. Each time you had a reason, each time you felt that today was not the best moment. In this lesson we read of a man whose “wait a little” finally waited until the last night.

Daniel chapter 5 begins at a great feast: “Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand.” Imagine the scene: the lamps blazing, laughter without end, wine cup after cup. The text does not say this night was unusual in any way; judgment often draws quietly near on just such a night. Then comes that decision: “Belshazzar, while he tasted the wine, commanded that the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem be brought.” Notice the moment: while he tasted the wine, not when he was sober, but when the wine was at its height.

These vessels were from the temple of God in Jerusalem, originally for serving God. Now they were brought for amusement, to raise a cup to gods made of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. The most dangerous thing is often not one great sin but, in a relaxed moment, treating holy things as things for amusement. Perhaps it is not gold and silver vessels; it is a stretch of time originally meant for serving the Lord, a gift originally meant for him, a Lord’s Day that originally belonged to him, and in relaxed moments we casually use it elsewhere.

Then verse 5 says: “In the same hour, the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall of the king’s palace.” Not an angel, not a voice, only a hand, part of a hand. It wrote opposite the lamp stand, in the place where the light was brightest. God does not need to say much; one hand is enough. The king’s face was changed, his thoughts troubled him, the joints of his thighs were loosened, and his knees struck one against another. The thousand lords, the gold and silver vessels, the feast: none of it mattered any more. When God’s hand appears on the wall, the strongest part of a person is often the first to give way.

He did what his predecessors had done: he summoned the wise men and promised a great reward: purple, a chain of gold, the third place. But the wise men could not read the writing. Not only could they not interpret, they could not even read. Human wisdom, before God’s handwriting, could not take even the first step. Just when the whole room was in panic, one person came in: the queen mother. She was the only one in the whole scene who spoke quietly: “O king, live forever; don’t let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your face be changed.” She did not scream and did not blame; she only remembered, and she remembered a name: Daniel. Some people, in the midst of chaos, are not the strongest but the ones who remember.

Please bring this picture back into your own life: is there a place where, when you are most relaxed, you most easily loosen your grip? Perhaps a weekend night, a dinner, a moment when no one sees. Between the holy and the ordinary there is often no clear wall; it is a very small voice in our heart, at that moment, that reminds us: this is the Lord’s. May we be willing to hear that voice.
What do the vessels of the temple mean for us today?

The New Testament says that the believer’s body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, and our time, gifts and money are also entrusted to us by God. This chapter does not ask us to hold a special superstition about any object, but reminds us that holy things must not be treated as casual things. You can ask yourself: which part originally prepared for God have I grown used to using casually? Find it, and hand it back to God in prayer; this is the lesson of this chapter for us. You can begin with the thing you use most often, such as your phone or your calendar, and ask: is there a part of this that is God’s, which I have taken for amusement?
II. Not Speaking for a Reward, Speaking Only for the Truth (5:13–24)

Daniel was brought before the king. The king asked him: “Are you that Daniel of the children of the captivity of Judah?” Listen to this address: “of the captivity.” This king remembered only his label, not his record. People are often like this; they remember only your label, and not what you have done. Daniel did not argue, and did not state his credentials. The king repeated that great reward: purple, a chain of gold, the third place. This was an invitation of power: if you speak, you will be the third man in this kingdom.

Listen to Daniel’s answer: “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.” He did not rage and did not bargain; he only said very clearly: this is not why I came. Only one who does not speak for a reward can say the truth others do not like to hear. Because what he was about to say was not good news.

He spoke first of history: God gave Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, greatness, glory and majesty, and all peoples, nations and languages trembled before him; but his heart was lifted up, and he was deposed from his kingly throne, lived with the wild donkeys and ate grass as oxen, until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men. This is the whole story of chapter 4, condensed into a few sentences, spoken to this night and this man. Then he turned and pointed directly at Belshazzar: “You … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.”

Please hear this sentence slowly. He did not say “you did not know”; he said “you knew, and did not bow.” The greatest debt is not ignorance, but knowing and still not humbling oneself. This sentence is especially important for us today: we have heard much truth, read many verses, know many stories; what we lack is often not information but a bowed head. Is there one thing you know very clearly God has already spoken about, yet you are still putting it off, still finding reasons?

Then he made the charge concrete: you lifted yourself up against the Lord of heaven, you brought the vessels of his house and drank from them, you praised gods that cannot see or hear, and you have not glorified the God in whose hand your breath is. This sentence is very near: every breath you take is in God’s hand. At last he said: “Then the part of the hand was sent from before him, and this writing was inscribed.” The writing on the wall was not without cause; it had a reason, a charge and an interpretation. God’s judgment is never sudden; it comes after long patience.

When Daniel said all this, the king’s thousand lords were all present. He did not avoid the crowd, and did not soften it with a roundabout manner. But there is a delicate point in his words: he began with what the king knew well, with the king’s father, with the history the king had seen with his own eyes. A truly wise reminder is not to throw down a new accusation, but to set before a person again what he already knew.
Daniel refused the rewards, so why did he later put on the purple? Is that not a contradiction?

It is not. What he refused in 5:17 was “speaking in order to get a reward”; the purple of 5:29 was ordered by the king himself after he had finished. The order is important: he did not change his interpretation because of a reward, and did not ask the king for anything beforehand. He put on the purple and was still only a servant; that very night the king was slain, and everything changed hands again. What we can learn is not to treat a reward as a condition of faithfulness; and when a reward comes, not to treat it as our own credit. Remember too that his interpretation was very clear yet had no mockery in it; this is the pattern we who speak the truth should learn.
III. The Light of the Original: Know, Balances, Wanting (5:22, 25–28)

The original of this chapter has three words worth reading slowly. The first is know, the Aramaic יְדַע (yeda). It recurs in chapter 4: “that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” Nebuchadnezzar paid the price of seven times to “know”; Belshazzar “knew all this,” yet paid no price and did not humble himself. The same word, in these two chapters, speaks of two kinds of people: one learned in the low place, one would not learn in the high place.

The second is balances, the Aramaic מֹאזַנְיָא (mozanya). TEKEL: you are weighed in the balances. The picture of balances in the Old Testament is often connected with fairness: “just balances.” The balances are not meant to shame people, but to show true weight. You may resist this picture, or you may accept it: God’s standard is real, and also fair.

The third is wanting, the Aramaic חַסִּיר (chasir), meaning lacking, deficient. “You are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.” Notice that this word does not say “you are bad” but “you are not enough.” No one before God is enough. This “not enough” is the starting point of the gospel of the whole Bible: only those who are not enough need a Lord who makes up for us.

These three words together are the route of this chapter: to know, then to be weighed, then to be shown wanting. But we need not stop here. The New Testament says that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us, and in this God’s love toward us is shown. The balances are still real, but there is one who already stands on our side.

Today you can quietly place these three words in your own situation: what do I “know”? By what have I been “weighed”? Where am I “wanting”? Then lay these three answers one by one before the cross. You will find that what truly sets a person free is not having no shortfall, but knowing that someone has already paid it in full.
Are “MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” units of weight, or verbs?

Both readings are possible. The four words of the original can be read as three units of weight, mina, shekel and half-shekel, or as three verbs, numbered, weighed and divided. Daniel’s interpretation takes the second, and brings out a wordplay: “divided” and “Persia” share the same root. We need not dwell here too long; the point is: what people see is writing, what God means is a verdict, and it takes the Spirit of God to point it out. In this way, our reading of the original is not for showing off knowledge but for hearing God more clearly. If you want to study further, you can ask a pastor or consult different commentaries, and set the views side by side.
Do the balances mean we must reach God’s standard by our own deeds?

No. The purpose of the balances is to show a person’s shortfall so that he knows he needs grace. The gospel of the New Testament does not cancel God’s standard, but says that Christ has already met that standard for us: he died for us, and rose again. We do not stand by our own weight, but by his. So facing the balances, we can honestly say: I am not enough, and can also say with peace: he is enough. This answer lets us on the one hand take the standard seriously, and on the other rest in grace; neither can be missing. So facing the standard, we need not run from it nor boast; we need only honestly rely on Christ.
IV. The Balances and That Night (5:25–31)

Now let’s look at the writing on the wall. “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.” Did the wise men fail to read it because it was too hard? Or because it was too direct? These words could be a merchant’s ledger, or God’s judgment. Daniel saw the second at a glance. He spoke it sentence by sentence: MENE: God has counted your kingdom, and brought it to an end. Notice, it is not “your kingdom is about to end,” but “God has already counted.” This is a process that began long ago: God, in patience, had been counting all along.

Then comes the theme of the chapter: “TEKEL: you are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.” You are weighed in the balances, and what is on the other side is not another person but God’s standard. Every person will be placed on these balances. This sentence is very solemn. But notice that when Daniel spoke of the shortfall, there was no mockery and no gloating. He only said it very clearly. This is how one who interprets judgment should be: not pleased, not exaggerating, only faithfully proclaiming.

The last word: “PERES: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.” This is the result. Then the text goes on: Belshazzar commanded that Daniel be clothed with purple, a chain of gold put about his neck, and a proclamation made that he should be the third ruler. This king kept his promise; he did not kill the one who brought the word, yet he did not repent either. His action was a perfectly complete courtesy, without one repentance.

Then comes the shortest narrative of the whole book: “In that night Belshazzar the Chaldean King was slain.” Just this one sentence, no description, no scene. This night began with a great feast and ended in a sudden change of dynasty. God’s judgment is not always loud; it can be quiet, yet on time. The last verse: “Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.” The name changed, but have you noticed: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will. This kingdom is still this kingdom.

Daniel, that night, put on the purple, and before daybreak the king had changed. He did not rise higher because of it, and lost nothing because of it, for he knew that his position had never been given by the king; it was given by God. This is the best rest for us whenever our position rises or falls. Your name card will change, your title will change, and your identity will be redefined by others; but the God in whose hand your breath is has never changed.

You may ask: if God has already counted, are people left with no chance? The text’s answer is that the chance lies behind us. Nebuchadnezzar’s story was Belshazzar’s chance; those thousand nights, every moment when he could have bowed his head, were chances. God’s patience is not so that we can put it off one more day; it is to give us one more chance to turn back.
“That very night the king was killed”: does this mean God’s judgment always comes this suddenly?

No. The judgment in this chapter comes after long patience: Nebuchadnezzar’s story had already happened before Belshazzar’s eyes, and he had many chances, yet he did not bow. Many times God’s patience looks like silence in human eyes. The text reminds us not to take God’s patience as God’s permission. Even more, we must not turn this chapter into material for frightening others; take it as a reason to bow our own heads today. What the text gives people is a chance, not fear; an invitation, not a threat. So bowing today need not wait for someone to remind us, nor for something to go wrong.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to teach “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” as a code for working out some nation or event of our day. Daniel’s interpretation points to the end of Babylon that very night; the text does not ask us to turn it into a tool for counting days or identifying nations. Turning this passage into a guessing game makes us forget what we are really meant to do: bow our heads.

The second deviation is to teach the judgment as gloating over others, or to use the “balances” to pass judgment on what others lack. When Daniel spoke of what was lacking, he did not mock and he did not gloat; this chapter is spoken to everyone who knows and yet does not humble himself, ourselves included. Weigh yourself first, then talk about others.

The third deviation is to teach the “balances” as “people must reach a standard by their own works to be saved.” The balances reveal what is lacking so that people may see their need; the gospel is that Christ already stands on our side, not that we stand by our own weight. Teaching this chapter as an exam of works makes people more anxious, not more free.

The fourth deviation is to teach Daniel’s refusing the rewards (5:17) and later accepting the purple robe (5:29) as inconsistency or hypocrisy. What he refused was speaking on the condition of a reward; the reward was something the king ordered afterward on his own, and Daniel never made it the precondition of his interpretation. The point is the order, not the purple robe.

The fifth deviation is to use this chapter to frighten people who have not yet believed, saying, “If you still don’t believe, you will end up like Belshazzar.” The point of this chapter is knowing and not humbling oneself; its invitation is to bow today. Threats cannot make anyone love the Lord; it is God’s grace and patience that lead people to repentance.
I often put things off. Am I like Belshazzar?

Putting things off is not necessarily Belshazzar’s condition, but this chapter does hold up a mirror: we know, and we have not yet done it. You can first ask honestly: am I putting it off because I am afraid, because I am tired, or because I do not actually want to let go yet? If it is one of the first two, bring that weakness to God and ask him to help you; if it is the third, you need a more direct humbling. Whichever it is, please do not face it alone. Find a companion and put that matter on the calendar with a specific date. You can also ask a companion to set a specific date with you, and on that day to ask you one question: did you do it?
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to saying “let’s wait and see.” Wait and see, wait a little longer, watch a bit more. In a Chinese setting this phrase is often a kind of wisdom: not impulsive, not rash. But in spiritual matters the same phrase can become a way of putting things off. We know very well that God has already spoken; about our family, our marriage, our work, God has already pointed a direction, and yet we say, “let’s wait and see.” This chapter does not ask us to be reckless; it invites us to be honest: when I say “let’s wait and see,” am I seeking wisdom, or avoiding humbling myself?

The second question: we care a great deal about face, and about other people’s face. In this chapter Daniel had to say to the king, in front of a thousand nobles: you have been weighed in the balances and found lacking. That is an occasion that calls for great wisdom and courage. In a Chinese setting we seldom say to someone’s face what he lacks; partly to protect the relationship, and partly because we are afraid. The direction this chapter gives us is: respect first, then honesty; not in order to win, and not in order to shame, but so that this person still has a way forward. Some words left unsaid are love; some words left unsaid are fear. We need to tell them apart.
What should I do if I find I need to tell an elder or a supervisor a hard truth?

First pray for this person, and check your motive: am I doing this for his good, or to prove that I am right? Then choose a suitable time and place, and speak privately and quietly. First acknowledge what the other person has given, then say clearly what you have seen, and finally offer a concrete way forward. If the matter involves safety or an imbalance of power, please first seek the counsel of a trusted companion or pastor; you do not have to carry it alone. Daniel spoke the truth in front of the king without any mockery, and that is a pattern we can learn from. If you are not sure how to begin, you can also write down what you want to say first and ask someone you trust to read it through once.
VII. Living Out 321: Once We Know, We Bow Our Heads

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. Although he knew who he was, he humbled himself, was obedient to death, even death on a cross. He was not one who knew and did not bow; he was one who knew, and bowed. The Bible is my Standard, because this chapter is not asking us to know one more story; it asks us to respond after we know. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because bowing the head does not rest on willpower; it rests on someone inside, who gently reminds me when I say “just a little longer.”

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that even on a relaxed evening he is my Lord; not only on the Lord’s Day, but also at my banquet, in my time, in my money. Let Jesus receive all the glory means giving back to God what was his all along: my breath, my gifts, the position I hold. The one purpose: to build God’s system. In God’s system there are people like the queen mother, who remember you; there are people like Daniel, who speak what must be spoken without seeking a reward; and we are, together, a community that watches over one another.

Changing our mindset changes our life: when we think “knowing” is the same as “having,” our life stays in information; when we realize that “knowing” must become “bowing the head,” our life begins to change. From self to selflessness: the person with self says “I know, let me think about it,” and the selfless person says “I know, Lord; today I will do it.”

In the family, this means we no longer say, “I’ll apologize when the children are older,” but bow our heads now; in the workplace, it means we no longer say, “I’ll deal with that matter after this project is over,” but do it today; in the church, it means we no longer say, “I’ll serve when there’s an opportunity,” but take the first step this very week. Bowing the head is a matter for today.
How do we concretely practice “once we know, we bow our heads” in everyday life?

You can start with three very small steps. First, write down in one sentence the thing you know. Second, write down one smallest next step, such as making a phone call or saying one sentence of apology. Third, agree on a specific time; do it before that time, and tell a companion. Bowing the head is not an emotion; it is an action. Do not wait until you feel ready; you can act first and let your heart follow slowly. The action is small, but little by little it teaches your heart to obey again. A month later, look back, and you will see that your heart is a little softer than before.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, One Night

The proud type says, “I know; I’m just busy right now.” What you know may really be a great deal, but knowing is not bowing the head. Please set down the phrase “I know” and answer only one question: what will I do today?

The fearful type says, “I’m afraid that once I bow my head, I will lose even more.” What you fear losing may be face, position, relationships. But this chapter lets us see that what God wants is not to humiliate you, but to bring you back into his hand; the God who holds your breath in his hand will not make you lose in order to frighten you.

The ashamed type says, “I have put this off for so long; God must be very disappointed in me.” Belshazzar’s end is a warning, not your end. If you bow your head today, God is right here. However long you have delayed, as long as you turn back, he still stretches out his hand.

The wounded type says, “I have bowed my head before, and all I got was more hurt.” That wound is real. Please do not use this chapter to push yourself to bow your head to anyone right away. First speak your wound before God, and ask a safe companion to walk with you; when you are ready, take the next step.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day be quiet for three minutes and say to God: the one thing I know, today I will bow my head.
Second, write down one thing you have long known you should do but keep putting off, and write down a specific date.
Third, find a companion; tell each other the one thing each of you has been putting off, and agree on a time to report back.
Fourth, review your time and your money once: which part was meant for God but has been taken to liven up a party? Give it back to God.
Fifth, for someone who is in a panic, say one quiet word and pray for him, as the queen mother remembered Daniel.
I declare: the breath in my hand was given by God, and I will give the glory to him.
I declare: once I know, I will bow my head; no putting it off, and no making excuses.
I declare: I do not stand by my own weight; I rely on Christ, who already stands on my side.
I declare: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men; my position was given by him, and I will be faithful.

Daniel chapter 5 begins with a lively banquet and ends with the quietest sentence: that very night Belshazzar was killed. One hand, one wall, four words, one kingdom, a new ruler. What this chapter gives us is not a frightening story but a clear invitation: the thing you know, bow your head over it today.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that “just a little longer.” The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he is also the Lord who stands for us on the other side of the balances. The focus is not how much I fall short, and not how hard I try, but the Lord who has already made up for what I lack.
May God make us bow our heads once we know; may we remember who is Lord even on the most relaxed evening; until his kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.

1. ★ 5:2 In the midst of his drinking, Belshazzar brought the vessels of the temple to liven up the party. Is there a place where, when you relax, you carelessly treat holy things as everyday things? Please give one example.
2. ★★ 5:22 says, “you have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.” Is there something you have known and yet have not bowed your head over? Please say it in one sentence.
3. ★★ When you know you should do something but keep putting it off, what reason do you usually give yourself? Please give the most recent example.
4. ★★★ Think quietly about one thing: what is it you are most afraid of losing if you bow your head? Now write it down, and write down the one sentence you most want to say to God.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 5:22 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches procrastination, shame and the feeling of being accused; if someone mentions long-term self-blame, a major failure or the loss of a loved one, do not press for details, do not ask them to let go right away, do not use this chapter to blame anyone, and check on them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 5:6 says the king’s face changed and his knees knocked together. Is there a moment when God’s reminder suddenly appeared and made you stop? Please give one example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 5:22 or 5:27. Which phrase is God speaking to you: “though you knew,” “balances,” or “lacking”? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 Daniel says “the greatest lack is knowing and not humbling oneself.” What difference does this make to something you are putting off right now?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Say to the person next to you, “I know now; today I will bow my head,” and name that one thing. Just one sentence; no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Do】 This week, in which matter will you turn “knowing” into “doing”? Please name the person, the time and the place.

Leader’s reminder: Go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, ask only for one sentence, one name, one time, with no need to tell stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort, do not press for details, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” look after them privately after the meeting, and help them find professional support if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.

10. ★ Is there someone among your family or colleagues who is in a “panic”? Please say his or her name, and decide that this month, like the queen mother, you will take the initiative to say one quiet word.
11. ★★ Is there something your church or group all know should be done but keeps putting off? Please say what it is, and where you could start.

12. ★★ Is there a place where you dare not speak the truth because you are “afraid of losing face”? Please name the person or the occasion, and decide that this week you will first pray for him, and then find a suitable moment.

13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “you have been weighed in the balances, and Christ already stands on your side.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not use the “balances” in the group to weigh others, and do not discuss anyone’s eternal end. If someone shares his wounds, long-term hopelessness, or the reason he dares not bow his head before anyone, do not press for details and do not ask for forgiveness; check on him privately after the meeting.
Let everyone gently close their eyes and place before God the one thing written down today. Read 5:22 together: you have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.

The leader prays for each person: God, teach us to bow our heads once we know, and let us take that step in the ordinary days of this week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

6.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 6 · Daniel Chapter 6
6.title: Praying as He Had Always Done—Window, Pit, Living God
blocks: I. A Daily Life with Nothing to Hold Against It, and a Law Made Just for Him (6:1–9)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Let me first ask you to think: if one day your boss, your colleagues or your neighbors examined your life carefully, going through your accounts, your words, your time, one thing at a time, what would they find? Today we read about a man who was examined this way; they searched for a long time, and in the end could reach only one conclusion.

Daniel chapter 6: a new king, a new regime. Darius appointed one hundred twenty satraps, and over them three presidents, and Daniel was one of them. The text says: “Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.” He had walked through one empire and into another, and was not pushed out. Why? Because of his steady faithfulness. Then comes that very old story: someone does well, and someone else begins to look for ground against him.

Verse 4 says: “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.” They searched everywhere, accounts, administration, speech, and found nothing. The strongest witness is not a beautiful speech but a daily life no one can find fault with. So they came to a conclusion: “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.” This is the highest praise an enemy gave Daniel. They admitted that this man’s only weakness was his obedience to God. The reversal is ironic: they wanted to find his fault, and found his greatest glory.

Then they designed a law. They did not go straight to accuse Daniel; they were clever: “whoever asks a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.” The law sounded good, it honored the king; it did not mention Daniel in a single word; yet it turned Daniel’s daily life into a crime. Notice how they put it: the presidents, deputies, satraps, counselors and governors of the kingdom, all consulted together. All of them. Yet Daniel was also a president, and was never asked. It is a very common method: to use “everyone is doing it” to apply pressure.

The most dangerous law is not the one that plainly targets you, but the one that looks ordinary and happens to keep you from worshiping as usual. Then Darius signed. This act made the king too a prisoner: the law he had established, even he could not take back. A law made by man can trap the one who made it, and that is a foreshadowing. But please pause here first and think: in your own setting, are there seemingly ordinary rules that make you pay a price to worship as usual? They may not be a law; they may be a habit, a pressure, or a phrase like “everyone does it.”

Daniel’s daily life was not the display of a perfect personality but long years of faithfulness: on time, honest, not greedy, not lazy. These very ordinary things look unremarkable in peaceful days, but when pressure came they became his firmest protection. We easily want to become brave only in a moment of crisis and forget that courage is trained, little by little, in ordinary life.
Why can devotion be treated as a crime?

Because an innocent person makes other people’s guilt show, and because those in power demand total loyalty, while a devout person gives his “final loyalty” to God. These two reasons often exist together. The text does not ask us to go looking for chances to be persecuted, nor to call every criticism persecution. What we can do is what Daniel did: first make our daily life one no one can find fault with, then let God be Lord. You can begin with one small thing near you, and make your daily life a little cleaner and a little more honest.

Now we come to the quietest verse of this chapter: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.” He knew, and then, as before. Notice what he did not do: he did not call a press conference, did not rally companions, did not go around asking for help, and did not hide.
