He simply went home, went upstairs, and went to that window. The greatest witness is often not a big action but carrying on as usual under pressure.

Notice a few details. First, the window faced Jerusalem. This was Solomon’s hope in the temple dedication prayer: when the people are carried away captive and pray toward this house, God will hear. His window was a memory of home and also a direction of hope. Second, the window was open; the original suggests it was always open, not for today but as his daily habit. He did not open the window specially to make a statement, nor close it to avoid trouble. Third, he knelt, prayed and gave thanks. Do you hear it? A man about to be thrown into the lions’ den has thanksgiving in his prayer. Fourth, “as before”: these words are the strength of the whole chapter. He did not increase the number of times because of danger, and did not reduce it because of danger. He did not perform, and he did not retreat.

Then they came and found Daniel praying and making petition before his God. They went to the king, first made the king nod, and then brought up Daniel’s name, calling him “Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah.” Notice what they called him: not “your president,” not “Daniel, who has served the king for years,” but only “of the captivity.” It is a stripping of identity: turning a man from a contributor into an outsider. And the phrase “pays no attention to you” is exactly the wording used against the three friends in chapter 3. The enemy’s language is always alike.

Then the king: “Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him.” This king was not a bad man; he loved this man, he wanted to save him, and he spent the whole day looking for a way. But his way was blocked by his own signature. The accusers came again: “Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians, that no decree nor statute which the king establishes may be changed.” Human power can set up laws, but it cannot save a man from a law it has set up itself. Do you remember Nebuchadnezzar’s sentence in chapter 3? Who is that god who will deliver you out of my hands? In this chapter the king himself becomes the one asking the question: who can deliver me from the law I made myself? Only God can answer that question.
If I cannot kneel down and pray three times every day, is my prayer not enough?

No. Daniel’s “three times a day” was his devotional habit over many years, not a number set by the law. The point of this chapter is “as before”: continuity, not the number. You can find a rhythm that suits you, morning, noon, bedtime, or one session of ten minutes; what matters is that under pressure you do not change it out of fear. If your body, your work or the care of your family makes a fixed schedule impossible, God also sees your heart, and you can begin with the smallest session. If your time cannot be fixed, you can fix a “starting point” instead, for example one quiet minute before you turn on the computer each time.
III. Light from the Original: As Before, Serve, Trust (6:4, 10, 16, 23)

The original of this chapter has three words worth reading slowly. The first is “as before,” Aramaic מִן־קַדְמַת דְּנָה (min qadmat denah), meaning “from earlier times,” that is, continuity over many years. “As before” stresses not this one time but the long years. You can imagine that a man who does not waver in the fire did not learn not to waver in the fire; he stood firm in ordinary days, one day at a time.

The second is “serve,” Aramaic פְּלַח (pelach), which we already met in chapter 3: “our God whom we serve.” In 6:16 the king of this chapter says: “Your God whom you serve continually,” and the original uses תְּדִירָא (tedira), meaning “continually.” This word appears only twice in the whole book, both in this chapter, both spoken by the king. The king did not know Daniel’s God, but he saw Daniel’s long years of service. Witness is often seen by unbelievers in everyday life.

The third is “trust,” Aramaic הֵימִן (hemin). 6:23 says: “because he had trusted in his God.” This word shares a root with the “faithful” (מְהֵימַן) of 6:4. His faithfulness and his trust are one and the same thing: he was faithful because he trusted, and he trusted, so he was faithful. This means we need not think of “trust” as a feeling; it is a continual, everyday, steady entrusting.

Put these three words together and they are the route of this chapter: “as before” is time; “serve” is the object; “trust” is the foundation. You can ask yourself: do I have an “as before” habit? Whom do I serve? What do I trust? These three questions are much easier to ask in ordinary days than at the edge of the lions’ den.

Today you can use these three words for a very simple check. As before: do I have a fixed time each day to meet with God? Serve: where have my time and strength been flowing lately, and to whom? Trust: when pressure comes, do I put my weight on my own methods, or in God’s hand? You need not answer everything at once; answer one a day, and bring the answer into prayer.
Does “innocence” mean that Daniel had no sin at all?

No. The original זָכוּ (zakhu) is a courtroom word meaning that on this one accusation he was clear. Elsewhere Daniel often confessed his own sins and the people’s (see chapter 9). When he said this he was bearing witness to the king: before God and before the king I have done nothing to harm the king. So we need not read this verse as “the righteous do not suffer,” and we need not be afraid, because of our weaknesses, to say “in this matter I am clear.” Honesty is needed on both sides. Honestly admitting weakness does not diminish your witness; it makes people believe you more. His honesty made his witness stronger.
“Trust” and “faithful” share one root; what does that mean for us?

It means that faithfulness is not held up by gritting our teeth; it grows from trust. If you only think “I must be more faithful,” you will be very tired; if you think “I will trust more in the God who is trustworthy,” you will find that faithfulness is a natural result. So when you feel you are not faithful enough, you can first ask: have I put my weight in a place that cannot bear it? Then slowly move it into God’s hand. Once a week, look back and see where you put your weight most steadily. You need not change all at once; just move your weight a little toward God each day.
IV. The Mouth of the Den, Dawn, and Two Endings (6:16–28)

Daniel was thrown into the den. The text does not describe his reaction; it records only the king’s sentence: “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.” This sentence is a little like comfort, and more like a man with no assurance grasping, at the last moment, at the one hope left. Notice that word: continually. What the king saw was not one brave moment of Daniel’s but his long years. A person’s trust in a time of crisis is built up, day by day, in ordinary days. Then a stone was laid at the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and the signet of his nobles. This picture reminds us of another mouth of a tomb, another stone; we do not treat it as a type, we only say: it reminds us.

Then the king’s night: “passed the night fasting. No musical instruments were brought before him; and his sleep fled from him.” That night the king was less at peace than Daniel. Human power can seal a den, but it cannot seal a conscience. At dawn the next day the king went in haste to the den of lions and cried out in a troubled voice: “Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?” Look at his title for him: servant of the living God. He had not said that yesterday. One night of silence changed his title.

Then Daniel’s voice, and his first words: “O king, live forever!” A man who had just come out of the lions’ den did not blame, did not accuse, did not cry injustice; he first blessed the king who had thrown him in. When hurt, still blessing: this is one picture of selflessness. Then he gave his witness: “My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.” The one who shut the lions’ mouths was God, not his prayer and not his faith, but the angel God sent. The text says: “no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.” This sentence is not saying how great Daniel’s faith was, but that the One he trusted is trustworthy.

Finally, two endings. One is very heavy: the accusers, together with their wives and children, were thrown into the den. We cannot pretend this verse is not there. Ancient laws often punished whole families; the text describes and does not say it was good. Deuteronomy 24:16 says each man shall be put to death for his own sin. When we read this verse we are not celebrating and not making excuses for any violence; we only see that the one who used harming others as his means finally fell into the pit he dug himself, and that innocent family members were drawn in as well, which is the bitter fruit of sin.

The other is very glorious: King Darius sent a decree to all the earth: “men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end.” Do you remember chapter 4? Nebuchadnezzar’s decree said almost the same words. Two foreign kings bear witness to all the earth of the same God. The last verse: “So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” He outlived one empire, and then another. From the youth of chapter 1 he walked to here, a man who carried on as usual: resolving as usual, serving as usual, praying as usual.
Does the story of the lions’ den mean that as long as you pray, you will surely not be hurt?

No. In chapter 3 of the same book the three companions said: “But if not.” They might be saved or might not, but their faithfulness was not conditional on the result. Daniel’s rescue was God’s work, and we do not turn it into a formula. Many faithful people prayed and still suffered, even died as martyrs, and it was not because their faith was less. The hope of this chapter is that God is with us in the den, and that in the dark of night God was not asleep. So when we read this chapter we can say both “God is trustworthy” and “I will still hold fast.” We do not make promises on God’s behalf that he did not make, and we do not take away the comfort he has already given.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to teach Daniel’s prayer as “believers may break any government law at any time.” Daniel was faithful in serving the king in everything reasonable and gave way only on the one matter of “asking from God.” Acts 5:29 says, “We must obey God rather than men,” which is a line between obedience and apostasy, not a pass for defiance. We need to discern, not to make excuses.

The second deviation is to teach the punishment of the accusers’ wives and children in 6:24 as a retribution God delights in, or to use it to curse enemies. The text describes an ancient punishment that fell on whole families and does not say it was good; Deuteronomy 24:16 says each man shall be put to death for his own sin. We do not defend any violence, and we do not take this verse as material for revenge.

The third deviation is to teach Daniel’s rescue as “as long as you pray, you will surely not be hurt.” His rescue was God’s work; chapter 3’s “But if not” is in the same book. Some people prayed and still suffered, even died as martyrs, and it was not because they had less faith. Do not use this chapter to blame anyone who is suffering.

The fourth deviation is to teach “praying as usual” as a public performance, or to encourage public declarations in dangerous places. Daniel went back to his own house with his window open; he did not call a press conference. For brothers and sisters under persecution, we must protect people even more, and not make public any details that could be traced. Quiet is not weakness; protecting is also love.

The fifth deviation is to turn this chapter into a slogan of “fighting the world.” Daniel did not curse the king, did not criticize the system, and did not rally crowds; he simply carried on as usual. His witness began with a daily life no one could find fault with, went on to kneeling under pressure, and then to blessing when hurt. This is a different kind of power: not the power of confrontation, but a quiet, faithful power.
If I am in a setting where I cannot make my faith public, how do I “carry on as usual”?

Carrying on as usual is not necessarily public. Within safe limits you can keep your relationship with God: quiet prayer, thanksgiving in the heart, low-voiced intercession with trusted companions. Daniel’s window was open, but he was in his own house. You do not need to put yourself or others in danger to prove your faith. Protecting yourself and your brothers and sisters is wisdom; staying open to God in your heart is faithfulness. God sees, and God remembers. Your peace is that God is still with you, not that the situation is certainly safe. Protecting people is the gentlest application of this chapter.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to “going along.” Going along with the boss, with the family, with the circumstances; in a Chinese setting this is often a virtue and also a kind of wisdom. But after going along for a long time we slowly find that some things have been quietly adjusted: prayer time has been shortened, attendance on the Lord’s Day has dropped, and the thanks before a meal has become an embarrassed motion. This chapter does not ask us not to go along; it invites us to ask ourselves: in which things has my going along become a change? If one day a small rule made it cost you something to carry on as usual, what would you do?

The second question: we often say “keep a low profile,” and we are very afraid of “being talked about.” In this chapter Daniel was neither high-profile nor hiding. His way was to carry on as usual. This gives us a great insight: a low profile does not mean hiding your faith; a high profile does not mean courage. True courage is not changing your daily life because of other people’s eyes. You can stay faithful in quietness, and when needed, calmly state your position. The point is not the volume but the continuity.
What should I do if my family does not understand my praying, or even opposes it?

You can respect first, then persevere. First respect your family’s feelings, without criticizing or arguing; then, within what does not provoke conflict, find a fixed time and place, such as early morning, bedtime or a quiet corner, to meet with God. You can also, in your actions, love your family well first and let your daily life be a witness. If there is pressure, bring the matter to a trusted pastor or companion and pray together; do not carry it alone. Daniel’s way was to carry on as usual, not to confront. If you feel powerless, you can also ask a companion to keep a fixed time of prayer for you.
VII. Living Out 321: The Window Open Toward Him

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. Luke says Jesus came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives, and under the greatest pressure still returned to the Father and said: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” The Bible is my Standard, because a window toward Jerusalem comes from God’s word and God’s promise, not from emotion. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because under pressure we do not need more willpower; what we need is a Spirit who is with us, so that I can still kneel.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that before any law, rule or unwritten rule, I still return to him first. Let Jesus receive all the glory means that when we are rescued, we say: God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths; it was not my faith and not my cleverness. The one purpose: to build God’s system. In every kingdom there are people whose windows are open toward him; they are not confronting and not performing, only carrying on as usual. People like this, reminding one another, become a silent but firm witness.

Changing our mindset changes our life: when we think “my circumstances decide my worship,” our life is pushed along by circumstances; when we know “God is the reason I worship,” our life has roots. From self to selflessness: the person with self says “first I protect myself, then I talk about worship,” and the selfless person says “first I return into his presence, and I leave the rest in his hand.”
How do we concretely practice “as usual” in everyday life?

You can begin with a fixed time and place, for example after getting up each morning or before bed each night, and prepare a “window” for yourself: a small, fixed place to meet with God. Add a very small ritual, such as first saying one sentence of thanks and then one sentence of request. When pressure comes, do not make it harder and do not suddenly stop; just keep the smallest session. A month later you will find that this small habit has become your steady strength. A month later you will see that this small place has shielded you from many unnecessary shakings.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, One Window

The proud type says, “I must let people see my faith, or else it is weakness.” This motive may come from courage, but it may also be mixed with wanting to be seen. Daniel did not call a press conference; he simply carried on as usual. You can ask yourself: am I doing this to be seen, or for God?

The fearful type says, “I’m afraid that if I pray as usual, I will lose my job, my relationships, even my safety.” This fear is real. This chapter does not say there is no danger; it says God is in the den, and God is at dawn. If your situation is truly dangerous, please first protect yourself and others, and stay open to God in your heart; this too is carrying on as usual.

The ashamed type says, “I have already changed my habits; I have no right to go back.” Your window can be opened again. God is not counting how many days you closed it; he is at the window, waiting for you to come back. Today is the first time.

The wounded type says, “I was hurt because of my faith; I dare not carry on as usual again.” That wound is real. Please first find a safe person for yourself and tell your story. Do not force yourself to go back to the way things were all at once; you can begin with the smallest session, and God does not hurry you.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day at a fixed time and place, pray and give thanks quietly for five minutes, not shortening it because of busyness or circumstances.
Second, write down the most recent spiritual habit you changed because you feared trouble, and write down one smallest step to restore it.
Third, find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: as usual; no showing off, no comparing.
Fourth, for someone who has hurt you, say one word of blessing each day, without needing him to know.
Fifth, in the setting where you are, do one unnoticed daily thing that no one can find fault with, so that your witness builds up in ordinary days.
I declare: my window is open toward God; I will pray as usual and give thanks as usual.
I declare: the one who shut the lions’ mouths was the angel God sent; my safety is in his hand.
I declare: when I am hurt, I can still bless.
I declare: God is the living God, and his kingdom will not be destroyed; no law or pressure will take my worship from me.

Daniel chapter 6 begins with a daily life no one could find fault with and ends with a decree sent to all the earth. A law made for one man, a window open toward Jerusalem, a sealed den, a dawn. What this chapter gives us is not a story about courage but a story about continuance: one man who, under pressure, carried on as before.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that window. Today, is your window open, or closed? The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, and he is also the Lord who, in Gethsemane, went as usual to the place where he prayed. The focus is not how brave I am and not how dangerous my circumstances are, but the living God.
May God make us carry on as usual under pressure, and still bless when hurt; until his kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 6:10 says Daniel did it “as he did before.” Do you have a spiritual habit that you keep every day? Please name one, and say whether you have changed it recently because of pressure.
2. ★★ The decree in 6:7 did not mention Daniel’s name, yet it made his daily life illegal. Is there a similar pressure or rule in your life? Please say it in one sentence.
3. ★★ When someone calls you one of “the exiles” or an “outsider,” what is your first reaction inside? Please tell about the most recent time you were labeled.
4. ★★★ Think quietly about one thing: what is it you are most afraid of losing by worshiping as usual? Now write it down, and write down the one sentence you most want to say to God.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 6:10 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches being excluded, being misunderstood and faith under pressure; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not ask for the place or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record any traceable information, and check on them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 6:4 says the enemies could find nothing to hold against Daniel. Is there a place where your daily life can be one no one can find fault with? Please give an example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 6:22. Which phrase is God speaking to you: “sent his angel,” “shut the lions’ mouths,” or “innocence”? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 In 6:21 Daniel blesses the king first. What difference does this make to the person who has hurt you and whom you face now?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Say to the person next to you, “My window is open toward God,” and name one thing you want to keep doing as usual. Just one sentence; no need to explain.
9. ★★★ 【Do】 This week, at what time and in what place will you keep one fixed prayer? Please say the time, the place and the person.

Leader’s reminder: Go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Step】, and leave enough time for each step. At 【Say】, ask only for one sentence, one name, one time, with no need to tell stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort, do not press for details, do not say to a person who is weeping, “You need to have faith,” look after them privately after the meeting, and help them find professional support if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Is there someone among your family or colleagues who is under pressure because of faith? Please say his or her name, and decide to take the initiative to pray for him once this month.
11. ★★ Is there something in your church or group that, because of circumstances or pressure, has quietly changed from what it was? Please say what it is, and where you could start.

12. ★★ Is there an occasion where you dare not say “let me pray first” because you fear trouble? Please name the person or the occasion, and decide that this week you will say it calmly in one sentence.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “God is with you in the den.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not discuss anyone’s political position in the group or draw conclusions about any regime, and do not use 6:24 to comment on anyone’s family. If someone shares his wounds, long-term fear or the experience of losing a loved one, do not press for details and do not ask for forgiveness; check on him privately after the meeting.

Let everyone gently close their eyes and place before God the one thing written down today. Read 6:10 together: three times a day he knelt on his knees before his God, prayed and gave thanks, as he did before.

The leader prays for each person: God, teach us under pressure still to carry on as usual, and when hurt still to bless; and let us take that step in the ordinary days of this week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will do this week?”

7.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 7 · Daniel Chapter 7
7.title: The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man—Beasts, Thrones, Son of Man
blocks: I. The Four Winds of Heaven and the Beasts from the Sea (7:1–8)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Have you ever been jolted awake in the middle of the night by a dream? Your heart racing, your palms sweating, you sit on the edge of the bed and tell yourself: it was only a dream. But the picture is still there. Today we read a dream that frightened even Daniel. The six chapters before were his story in other people’s courts; from chapter 7 on, it is the vision he himself saw, in bed.

The text says: “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon Daniel had a dream and visions of his head on his bed. Then he wrote the dream and told the sum of the matters.” Notice this act: he wrote the dream down. Not to frighten people, but to leave it for those who would come after. So this chapter was written for us. Then the vision begins: “I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea.” In the Bible the sea is often a symbol of unrest and surging, the place where the nations churn. But look: whose wind is it? Heaven’s wind. Even the chaos of the sea has a hand above it.

Then four great animals came up from the sea. Notice the direction: not coming down from heaven but growing out of chaos. The first was like a lion with eagle’s wings, the king of beasts joined to the king of birds, how majestic. But the text goes on: “I watched until its wings were plucked, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made to stand on two feet as a man. A man’s heart was given to it.” Wings plucked, made to stand, given a man’s heart. Is this picture familiar? In chapter 4, an exalted king was brought low and then given a man’s heart. And look: these verbs are all passive: plucked, lifted up, given. Even a beast is treated this way; how much more a man. This means we need not put all our eyes on the beast’s teeth.

The second was like a bear, with three ribs in its mouth between its teeth, and “they said this to it: ‘Arise! Devour much flesh!’” Even the command to devour was spoken by someone. The third was like a leopard, with four wings and four heads, “and dominion was given to it.” Given: it too was given. Its speed was not its own ability. Do you hear it? Not one of the four beasts seized its own power. This is the first reminder this chapter gives us: even the fiercest power is permitted.

The fourth does not even have a name, because no animal can be compared to it: “awesome and powerful, and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth. It devoured and broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet,” and it had ten horns. Then another horn came up, a little one, “in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.” About these beasts and this horn there have long been various views; we set them side by side in the issues, without charting a timetable and without identifying anyone today. What the text wants us to see is the feature: it speaks big words. Have you ever met in life a voice so loud that it seems no one can answer it? This dream wants to tell you: the mouth that speaks big words will not have the last word. Such voices often appear not only in the dark; they may appear in an office, in a family, even in a church meeting. So today we are not here to match verses to people and look for who the little horn is; we first ask: in my own words, is there a bit of big talk meant to prop myself up?
All four beasts are “given”; how does this help me face pressure?

It helps this way: you need not see pressure as a power with no limit and no master. The text uses passive verbs to tell us: wings plucked, a man’s heart given, dominion given, and even the command to devour has a source. This does not say the pressure does not hurt, and does not say oppression is good; it says it is not the last word. When you face a very great power, you can first ask: who is permitting it? Does it have a limit? Asking this slowly turns trembling into quiet prayer. You can also write in a journal one power that frightens you now, and beside it one sentence: this is permitted, and it has a limit. After writing this a few times, you will find that a distance slowly appears inside you.
II. The Throne Is Set Up, and the Books Are Opened (7:9–12)

The rhythm of the text changes at verse 9. Before, it was one beast after another; now it is one sentence: “I watched until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat.” No clamor, no army, only a throne, quietly set up. The beasts are busy scrambling for position; in heaven a place was long since prepared.

The one sitting on it is the Ancient of Days, literally “the aged of days.” This is not the old of decline but the old of one who was there before all days. The beasts before were all newcomers; he is the one who has always been. “His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.” This is purity and also holiness, so holy that no one dares look at it. Then the numbers: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him. Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.” These numbers are not for you to count but for you to feel: in heaven there is an order we cannot see, larger than all the armies of earth.

Then the most comforting words of this passage: “The judgment was set. The books were opened.” Judgment is carried out seated, unalarmed, unhurried. The books are opened, and nothing is missed. Have you ever been wronged? Have you ever seen something that no one dealt with? Have you ever thought: is this just going to be left like this? This verse is speaking to you. It is not meant to frighten you but so that you can let go, and hand the matter of revenge to the One who sits.

Verses 11 and 12 speak of the end: “the animal was slain” because of “the voice of the great words which the horn spoke.” You see, the little horn’s greatest power was its mouth, and its end came because of its mouth. As for the rest of the beasts, “their dominion was taken away; yet their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.” Here is a gentle detail: the other beasts had their dominion taken away, yet their lives were prolonged. God’s judgment has measure. Even the season and the time were not set by them. This passage changes history’s end from a free-for-all into a throne that was set up. So when the world feels chaotic, you can first place one picture in your heart: a throne has been set up; someone has already sat down. Your prayer is not speaking into thin air; it is spoken to the One who sits.
Will the picture of “judgment” make me more afraid, not more at rest?

It depends on which side you read from. The picture of the text is: the Judge sits, the books are opened, the mouth of evil is stopped, and the wronged are vindicated. For the oppressed this is rest; for someone with a debt on his heart it is an invitation to come back into the light. We need not turn this scene into a threat, and we need not use it to find excuses for our own revenge. What you can do is bring your wrongs and your debts before the One who sits, and say: please deal with this, and have mercy on me. If you have a very concrete debt in your heart, do not put it off; today in quiet, tell God about it sentence by sentence; and if you need to apologize to someone, take one small step this week.
III. Light from the Original: One Like a Man, the Saints, Given (7:13–14, 18, 27)

The original of this chapter has three groups of words worth reading slowly. The first is “one like a son of man,” Aramaic כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ (kevar enash). “Son of man” is literally “son of a man,” and in Aramaic it very often means simply “a human being”; with “like” in front it is “one like a human being.” Set it against what came before: the beasts were “like a lion,” “like a bear,” “like a leopard,” and this one is “like a man.” Human kingdoms in history have often been beastly; the kingdom God establishes has a human face.

The second is “brought near.” Aramaic הַקְרְבוּהִי (haqrevuhi) means “was brought near.” He did not walk up to the throne by himself; he was brought before the Ancient of Days. Then “dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom”; that verb is the same kind of passive as the beast’s “dominion was given to it.” The beast devours; the son of man receives. The beast seizes; the son of man is entrusted. The true kingdom is not taken by force; it is entrusted.

The third is “serve” and “receive.” Aramaic פְּלַח (pelach, to serve): in chapter 3 everyone was commanded to serve the golden image; in this chapter “all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.” The same words, two kingdoms: one forced, one truly worthy. And “receive,” Aramaic קַבֵּל (qabbel): in 7:18, “the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom,” is the same verb as Darius “received the kingdom” in chapter 5. The kingdom is something received.

These three groups of words together are the route of this chapter: like a man, brought near, given. You can ask yourself: do I often try to get a position by seizing, by big words, by my own strength? God’s way of giving to us is receiving. This is an honest question: it is not that we do not need a place, but that we need to discern which places God gave and which I grabbed for myself.
How does the title “Son of Man” connect to Jesus in the New Testament?

The New Testament makes the connection. At his trial Jesus said to the high priest: “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming on the clouds of the sky.” Many see here a link to Daniel 7:13. We follow the New Testament in saying so, and we also respect the different readings that have long existed, as an individual, as a representative of the saints, or as both, which are set side by side in the issues. We do not set the son of man against the saints: Jesus is King, and he also makes those who belong to him receive the kingdom. Reading it this way lets us see him more, and also see ourselves more as those who are given. So when someone asks you, “Who is the son of man?”, you need not hurry to give one only answer; you can say: I see this one brought to God and given the kingdom; and I too am among those who are given.
IV. One Like a Son of Man, and the Saints Receive the Kingdom (7:13–28)

We come to the high point of the whole book. “I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.” Before, beasts came up from the sea; now one like a man comes with the clouds of heaven. The kingdoms of the beasts rise and fall; this kingdom is everlasting and will not pass away. This joins in one line with the words of chapters 2, 4 and 6. These words give everyone in a troubled age a steady direction.

Then what about Daniel? The text says: “my spirit was grieved within my body, and the visions of my head troubled me.” A man who did not waver in the lions’ den this time was frightened by a dream. Faith is not the absence of feeling. But he did one thing: “I came near to one of those who stood by, and asked him the truth concerning all this.” He did not pretend to understand and did not guess by himself; he came near and asked. The thing you fear most can also be brought before God in this way. This is what real faith looks like.

The attendant’s explanation was short: “These great animals, which are four, are four kings, who will arise out of the earth. But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.” The word “But” is the turn of the whole explanation: before, beasts that rise; after, an everlasting kingdom. The saints’ receiving the kingdom is also a receiving. The people you belong to may be very small in the world’s eyes, but the text says they will receive the kingdom. This is not a hope with pride in it but a hope with humility: we receive the kingdom not because we are strong but because the kingdom is given.

What Daniel most wanted to know was the fourth beast, because that one was the hardest to face. He was honest; you do not need to pretend you are not afraid. The attendant said this king “will speak words against the Most High, and will wear out the saints of the Most High. He will plan to change the times and the law; and they will be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.” All three actions put God somewhere else: speaking big words belittles God; wearing out the saints attacks those who belong to God; changing the times and the law means rewriting the norms God has set. “A time and times and half a time” is in the original “a time, two times, and half a time”; we do not decide its length for it, and we do not count days; what we see is the direction: the saints given into his hand is limited, bounded, and has an end.

Notice this turn: “until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.” What you have suffered was not suffered in vain; what you are waiting for is not something you will wait for in vain. The text does not say which day, so we do not count. And finally: “But the judgment will be set, and they will take away his dominion, to consume and to destroy it to the end. The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High.” All the kingdoms of the earth will in the end be handed to those who never scrambled for them. It is the gentlest and also the most subversive sentence.

Then Daniel: “my thoughts much troubled me, and my face was changed in me; but I kept the matter in my heart.” He was still alarmed; he did not hurry to explain and did not hurry to proclaim; he first kept it. Some words, when God gives them to us, are not to be spoken at once but to be kept in the heart first, so that they change us. When we cannot yet fully understand, we can first keep it, and go on being faithful. This is something we can practice every day: take one thing received today, do not rush to say it, keep it in the heart first, and in prayer let God slowly make it clear to us.
If the saints are “overcome,” is the hope of receiving the kingdom empty?

No. 7:21 says plainly that this horn made war with the saints and prevailed against them; the text is honest and does not say believers are never hurt. But then comes “until”: until the Ancient of Days came and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. The hope is not that suffering is removed right now, but that suffering has a limit, and that One who sits in judgment is watching. For those who are suffering this is comfort; for those who are not it is a reminder: do not make light of, or make use of, someone else’s suffering. Remember also that this hope is a hope held with patience: you need not deny pain, and need not force yourself to look strong; you only need, in the pain, to keep an open heart toward the One who sits in judgment.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to match the four beasts one by one to certain nations or organizations of today, and set out a timetable. The four beasts have long been read in different ways, and these notes set them side by side without charting a schedule. The point of this chapter is “given and judged,” not to make people count days.

The second deviation is to identify the little horn with a person or regime of today and call him the antichrist. The text describes features: speaking big words, wearing out the saints, planning to change the times and the law, and names no one of today. Identifying someone makes the congregation panic and also hurts the innocent. The fruit of this chapter is patience, not panic.

The third deviation is to teach “one like a son of man” as having only one acceptable answer, belittling other readings, or setting the son of man against the saints. The son of man and the saints have long been read as individual, as collective, and as both; in the New Testament Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, and we see the connection while respecting each view.

The fourth deviation is to teach “the saints will receive the kingdom” as “believers will surely win and not be hurt.” 7:21 says plainly that this horn made war with the saints and prevailed against them; receiving the kingdom comes after the judgment and is given, not an exemption from suffering right now.

The fifth deviation is to use the theme of judgment to frighten people, or to find excuses for our own revenge. The Judge sits to give judgment, and the books are opened; our responsibility is to hand the matter to him, not to pick up the sword ourselves.
How should I respond when someone is keen to use this chapter to chart a “timetable of the last days”?

You can first affirm his zeal for God’s word, and then gently return to the purpose of the text. This chapter says plainly that the description of the four beasts and the little horn is so that the saints would know: power is given and will be judged, and the kingdom will be given to the saints of the Most High. The text gives no date and does not ask anyone to count. You can ask him: does this way of arranging things make you love the Lord more and be more patient, or more anxious and more eager to persuade others? If the latter, it is time to return to the text. Finally, one reminder: discussion can have warmth, but should not have winners and losers. If you can accompany the other person back to the text, and back to loving the Lord and loving others, that conversation is already a very good witness.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to “those who read the times are wise.” Facing a very great power, we have learned to watch which way the wind blows, not to stick our necks out, and to protect ourselves first; in a Chinese setting this is often a wisdom, and also the experience of long years of protecting family. This chapter does not ask us to be reckless, and does not ask us to confront; it asks us to see that the wind is heaven’s wind and the throne is set up. You can be cautious, you can be quiet, but you need not let “the way things are going” become your god.

The second question: we often say “bear it for a moment and the waves will calm,” and we are used to swallowing a wrong. Some people carry the pain for years because of it; some finally explode in revenge. This chapter gives a third way: the books are opened, and the Judge sits. Handing the wrong to him is neither suppression nor revenge but speaking it honestly, and then letting go, into his hand. If the matter involves harm or violence, please also find safe people and professional help, and do not carry it alone.
I am used to “bearing it”; how is that different from “handing the wrong to God”?

“Bearing it” is often swallowing the words and going on hurting; “handing it to God” is saying the words out loud, to the One who will listen. The difference is whether there is someone to say them to. Each day you can use three sentences to tell God: how this hurt me, how I want to deal with it, and now I hand it to you. When needed, find a reliable person or a counselor to walk with you. Handing it over does not mean the matter is not important; it means you no longer use your own strength to carry a judgment that was never yours to carry. Also, if you are in a setting where you cannot speak, you need not force yourself to hand it over by speaking; writing it down, praying, or talking with a safe person are all possible ways.
VII. Living Out 321: The Throne Has Been Set Up

The three foundations: Jesus is my Role Model. Jesus called himself the Son of Man and said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve”; he gains the kingdom not by devouring but in the form of a servant. The Bible is my Standard, because our attitude toward the four beasts, the little horn and the son of man does not rest on guessing but only on what the text itself says: given, judged, the kingdom given to the saints. The Holy Spirit is my Guide, because before great powers we do not need more panic; we need a Spirit who is with us, so that I can be quiet and still be faithful.

The two core values: Let Jesus be King means that before all big words and pressure we still keep our focus on the throne, acknowledging that the kingdom, dominion and glory are all given. Let Jesus receive all the glory means that when we receive the kingdom, we do not say it is our merit but say: he gave it. The one purpose: to build God’s system. The saints of the Most High do not scramble but receive; in the chaos they remind one another: the throne has been set up, and the kingdom will surely be given.

Changing our mindset changes our life: when we think “power decides everything,” our life is chased by the teeth of the beasts; when we know “the throne has been set up,” our life has rest. From self to selflessness: the person with self props himself up with big words and power; the selfless person sets down power, returns to his place, and lets man be man and God be God. This is not a slogan but a daily practice of returning to one’s place: today, have I handed over what is not mine?
How do “selflessness” and “seeing the throne” connect?

They connect this way: someone who sees the throne no longer needs to be a throne himself. People with self are often afraid: afraid of being crushed, afraid of being overlooked, so they prop themselves up with big words and control. To see the throne is to see that someone is seated and someone is in charge; I can return to my place, do what I should, and hand over what is not mine. Then selflessness is not losing myself but no longer spending strength to hold a position that does not belong to me. A very simple practice: every night before sleep, ask yourself two questions: today, was there something I tried to prop up? What can I hand over? Then, in bed, say it in one sentence.
VIII. Four Kinds of Hearts, One Throne

The proud type says, “I will use big words and bearing to let people know I am not to be trifled with.” This heart may also be afraid of being looked down on. The text reminds us: the mouth that speaks great things is finally stopped by judgment. You can ask yourself: are my words propping myself up, or serving others?

The fearful type says, “The power before me is too great; I dare not speak, and I dare not believe.” This fear is real; even Daniel was alarmed. Please, like him, come near and ask; bring the thing you fear most before the throne. If your situation is truly dangerous, first protect yourself and others, and still stay open to God in your heart.

The ashamed type says, “What I have done in the past, if the books were opened, how could I face it?” Please remember that the One who opens the books is also the One who gives the kingdom to one like a son of man. You can honestly bring your debts before him, asking for mercy and for cleansing, instead of hiding.

The wounded type says, “I have been deeply hurt, no one has vindicated me, and I dare not trust again.” That wound is real. The text does not ask you to pretend nothing happened; it says: one sat, and the books were opened. Please first find a safe person for yourself and tell your story; do not ask yourself to forgive at once, and do not force yourself to have faith at once. God does not hurry you.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, every day spend five minutes bringing one power that frightens you before God, saying only: the wind is heaven’s wind, and the throne has been set up.
Second, write down the most recent sentence that made you shrink or made you want to speak big words, and write down one small step back to your own place.
Third, find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one phrase: the throne is set up; no comparing, no showing off.
Fourth, take one revenge, accusation or worry you cannot give away, hand it in one prayer to the One who sits in judgment, and do not bring it up again.
Fifth, in the setting where you are, do one small, faithful thing that does not grab for power or speak big words, so that your witness builds up in ordinary days.
I declare: the wind is heaven’s wind; the throne has been set up; I need not be chased by the teeth of any beast.
I declare: I will not prop myself up with big words; I return to my place, letting man be man and God be God.
I declare: the books are opened, and I can hand my wrongs and my debts to the One who sits in judgment.
I declare: the kingdom is given, not seized; I will receive it and be faithful, until Jesus reigns as King.
How can I make “the books are opened” a daily practice, and not a distant picture?

You can use five minutes in the evening. For the first minute, be still and say: Lord, you are seated. Then say out loud the heaviest thing of the day, whether what someone did to you or what you did to someone. Then in one sentence hand it over: this matter, I give to you. Finally, if there is an apology or reconciliation needed, write down one small step for tomorrow. Done this way, the books are no longer carried by you alone but placed each day before the One who sits. You can do it slowly, not all at once; even if you only get halfway, God sees, and encourages you to come again tomorrow. That is enough.

Daniel chapter 7 begins with a dream in the night: four beasts in the sea, and in the end a throne quietly set up; one like a son of man is brought before him and given the kingdom; the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom forever. The teeth of the beasts are real; the throne is real too. What this chapter gives us is not more guessing about the beasts but more trust in the throne.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to that night. What do you fear most right now? Perhaps a very great power, perhaps a big word that keeps ringing, perhaps a question you dare not ask. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our Role Model, he is our King, he is the Lord who was brought before the Ancient of Days and given the kingdom, and who also makes those who belong to him receive the kingdom. The focus is not how great the beasts are and not how afraid I am, but the God who sits.

May God let us see the throne in the chaos; when we do not understand, keep the matter in the heart and go on being faithful; until his kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 7:2 says the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea. Is there a situation in your life now like “wind rising on the sea”? Please say it in one sentence.
2. ★★ 7:1 says Daniel wrote this dream down. Is there a “dream” or worry that you dare not say aloud but need to tell God? Please say it in one sentence.
3. ★★ The little horn of 7:8 had eyes and a mouth speaking great things. Have you met a very loud voice that made you dare not answer? Please say in what kind of setting, with no need for details.
4. ★★★ Think quietly about one thing: that power you fear most, if it were only “given,” how would your heart be different? Please write one sentence to God.

Leader’s reminder: Please first read 7:9 and 7:10 quietly, and then begin. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches oppression, fear and wrongs; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not ask for the place or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record any traceable information, and check on them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ 【See】 The beasts of 7:4–6 had wings, a man’s heart and dominion, all given to them. In your life, have you seen a power that was “given”? Please give an example.
6. ★★ 【Hear】 Read 7:9–10. Which sentence is God speaking to you: thrones were placed, the books were opened, or he sat in judgment? Please say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ 【Think】 The one like a son of man in 7:13–14 was brought near and given. How does this change your view of “position” and “striving”?
8. ★★ 【Say】 Say to the person next to you: “The wind is heaven’s wind,” and name one thing you will hand over. Just one sentence; no need to explain.

9. ★★★ 【Do】 In 7:28 Daniel kept the matter in his heart. This week, what is one thing you do not yet understand that you will first keep in your heart while remaining faithful? Please name the matter and the time.

Leader’s reminder: go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Do】, leaving enough time for each step. At 【Say】, only one sentence, one name, one time is needed; no story. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “you must have faith” to someone who is weeping; check on them privately after the meeting, and help them seek professional help if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Is there someone among your family or colleagues living under great pressure or fear? Please say his or her name, and decide to take the initiative to pray for him once this month.
11. ★★ Is there a “big word” or “the way things are going” in your church or group that makes everyone quietly afraid to speak the truth? Please say what it is, and where you could start.
12. ★★ Is there a wrong or a debt you have never handed over? Please name one, and decide that this week you will hand it over in one prayer.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear that “the throne has been set up.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s reminder: Please remind everyone especially: do not match the four beasts or the little horn to any country, regime or person in the group, and do not count days or chart a timetable. If someone shares his wounds, long-term fear or the experience of losing a loved one, do not press for details and do not ask for forgiveness; check on him privately after the meeting.
Let everyone gently close their eyes and place before God the one thing written down today. Read 7:9 together: I watched until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat.

The leader prays for each person: God, teach us to see the throne in the chaos; when we are wounded, to hand our wrongs to the One who sits; and let us take that step in the ordinary days of this week. Before the meeting ends, ask one another: “What is the one thing you will hand over this week?”

8.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 8 · Daniel Chapter 8
8.title: The Ram, the Goat, and the Little Horn—Sheep, Horn, Sanctuary
blocks: Peace, brothers and sisters. Have you ever, on some night, stared at the ceiling and asked one question: how long? How long will this illness last; how long will this unfairness last; how long will this prayer without an answer go on? In this lesson we read a very special picture: it is not only people who are asking; the holy ones in heaven are asking too. This is Daniel chapter 8.

First notice a change. From this chapter on, the language of the original returns from Aramaic to Hebrew. Why? There have long been different views, and we set them side by side in the issues rather than conclude here. You do not need to agree with any one of them in order to read this chapter. We can quietly see this much: the long section before spoke of the affairs of the nations, and now, speaking of the sanctuary, the holy people and the end, it uses the holy people’s own language.

The text says: “In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, even to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first.” Notice that verb: appeared. The vision appeared to him; he did not go looking for it. Then, in the vision, he was at Susa, by the river Ulai. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and there was a ram with two horns; both horns were high, and the later one was higher. “I saw the ram pushing westward, northward, and southward. No animals could stand before him. There wasn’t any who could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and magnified himself.”

Next came a male goat, from the west, crossing the whole earth, not touching the ground, with a notable horn between his eyes. He ran at the ram, broke its two horns, threw it to the ground and trampled it. Then again that sentence: there was none who could deliver the ram out of his hand. Before a great power people are helpless; this is true, and the text does not deceive you. But look at the next verse: “The male goat magnified himself exceedingly. When he was strong, the great horn was broken.” When he was strong, the great horn was broken. The highest point of power is often also the beginning of the turn.

Please remember the undercurrent of this chapter: magnifying oneself. This verb is used of the ram, of the male goat, of the little horn, and later of the little king. One word, four different subjects. It tells us that whichever power it is, as long as it forgets that it was given, it walks the same road and makes itself great. We heard this story in chapter 4: a king stood on the roof of his own palace and said, “Is not this what I have built?” This chapter is only the same story in the shape of different animals.

One more thing must be said plainly. Later in this chapter the text itself opens the symbols: the two-horned ram is Media and Persia; the male goat is Greece. This is one of the rare places where the text says it directly. So we follow what it says, without adding and without carelessly changing. As for the names of “the first king” and of the “four kingdoms,” the text does not give them, and we do not speak for it. The purpose is to give us steady footing as we read the vision: what the text says, we say; what it does not say, we do not say for it.
Why does “magnify himself” keep recurring in this chapter?

Because the text wants us to see that pride is a road, not one person. The ram, the male goat, the little horn and the little king have different names but the same action: making themselves great. This reminder is not only for distant powers; it is for each of us. When we have been given something, that is when we most easily forget that it was given. You can use this word to examine yourself: today, in which matter did I want to make myself great? Then put it back in God’s hand. You might also write in a journal the one thought today in which you most wanted to make yourself great, and beside it write one line: this was given. After practicing this a few times you will find that the strength clenched in your heart slowly loosens.
II. The Little Horn, the Sanctuary and the Question from Heaven (8:9–14)

Out of one of the four horns came a little horn. Notice: first “little,” and then it grew great toward the south, toward the east and toward “the glorious land.” In the Bible, “the glorious land” often means the land God promised to his people. The direction of this horn pointed to where God’s people were.

Then its three actions. First, it grew great to the host of heaven, cast some of the stars to the ground and trampled on them: it pulled the things of heaven down and put them under its feet. Second: “Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down.” This lays hands directly on God. Third, the sanctuary was cast down. For one person to carry off another’s home is one thing; to tear down the place where a people worship God is another, for that is where they meet with him.

Then the text says something very heavy: “The army was given over to it together with the continual burnt offering through disobedience. It cast down truth to the ground, and it did its pleasure and prospered.” “Was given over” is in the passive. The text does not say whose sin it was, and does not say that every suffering is because of someone’s sin. Please do not turn this verse into blame on those who suffer. What we see is only this: evil has a season of prospering. If you are watching someone who speaks big words, tears down God’s house, and seems impossible to stop, you are not the first to be confused. The text wrote this honestly.

About this little horn there have long been different readings. Many scholars think it refers to a king of the Greek period who defiled the sanctuary and abolished the continual burnt offering; some think the description also foreshadows a later figure; others stress that the text gives a pattern. We set the views side by side in the issues; we do not identify anyone today, and we do not set a timetable. What we see is its direction and its end.

Then I heard a voice from heaven: “Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, ‘How long will the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot be?’” Did you hear it? This question was not asked by Daniel; the holy one in heaven asked it. How many times in the Psalms the holy people cry like this: Yahweh, how long? This is not unbelief; it is an honest faith. If you have asked it, you need not feel weak because of it. Heaven has asked too. At this point, please pause, and quietly say your own “how long.” No need to dress it up, and no need for an answer.

The answer is a number: “To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.” The original counts evenings and mornings. This number has long been read in different ways, and we do not use it to count days. For the point of the answer is not the number but the second half: the sanctuary will be cleansed. The verb in the original is more like saying that the sanctuary is declared right again. This destruction has a limit: there is an evening, and there is also a morning. For someone in the dark of night this is a great comfort: the night is numbered. This is the hope we can hold in our hands: not a date, but a direction.
Does a question like “How long?” mean my faith is not enough?

No. The text itself records that the holy one in heaven asked how long the vision would last, and the Psalms are full of such prayers. An honest question brings the question to God; it does not bury it in the heart, and it does not leave him. Unbelief is no longer bringing the question to God, or turning to trust some other way out. You can take “how long?” as a prayer and say it together with your tears. God did not blame the holy one in heaven and will not blame you. He gives only a gentle answer: there is a morning. If you often have this question lately, you can also find a safe friend or a pastor and say it aloud, and let someone ask it with you. That too is a way of being raised up.
III. Light from the Original: Magnify Himself, Evenings and Mornings, Set Upright (8:4, 14, 18)

Three words in the original of this chapter deserve a slow reading. The first is “magnify himself,” Hebrew הִגְדִּיל (higdil). Its root is גָּדַל (gadal), “to become great”; in the causative form the verb means “to make himself great.” It appears four times, in 8:4, 8, 11 and 25: the ram, the male goat, the little horn and the little king. You can think of it as a stamp: whoever wants to make himself great is under this stamp. And in the prayer of Daniel in chapter 9 we will see another kind of “great”: God’s greatness.

The second is “evenings and mornings,” Hebrew עֶרֶב בֹּקֶר (erev boqer). Together these two words recall Genesis 1: there was evening and there was morning. The original does not say “days,” so whether the two thousand three hundred is 2,300 days or 1,150 days, with an offering each morning and evening, has long been read in different ways. We do not count days. What we see is the suggestion in this language: night was never the last word; after it comes morning.

The third is “set me upright,” Hebrew וַיַּעֲמִידֵנִי (vaya'amideni). Its root is עָמַד (amad), “to stand,” here in the causative form: “made me stand.” Do you remember 8:4? “No animals could stand before him”: the same root. This chapter has an undercurrent of standing. The ram could not stand; Daniel, asleep on the ground, was raised by a hand and stood where he had stood. We are able to stand not because we are strong but because we have been raised.

These three words together are the route of this chapter: those who make themselves great cannot stand; the one in the dark of night waits for the morning; the one who is frightened and asleep is raised up. You can ask yourself: which word am I in lately? Am I wanting to make myself great, waiting in the dark, or needing to be raised up? Today you might choose one of the three words as your prayer for this week.
How does the root “stand” help me live today?

It helps this way: you do not have to stand by your own strength. In this chapter the ones who cannot stand are the proud beasts, and the one who can stand is the one who was raised up. So when you feel you can hardly stand, do not blame yourself first; lift up your hands first and say: Lord, raise me up. Then do one small thing today: get up, wash, make one phone call. These small things are the first steps of someone who has been raised up. Your standing is not proof that you are strong; it is proof that he raised you. So you need not become the strongest person, only a person willing to be raised. Each morning, say first: Lord, raise me; and then begin your day.
How should I read the two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings so that I do not go astray?

You can read it this way. First, admit there are different readings, and do not treat one as the only one. Second, do not use it to calculate dates, and do not use it to endorse any event. Third, hold the text’s own point: this destruction has a limit, and the sanctuary will be vindicated. Fourth, let it change how you live today, not how you calculate tomorrow. Read this way you need not be an expert, and you will not fall into the pit of timetables; you will instead be quieter and more hopeful. The road the text gives is quiet: no arguing, no calculating, only holding this one point and bringing it into today’s prayer.
IV. Gabriel’s Explanation and the Man Who Was Sick for Some Days (8:15–27)

When Daniel had seen the vision, he “sought to understand.” This is a very good habit: having seen, he was not in a hurry to speak, nor in a hurry to worry; he wanted to understand. Then one with the appearance of a man stood before him, and at the same time a voice called: “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.” This is the first time in the whole Bible that an angel’s name appears. Gabriel means “mighty one of God.” Notice that a voice commanded him. Understanding is given; it is not something you squeeze out by hard thinking.

Then Daniel’s reaction: “So he came near where I stood; and when he came, I was frightened, and fell on my face; but he said to me, ‘Understand, son of man; for the vision belongs to the time of the end.’” Even Daniel was frightened. The angel called him “son of man,” the Hebrew form of address, meaning: you are a human being, a finite one. In Ezekiel, God addresses the prophet this way too. This is a different word and a different position from the one in chapter 7 who came with the clouds of the sky like a son of man; we do not mix the two together. This form of address is not praise but a reminder: you are only a man, so you need to be raised up.

Then the text says: “Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me, and set me upright.” Even before the most important revelation, a man falls asleep. And the first thing the angel did was not to blame him but to touch him and set him upright. Before, the ram could not stand; now Daniel is raised up by a hand. The first act of God’s messenger toward a weak man is to raise him up. Then the angel said: this belongs to the appointed time of the end. What was given to Daniel was understanding, not a schedule of days. This is an important order: first be raised, and only then have strength to stand; first be touched, and only then have strength to work.

At the end of his explanation the angel speaks of a king “of fierce face.” The text gives his features: understanding dark sentences, great in power but not by his own power, prospering in what he does, destroying the mighty ones and the holy people, magnifying himself in his heart, standing up against the prince of princes; “but he will be broken without hand.” This reminds us of the stone in chapter 2 that was cut out without hands. The text does not connect the two, and we say only that it reminds us: people cannot save people, but there is One who does not need human hands. Who this king is we set side by side in the views; we do not identify anyone today.

Finally the angel said: “seal up the vision.” Not because it is unimportant, but because the time has not yet come. Then comes the most ordinary and most comforting verse: “I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick for some days. Then I rose up, and did the king’s business. I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it.” Having seen the greatest vision, he was sick. Even spiritual people get sick. Then he rose up. This rising is something only one who has been raised up can do. Then he did the king’s business: he returned to his post. Even the one who saw did not understand it all. The practice this verse gives us is: when you do not understand, return to your post. So today, if you feel you do not understand, do not hurry to find answers; first return to your post and do well the one thing in front of you. That is a very good beginning.
Having seen so great a vision, why did Daniel still go back to the king’s business?

Because a vision is not meant to make people leave their posts but to make them more faithful at their posts. He saw suffering and the end, yet he did not resign, hide, or spread panic and preach it everywhere. He was sick, he rested, and then he rose and did the work in front of him. This is a very steady posture when we do not understand: not chasing the answer with our own strength, and not putting down today’s responsibility. Your post may be an office, a kitchen, a classroom or a hospital ward; doing it well is also worship. This is not passivity but a deeper faithfulness: you hand the outcome to God and finish today steadily.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to calculate the “two thousand three hundred” as calendar dates, or to match it to some event of today. The original has two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings, which has long been read in different ways; these notes set them side by side and do not count days. What the text wants us to see is that this destruction has a limit.

The second deviation is to identify the little horn or the little king as some figure or regime of today, calling him the antichrist. The text gives features and an end; it names no one today. Identifying someone makes the congregation panic and hurts the innocent. The fruit of this chapter is endurance, not panic.

The third deviation is to confuse the “son of man” of 8:17 with the “one like a son of man” of chapter 7. The former is Hebrew, addressing Daniel as a finite human being; the latter is Aramaic, describing the one who came with the clouds of the sky. The wording and the position of the two differ, and we do not force them together.

The fourth deviation is to turn the “through disobedience” of 8:12 into “people who suffer must have done something wrong.” The text does not say whose sin it was, and does not say that every suffering is because of someone’s sin. For the suffering we do not blame; we only accompany.

The fifth deviation is to use “seal up” as a reason to refuse to learn, or conversely to use our own guesses to add authority to this vision. “Seal up” says the time has not yet come; we need not understand it all now, and we need not pretend to.
What should I say to someone who is very sure and gives the exact date of the “two thousand three hundred days”?

You can first affirm his zeal for God’s word, then ask gently two questions. First, does the original say days, or evenings and mornings? Second, does this way of counting make you love the Lord more and be more patient, or become more anxious and more eager to persuade others? Then return to the purpose Gabriel gave: to make people understand, not to give a schedule of days. You need not argue and need not win; you can close with one sentence: what comforts me most in this chapter is that the night is numbered and the morning will come. And remember to stay gentle as you answer, so it does not turn into a debate; your aim is to bring him, and yourself, back to the purpose Gabriel gave: understanding, and hope.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are used to “calculating.” Calculating feng shui, calculating days, calculating luck, calculating the right time; in a Chinese setting this is often a search for a little security in the midst of unease. The two thousand three hundred of this chapter is easily taken up for calculating. But the text wants us to see that what God gives is understanding, not a schedule of days; the morning will come, not on a particular date. You can be quiet and patient; do not let “calculating” take the place of “trusting.”

The second question: we often “hold on.” However tired, we finish the work; however much it hurts, we say nothing; however little we understand, we pretend there is no problem. This holding on is a virtue, and also a burden. This chapter gives another posture: being raised up. Daniel was frightened, fell asleep, got sick, and then, raised by a hand, rose to do his work. You can let yourself be raised up first, and then return to your post. If your weariness or unease has lasted a long time, please find a safe person or professional help, and do not hold on alone.
I am used to “holding on.” How do I learn to “be raised up”?

You can start with small things. First, say it aloud: find someone reliable, or tell God, “I cannot hold on.” Second, rest. Being sick for some days was Daniel’s reality; you can give yourself a day, an afternoon. Third, accept help: let someone take one small thing from you. Fourth, return to your post with a lighter posture. Being raised up is not weakness; it is admitting: I am a man, a finite man, and he is the God who raises people. In this way your faithfulness will last longer than holding on. The process need not be finished at once; every small “being raised up” is God’s grace, and every one is a step toward being more like Jesus.
VII. Living Out 321: The Night Is Numbered, and the Lord Raises Me Up

Three foundations: Jesus is my example. He took Peter’s mother-in-law by the hand and raised her up, and he stretched out his hand and touched a leper, and said, “I will. Be made clean.” He is also the Lord who, when the disciples fell asleep, did not blame them but brought them back to prayer. The Bible is my standard: for “how long?” and “two thousand three hundred” we do not rely on guessing but on the point the text itself gives: there is a limit, and the sanctuary will be vindicated. The Holy Spirit is my guide: when we do not understand, we do not need more panic; we need a Spirit who is with us, to make me still and to stand me up.

Two cores: Let Jesus reign, which means handing the question “how long?” to him, not putting a schedule of days in place of trust in him, and, once raised up, returning to today’s duties and post. Let Jesus receive all the glory, which means saying, as we stand up: it was not that I am strong, it was that he raised me. One purpose: to build God’s system. This system is a people who have been raised up, who accompany one another when they do not understand, who do not frighten one another and do not set up schedules of days; each returns to his post and faithfully does the work in front of him.

Change the concept and the life changes: when we think “only if I know the days will I feel secure,” our life is pushed along by unease; when we know “the night is numbered, and the Lord raises me up,” our life has rest. From the self-life to the no-self life: the self-life uses calculating and holding on to prove itself; the no-self life lets go of calculating and lets go of holding on, lets God be God, and lets itself be one who is raised up. A life like this has nothing to prove and nothing to chase; it is quietly raised up, and quietly returns to its post.
