What does “being raised up” have to do with having no self?

The relationship is direct. A person with self always wants to stand by his own strength, so he fears falling and fears being seen to fall; a person without self admits that he will fall asleep, get sick and fail to understand, and admits that there is a hand that will raise him. Having no self does not mean becoming nothing; it means no longer using our own strength to hold up the look of standing very straight. When you learn to say, “Lord, raise me up,” you begin to enter the no-self life, and you find that standing because you were raised is steadier than standing by holding on. As you live this way, those around you will slowly be affected too: no longer pressing one another with calculating and holding on, but encouraging one another by raising up.
VIII. Four Kinds of Heart, One Touch

The proud type says: “I must know the days first, so I will not lose out.” This heart may also be afraid of being deceived, afraid of being left behind. The text reminds us that what was given to Daniel was understanding, not a schedule of days. You can ask yourself: do I want to know in order to love the Lord, or in order to beat others?

The fearful type says: “I am afraid that what this chapter says will happen to me.” This fear is real. Please remember that the end of this chapter is that the sanctuary will be vindicated, the night is numbered, and the first thing the angel did was to raise up. If your situation is truly dangerous, first protect yourself and others, and in your heart stay open to God.

The shame type says: “I do not understand, and I dare not ask, afraid others will think I am not spiritual enough.” Even Daniel said that no one understood its meaning. You may ask, and you may not understand. Shame is not a condition for entering this chapter. You can be quiet first, and then ask slowly.

The hurt type says: “I was once blamed: you suffer because you have sinned.” This wound is real. Please first find a safe person for yourself and tell your story. This chapter does not ask you to blame yourself; it says there is a hand that touches you and sets you upright. You do not have to have faith at once, and you do not have to forgive at once; God does not hurry you.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, each day be quiet for five minutes, say one “how long” to God, and then say only one sentence: please raise me up.
Second, write down one matter for which you are anxious to know the days or the outcome, and write down one small thing you can do today so that you are not trapped by that question.
Third, find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one sentence: the night is numbered; we pass on no schedule of days and do not frighten one another.
Fourth, on days when you do not understand, are very tired or are in pain, still do well the one task in front of you, for example going to work on time or caring for your family.
Fifth, when someone wants to use this chapter to set up a timetable, gently bring him back to the purpose Gabriel gave: to give understanding, not to cause panic.
I declare: the night is numbered, the morning will come, and I need not be bound by days I do not know.
I declare: I will not let calculating take the place of trust; I hand my “how long” to God.
I declare: when I am frightened and asleep, God’s messenger also touches me and sets me upright.
I declare: I may not understand, and still return to my post and faithfully do the work in front of me, until Jesus reigns.

Daniel chapter 8 begins with a vision: a ram, a male goat and a little horn, one verb, magnifying themselves. In the middle is the question from heaven: how long? The answer is a number with evenings and mornings in it. At the end is a man who was raised up, who was sick for some days, and then rose up and did the king’s business. What this chapter gives us is not a schedule of days but a gentle answer: the night is numbered, and the Lord raises me up.

Brothers and sisters, let us go back to that night. Which “how long” do you most want to ask now? Say it to God; no need to dress it up. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our example, he is our King, he is the Lord who stretches out his hand, touches people and raises them up. The focus is not whether I can calculate the days, nor how strong I am, but the God who raised me up.

Lord, may we, when we do not understand, still return to what we should do today; when we are frightened and asleep, be raised up by you; until your kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 8:13 says the holy one in heaven asked, “How long?” What was the “how long” you most often asked the adults when you were small? Do you still have a similar question now?
2. ★★ 8:1 says the vision “appeared” to Daniel. Is there something you very much want to understand but have not yet understood? Please say it in one sentence.
3. ★★ What is the one “how long” you most want to ask God now? Please say it in one sentence; no need to dress it up.
4. ★★★ In quiet, please think of one thing: if this night were “numbered,” what would be different in your heart? Please write one sentence to God.

Leader’s note: Please begin by quietly reading Daniel 8:13 and 8:14. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches illness, not understanding and long waiting; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not press for location or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record anything that could be traced, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ [See] 8:4, 8, 11 and 25 all use “magnify himself.” In life, have you seen an example of someone “wanting to make himself great”? Tell one, without naming anyone.
6. ★★ [Hear] Read 8:14 and 8:18. Which sentence does God say to you: “the sanctuary will be cleansed,” “he touched me,” or “set me upright”? Say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ [Think] 8:26 says to seal up the vision, because the time has not yet come. How does this change your need to “know the days”?
8. ★★ [Speak] Say one sentence to the person next to you: “The night is numbered, and the Lord raises me up,” and say the one thing you will hand over. Only one sentence; no explanation.
9. ★★★ [Do] In 8:27 Daniel was sick for some days, then rose up and did the king’s business. This week, what post or task will you return to? Please say the task and the time.

Leader’s reminder: go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Do】, leaving enough time for each step. At 【Say】, only one sentence, one name, one time is needed; no story. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “you must have faith” to someone who is weeping; check on them privately after the meeting, and help them seek professional help if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who is “holding on” and does not dare say he is tired? Please say the name, and decide to reach out to him once this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there anyone keen on using Scripture to set up a schedule of days? Please say how you could gently bring everyone back to the purpose of “giving understanding.”
12. ★★ Is there something you very much want to know “when it will get better”? Please say one, and decide this week to hand it over with one sentence of prayer.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear “the night is numbered, and the Lord raises me up.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s note: Please remind especially: in the group, do not match the little horn or the little king to any country, regime or person, and do not count days or set up timetables. If someone shares their own illness, long waiting, or the experience of being blamed with “you suffer because you have sinned,” do not press for details, do not ask them to forgive, and look after them privately after the meeting.
Please close your eyes gently and put before God the one “how long” you wrote down today. Read together Daniel 8:18: “he touched me, and set me upright.”

Let the leader pray for each person: Lord, teach us, when we do not understand, to be raised up by you; when we are frightened and asleep, to be touched by you; and in the ordinary days of this week, to return to our posts. Before dismissal, ask one another one sentence: “What is the one thing you will return to this week?”

9.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 9 · Daniel Chapter 9
9.title: Prayer and the Seventy Sevens—Book, Prayer, Seventy
blocks: I. Learning from the Books: Not Calculating but Praying (9:1–3)

Peace, brothers and sisters. If one day you read one of God’s promises, what is your first reaction? Do you take out a calculator and start to calculate, or do you kneel down? In this lesson we read of a man who read a promise and did not pick up a pen; he fasted, put on sackcloth and ashes, and turned his face to God. This is Daniel chapter 9, the chapter in the whole book most like a prayer book.

But this chapter does not begin with prayer; it begins with reading. The text says: “In the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet, for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years.” He was reading Jeremiah. In Jeremiah there are two places that speak of seventy years. He had read them. Please notice that what he read was “the books,” and in the original this is plural: the scrolls. By then God’s word had already been collected and was read over and over. He did not rely on dreams or on visions; by reading what God had already said, he understood the time. This gives us a very practical reminder: to understand God’s heart today, the steadiest road is also to return to what he has already said, reading it again and again, thinking it over again and again, and not running after fresh prophecies.

Then what did he do? An ordinary person who read “seventy years are fulfilled” might calculate the days, might get excited, might say: it is nearly time. Daniel did not. The text says: “I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.” He turned his face to God. This is the first lesson of this chapter: God’s promise is not for calculating; it is for praying.

Why? Because a promise is a word of relationship, not a timetable. When God said seventy years, he was not sending Daniel a countdown timer; he was saying: I remember you, and I will bring you back. When Daniel read this sentence, his reaction was: I must go and meet the God who is speaking. Is there a promise of God in your life that you have always wanted to calculate? Perhaps about a child, a job, the reconciliation of a family. Try, like Daniel, first putting down the abacus and turning your face to him. Such a turning needs a little courage, because calculating often gives us a feeling of control, while prayer needs us to let go.

As for fasting, sackcloth and ashes, these outward postures are not the goal; they are ways of putting the whole person down. Your body and your circumstances are not the same as Daniel’s, and you need not do exactly the same. What God looks at is the heart that turns its face to him.
When I read God’s promise, how do I avoid only “calculating,” and truly “pray”?

You can try three steps. First, copy that promise on paper, without adding any explanation of your own. Second, write down the urge to calculate too: “I want to know, when?” Third, put the two sheets before God and pray one sentence: Lord, I give you this promise, and my heart that wants to calculate. Doing this does not suppress your expectation; it lets expectation return to relationship. You will find that when the face is turned to God, waiting changes from anxiety to quiet. You can do this small practice once each morning, and a week later look back at your heart: has it slowly turned from calculating to relying?
II. We Have Sinned and Done Wrong; Righteousness Belongs to Him (9:4–14)

Then he opened his mouth: “I prayed to Yahweh my God, and made confession, and said, ‘Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments.’” Please notice this order: first praise, then confession. God is the one who keeps covenant and shows loving kindness; this is the foundation of the whole prayer. He was not confessing to a cold judge but to a covenant-keeping God. Before confession there is first loving kindness. If you feel you are not qualified to open your mouth, begin with this sentence: Lord, you keep covenant, you show loving kindness.

Then five verbs: “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even turning aside from your precepts and from your ordinances.” Please notice that every verb is “we.” Not one is “they.” This is not easy. Daniel is the most praised man in the whole book, and the text records no fault of his. Yet when he prayed he said “we.” This is the posture of an intercessor: he puts himself inside the people and does not stand outside pointing the finger. Have you ever prayed for a group you belong to, a family, a church, a country? When you prayed, did you say “they” or “we”? This “we” turned his prayer from the mouth of one man into the mouth of a people.

Then comes the hinge of this passage: “Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face”; and then, in verse 9: “To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him.” The sentence pattern is the same, and the content is turned over. Righteousness belongs to him; shame belongs to us; and mercies and forgiveness also belong to him. This sentence, placed in the middle of the confession, is the hinge of the whole prayer. Without it, confession would become only heavy self-blame.

Then he mentions the curse in the law of Moses, poured out on them. For many modern readers this is hard, and we talk about it in the issues. Daniel’s point is: he did not defend God or make excuses for him; he only said that God is righteous, and that all this is not that he broke the covenant but that we did. In verse 13 he adds a very deep word: “Yet we have not entreated the favor of Yahweh our God, that we should turn from our iniquities and have discernment in your truth.” The calamity had come, and they had not yet turned. True repentance begins with admitting, and also with believing that God is still willing to listen.

Please do not turn this passage into blame on those who suffer. This is Daniel, on behalf of the whole people, speaking a review of history before God. He himself was one of the exiles. If you are suffering, the text does not ask you to say “I deserved it”; it wants you to know that there is a God who is righteous and also merciful, and you may bring your pain, and your weakness, into his presence.
Will confessing with “we” make me responsible for other people’s sins?

No. “We” does not mean carrying others’ sin; it means not standing outside to judge. You are still responsible only for your own conduct, but before God you are willing to stand together with the family, church or country you belong to, and say: we need mercy. This is a kind of humility, and also a kind of love. You can open your mouth this way: Lord, our family has been wrong in this matter; I have a share in it too. Saying it this way is not self-blame but bringing the whole relationship before God so that he may heal it. You can also find a companion and open your mouths with “we” together, so that confession is no longer a lonely thing but two people walking together toward mercy.
III. Light from the Original: Confess, Cast Down, Greatly Beloved (9:4, 18, 23)

Three words in the original of this chapter deserve a slow reading. The first is “confess,” Hebrew וָאֶתְוַדֶּה (va'etvaddeh). This root יָדָה (yadah) in Hebrew means both “to give thanks” and “to confess.” Confession and praise are in the same root: admitting what we are, and admitting what God is. This is why Daniel’s confession begins with praise: great and dreadful, keeping covenant and showing loving kindness.

The second is “cast down,” Hebrew מַפִּילִים (mappilim). 9:18 says: “we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.” The WEB renders it “present”; the verb literally means “to cause to fall”: we cause our petitions to fall before you. Like putting down a heavy load. That load is shame, desolation, helplessness. He did not say, “Lord, look how repentant we are”; he said, “look at your mercy.”

The third is “greatly beloved,” Hebrew חֲמוּדוֹת (chamudot). Literally “desired, very precious.” Gabriel said to Daniel: “for you are greatly beloved.” This name appears three times in this book (9:23, 10:11, 10:19). Think about it: he was beloved before he prayed, not beloved because he prayed well. Prayer is not an exchange to earn love; it is speaking within love. This lets us say quietly: I do not open my mouth because I have done well enough; I dare to open my mouth because I am loved.

Together these three words are the route of this chapter: confession begins with praise; petition puts the load down; and the answer comes from the certainty of being “greatly beloved.” You can ask yourself: is my prayer trying to “exchange” something, or to “set something down”? Am I proving whether I am worthy, or admitting his mercy? Today, choose one of these three words as your prayer for this week: praise, setting down, or receiving being loved.
How do I actually “set the petition down”?

You can use a very simple action: put your hands palm up on your knees; then say the heaviest thing you have, as if pouring it out of your hands and setting it before God. Then close with one sentence: not because of my righteousness, but because of your mercy. No need to say much, and no need to say it beautifully. This action exchanges “I will prove” for “I will entrust.” You will find that the lightness after prayer is not because the matter is solved but because you no longer carry it alone. If it is hard for you to say, do not force it; you can start practicing with something very small. God does not hurry you; he waits for you.
Is “greatly beloved” said only to someone like Daniel?

Gabriel said it to Daniel, but this name was not because he was especially perfect; it is because God loves those whom he loves. The New Testament also tells us that in Christ we are called beloved children. You need not, because you feel you are not good enough, push this sentence off onto someone else. In today’s prayer you can try saying one sentence to yourself and to God: I am loved by you. This is not pride but a quiet, self-releasing trust. In other words, you need not first qualify in order to be loved; you are loved first, and then you learn how to respond. This order changes everything.
IV. The Word Has Gone Out; the Seventy Sevens (9:15–27)

Then the prayer enters its most moving stretch. He first remembers the exodus from Egypt: “who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have gotten yourself renown, as it is today.” In the darkest hour he first remembers what God has done. Then he says: “My God, turn your ear, and hear. Open your eyes, and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name; for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.” Please read this sentence slowly. Even prayer is not our merit. This is a very good order: first look back at what God has done, and then open your mouth about what God is to do now. Your prayer can begin this way too: think of one thing God has already done for you, say it, and then say your need.

Then three short cries: “Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do. Don’t defer, for your own sake.” Hear, forgive, act. The last ground is “for your own sake,” his name. The whole prayer moves from the people to God’s name. This is the steadiest place in prayer: what we ask is not our face but his name. If you have ever measured your prayer by “am I worthy?” this passage will set you free. You need not be worthy; you only need to set your petition down. This is a very deep freedom in prayer: no need to prove, no need to pretend, only to come.

Then the prayer was not yet finished. The text says: “while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me.” Gabriel arrived, not at the end of the prayer but in the middle of it. He said: “At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, and I have come to tell you; for you are greatly beloved.” Do you have a prayer that looks as if it has no answer yet? The text says the word has already gone out. He moves earlier than we do. And there is “the time of the evening offering”: the temple was gone, the evening offering had stopped, but Daniel still remembered that hour. He carried the altar into his own prayer. This teaches us a quiet waiting: not hurrying, not doubting, only believing he is already on the way.

Then the answer came: “Seventy weeks [literally, sevens] are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy.” This verse is the most studied in the whole book, and the one that most easily leads people to calculate days. Let us say plainly first: these notes do not count days and do not set up a timetable. There have long been many different readings, and we set them side by side in the issues.

We look at the direction of this verse. What Daniel prayed was: the seventy years are up; forgive, and let Jerusalem be desolate no more. God’s answer was a larger vision: the seventy years stretched into seventy sevens. Then six things were listed: to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make atonement for iniquity, these three about sin; to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up the vision, to anoint the most holy, these three about fulfillment. Not one of these six is military or political; all deal with sin and righteousness. God’s answer to Daniel was not a schedule of days but a promise that sin would be dealt with.

The last three verses are the hardest passage in the whole book: the Anointed One is cut off, desolation is decreed, and the end is decreed too. There have long been many readings; we set them side by side and set up no chart. We see only three things. First, the order of the text: first rebuilding, then the Anointed One is cut off, then destruction and war. Second, the word that recurs: desolation, which reminds us of chapter 8. Third, the last sentence: the one who destroys is, in the end, met by God’s wrath poured out. This passage is not meant to make people anxious but to say: desolation is decreed, yet desolation also has an end. So when you read a text this hard, you might pause first and return to that prayer, to that sentence: not because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.
Reading such a hard text as the seventy sevens, what should I do?

You need not be an expert to read this chapter. First, put the emphasis back on prayer: this is the answer to Daniel’s prayer. Second, hold the six things: sin is dealt with, and everlasting righteousness is brought in. Third, admit that there are different readings, and respect other brothers and sisters. Fourth, do not use it to calculate days, and do not use it to frighten people. You can say to yourself: I do not need to understand all of this verse; what I need is to trust more in the mercy of God who deals with sin. Then you have read this chapter rightly. Also, if in this process you feel anxiety rising, return to the simplest sentence: Lord, have mercy on me. That sentence is already enough.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to calculate the seventy sevens into dates, or to lay out a timetable of history and the end. The original says only “seventy sevens,” and does not say days, months or years; there have long been different readings, and these notes set them side by side and do not count days or set up a chart. The point of this verse is that sin and righteousness are dealt with.

The second deviation is to turn “the commandment went out” into: if only you pray, God will surely answer in our time and in our way. What the text says is that God’s word had gone out as the petitions began; it does not say that we can control the outcome; Daniel waited for God’s work, and still asked on the ground of mercy.

The third deviation is to turn “we have sinned” into condemning the victims, or to turn collective confession into blaming those who suffer. Daniel confesses before God on behalf of the people; he does not blame any individual who suffers. For the suffering we do not blame; we only accompany and show mercy.

The fourth deviation is to identify 9:26–27 as some figure or regime of today, or to call brothers and sisters who hold a different reading unbelieving. The Anointed One, the most holy, and the people of a prince have long been read in many ways, and these notes set them side by side; we identify no one today, and we respect the faithfulness of each tradition.

The fifth deviation is to turn “not for our righteousness” into “so I need not repent.” Daniel confesses through the whole chapter; mercy and repentance are not opposed but two sides of the same prayer.
Someone uses this chapter to “prove” a certain end-time timetable. How should I respond?

You can first listen, then return to the purpose the text itself gives. You can gently ask him three questions: does the original of this verse say “days”? Does this way of counting make you love the Lord more and be more patient? Are the six things the text gives not all dealing with sin and righteousness? Then share your own point: this chapter is the answer to a prayer, and its end is mercy. You need not win; you only need to bring the atmosphere from arguing back to reverence. Many times a quiet witness is stronger than a debate. Finally, remember that your aim is not to beat the other person but to let him see that a merciful God is still waiting for everyone.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to “merit” and “worthiness.” From childhood we learn that you must do good to have blessing, and be good enough to deserve help. So we naturally measure our prayer with the same ruler: am I spiritual enough today? I have made so many mistakes; will God still listen? This chapter gives another road: the petition is not for our righteousness but for his great mercy. You may be not good enough, and still come.

The second question: we are very afraid of “losing face,” and afraid of making others lose face. So we often do not say “we were wrong,” but say “they” or “those people,” or say nothing at all. Daniel confessed with “we,” his face covered with shame, and yet he did not hide from God. His prayer shows us that admitting is not the end of losing face but the beginning of healing. If you are in a setting where you cannot say publicly that you were wrong, first say it before God, and find a safe person to walk with you.
I am used to measuring myself by “worthy or not.” How do I change?

You can do one small practice each day. In the morning, do not ask “am I worthy today?” but ask “what shall I set down today?” Put shame, weariness and failure before God one by one, and say: not because of my righteousness, but because of your mercy. Then thank him in one sentence for accepting you. After a few weeks of practice you will find that your prayer is no longer an examination but an act of coming home. If this habit is too deeply rooted, you can also ask a pastor or counselor to walk with you. If this habit cannot be changed, you can also ask a pastor or counselor to walk with you; this is not weakness but wisdom.
VII. Living Out 321: For Your Own Sake, Do Not Delay

Three foundations: Jesus is my example. He taught us to pray, and also opened his mouth with “we”: “Our Father in heaven”; on the cross he spoke for others: “Father, forgive them.” The Bible is my standard, because for the seventy sevens we do not rely on guessing but on the point the text itself gives: this is the answer to a prayer, the dealing with sin and righteousness. The Holy Spirit is my guide, because in confession and petition we do not need more self-blame; we need a Spirit who is with us, to let us see God’s mercy and to make us willing to say “we.” A prayer like this and the prayer of Jesus go the same direction: may your name be kept holy.

Two cores: Let Jesus reign, which means bringing God’s promise to him in prayer, not letting calculating take the place of trust in him, and, in confession, not defending ourselves but looking only to his mercy. Let Jesus receive all the glory, which means that when the answer comes we say: it was not that I prayed well; it was his great mercy, for his own name. One purpose: to build God’s system. This system is a people who pray with “we”: not standing outside pointing the finger, but confessing together, interceding for one another, and placing the petition on God’s mercy.

Change the concept and the life changes: when we think “God responds because I am good enough,” our prayer is an examination; when we know “he responds because of his mercy and his name,” our prayer is a homecoming. From the self-life to the no-self life: the self-life props itself up with qualification and calculation; the no-self life puts down the abacus, puts down qualification, sets the petition down, and lets man be man and God be God.
What does “no self” have to do with “we confess”?

The relationship is deep. A person with self always wants to assign sin to others, or to clear himself; a person without self is willing, before God, to stand with others and admit that we need mercy. Confessing with “we” is putting down the position of “I am a good person, they are bad people” and returning to my place: I am a man, and I need mercy. This is not losing oneself but no longer using strength to keep up an untrue image. You can begin with a small thing: this week, in one conflict, first say one sentence: “I have a share in this too.” Sometimes one sentence, “I have a share in this too,” can loosen a tense relationship a little; this is the power of having no self, and the gift this chapter brings us.
VIII. Four Kinds of Heart, One Prayer

The proud type says: “I must first figure out this prophecy, so I will not be deceived and will not lose out.” This heart may also want to control, to not lose to others. Daniel prayed first; he did not calculate first. You can ask yourself: do I want to know in order to love the Lord, or in order to control?

The fearful type says: “This chapter is too hard, and it speaks of destruction and desolation; I am afraid.” This fear is real. Please remember that the end of this chapter is that God deals with sin and brings in everlasting righteousness; desolation is decreed, and the end is decreed too. You can first put your fear before God, sentence by sentence; you need not understand it all to be able to rest.

The shame type says: “I have made so many mistakes; I have no right to pray.” This is exactly what this chapter most wants to say to you: the petition is not for our righteousness but for his great mercy. You need not become good first and then come; you can come with your shame. Shame belongs to us; mercy belongs to him.

The hurt type says: “I was once told that I suffer because I have sinned.” This wound is real. Please first find a safe person for yourself and tell your story. This chapter does not ask you to blame yourself; it says there is a God who is righteous and also merciful. You do not have to have faith at once, and you do not have to forgive at once; God does not hurry you.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, each day spend five minutes reading one verse of God’s promise; do not calculate, only turn your face to him and say one sentence: have mercy, for your own name’s sake.
Second, write down one promise you want to “calculate,” and write one sentence of prayer you can say to God in place of that calculation.
Third, find a companion and agree once a week to pray together with “we” for a group you belong to, without blaming others.
Fourth, at a fixed time each day, like the “evening offering,” be quiet for five minutes and put the day’s burden before God.
Fifth, when someone wants to use this chapter to calculate days or set up a timetable, gently bring him back to prayer and mercy, so that people love the Lord more rather than become more anxious.
I declare: I do not take God’s promise to calculate; I take it to pray.
I declare: not because of my righteousness, but because of God’s great mercy, I set my petition down.
I declare: I pray with “we,” not standing outside pointing the finger, and not hiding from God’s face.
I declare: God’s word has already gone out as I open my mouth; I am greatly beloved, and I will wait quietly, until Jesus reigns.

Daniel chapter 9 begins with a man reading and ends with the promise of the seventy sevens. In the middle is a very long prayer: first praise, then confession with “we,” then the petition placed on God’s great mercy. Before the prayer was finished Gabriel flew to him and said: the commandment went out, for you are greatly beloved. What this chapter gives us is not a schedule of days but a gentle answer: sin is dealt with, everlasting righteousness is brought in, and you are loved.

Brothers and sisters, let us return to that moment: he read the seventy years and did not calculate; he turned his face to God. Is there a promise you have always wanted to calculate? Put down the abacus and turn your face to him. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our example, he is our King, he is the Lord who deals with sin for us and brings in righteousness. The focus is not whether I calculate accurately, nor whether I am worthy, but the God of great mercy.
Lord, teach us to take the promise to prayer; to confess with “we” and ask on the ground of mercy; and, when your word goes out, to wait quietly. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 9:2 says Daniel read the seventy years in the books. Which promise of God have you read lately that moved you especially? Please say it in one sentence.
2. ★★ 9:20 says Daniel confessed his own sin and the sin of the people as he prayed. When did you last admit “I have a share in this too,” and in what matter? Please say it in one sentence.
3. ★★ Is there a promise of God for which you have always wanted to “calculate” the time? Please say what it is; no need for details.
4. ★★★ In quiet, please think of one thing: if your petition did not need to be qualified, only set down, what would be different in your heart? Please write one sentence to God.

Leader’s note: Please begin by quietly reading Daniel 9:18. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches shame, guilt and prayers long unanswered; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not press for location or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record anything that could be traced, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ [See] In 9:5 Daniel confesses with “we.” When you pray for your family, church or country, do you usually say “they” or “we”? Please say about the most recent time.
6. ★★ [Hear] Read 9:18 and 9:23. Which sentence does God say to you: “for your great mercies’ sake,” “the commandment went out,” or “you are greatly beloved”? Say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ [Think] 9:24 says the seventy sevens are to deal with sin and righteousness. How does this change your need for a “schedule of days”?
8. ★★ [Speak] Say one sentence to the person next to you: “Not for my own righteousness, but for his mercy,” and say the one thing you will set down. Only one sentence; no explanation.
9. ★★★ [Do] In 9:21 Gabriel arrived in the midst of the prayer. This week, which prayer without an answer will you keep setting down? Please say the matter, the time and your companion.

Leader’s reminder: go in the order 【See】【Hear】【Think】【Say】【Do】, leaving enough time for each step. At 【Say】, only one sentence, one name, one time is needed; no story. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “you must have faith” to someone who is weeping; check on them privately after the meeting, and help them seek professional help if needed.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who feels “I am not good enough, not worthy to be loved”? Please say the name, and decide to pray for him once this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there a habit of using “they” to talk about problems? Please say what it is, and say where you could first change it to “we.”
12. ★★ Is there something for which you need to admit before God “I have a share in this too”? Please say one, and decide this week to say it in one sentence of prayer.

13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear “the petition is not for our righteousness but for God’s great mercy.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s note: Please remind especially: in the group, do not argue about how to calculate the seventy sevens, and do not match the Anointed One or the one who makes desolate to any person or regime. If someone shares their own guilt, being blamed with “you suffer because you have sinned,” or prayers long without an answer, do not press for details, do not ask them to forgive, and look after them privately after the meeting.

Please close your eyes gently and put before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read together Daniel 9:18: “we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.”

Let the leader pray for each person: Lord, teach us to take the promise to prayer; to confess with “we” and ask on the ground of mercy; and to take that one step in the ordinary days of this week. Before dismissal, ask one another one sentence: “What is the one thing you will set down this week?”

10.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 10 · Daniel Chapter 10
10.title: From the First Day You Set Your Heart to Understand—Hand, Prince, Spirit-Prince
blocks: I. Three Weeks of Mourning, and a Glory Only He Saw (10:1–9)

Peace, brothers and sisters. Have you ever mourned? Not over your own affairs but for others: for a child’s future, for the state of a church, for a place you love. In this lesson we read the mourning of an old man. He mourned three whole weeks, and then God’s answer came. This is Daniel chapter 10, and the beginning of the last vision of the whole book.

The text first gives the time: “the third year of Cyrus king of Persia.” Notice that this is already the Persian era; Babylon is past. But Daniel is still here. His name is still called Belteshazzar, the name Babylon gave, which has followed him all along. But in this chapter he is still Daniel. The text says: “the thing was true, even a great warfare.” The meaning of the original has long been read in different ways, and we set them side by side in the issues. We can quietly say first: this is a word about something hard and very great.

Then Daniel himself: “In those days I, Daniel, was mourning three whole weeks. I ate no pleasant bread. No meat or wine came into my mouth. I didn’t anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled.” Why was he mourning? The text does not say, and we do not supply it. We only see that he was not a man for himself alone. His mourning was for the future of God’s people. Such mourning is not weakness; it is love.

Then the vision came: by the Tigris, he lifted up his eyes and saw a man clothed in linen, with pure gold of Uphaz at his waist, his body like beryl, his face like lightning, his eyes like torches, his arms and feet like burnished bronze, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude. This is a glory beyond description. Who is this? There have long been different readings: some think he is a glorious angel; some think he is Christ, because Revelation chapter 1 has a similar description; and some say the text does not say, and we need not guess. We set the views side by side and do not decide for you.

Please notice another detail: “I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves.” There is an experience others cannot see. You may have had it: a burden others do not understand; a moment only you and God know. Please do not doubt its reality because no one saw; and please do not feel alone because others did not see. God is the one who sees.

Then Daniel’s reaction: “So I was left alone, and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; for my face grew deathly pale, and I retained no strength.” A man who had mourned for the people for three weeks, at the sight of the glory, fell down. This reminds us of chapter 8, where he also fell asleep. Before glory man has no strength; this is honest. But this chapter does not stop here. Next, a hand came.

Perhaps you are mourning for someone right now: a child who has gone astray, an elder who is gravely ill, a church that is struggling. You need not dress this mourning up as full confidence. Daniel’s mourning was real, and God answered him with reality. You can first sit down in a quiet place and say that person’s name, not beautifully, only honestly. This small act is often the beginning of intercession.
Is mourning for others a kind of unbelief?

No. Mourning for others is an expression of love. Daniel mourned for the people three weeks; the text does not blame him, and instead, while he mourned, God sent a messenger to answer him. The real question is not whether you mourn but whether you bring your mourning before God. You can fix a time each day, say to God the person or matter that makes you mourn, and then place it in his hand. Then mourning is no longer a burden carried alone but becomes intercession. After practicing this for a few weeks you will find that mourning is no longer only a stone pressing on your chest but becomes a small road into God’s heart.
II. A Hand, a Name and the Words “From the First Day” (10:10–14)

The man on the ground did not stand up by himself. The text says: “Behold, a hand touched me, which set me on my knees and on the palms of my hands.” Notice this picture: he had not yet stood; he only rose a little on his knees and palms. This is a very gentle, step-by-step raising. God does not force a man who has fallen to stand straight at once; he first touches him and lets him prop himself up a little with knee and hand.

Then the first words the visitor spoke were not blame and not a command but a name: “Daniel, you greatly beloved man, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright; for I have been sent to you, now.” Do you remember? In chapter 9 Gabriel called him this too. A man on the ground without strength, before any other words, was first called greatly beloved. This is what God says first to the weak: not “be strong” but “you are beloved.” Then the text is honest: “I stood trembling.” When he stood, he was still trembling. God does not require that we stop trembling before we stand. We can tremble and stand at the same time.

Then the most important verse of this chapter: “Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard. I have come for your words’ sake.” Notice three things. First, do not be afraid: this is the first thing God’s messenger said to a trembling man. Second, from the first day: not the twenty-first day, not when the fasting reached three weeks, but from the first day, his words were heard. Third, I have come for your words’ sake: his prayer was the reason the messenger came.
Have you prayed a long time and had no response? Sometimes we think God has not heard. This verse says to you: from your first day, your words were heard. Delay does not mean not heard.

Then the text says: “But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me because I remained there with the kings of Persia.” This sentence has long been read in many different ways: some think it is a spiritual power; some think it is the ruler of Persia or his representative; and some think it is a language in which heaven and earth correspond. We set the views side by side and say plainly: we do not turn this verse into teaching on territorial spirit warfare, and we do not teach you to identify or attack the spirit of a place. What this verse gives us is a deep comfort: over your prayer, in heaven, much is going on that we cannot see. You need not know the details; you only need to know: the words have been heard.

One more small picture is worth pausing over: the hand set him on his knees and palms and did not pull him straight to standing at once. God knows how much a person can bear, and he is not in a hurry. You need not be in a hurry either. If today you can only prop yourself up a little, that is already grace; you need not compare your speed with others, and need not blame yourself for being too slow.
How do I use the words “from the first day” in my own waiting?

You can use them this way: each morning, do not ask “is there an answer today?” but say, “From the first day, you heard.” Write this sentence on paper and put it where you see it every day. Then divide your waiting into two parts: what you have heard, and what I can do. What I can do is one small thing today; what you have heard is my whole waiting. Then your waiting is no longer empty but a journey that has been heard and held. Please remember, this is not a formula and does not guarantee the answer will come at once; it only brings you from anxious guessing back to a resting assurance: he heard.
III. Light from the Original: Greatly Beloved, First Day, Touch, Strong (10:11, 12, 18, 19)

Four words in the original of this chapter deserve a slow reading. The first is “greatly beloved,” Hebrew חֲמוּדוֹת (chamudot). Literally “desired, very precious.” In this book it appears three times: 9:23, 10:11, 10:19. All three were said at the moment when Daniel was weakest and most in need. This name is not a reward but an acceptance: you are beloved, whether or not you have strength now.

The second is “set your heart,” Hebrew נָתַתָּ לִבְּךָ (natata libbekha), literally “you set your heart here.” “Setting the heart to understand” is putting the whole heart on understanding. It is joined with “humble yourself” (לְהִתְעַנּוֹת): on one side placing the heart on understanding, on the other humbling oneself before God. These two things are, the messenger said, the reason his words were heard. Notice that it is not because he did much, but because he set his heart in the right place.

The third is “touch,” Hebrew נָגַע (naga). This word appears three times in this chapter: in 10:10 a hand touched him, in 10:16 one touched his lips, and in 10:18 one touched him again. Three touches, three results: standing, opening the mouth, strength. In the Bible, touch is often the closest act between God and man. You can think of it: Jesus too often used his hand to touch people.

The fourth is “strong,” Hebrew חָזַק (chazaq). In 10:18, “strengthened me” (Piel, to make strong); in 10:19, “be strong” (a command); in 10:19, “I was strengthened” (reflexive); in 10:19, “you have strengthened me” (Piel). The same root, four times in all. See the order: first he is made strong, then commanded to be strong, and then says: you have made me strong. Strength is given, and also answered.

Please notice again: this chapter does not teach us a formula; it shows how a gentle God treats a weak servant. We put the emphasis on his work, not on our method, because methods make people tense, and knowing him lets people rest.
How do “setting the heart to understand” and “humbling yourself” fit together?

The way they fit is that one is upward and one is downward. Setting the heart to understand is putting the heart on God’s word and God’s heart; humbling yourself is lowering yourself before God and admitting your limits. With only the former it can become the pride of pursuing knowledge; with only the latter it can become heavy self-blame. Together they let you be hungry and humble at once. When you read the Bible you can pause and say to God in one sentence: I want to understand, but I also know I need you. Then your reading is not only adding knowledge but, in humility, being led step by step by God’s word and God’s Spirit, becoming softer the more you read.
How can I experience God’s “touch” today?

From several channels. First, in quiet prayer, put your hand on your chest and say to yourself: I have been touched. Second, through a friend willing to stay with you: an embrace, a word, a bowl of hot soup. Third, through Scripture: read this chapter slowly and read the word “touch” into your heart. God’s touch often comes through people and through his word. If you feel alone for a long time, please find a safe person to walk with you, and if needed, professional help. If you long feel that no one comes near you, pray, and also actively find a reliable companion, and let God’s hand reach you through a human hand.
IV. The Speechless Man Touched Twice (10:15–21)

Then the text says: “When he had spoken these words to me, I set my face toward the ground, and was mute.” He fell again, unable even to speak. Then: “Behold, one in the likeness of the sons of men touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth, and spoke and said to him who stood before me, ‘My lord, by reason of the vision my sorrows have overtaken me, and I retain no strength.’” Touched. Lips. God not only raises people to stand; he also lets the mute open their mouths.

Look at the first thing he said: “For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? For as for me, immediately there remained no strength in me. There was no breath left in me.” He was honest. He did not pretend to be strong and did not say “I am fine.” He said his helplessness just as it was. God does not despise such words. You can pray this way too: Lord, I have no strength, I cannot find words, I come to you just like this. Heaven hears a prayer like this.

Then the text says: “Then one like the appearance of a man touched me again, and he strengthened me.” This is the second touch. The first raised him to stand; this one gave him strength. Then came the command: “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid. Peace be to you. Be strong. Yes, be strong.” See this order: first he touched, first he gave strength, and only then said, “be strong.” This is not asking a man without strength to make himself strong; it is first making him strong, and then telling him to be strong.

You may have had such moments: told “be strong” and with no strength. This passage tells you: true strength is not gritted teeth; it is touched into you, spoken into you, given. In the end he said: “Let my lord speak; for you have strengthened me.” He had strength not because of himself but because of you. This is the strength of having no self.

Then the visitor said: “Do you know why I have come to you?” He said he would still return to fight, and afterward the prince of Greece would come. We likewise do not turn it into a tool for predicting geopolitics. At the end he said: “I will tell you that which is inscribed in the writing of truth. There is no one who holds with me against these, but Michael your prince.” In heaven there is a book of truth; what God will accomplish is already written, not on a sudden whim. History is not a tangle of threads; one has already written its direction. You are not alone. This chapter ends very quietly: no dates, only one answer: your words were heard; you were touched twice; be strong; there is a book of truth.

Please imagine: on your most weary night, you cannot say anything, only tears. Then a hand gently touches your lips, and you are able to open your mouth. This is not a romantic imagining but the picture of promise the text gives us: God knows our muteness, and knows how to let us open our mouths again. You only need to come; that is enough.
Can I use the words “be strong” to comfort others?

You can, but please follow the order of the text: first touch, then speak. To a person with no strength, saying “be strong” at once is often stopping his tears. You can first sit with him a while and say: I am here; ask him: what do you need? If needed, give him a bowl of hot soup, an embrace. When he has a little strength, then say: I believe you are beloved, and I believe God will give you strength. Then “be strong” will not become pressure but blessing. Also watch your tone: first accompany, then encourage, so that the other feels held rather than demanded of; this is God’s order.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is to turn “the prince of Persia withstood me twenty-one days” into “if a prayer has no answer, it must be blocked by a territorial spirit.” The point of the text is: from the first day, your words were heard; the description of the prince and of Michael has long been read in different ways, and these notes set them side by side and do not teach identifying or attacking territorial spirits.

The second deviation is to turn the three weeks of fasting into “to get an answer you must fast for a certain number of days.” Daniel’s fasting was an expression of mourning and of humbling himself, not a condition for exchanging for an answer; those with health conditions should first consult medical care, and God looks at the heart.

The third deviation is to declare that the man in linen is Christ, or to insist he is a particular angel, and belittle other readings. The one who comes in 10:5–6 has long been read variously as an angel, as Christ and so on; these notes set the views side by side and say no more than the text.

The fourth deviation is to use “be strong” to tell the weak to be strong at once, or to blame them for not having enough faith. The order of the text is that he first touched and first gave strength, and only then said, be strong; toward those who are hurting or have lost their strength we first accompany and do not blame.

The fifth deviation is to turn this chapter into a tool for predicting history, saying that the princes of Persia and Greece are certain countries or powers of today. The text does not say this; we set up no timetable and identify no one today.
Someone uses this chapter to teach “territorial spirit warfare.” How should I respond?

You can first affirm his seriousness about the spiritual world, then gently return to the text: what this chapter says is that Daniel’s prayer was heard from the first day; the prince and Michael are background the messenger gave Daniel, and there is no command for us to identify or attack the spirit of a place. You can ask: does this teaching make you trust God more, or become more tense? Then bring the focus back to 10:12: setting the heart to understand, humbling oneself before God, and God heard. No need to argue; bring the atmosphere back to quiet. Finally, bring it back to the text’s own point, so that people love the Lord more and are quieter, rather than more tense and more afraid of things the eye cannot see.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to “not making people worry.” Children toward parents, parents toward children, friends among themselves, we are used to keeping mourning in the heart and saying with a smile, “I am fine.” Daniel was also a man who could endure, but in this chapter he honestly said, “I have no strength.” You can learn to say one true sentence in front of a suitable person too. If your situation does not allow telling people, you can first tell God.

The second question: we are very used to the expectation that “asking brings an answer,” and easily read “no immediate response” as “God is ignoring me” or “I have not done enough.” This chapter gives another way of seeing: from the first day your words were heard; the delay is because there are things in heaven we cannot see. This is not a formula, and not every delay has an explanation, but it gives us a rest: he heard.
It is very hard for me to say “I have no strength” in front of people. How do I begin?

You can begin with three small steps. First, say it to God, in writing or aloud, not beautifully. Second, choose someone you trust and say only one sentence: I have been very tired lately. No need to explain much. Third, if the other responds well, say a little more; if not, do not blame yourself; try another person, or a pastor or counselor. Telling the truth is not weakness; it gives another a chance to love you, and gives God a chance to touch you. This is a practice that takes time; give yourself patience, and give those around you patience; God’s hand is always there.
VII. Living Out 321: First Touch, Then Speak: Be Strong

Three foundations: Jesus is my example. In his extreme anguish an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him; he is also the Lord who often stretched out his hand, touched people and raised them up. The Bible is my standard, because for the prince of Persia and Michael, and for the twenty-one days, we do not rely on guessing but on the point the text itself gives: from the first day, your words were heard. The Holy Spirit is my guide, because in weakness we do not need more gritted teeth; we need a Spirit who is with us, to touch our lips and give us strength.

Two cores: Let Jesus reign, which means in delay still bringing our words to him, not explaining God’s silence for him, and letting him touch our lips and give us strength. Let Jesus receive all the glory, which means that when we stand up we say: it was not that I am strong; he gave me strength. One purpose: to build God’s system. This is a people who touch one another and strengthen one another: accompanying when someone mourns, waiting when someone is speechless, not hurrying when someone trembles; not teaching people to attack unseen powers but teaching them to be touched first and then stand.

Change the concept and the life changes: when we think “being strong is my own responsibility,” our life is held up by gritted teeth; when we know “strength is given,” our life has rest. From the self-life to the no-self life: the self-life proves itself by pretending to be strong; the no-self life honestly says it has no strength, lets God touch, lets God give strength, and lets man be man and God be God.

So when we read these hard-to-understand descriptions, we can rest in stopping where the text stops, neither adding nor taking away; to remain honest and humble about what is uncertain is itself a respect for God’s word.
What does “no self” have to do with “being touched”?

The relationship is that being touched requires putting down defenses. A person who feels “I must hold up by myself” finds it hard to let others, even God, come near. Having no self is not disappearing but being willing to be touched. You can try: on an occasion where you want to pretend all is well, gently say one true sentence and see what happens. Most of the time you will find that the feeling of being held is stronger than holding up by yourself. Practicing no-self in this way, you will slowly learn that the rest of being held is deeper and longer lasting than the strength of toughing it out alone, and it also better lets you accompany others along the same road.
VIII. Four Kinds of Heart, One Hand

The proud type says: “I must make myself strong and not let anyone see my weakness.” This heart may be afraid of being looked down on, afraid of losing control. Daniel was also a strong man, yet in this chapter he honestly said: I have no strength. You can ask yourself: is my strength for loving the Lord, or for proving myself?

The fearful type says: “I am afraid God has not heard my prayer; I am afraid there will never be an answer.” This fear is real. Please remember the text says: from the first day, your words were heard. Delay does not mean not heard. You can write this sentence on your palm and read it every day.

The shame type says: “I am so weak, so speechless; how can I be worthy of being beloved?” What this chapter most wants to say to you is: greatly beloved man. He was called this while he was on the ground, speechless. You need not become strong first to deserve being loved. You can come with your shame.

The hurt type says: “When I most needed it, no one touched me or raised me up.” This wound is real. Please first find a safe person for yourself and tell your story. This chapter does not ask you to forgive at once or to have strength at once; it says God’s hand touches again and again, and he does not hurry you.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, each day pray one sentence: from the first day, you heard; set down one matter you have waited long for.
Second, write down one thing in which you pretend to be strong, and write one sentence you can honestly say to God: I have no strength.
Third, find a companion and agree to remind each other each day with one sentence: your words were heard; do not explain God’s silence for the other.
Fourth, on your most tired day, first rest, eat and sleep, then return to prayer; do not take weariness as spiritual failure.
Fifth, when someone wants to use this chapter to teach territorial spiritual warfare, gently bring him back to 10:12: setting the heart to understand, and being heard.
I declare: from the first day, my words were heard; delay does not mean not heard.
I declare: I am a greatly beloved one; I need not pretend to be strong, and I can stand even while trembling.
I declare: God first touches me and gives me strength, and only then says: be strong.
I declare: in heaven there is a book of truth, history is not a tangle of threads, I am not alone, and I will rest, until Jesus reigns.

Daniel chapter 10 begins with the mourning of an old man: three weeks, no pleasant bread, no oil. He saw glory, fell to the ground, and was speechless. Then a hand touched him, a voice called him a greatly beloved man, and said: from the first day, your words were heard. He was touched twice before he was told: be strong. What this chapter gives us is not a method of warfare but a gentle answer: you were heard, you were touched, you are not alone.

Brothers and sisters, let us return to those three weeks. Do you have a mourning for someone else? Do you have a prayer you have waited long for? Bring it before God. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our example, he is our King, he is the Lord who stretches out his hand and gives people strength. The focus is not how strong I am, nor how many battles in heaven we cannot see, but the God who heard us from the first day.

Lord, may we in delay believe that we were heard from the first day; in weakness let you touch our lips and give us strength; until your kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ 10:2 says Daniel mourned three whole weeks. Is there something you have mourned or worried about for someone else for a long time? Please say it in one sentence.
2. ★★ 10:7 says only he saw this vision, and those with him did not. Do you have a burden that others cannot see and only you and God know? Please say one; no need for details.
3. ★★★ In quiet, please think of one thing: if your words were heard from the first day, how would your waiting be different? Please write one sentence to God.
4. ★ Please say in one sentence: this week, at what fixed time will you bring one worry or mourning before God? Say the time and the place.

Leader’s note: Please begin by quietly reading Daniel 10:12. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches mourning, long waiting and having no strength; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not press for location or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record anything that could be traced, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ [See] In 10:8–9 Daniel fell down at the sight of the glory. When have you also felt “no strength”? Please say one time.
6. ★★ [Hear] Read 10:11–12. Which sentence does God say to you: “greatly beloved man,” “don’t be afraid,” or “your words were heard”? Say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ [Think] 10:18–19 first touched, first gave strength, and only then said: be strong. How does this change your view of “be strong”?
8. ★★ [Speak] Say one sentence to the person next to you: “I have a prayer I have waited long for,” and say what it is. Only one sentence; no explanation.
9. ★★★ [Do] In 10:16 Daniel honestly said he had no strength. This week, to whom will you say one true sentence, “I have no strength”? Please say the name and the time.

Leader’s note: Follow the order [See], [Hear], [Think], [Speak], [Do], and leave enough time for each step. In [Speak], only a sentence, a name and a time are needed; no stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “have faith” or “be strong” to someone who is crying; look after them privately after the meeting, and if needed help them seek professional help.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone who is mourning yet says “I am fine”? Please say the name, and decide to sit with him for a while this month.
11. ★★ In your church or group, is there anyone in the habit of answering others’ tears with “be strong”? Please say one instance, and say how you could first accompany and only then encourage.
12. ★★ Is there something for which you need to say to God, “from the first day you heard”? Please say one, and decide this week to set it down with one sentence of prayer.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear “your words were heard.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s note: Please remind especially: in the group, do not identify or attack the spirit of any place, and do not match the princes of Persia and Greece to any country or person of today. If someone shares their own mourning, long waiting or the experience of losing a loved one, do not press for details, do not ask them to forgive, and look after them privately after the meeting.
Please close your eyes gently and put before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read together Daniel 10:12: “your words were heard. I have come for your words’ sake.”

Let the leader pray for each person: Lord, teach us in delay to believe we were heard from the first day; in weakness to let you touch us and give us strength; and to take that one step in the ordinary days of this week. Before dismissal, ask one another one sentence: “What is the one thing you will set down this week?”

11.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 11 · Daniel Chapter 11
11.title: The King of the North and the King of the South—King, King, Wise Ones
blocks: I. Someone Else’s Battlefield, Our Land (11:1–4)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today I would like to begin by asking you to imagine a picture: the place where you live has become someone else’s road to war. Great men meet over it, make alliances, break covenants, passing through again and again; and you are only the one passed through and decided about. Your home, your school, your church are all at the edge of someone else’s chessboard. If you have felt this, then Daniel chapter 11 was written especially for you.

This chapter begins with a very unremarkable sentence: “As for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.” The speaker is still the messenger of chapter 10. Notice: as soon as he opens his mouth, he lifts our eyes from earth to heaven. The first year of Darius is just when Babylon had fallen; Daniel at that time did not know that in heaven someone was standing up and supporting. However fast empires change on earth, in heaven there is one who has stood all along.

Then the messenger uses a very weighty word: “truth.” He says, “Now I will show you the truth.” The long run of kings and kings that follows is not a novel and not casual guessing but something spoken of as “true.” Three more kings in Persia; the fourth is far richer and stirs up all to attack Greece; then a mighty king rises, rules with great dominion and does as he pleases. But the text goes on: as soon as he rises, his kingdom breaks and is divided toward the four winds of heaven, and does not go to his posterity.

Most readers through the ages have read this mighty king as the beginning of the Hellenistic age; for the details, the matchings differ from one reading to another, and we set them side by side among the issues. Here we do not match every name; we first hold on to a very practical reminder: the moment a man is strongest is often the moment his kingdom breaks most easily. This makes us think of the image in chapter 2: even the most majestic head of gold was only one stage.

Please be quiet here a moment: have you put your security on something that looks very strong? A very secure job, a very influential person, a very large organization? These things are not necessarily bad, but what the text says is: all of them will have a time of breaking; and the one who was standing in the first year of Darius is still standing today.

Think again: why did the messenger mention the first year of Darius in the very first sentence of chapter 11? Perhaps he wanted Daniel to know that everything he now saw had not begun to be arranged only today. Before you knew, heaven was already standing for you. Such seeing gives us a little more quiet and a little less panic in the face of uncertainty.

Perhaps you stand in a very small place and feel your prayer is of no account. Please remember: in the first year of Darius, the one the messenger stood up to support was a small people passed through in turn by great empires. God in history often does his greatest work from the most unremarkable position; your position is among them.
How can I use the sentence “I stood up to confirm and strengthen him” in my situation today?

You can use it this way: take this verse as a reminder, not as a doctrine of angels. The reminder is: behind the situation you can see, there is a support you cannot see, which began in the first year of Darius. Each morning you can say one sentence to yourself: today, the place where I am is not only someone else’s battlefield but a place where someone stands beside me. Then name the person or matter you worry about most and hand it to the God who stands unmoved. This practice does not deny the hardness of your situation; it slowly brings your eyes back from seeing only the movements of great men to the God who has stood all along.
II. Kings of the South and of the North, and One Word: Cannot Stand (11:5–20)

From verse 5 the text begins to speak of the king of the south and the king of the north; over a dozen verses it is one coming and going after another: marriage, alliance, broken covenant, war, triumph, retreat. Many readers get lost here, because the names are not spelled out and the details are many. Most readers through the ages have understood the two kings as two dynasties of the Hellenistic age, around Egypt and Syria; the matchings of details differ from one reading to another. These notes set them side by side, do not match them one by one for you, and set no dates for these events.

I would like to ask you not to be dragged away by the details but to hold on to three words the text itself repeats. The first is “stand.” The text says again and again that no one can stand before him, that the arms of the south cannot stand, that this thing will not stand. This word in the original is exactly the undercurrent of the whole book: stand. Human strength falls one after another. The second is “fall”: the commander will stumble, fall, and not be found. The third is the “glorious land”: the two kings go back and forth, and both must pass through it and use it.

Notice that marriage: the daughter of the king of the south is sent to the king of the north to make a covenant. It looks like a covenant of peace. But the text says just one thing: the strength of this woman’s help cannot stand. The most beautiful covenants of men often wrap the deepest calculation, and the text finishes such a covenant with two words: cannot stand.

There is one more detail worth a pause: the text says that “violent ones” want to “fulfill the vision” yet will fall. The meaning of the original is wanting to “make the vision stand.” This is a very painful reminder: some want to accomplish God’s word with their own hands, and fall as a result. God’s plan does not need us to push it forward by scheming.

Not one line of this passage says which king God’s people should follow. This is important: the text does not teach us to take sides but to see that when great nations fight each other, God’s people are to fix their eyes on the God who stands unmoved, not on who wins and who loses. Then we will not lose our peace in the rise and fall of the news.

Please take this passage as a mirror: in our life too there are many comings and goings between north and south, many beautiful alliances wrapping motives not so beautiful. You can ask yourself quietly: among the alliances and relationships I am now relying on, is there one that was gained by calculation? No need to hurry to condemn; simply to see honestly is already a step taken.

One more thing is worth adding: although the text gives so much space to kings and kings, not one line puts God’s people against these kings to attack anyone. Their task is to “stand,” and to “know God.” This reminds us that in turbulent years, holding one’s own place matters far more than commenting on someone else’s place.
When I read this long stretch of history it feels remote. How should I read it so that it helps?

You can read it with three questions: First, in this passage, what can stand and what cannot? Second, the thing I am relying on now: which side does it belong to? Third, if I were the people being passed through, what comfort does this passage give me? Write these three questions in a notebook, and use them each time you read historical details like these. You will find that although the names are unfamiliar, human nature is very familiar; and what the text gives is not a history lesson but the wisdom of how to stand firm on someone else’s battlefield. This is a habit that builds up slowly; you need not understand every detail at once, and each time you see a little more, that is progress.
III. Light from the Original: Stand, Contemptible, Appointed Time, Know (11:1, 21, 27, 32)

In the original of this chapter there are four words worth a slow reading. The first is “stand,” Hebrew עמד (amad). From the start of Daniel this word has been moving beneath the surface: standing before the king, standing before the image, standing before the throne in heaven. In this chapter it appears most often: cannot stand, no one can stand before him, I stood up to support. Human strength is a strength that cannot stand; and on God’s side, someone stands and supports.

The second is “contemptible,” Hebrew נִבְזֶה (nivzeh). Literally “one who is despised,” a passive form: this man, in men’s eyes, originally had no right. He gains the kingdom not by lawful succession but by “smooth words” (חֲלַקְלַקּוֹת). This word appears again and again in 11:21, 11:32 and 11:34: smooth words are the language of this age. The truth is not always pleasant to hear, but smooth words most easily make people fall.

The third is “appointed time,” Hebrew מוֹעֵד (mo'ed), often joined with קֵץ (end): “the end will still be at the appointed time.” This word recurs in 11:27, 11:29 and 11:35.
