Its meaning is “the designated time.” This time is not in the king’s hand but in God’s. The fourth is “know,” Hebrew יָדַע (yada), “knowing in relationship,” not merely knowing some information. “The people who know their God will be strong, and take action.” This sentence is the heart of the whole chapter.

Finally, please join these four words into one line: standing is the mark of God’s side; smooth words are the language of the other side; the appointed time is the boundary God gives history; knowing is the only thing needed on our side. You need not grasp all the details of the original at once; only remember: in darkness, the one who knows God, held up, can stand.

If you want to bring this lesson into daily life, you can try this small practice: whenever you hear news that makes you tense, first say silently, “the end belongs to God,” then say silently, “today I will know him,” and only then decide whether to keep watching and whether to forward it. These three steps take less than a minute, yet little by little they change your heart.
Why are “smooth words” the key word of this chapter?

Because it is the hardest power to guard against: it uses no sword, only good words. 11:21 says the contemptible man gains the kingdom with flattery; 11:32 says he corrupts, by flatteries, those who act wickedly against the covenant; 11:34 says many join themselves to the fallen wise with flatteries. Such words often sound very warm and reasonable, yet lead people away from the truth. When you hear words that are especially pleasing, you can pause three seconds first and ask yourself: is there truth in these words? What do they ask me to pay? This small pause is the beginning of drawing near to the truth. When you meet words especially pleasing and especially to your liking, take still more care, because what smooth words do best is make people lay down their guard.
What is the difference between “knowing God” and “knowing a lot about God”?

The difference is relationship. Knowing a lot about God can come from reading; knowing God needs time and ordinary days. Think: you know a friend not because you have read his file but because you have eaten with him, walked through low valleys with him, been silent together. Knowing God is the same: on ordinary days, spend a little time each day drawing near to him; on nights with no answer, still speak to him. In chapter 10 God first touched Daniel and gave him strength; the strength in this chapter shares a root with “support” in 11:1. So knowing God is not the result of gritted teeth but of one who is held up, still standing in the darkness.
IV. The Contemptible Man, Lying at One Table, and the Defiled Sanctuary (11:21–35)

Then the text draws the camera close and rests it on one man: “In his place a contemptible person will stand up.” Many through the ages have read this “despised man” as a ruler who persecuted God’s people; others read from other angles, and we set them side by side. We need to say plainly: these notes do not connect this man to any person of today, nor use him to label anyone in the future in advance. What we need to recognize is his way: flattery, deceit, scheming, scattering wealth.

We are not strangers to such a way. It rests not on lawful trust but on pleasing people, on smooth words, on handing out benefits to buy hearts. It exists in companies, it exists in clans, and sadly, sometimes it exists in churches too. But the text leaves one line: “...even for a time.” However refined his plans, they lie inside a boundary.

Then there is that table. Two kings sit at one table, eating and telling lies, each thinking in his heart how to harm the other. The verdict the text gives this scene is short: the plan will not prosper, for “the end will still be at the appointed time.” The end is not in their strategies but in a timetable they cannot touch. We must be especially careful: this sentence does not teach us to count days; it teaches us to let go: the end belongs to God.

Next, the camera turns to the sanctuary: his heart is against the holy covenant, he profanes the sanctuary, takes away the continual offering and sets up the abomination that makes desolate. This echoes the descriptions in chapters 8 and 9. For this passage too, different historical matchings have been offered through the ages; we set them side by side and set no date for it. In such darkness the text leaves two groups: one is the people drawn away by smooth words; the other is “the people who know their God,” who are strong and take action.

Finally, the wise. They make many understand, yet fall by the sword, in flame, into captivity and plunder. The text gives their falling a meaning: to refine the rest of them, to make them pure and white. This is hope for those who suffer; please do not take this verse and say to someone who is suffering, “this is God refining you.” We should become the “little help” in the text: accompany first, and speak afterward.

Perhaps you ask: since the text says this, how should we face real darkness? The answer: do not flee, do not exaggerate, and do not add our own lists to it. We honestly see the power of darkness, and honestly admit that we do not need to see all the details before we can stand firm. We need only, today, in our own place, to know God, and to become that little help to one person beside us.

Notice one more detail: when the wise fall, the text says they are “helped with a little help.” These words are small but very true. God’s help is often not removing all the pain at once but giving strength little by little at the moment of greatest need. If we learn to treasure that little by little, we will not miss the grace God has already given for lack of seeing a great miracle.
Does the fall of the wise mean that God lets good people suffer for a purpose?

The text gives this situation one meaning; it does not say all suffering is for this purpose. To a person who is suffering, we should not hurry to explain on God’s behalf, nor say, “this is God refining you.” You can first sit beside him and ask: what do you need? When needed, give him a bowl of hot soup, an embrace, a stretch of time without words. When he has strength, if he himself asks, we can slowly read this verse together. This verse is hope written for a suffering people, not a standard answer in the hands of those standing by. If someone beside you is suffering, remember: accompanying needs no beautiful words, and a figure who does not leave is often more powerful than a hundred explanations.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is matching the kings of the south and north, one by one, with certain countries or people of today. The text’s vantage point is the glorious land, and the matching of details has long been read in many ways; these notes set them side by side, put no label on any person of today, and set no dates.

The second deviation is directly identifying the abomination of 11:31, or the self-exalting king from 11:36 on, as a particular person today, or using it to draw up an end-time timetable. These notes set the various readings side by side, state plainly that we identify no antichrist, and count no days.

The third deviation is using 11:35 to tell a suffering person, “this is God refining you.” This verse is hope for a suffering people, not a standard answer in the hands of bystanders; to those who are losing something, we first accompany, and we do not explain suffering on God’s behalf.

The fourth deviation is turning “knowing God” into how much knowledge one has or how much one serves, and using it to judge who is truly strong. Knowing is living in relationship with God; being strong is being held up by God, from the same root as “support” in 11:1.

The fifth deviation is that, because the details of this chapter are hard to match, one says the whole book is unreliable, or forcibly uses one reading to attack brothers and sisters who hold another view. We honestly admit the difficulty and hold on to the clearest point: his end will come, and no one will help him.
Someone insists this chapter can precisely predict world events. How should I respond?

You can first affirm his seriousness about the Bible, then gently ask three questions. First, does the text itself name anyone? Second, have interpreters through the ages read it differently? Third, does this reading make the congregation love the Lord more and be more patient, or become more panicked? If the latter, it has departed from the purpose of the text. Then bring the atmosphere back to 11:32: we do not need to know all the details; we only need to know God and be strong and take action today. No need to argue and no need to win; put the center of the conversation back on learning together and being humble together. Please also give yourself and the other a little room: between different readings we can learn from one another, and need not hurry to decide a winner.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to “keeping our heads down to survive” in a large environment. The experience of many Chinese families is that in situations they do not decide, they learned not to speak, not to offend, not to stand out. In many cases this is wisdom, but it can also turn “smooth words” into the language of survival: saying what is pleasant and safe, and no longer speaking the truth. This chapter reminds us: those who know God can, without provoking, still speak the truth and still hold to the covenant.

The second question: we are also easily fascinated by “big events”: the news, the situation, predictions, the end times. Some lose sleep over it, some quarrel over it, some use it to identify others. What this chapter gives us is not more predictions but the rest of an ending that belongs to God. You can practice spending five minutes before reading the news to read one verse of his word; after reading, tell God your worries. Then the news is no longer your master.
In an environment where faith cannot be expressed openly, how does this chapter help me?

What it gives you is not a brave slogan but an inner anchor: knowing God in daily life and holding to his covenant, with no need for anyone to see. In a safe time you can quietly read one verse of his word and pray, leaving no traceable mark and needing to prove nothing to anyone. If there are trustworthy brothers and sisters, you can support one another in a safe place. Do not force yourself to do more than you can bear; God sees your heart and also sees your situation. This quietness is not passivity: in a situation where one cannot speak, still holding on to the relationship with God is itself a kind of strength.
VII. Living Out 321: Knowing Him, Strong in the Darkness

Three foundations: Jesus is my example. Facing the greatest power, he used no smooth words; he spoke the truth, went silently to the cross, and entrusted himself to the righteous Father. The Bible is my standard, because before the many hard details of this chapter we do not rely on guessing or matching but on the point the text itself gives: the end belongs to God, and only the people who know their God will be strong and take action. The Holy Spirit is my guide, so that in dark days we know God and not merely know about him, and are not led around by fear.

Two cores: Let Jesus reign, which means putting our security on the God who stands unmoved, not on any king, relationship or organization that will fall; the ending is handed to him, and we do not count his days for him. Let Jesus receive all the glory, which means that when we are strong and take action we say: it is not that I grit my teeth and hold on; he holds me up. One purpose: to build God’s system. This is a people who know God: in turbulent times supporting one another, accompanying first when someone falls, not leading people by fear, and not using Scripture to identify anyone.

Change the concept and the life changes: when we think “security comes from standing on the right side,” our life is tense; when we know “security is being held up by the God who stands unmoved,” our life has rest. From the self-life to the no-self life: the self-life needs to see through history and identify others before it feels safe; the no-self life needs only to know God to stand in the darkness, letting man be man and God be God.

Think: what does no-self look like in this chapter? It is not silence, nor withdrawal, but putting down the burden of “I must be in control.” A person of no-self, in turbulent times, can instead be quieter and have more room to accompany others, because his heart is no longer tied to the situation but occupied by Jesus.

We should also remind ourselves: 321 is not a standard for attacking others but a mirror for ourselves. When we read of the contemptible man and the self-exalting king, let us first ask: is there some shadow of the same in my own heart? Humility overcoming pride begins with me; changing concepts begins with me.
What does “no-self” have to do with “knowing God”?

The relationship is this: the self-life puts its security where it can see through, calculate accurately and stand on the right side; the no-self life puts its security on God and so need not see through everything. You can try an exercise: whenever you cannot help wanting to “find out who is who,” stop first and ask yourself: am I doing this out of love for the Lord, or to give myself a sense of security? Then say one sentence: Lord, I do not need to know everything; I only want to know you. This practice will slowly bring your heart from chasing the situation back to knowing him. In time you will find yourself less eager to figure everything out and more held up by God, standing quietly.
VIII. Four Kinds of Heart, One Ending

The proud type says: “I want to see the situation clearly and know who is who, so that I have the lead.” This heart may be unwilling to be kept in the dark. But this chapter says the end belongs to God. You can ask yourself: is my “figuring it out” for loving the Lord, or for seizing the lead?

The fearful type says: “The situation is so chaotic and I am very afraid; I am afraid the worst will happen.” This fear is real. Please remember the text says the end is still at the appointed time, and that for him who comes to his end, no one will help. You can reduce the information that makes you panic and leave a little more time to know God.

The shame type says: “I was deceived by smooth words before; I am ashamed; how could I be so naive?” Being deceived does not mean you are unworthy of love. The text sees the power of smooth words; you can bring this shame before God and tell him, and tell one safe person too.

The hurt type says: “In my darkest time no one held me up.” This wound is real. The text says that when they fall, they are helped with a little help. We do not make your wound lighter, and do not ask you to forgive at once; you can slowly find one safe person, and let God, through a person, become that little help.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, each day spend five minutes, not to ask for anything, only to read one verse of his word and say to him: I want to know you.
Second, write down three things you habitually treat as security, and beside each write one sentence: this is not my king.
Third, sit for a while with someone who is falling; accompany first, do not hurry to explain, and do not say “this is God refining you.”
Fourth, before the next time you hear smooth, pleasant words, pause three seconds and ask yourself: is there truth in these words?
Fifth, when someone wants to use this chapter to draw up a timetable or point at someone, gently bring him back to 11:32: we only need to know God.
I declare: human scheming has a boundary, the end belongs to God, and I need not count his days for him.
I declare: I will not rely on powers that cannot stand; my security is the God who stands unmoved.
I declare: I will know God, be held up by him in the darkness, and be strong and take action.
I declare: I will become that little help, accompanying those who are falling, until Jesus reigns.

Daniel chapter 11 is the longest and hardest-to-read chapter of the whole book, and also the one most easily misused. It speaks of many kings, many wars, and many names we can no longer be sure of. But if by the end we remember only one thing, let it be this: “Yet he will come to his end, and no one will help him.” In the end the self-exalting man has no one standing beside him, while the people who know God have a great prince who stands always on their side.

Brothers and sisters, let us return to the first picture: the place where you live has become someone else’s battlefield. You need not see through the whole situation and need not identify anyone; you need only, today, to know God. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is our example, he is our King, he is the Lord who stands unmoved and holds us up to make us strong. The focus is not how well I understand the situation, nor how frightening others are, but the God who rules history.

May God let us, on someone else’s battlefield, still know him; among smooth words, still speak the truth; when someone falls, become that little help; until his kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ In one sentence, tell about a time when the place where you were became someone else’s battlefield. Only one sentence, please.
2. ★ 11:1 says that in the first year of Darius, someone in heaven stood up to support. Is there a situation in which you feel decided by others? Please say one; no need for details.
3. ★★★ In quiet, please think of one thing: what do you habitually put your sense of security on? Work, connections, an organization, or something else? Please write one.
4. ★ Please say in one sentence: what was a smooth, pleasant word you heard recently?

Leader’s note: Please begin by quietly reading Daniel 11:32. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches the experience of pressure from the larger environment, of being forced into silence and of being hurt by smooth words; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not press for location or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record anything that could be traced, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ [See] 11:21–24 says the contemptible man gained the kingdom with flattering words. Have you ever been moved by smooth words and only later found something wrong? Please tell about one time.
6. ★★ [Hear] Read 11:32. Which phrase does God say to you: “know God,” “be strong and take action,” or “only you”? Say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ [Think] 11:35 says the wise fall to refine them. When can this verse comfort people, and when might it hurt them? Please say your view.
8. ★★ [Speak] Say one sentence to the person next to you: “I am standing in a situation I do not decide,” and say what it is. Only one sentence.
9. ★★★ [Do] This week, which person who is falling will you accompany? Please say the name and the time, and say how you will accompany first without hurrying to explain.

Leader’s note: Follow the order [See], [Hear], [Think], [Speak], [Do], and leave enough time for each step. In [Speak], only a sentence, a name and a time are needed; no stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “this is God refining you” or “have faith” to someone who is crying; look after them privately after the meeting, and if needed help them seek professional help.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.
10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone under pressure from the larger environment? Please say the name, and decide to reach out to him this month.

11. ★★ In your church or group, is there anyone in the habit of using Scripture to identify others, or of drawing up timetables? Please say one instance, and say how you could gently bring the atmosphere back to knowing God.
12. ★★ Is there something in which you need to put down the heart of “I must see clearly”? Please say one, and decide this week to hand it to God with one sentence of prayer.

13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear “only the people who know their God will be strong and take action.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s note: Please remind especially: in the group, do not match the kings of the south and north or the self-exalting king to any country or person of today, and do not draw up timetables. If someone shares an experience of being hurt, persecuted or losing a loved one, do not press for details, do not ask them to forgive, and look after them privately after the meeting.
Please close your eyes gently and put before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read together Daniel 11:32: the people who know their God will be strong and take action.

Let the leader pray for each person: Lord, teach us on someone else’s battlefield still to know you; among smooth words still to speak the truth; when someone falls, to become that little help. Before dismissal, ask one another one sentence: “What is the one small thing this week by which you will know God?”

12.vol: Study Notes on Daniel 321, Lesson 12 · Daniel Chapter 12
12.title: Go Your Way Until the End—Rest, Awake, Rise
blocks: I. An Old Man and a Figure Who Stands Up (12:1)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today is our last lesson in the book of Daniel. I would like to begin by asking you to imagine an old man: he walked through Babylon, he walked through Persia, he saw several kings rise and fall; he grew up in the king’s palace, spent a night in the lions’ den, and mourned three weeks by the river. Now he comes to the last vision of his life. What do you think he most wanted to hear? A complete timetable? An answer that would untie all his questions? Today’s chapter tells us: no. What he received was a very quiet sentence.

This chapter begins with a “stand up”: “At that time Michael will stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there will be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time.” Do you remember? The word “stand” has been moving beneath the surface since chapter 1: the young men stood before the king, the three friends stood before the golden image, Daniel stood by the lions’ den. In chapter 10 the messenger said he had stood up to support; in chapter 11 no king could stand. Now, in the last chapter, it is Michael, the great prince of the children of your people, who stands up.

When is this “at that time”? It has long been read in different ways: some say it follows the stretch of darkness described in chapter 11; some say it is a still later time; and some say history and the end reflect each other here. We set these readings side by side, and must say plainly: these notes set no date for this “at that time” and do not tie it to any event of today. In Matthew 24 Jesus also used similar words to describe great tribulation; we respect this link, but do not use it to draw up a table.

The text gives two things, set against each other. The first is trouble: “such as never was.” This is a heavy word; we need not pretend darkness does not exist. The second is deliverance: “At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.” Please notice: Michael stands up not to make the trouble vanish but so that the people may be delivered in the trouble. God’s people were never promised that they would not pass through darkness; what they were promised is a great prince who stands beside them.

So the first reminder of this lesson may be this: in your darkest moment, please look up and see a figure who stands up. You need not stand firm by yourself, because there is one who stands for you. This is also the main melody of the whole book: the God of heaven rules, and his people, in other people’s kingdoms, still have someone standing beside them.

Perhaps you want to ask: if such a great prince stands up, why does my trouble still not end at once? This question is very real, and the text does not avoid it. It only tells us gently: the one who stands up is the one who is with you; his standing is not so that you will not pass through darkness but so that in the darkness you are not alone. This is a promise we can take hold of again every day.

Finally, please take this picture home: an old man sitting by a river hears someone say, “your people will be delivered.” He did not receive more answers, but he received more assurance. May you too, by your own river today, hear this sentence: there is one who stands up for you.
“Found written in the book”: how can I be sure my name is on it?

The point of this verse is comfort, not making people anxiously check themselves. Different theological readings of “written in the book” have long existed, and we set them side by side among the issues; but the New Testament tells us clearly that God remembers everyone who trusts in Christ and leaves no one out. You can practice this: each morning say one sentence to God: Lord, my name is in your hand, and today I will trust you. When you find yourself doubting because of weakness or failure, do not hurry to prove yourself by your performance; return to the great prince who stands up, and to the salvation Jesus accomplished for you, and let assurance rest on him and not on your feelings.

Then the text lights up one word: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” This is one of the clearest Old Testament verses on resurrection. Death is called “sleep”; and sleep is something one wakes from. Think of chapter 11: the wise fell by the sword, in flame, into captivity and plunder. They made many understand, and paid with their lives. Their story at the end of chapter 11 is all heaviness. But in chapter 12 God answers them: you will awake. Falling is not the end.

The verse goes on to say that some will have everlasting life, and some shame and everlasting contempt. This sentence is heavy; we should not pass over it lightly, nor turn it into a tool of fear. The scope of “many” has long been read in different ways, and the theological understanding of “everlasting contempt” also differs; we set them side by side among the issues. We first hold on to the most direct point: death is not the end, and God has a final justice and also a final hope. The New Testament too teaches resurrection, in John 5 and Acts 24; we need not build a complete end-time chart on this verse.

Then verse 3, which is one of my own favorites: “Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse. Those who turn many to righteousness will shine as the stars forever and ever.” This “wise” is the same word as in chapter 11. In chapter 11 they fall; in chapter 12 they shine. The same word, two scenes: on earth, they fall; in heaven, they shine. Failure in men’s eyes is, in God’s eyes, the brightness of the sky.

Notice how the text describes these people. Not “those of highest standing” and not “those of greatest achievement,” but “those who turn many to righteousness,” that is, those who turn people toward righteousness, toward God. Such a person is not necessarily a pastor and does not necessarily stand on a platform. A mother who prays for her children all her life; a colleague who bears witness to God by honest work; an elder who still blesses others from a sickbed: all of them are in this description.

Stars do not shine by themselves; they are set by God in the sky to guide people in the night. So we need not be proud, and need not be discouraged. Our task is not to shine the brightest but, in the night, not to go out. For whom can you be a little light today?

Please also think of the wise whom the world has not remembered: a person quietly praying for coworkers in a factory, a person singing hymns for the patient in the next bed, a son or daughter caring for a parent with dementia over many years. Their light may never be praised by anyone, yet God remembers each one. This verse is written for them, and for you if you are on such a road.
Think again: for whom can you be that little light today? Perhaps a phone call, a presence that does not preach, a prayer offered with no return. These small things, in heaven, are all stars.
How does the hope of resurrection comfort someone who has lost a loved one?

Accompany first, comfort afterward. Someone who has just lost a loved one usually does not need a long theology; he needs someone beside him. You can sit quietly first and let the other tell the story of that person, and when needed simply hand him a glass of water. When the other has strength and is willing, then gently read 12:2 together: many of those who sleep in the dust will awake. Treat this sentence as a hope being shared, not a conclusion one is required to accept. Remember too: grief is real and hope is real, and the two can exist together. This practice need not be rushed; take it slowly, and God is present in every honest beginning.
III. Light from the Original: Stand, Purified, Blessed, Rest (12:1, 10, 12, 13)

In the original of the last chapter there are four words worth a slow reading. The first is “stand,” Hebrew עמד (amad). The undercurrent of the whole book appears here for the last time: Michael “stands up” (12:1), the two by the river “stood” (12:5), and Daniel at last will “stand” (12:13). From the young men standing before the king in chapter 1 to the old man standing to receive his portion in the last chapter, this word strings the whole book on one line: standing is the final posture of God’s people.

The second is “be purified, be made white, be refined,” Hebrew בָּרַר, לָבַן, צָרַף, three verbs that in 12:10 are all reflexive or passive in form; and the same set of words as in 11:35. This lets us see that purity does not come from ourselves, still less from comparison; it is brought out in God’s hand. This is very close to the “no-self” of 321: we do not make ourselves clean; we are willing to be refined by God.

The third is “blessed,” Hebrew אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei). It is the word that opens the Psalms: “Blessed is…” In 12:12 it is joined with “waits” (חָכָה): blessed is the one who waits. This “waiting” is not idle waiting but a watching with hope. What the whole book finally gives God’s people is not a day but a posture.

The fourth is “rest,” Hebrew נוּחַ (nuach). It is not only a gentle way of saying death; it also means “to find rest,” and in Genesis Noah’s name is related to it, meaning “comfort” and “rest.” In 12:13 God says to Daniel: you will rest. This word brings the whole book back to a gentle end.

When we join these four words, we see a very complete road: first standing, the final posture of God’s people; then being purified, the work God does in his people; then blessed, the state of the one who waits; and last rest, an old man’s gentlest end. These four words are not four doctrines but the shape of a person’s whole life.
“Blessed is he who waits”: does this mean we are to wait passively?

No. This “waiting” is an active trust. Imagine a mother at the airport waiting for a child returning from far away: she is not doing nothing; she prepares the meal, tidies the room, looks up and watches. Waiting for God is the same: we keep reading Scripture, praying, loving others, doing what is before us, and at the same time place the time of the end in God’s hand. What is passive is the calculation of days; what is active is holding to trust in daily life. Such waiting is blessed waiting. Please remember, this is not a lesson finished at once but a journey that needs patience and also companions.
“Being refined” sounds painful. How can I face it?

You can admit honestly: being refined is usually not comfortable. We need not pretend to like it. But notice that the text uses the passive voice: be purified, be made white, be refined, which means that the one doing this is God, not you. All you need to do is not run from that hand. In the most painful moments you can pray simply: Lord, I do not understand, but I will not leave your hand. At the same time, please find a safe companion and say your pain aloud, and if needed seek professional help. Refining does not mean you grit your teeth alone. What God values is not how well you perform but that you are willing to come back to him with your real self.
IV. I Heard, But I Didn’t Understand (12:4–9)

Then the text enters a very honest passage. The messenger commands Daniel: “shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end.” In the ancient world, to seal was to keep a document safe, waiting for the time it should be opened. Then the text says: many will run back and forth, and knowledge will be increased. This sentence is often used to speak of technological progress in the last days; but the original “run back and forth” can also be read “examine closely,” so there are different readings through the ages; we set them side by side and do not turn it into a prediction about the times.

Then the camera goes to the river: two others, one on this side and one on that; in the middle, the one clothed in linen. One of them asks the last question of the whole book: “How long will it be to the end of these wonders?” You must know this question well; it is the cry of the Psalms, the cry of everyone waiting in the dark: how long. The man clothed in linen lifts his right hand and his left hand to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever, and gives an answer: a time, times, and a half.

Through the ages there have been many readings of this answer; we do not convert it into years and do not arrange it into any timetable. But please notice: this answer has no date, yet it has a guarantee: one who lives forever has sworn. Do you want a timetable, or a God you can trust? This chapter leads us from the former to the latter.

Then comes the most honest sentence of the chapter: “I heard, but I didn’t understand.” The speaker is Daniel, the man who understood in chapter 9 as he read Scripture, who set his heart on understanding in chapter 10. Here he says frankly: I do not understand. The text does not hide this and does not say he was therefore not spiritual enough. Even he had times of not understanding.

God’s answer is: “Go your way, Daniel.” This is not being sent away but being entrusted: now is not the time when you need to understand everything but the time when you need to keep walking. Not understanding does not stop us from walking the way God gives. This is the deepest comfort the whole book gives us.

If today you have something you do not understand, please do not hurry to find an answer to fill it. You can say honestly, as Daniel did: Lord, I heard, but I did not understand. Then listen quietly as he says: go your way. This conversation can happen in our lives again and again, and each time it happens it brings us a little closer to him.
I keep failing to understand when I read the Bible. Is something wrong with my spiritual life?

No. Even Daniel said “I heard, but I didn’t understand.” Not understanding does not mean you are not spiritual; it reminds us that some things need time, and also community. You can do this: mark the places you do not understand with a pencil; do not force yourself to understand right now; ask a brother or sister you trust, or read together in a group; then keep doing the part you already understand. God often makes us understand little by little only as we “go.” When we do not understand, still going is itself faith. May you in this process be held up little by little, and learn little by little to hold up others.
V. A Few Deviations We Must Recognize

The first deviation is using “a time, times, and a half” in 12:7 and the days of 12:11–12 to convert into years, months and days and draw up an end-time timetable. These numbers have long been read in many ways, historical, end-time and symbolic; these notes set them side by side and state plainly that we do not calculate, convert or draw up tables.

The second deviation is using the great trouble of 12:1 to identify some event or person of today, saying that it is the great tribulation or the antichrist. The point of the text is that in the trouble a great prince stands, and all found written in the book are delivered; these notes identify no event or person of today.

The third deviation is making the “everlasting contempt” of 12:2 a tool to frighten people or to judge that someone has already been condemned. This verse speaks of the final justice, and theologians have understood it in different ways; we pass final sentence on no one.

The fourth deviation is simply equating “knowledge will be increased” in 12:4 with technological progress, and using this to predict the end times. “Run back and forth” can also be read as examining closely and searching; there are different readings, and we set them side by side.

The fifth deviation is saying to someone who is grieving, “he is asleep, you need not be sad,” or using 12:2–3 to stop his tears. The hope of resurrection is real, but grief is real too; we accompany first, and when the other has strength we read together.
Someone is eager to predict the end times with this chapter. How should I respond?

You can first affirm his zeal for God’s word, then gently return to the text’s own point. You can ask three questions: First, does the text itself give a date? Second, have interpreters through the ages read it differently? Third, does this claim make the congregation love the Lord more and be more patient, or more anxious? Then bring the atmosphere back to 12:13: go your way, you will rest, you will stand. You need not win over the other and need not persuade everyone; you can let your own life of peace, patience and love be the quietest answer. If the other still insists, treat him with love and leave the arguing to the Holy Spirit.
VI. Two Real Questions in the Chinese Context

The first question: we are very used to finding security by “calculating.” Calculating fortunes, calculating days, calculating feng shui, calculating investments. This habit also easily comes into faith: we always want to know when, how, whether it has already come. This chapter answers us in one sentence: go your way until the end. When we turn the strength we spend calculating into strength for knowing God, our security moves from numbers to a God who swears and lives forever.

The second question: we are used to being silent before death. Many Chinese families do not talk much about death or resurrection, and pass over it with “just live well.” This chapter gives us a space in which we can talk: death is “sleep,” and sleep is something one wakes from; falling is not the end. In a safe time you can read 12:2–3 gently together with your family, and say to one another: we are not afraid to talk about this, because there is hope.
How can I talk about death and resurrection with family who do not yet believe?

You can begin from love, not from doctrine. Find a quiet, natural time, perhaps when the family mentions a relative who has died; you can say one sentence: I miss him too, and I believe that one day we will meet again. Then do not hurry to say much; let the other respond. If the other is willing to listen, then share the hope you read in Daniel: death is sleep, and sleep is something one wakes from. Do not use fear and do not force; let this hope be a gift that can be received or can be set aside. A little at a time is enough; being willing to begin is already saying to God: I trust you.
VII. Living Out 321: Go Your Way, You Will Rest, You Will Stand

Three foundations: Jesus is my example. He fell into the dust, rose on the third day, and became the firstfruits of those who sleep; he also said that of that day and hour no one knows. The Bible is my standard, so that before the many hard numbers of this chapter we rely not on calculation and not on identifying but hold only to the clearest point of the text: the end belongs to God. The Holy Spirit is my guide, who in our not-understanding still leads us on, so that we are purified and refined and, in the night, do not go out.

Two cores: Let Jesus reign, which means placing the end in his hand, not counting his days for him, and, when we do not understand, still going and still waiting. Let Jesus receive all the glory, which means that when we shine we say: this is not my light, it is his light; and when we stand up and receive our portion we say: all of this is his grace. One purpose: to build God’s system. This is a people who wait: purifying one another and turning many to righteousness; accompanying first when someone falls; and together keeping the witness this book leaves behind.

Change the concept and the life changes: when we think “security comes from working out the time exactly,” our life is anxious; when we know “security comes from a God who swears and lives forever,” our life has rest. From the self-life to the no-self life: the self-life demands to understand everything; the no-self life admits “I do not understand” yet is willing to go, letting man be man and God be God.

We also need to remind ourselves: 321 is not for finding a beautiful answer to this chapter’s difficulties but for keeping our heart within them. Jesus is my example, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; when we do not understand, these three foundations are the stones under our feet. Stepping on them, we can keep going until that day.
What does “no-self” have to do with “waiting”?

Waiting is itself a practice of no-self. The self-life cannot bear not knowing and always grabs something it can control, such as dates, predictions, identifications; the no-self life can remain at peace in not knowing, because it has returned the authority of control to God. You can try a simple practice: each time you want to “know more,” stop first and say to God: Lord, I place the time and the end of this matter in your hand. Then do one small thing that is before you. Then waiting turns from torment into a practice of trust.
VIII. Four Kinds of Heart, One Promise

The proud type says: “I must find out when and how it will happen, so that I can be at peace.” This heart may be afraid of being kept in the dark. But this chapter says the end belongs to God, and even Daniel said he did not understand. You can ask yourself: is my finding out for loving the Lord, or for seizing the lead?

The fearful type says: “I am afraid that when the great trouble comes I will not hold on, and I fear for my family.” This fear is real. Please remember the text says that in the trouble a great prince stands up, and everyone found written in the book will be delivered. You are not holding on by yourself; you are held up. You can reduce the information that makes you panic and leave a little more time to be quietly with God.

The shame type says: “I have read the Bible for so many years and still do not understand; I must not be good enough.” Even Daniel said he did not understand; you are not alone. You need not first become very understanding to deserve God’s charge; what God says is: go your way. You can bring this shame before God, and before a safe companion.

The hurt type says: “I paid a price for my faith and no one remembers.” This wound is real. The text says the fall of the wise is remembered before God, and they will shine. We do not make the wound lighter, and do not ask you to let go at once; you can slowly find a safe person and tell your story. God sees, and remembers.
IX. A Few Things You Can Do This Week
First, each day pray one sentence: I do not understand, but I am willing to go; and hand one waiting matter to God.
Second, write down one thing for which you want to find security by “working it out,” and beside it write one sentence: the end belongs to God.
Third, sit for a while with someone who is waiting or has lost a loved one; accompany first, do not explain for God, and do not frighten with numbers of days.
Fourth, each day do one small thing that brings someone nearer to God, such as one word of encouragement or one prayer; this is turning people to righteousness.
Fifth, when someone wants to use this chapter to draw up a timetable or identify the antichrist, gently bring him back to 12:13: we only need to go, to rest and to stand.
I declare: the end belongs to God; I do not count his days for him; I only wait for him.
I declare: when I do not understand, I am still willing to go, because he says to me: go your way.
I declare: I will be purified and refined, not go out in the night, and turn many to God.
I declare: I will rest, and at the end of the days I will stand and receive my portion, until Jesus reigns.

In twelve lessons we have walked through the book of Daniel. Chapter 1: a young man who purposed not to defile himself with the king’s food; chapter 2: the stone cut out without hands; chapter 3: “But if not”; chapter 4: the Most High rules in the kingdom of men; chapter 5: you are weighed in the balances; chapter 6: praying as he had done before; chapter 7: the Ancient of Days and the son of man; chapters 8 to 11: kings and kings coming and going, God first touching, and the people who know God being strong and taking action. Now we come to the last sentence: “But go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.”

Brothers and sisters, let us return to that old man. He did not receive a timetable, but he received a promise: go, rest, stand. The focus of this lesson is Jesus: he is the great prince who stands up, he is the firstfruits of those who sleep, he is the place of all our hope. The focus is not how much I understand, nor how frightening others are, but the God who has placed the end in his own hand.

May God let us, when we do not understand, still be willing to go; in the night, not go out; when we fall, believe that he will make us awake and shine; until his kingdom fills the whole earth. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
XI. Small Group Sharing: The Three “Hua”

Leader’s note: In this lesson we walk through the three “hua”: first take the words into our own hearts (internalize), then think them through together, say them aloud, and take a step (digest), and finally bring this lesson to people (transform).

Priority marks: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each “hua”; ★★ = second priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked 【Required】 must not be skipped; it may be completed at home.
Aim: let each person first take the Scripture into his own heart and see his own position, without rushing to discuss others.
1. ★ In one sentence, tell whether there is something you have waited a long time for and still have no answer. Only one sentence, please.
2. ★ 12:1 says that in the great trouble a great prince stands up. Was there a moment when you felt someone standing for you? Please say one; no need for details.
3. ★★★ In quiet, please think of one thing: if the end truly belongs to God, which thing that you meant to find security in by “calculating” can you put down? Please write one.
4. ★ Please name a grieving person you once accompanied, or who once accompanied you. What helped most that time?

Leader’s note: Please begin by quietly reading Daniel 12:13. Do not call on people to speak. This chapter touches death, bereavement, long waiting and not understanding; if someone is in a place where faith cannot be made public, do not press for location or details, do not ask for public testimony, do not record anything that could be traced, and look after them privately after the meeting.
The Second “Hua”: Digest (about 35 minutes · the main thread)
Aim: see yourself, hear God speak, think it through, say it aloud, and take a step, so that this lesson becomes your own words.
5. ★★ [See] In 12:8 Daniel said: I heard, but I didn’t understand. Is there something that is also like this for you? Please say one.
6. ★★ [Hear] Read 12:9 and 12:13. Which sentence does God say to you: “go your way,” “you will rest,” or “you will stand”? Say one sentence in your own words.
7. ★★★ [Think] 12:2–3 says that those who sleep in the dust will awake and the wise will shine. How do these two verses change your view of “falling”?
8. ★★ [Speak] Say one sentence to the person next to you: “There is something I do not understand,” and say what it is. Only one sentence; no need to explain.
9. ★★★ [Do] This week, which person who is waiting or grieving will you accompany? Please say the name and the time, and say how you will accompany first without hurrying to explain.

Leader’s note: Follow the order [See], [Hear], [Think], [Speak], [Do], and leave enough time for each step. In [Speak], only a sentence, a name and a time are needed; no stories. If someone’s tears fall, do not hurry to comfort and do not press; do not say “he is asleep, do not be sad” or “have faith” to someone who is crying; look after them privately after the meeting, and if needed help them seek professional help.
Aim: take this lesson out into the real relationships of family, workplace and church, and let the gospel keep multiplying.

10. ★ Among your family or colleagues, is there someone panicked by predictions of the end times? Please say the name, and decide this month, with a quiet presence, to help him bring his focus back to knowing God.

11. ★★ In your church or group, is there anyone in the habit of using numbers and dates to identify some matter or person? Please say one instance, and say how you could gently bring the atmosphere back to 12:13.
12. ★★ Is there something for which you need to say, “I do not understand, but I am willing to go”? Please say one, and decide this week to hand it to God with one sentence of prayer.
13. ★★★ 920 practice: find your “2,” the friend who most needs to hear “you will rest, you will stand.” This week share this lesson with him, and say his name on the spot.
14. ★★★ 【Required】 This week, tell this lesson in three sentences to a friend outside the church, and report back at the next group meeting: whom you told, where you told him, and how he responded.

Leader’s note: Please remind especially: in the group, do not use numbers, dates or events to draw up a timetable or identify the antichrist, and do not match the great trouble to any event or person of today. If someone shares an experience of losing a loved one, of being hurt, or of long hopelessness, do not press for details, do not ask them to forgive, and look after them privately after the meeting.

Please close your eyes gently and put before God the one thing you wrote down today. Read together Daniel 12:13: go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.

Let the leader pray for each person: Lord, teach us, when we do not understand, still to be willing to go; in the night, not to go out; when we fall, to believe that you will make us awake. Before dismissal, ask one another one sentence: “What is the step you will walk this week?”
